q.t: Discussed any other parts of your affordability agenda with him? You know, groceries, freezing the rent, anything else related to that, or is it just specifically housing?

a.t: It's a wide-spanning conversation. Housing tends to be the focus. Thank you all very much.

q.t:
Yesterday we heard the president say a word he doesn't use often, which is affordable. You mentioned that earlier. He's previously called it a "hoax," a "con job," things like that. Do you think he's changed or shifted on the issue, at least the rhetoric? Do you take any credit for that? How do you approach kind of that question of affordability with him?

And then I'd love to get specifics on this. When you think of Sunnyside Yard and the affordable aspect of it, kind of what percentage of affordable housing are we thinking there, what's a goal for you?

a.t:
You know, I want to be honest with you that that is exactly the reason why we're setting up the conversations at the highest level between our housing operations teams, as well as the White House, which is what the president and I agreed to do coming out of yesterday's meeting.

It will be a focus, however, is developing that scale of housing, ensuring that a significant portion is affordable, and also constructing what will effectively be an entirely new neighborhood in New York City. Because, as we know, one of the most difficult things in our city is to find land. And what this project would do is effectively create new land by creating a structure atop what is currently a rail yard.

And then to your first question, what I've said publicly and also said to the president is anything that could help a working New Yorker's life, that's what I want to focus on. That's what I want to talk about. And I appreciated the president's consideration of that when it comes to building more housing than we've seen in the city since the early 1970s, and the importance of stability in Haitian New Yorkers' lives and just how critical of a role they play in this city, not only as New Yorkers, but also as the New Yorkers who are oftentimes powering our economy, whether it is in health care, hospitality, construction.

And I shared that I'm hearing this not only from those New Yorkers, not only from my personal experiences of seeing and meeting these New Yorkers, but also from their pastors, from developers, from the executives of hospitals, from across the board in the city.

q.t: When did you go to the facility, and what did you observe there?

a.t:
I think it was maybe about a little more than a month ago. I can get back to you on the exact dates of it. What I observed there is both the improvements that our ACS staff have been able to deliver with newfound support, as well as the need for this to be something that is sustained.

And we need to provide, not only, you know — I was able to go with a number of the New Yorkers who are being held there into something called Elite Lounge, where they're being taught skills about — I think on that day it was running what was effectively a coffee shop.

I saw the recreation area. I saw the incredible artwork that a lot of those young people have come together to be a part of. There was also, they were preparing for a karaoke competition and so I heard a song that they were putting together.

But to me, these are young people who at some point will be returning home, and we need to ensure that they are equipped with the skills, the education, the training, so that they can flourish in our society. We're committed to doing that.

q.t:
I want to ask about the Horizons Juvenile Facility in the Bronx. Today, Council Member Stevens and the Legal Aid Society, as well as other community members, are having another visit of the site. They visited back in July. I asked you if you were planning to visit yourself. You said that you were working internally on setting something up and making changes regarding the oversight of overcrowding, security and safety.

Were you invited to go on this tour today? Have you set a date to go see the facility, and what internal conversations are you having about making changes and addressing, particularly, the overcrowding and the safety in that facility?

a.t: So, since you last asked me that question, I did visit the facility. I visited both Horizon and Crossroads. And we are firmly committed to not only providing the staff there with the support that they need but also ensuring that we are in full compliance because this is critically important in living up to not only the intent that we have of our administration, but also the importance of ensuring that we are providing all of the kinds of services that young people in detention need.

q.t: So, it didn't come up? You did not bring it up?

a.t: Focus was on the city.

q.t:
So, just following back up on the Israeli prime minister. So, you have called for his arrest, and you've called for the federal government to honor the ICC's warrant. Was this brought up with the president yesterday during your discussion at Gracie Mansion? And if it wasn't, why wasn't that brought up?

And then separately, just circling back to the influencer hearing that's happening with the Council members right now. So, there was a memo that we obtained that went out earlier this year from your chief counsel that explicitly said not to use WhatsApp or Signal — not with the caveat of if you have the permission.

So, how do you answer for the statement that was put out from City Hall afterwards that — from your lawyer, Ramzi Kassem — that they could use Signal with permission? Was this not being truthful? Was it not being understanding that this memo went out? I know there's a training also in March, so how do you score that, sir?

a.t:
Well, I think to quote the chief counsel, there are trainings and there are retrainings, and that will continue because for us, being in accordance with the record-keeping laws of the City is of paramount importance. I will defer to the chief counsel to answer more specifically to your question.

When it comes to your first question, the focus of the conversation that I had with the president was New York City and New Yorkers. That is a conversation that spanned Sunnyside Yard, as the president said, about Haitian New Yorkers as well as an appreciation of our Police Department. And when it comes to the prime minister, though, I've made very clear where I stand on that.

q.t:
I had another follow-up question about your conversation with the president yesterday. There was some reaction to the Sunnyside Yard discussion from local Queens officials, Julie Won and Donovan Richards. And the Queens borough president basically said he thought that there were other better uses, maybe more efficient ways to build housing that didn't involve building a super-expensive platform over this rail yard.

And Council Member Won basically suggested, you know, the local community wasn't consulted. The gist was kind of you're planning this thing with Trump without including the neighborhood of Sunnyside. What would be a response to those reactions?

a.t:
What we're speaking about would be the largest housing project in New York City since the early 1970s; the largest development in more than 50 years, which would construct 12,000 homes, 30,000 jobs. And as the president said himself yesterday, a significant number of those homes would be affordable to New Yorkers in terms of an intentional rate.

And to me, this is such a priority because of the fact that when we look at the cost-of-living crisis in our city, the number one driver is a lack of housing. And I will do everything in my power to build more housing in this city. And working with the president to fulfill an idea that has existed for 50 to 60 years; that to me is clearly an example of what could be done

q.t:
I wanted to ask you right now, the City Council's holding an oversight hearing on the Signal chat and what went wrong there. Nobody from your administration actually showed up. I wanted you to know why and why your administration doesn't think it's important to show up to this type of an oversight hearing.

And then I also wanted to get your response. The prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, today put out something on social media. In particular, he said, in particular, that "Shame on you, Mr. Mamdani, shame on you for supporting the Hamas terrorist monsters who butchered our people. Shame on you for inciting riots against New York Jews. I'm coming to the U.N. I'm going to tell the truth about our heroic soldiers and I'm gonna tell the truth about you."And I wanted to get your response to that post as well.

a.t:
Well, we all know that what the prime minister has said in that video is not true. What we do know to actually be the truth when it comes to the prime minister is that he is the subject of an International Criminal Court arrest warrant for alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity. And as the prime minister, he is the architect of a horrific genocide against Palestinians. And that just a few days ago, his military killed an 11-year-old boy in what is deemed to be a safe zone in Gaza. So, that is what I have to say to his video.

And then to your earlier question, as it pertains to Signal, you know, as I said alongside my chief counsel, our administration took corrective action to ensure that we're in accordance with the city's record-keeping laws. And I'm confident in the testimony that our administration is providing today, that it will be sufficient in answering the Council's questions.

[Crosstalk.]

q.t: So, yesterday at your press conference, you mentioned that you and President Trump talked about the importance of the Police Department here. I'm wondering if you can elaborate a little bit on that, and I'm wondering if, off of your remarks on Sunday, if one of the areas you found common ground with the president on was a crackdown on quality-of-life concerns. I know you had talked about it on Sunday as a little bit different, trees, potholes, etc.; and the president has embraced some version of, like, broken-windows policing.So, I'm wondering if you found common ground in that area or others, regarding—

a.t: The conversation as it pertained to policing was just a shared appreciation of the men and women of the NYPD. My remarks on Sunday at the U20 forum were about the importance of responding to potholes that need to be paved over, trees that need to be planted, the concerns that New Yorkers have on their block. But the conversation with the president was a much just broader appreciation.

q.t: I mean, they're saying kind of like, "oops, my bad." Can you respond directly to what DoorDash is saying?

a.t:
I've never heard someone describe $131.5 million settlement in that kind of a language. We are speaking about something that was sustained, something that was rampant for a quarter of a million workers, and something that would never have been acknowledged, let alone rectified, were it not for the courage of these very workers.

And we also know that when workers step forward, they are typically not welcomed in doing so. That is why we are also making clear that if any worker is retaliated against for the use of the app that we are now developing alongside Workers Justice Project, we're going to fast-track the retaliatory proceedings.

And to DoorDash, we want to make it very, very clear that we will continue to hold them accountable, as we will any other company, and we are not going to abide by the flagrant violation of the law. No matter the tone and the tenor of that kind of a statement.

[Crosstalk.]

q.t:
What we're hearing from you and your commissioner this morning is that these are very clear algorithms, a very clear pursuit of corporate profits kind of under the radar and thinking that the law is an option, to quote what you said.

So, I just wanted to know if you can directly respond to how DoorDash is characterizing this: "Simply put, we screwed up. Our mistakes meant some Dashers were underpaid or paid late. While these mistakes weren't intentional, that doesn't make them okay. We pride ourselves in excellence."So, can you just speak directly to their statement?

a.t: Was that published on the Notes app?

q.t: The first question, are Uber and Grubhub compliant under the minimum pay rules, as far as you're aware?

a.s: Brad Lander, Congressional Nominee, New York's 10th Congressional District
a.t: Law — minimum pay law.
Thank you to future Congressman Lander. It is indeed a law, and if they're not compliant, we're gonna have another big event like this one.

q.t: Laura, go ahead. Thank you. I have a two-part question. The first is, as far as you're aware, have other apps like Uber and Grubhub been compliant under the minimum pay rule? And then could you tell us, as far as the use of these greedy algorithms go, is this a problem that's limited to delivery apps, or is this something that you're seeing at other kinds of companies and other kinds of industries since everything uses tech these days?

a.t:
We are seeing across a number of different companies and a number of different industries a pursuit of profit no matter the cost. And we want to make it very clear that it does not matter how profitable your company is, how large your company, you have to abide by the laws of New York City.

They are not suggestions, they are requirements. And we are so appreciative of the workers who step forward and alert us to these violations because without them we would not have been able to put into place what is the largest labor settlement in New York City history.

And I'll pass it over to the commissioner to your first question.

You know, this is absolutely a huge problem. One of the things I find interesting, and I wonder if the deputy mayor would agree with me, you know, in Washington, everyone's searching, but what are we gonna do about all these algorithms? What are we going to do about AI?

We're showing what to do right here in New York City. We're saying we don't care what the algorithm spits out. If you're a delivery worker, you're entitled to about $22 an hour in the city of New York.

And what this enforcement action shows is that we can actually deliver on that commitment to put money back in people's pockets. So this is a problem across the economy. And New York City is showing the way for how government can address it.

q.t: Hi, uh, give me one second while I pull up my question. So, this could be answered by you or maybe the head of DCWP. Is there any concern — because Mr. Levine just said that this is proprietary data — is there any concern regarding this recording app that you guys have announced, that they might come back and say, "Well, that's our data; it's not theirs to even record." That they might sort of try to draw a line about it being theirs?

a.t: I'll say it in short, and then I'll pass it over to the commissioner to say it in long. No.

You know, for too long we have had this economy where these app companies collect vast amounts of data on individual workers, but neither individual workers nor government enforcers have visibility into what's happening across the board.

What we're doing with this settlement is we are ending that asymmetry. We are recognizing for the workers behind me, the deliveries they make, that's their data. The pay they earn, that is their pay. The disclosures they get, those are their disclosures.

So, there's nothing inappropriate at all about having that data directly transmitted to us, and it's making sure that the kind of underpayment scheme we saw here is not gonna be repeated in this city. All right.

q.t: So, I have one quick question, which is, is this new data going to be made public just like the other data is each quarter? And then my second question is, you know, all of these delivery workers are on the streets navigating the cycling infrastructure, they're riding bikes and mopeds, and they're dealing with the dangers of riding bikes in the city. Do you see these kinds of settlements as related to street safety and to your Vision Zero Safe Systems approach goals?

a.t:
I think that they are all part of how we can protect workers, because we know that it is delivery workers who spend the most amount of hours on our streets. They are the most exposed to either the presence or the absence of street safety infrastructure. And we want to make sure that not only are delivery workers being paid for the work that they do, not only are we holding app companies accountable to the law here in our city, but also that delivery workers are safe when they are using our streets.

And, you know, one of the reasons that I wanted to acknowledge our City Council member, Sandy Nurse, who was just here with us, was that one of the other things we've heard from delivery workers is: Can they access a bathroom?

And the other day, when the mayor of Mexico City was here, we met with a number of members of the Workers Justice Project, and one of the things that they proudly showed was a bathroom access card, a reflection of the fact that here in New York City, it is now the law that if you are delivering for a restaurant, you are allowed to use the bathroom of that restaurant. So all of this to us is part and parcel of it. Commissioner, the question on the—

A lot of the data DoorDash is going to be turning over is proprietary, so it won't be made public. And I think that speaks to what is so remarkable about the settlement. Council passed a really strong minimum pay rate law. It's complicated, though. The mayor has been committed to a government that can actually hold these companies accountable — that's not afraid of complicated problems.

And one of the things I'm really proud of is that we have some of the best data scientists and economists in the world — we're recruiting, by the way [at] nyc.gov/jobs — who are able to actually crunch — I mean, think about all the delivery data New York City generates. Folks all over the city delivering thousands of packages every day — we're gonna be able to track that to a very granular level and make sure that this kind of mass underpayment doesn't happen again in New York City.

q.t: You talked about the software that is being developed to track worker complaints. How long has that been in the works for, and what's the plan to get it up and running fully? Because DoorDash only has to comply for this for the next three years. So, what's the plan there?

a.t:
Well, let me just start by saying DoorDash's obligations to comply with the settlement start today. We're not waiting for the software to be developed. DoorDash will be obligated to submit regular reports to us, much more granular than they have to do under the ordinary minimum pay law. We are also requiring DoorDash to regularly attest under oath that they are in compliance with the law.

With respect to the app, this is something we've been thinking about for a long time. I mentioned in my remarks my experience in Washington, where I saw companies like Meta ignore court orders over and over and over again [and] treat the law as a suggestion. That isn't gonna be how things go in New York City.

That's why we were so intent on giving workers the power themselves to collect this data [and] transmit it to us so we can respond to violations. We're gonna roll out that software as soon as possible. You know, we now have the funding to put it in place, but DoorDash's obligation to follow the law starts today.

And just before we go to the next question, I want to just add that this is also part of a larger commitment to holding these delivery companies accountable. You have heard many of us on this stage and beyond speak about the importance of interrogating the algorithms that are behind the incentives for delivery workers when they make their deliveries and what they are pushed to do.

I just want to invite up our City Council member, Shaun Abreu, who's been a real champion and [has] focused on how to hold these kinds of companies accountable — in case you have anything you want to add.

Well, thank you for calling me, Mr. Mayor. I think that what the commissioner has done as well with doing information sharing with the DA's office has also been important for DCWP. Data sharing has been important in terms of enforcement actions, not only on the civil level but also [for] criminal penalties as well.

The Council has done a lot with tipping transparency laws. We've done a lot with pay transparency as well. And there's the commissioner's job, and he's doing a great job at enforcing those laws and giving it teeth. And so, [I'm] looking forward to that continuing. Thank you, Mr. Mayor.

q.t: Just so we get the math right, it's 260,000 deliveristas; thus, that's about $500 apiece. Is that correct? And when we've done any stories in the past that have involved inequality regarding delivery workers, the comptroller had been part of this. And the former comptroller — we've done many stories with him about this very thing. Did it play any role in conjunction with DCWP?

a.t:
I will let our commissioner add some specific details, but before doing so, what I will say is you are correct that this is about roughly 260,000 workers. Of those, more than 27,000 will be receiving more than $1,000. About a little over 4,000 will receive more than $5,000.

And what this speaks to is not only the largest delivery workers' settlement action in municipal history, but also New York City's largest-ever labor enforcement action. And what is so exciting is, as you've heard other speakers say today, we know that more than $115 million will go directly to workers.

And then of the remaining $16 million — it's civil penalties, it's costs, it's also the kind of investment that is required to create the app that the workers will now be able to use to record their experience with DoorDash. Because what we're looking for is to not just protect these workers, not just to protect the incredible worker who stepped forward, but also to protect every worker that joins this workforce in the days, weeks, months and years to come.

Commissioner, if you want to add anything —

I would just say briefly that we work closely with the comptroller on these cases all the time. This is one that we did on our own. Our new research and analytics division, which we announced the launch of last week, played a key role in crunching these numbers and delivering this victory for tens of thousands of New York City workers.

q.t:
And then my second question. I think a lot of people see your strategy around the president, curbing criticism of him. I feel like you don't often launch personal attacks against him. You don't talk about how often you speak or what you speak about when we typically ask you at press conferences.

And I think a lot of people see that as a way to kind of avoid incurring his wrath in a way. Especially with immigration enforcement. But we've seen since January that ICE arrests have increased since you became mayor.

So, I'm wondering, do you still think that this tactic is worth it to sort of take a softer touch with the president in exchange for maybe sparing New York City more enforcement? And is there a point where this no longer makes sense for you?

a.t:
You know, the president and I have both been very frank about the many disagreements that we have. And immigration is one of those places. We've both spoken about very different approaches, very different beliefs. And I will continue to have conversations with the president and, frankly, with anyone who can deliver relief to the people of this city.

And to me, you know, in the past meeting, at the meeting we spoke about Sunnyside Yard, we introduced that conversation. Thirty minutes after the last meeting, he called me to let me know that the list of students that we had put forward to him, that he was going to release one of them. Soon after that, he released another one of them. 

And frankly, if a meeting can be the difference between detention and dignity, it's a meeting worth taking. All while being honest about the disagreements that we do have. Thank you all very much.

q.t: Two questions. You said that you're taking the conversation about Sunnyside Yard to the next level. Can you give us any detail about what that means? I mean, you've already brought the plan to him before. So, what does the next level mean?

a.t: So, the conversations have been continuing about this project. What today we made an agreement on was that the conversation would now be elevated to a place where it's going to also be technical between our housing teams, our operations teams and the White House. And that is critically important because, as you heard earlier from the question from Crain's, yes, there's an aspect of this that is about financing. There's also an aspect of this about technical and legal authorization of the construction of a platform. That's what this kind of a conversation facilitates.

q.t: I wanted to ask you a little bit about how this meeting came about. Could you tell us a little more? Did you invite him? You know, did you expect to have certain things addressed while here? Did you have a sort of agenda before meeting him when he came here? And then the second question is, Hakeem Jeffries was strongly criticized for meeting with Jared Kushner, president's adviser. Do you think you should be criticized for taking time to meet with the president?

a.t:
Look, I think the — I said this in my opening remarks — that I committed over the course of the campaign, as well as while being in office, that I would meet with anyone, work with anyone that could deliver for New Yorkers. And in the previous meetings I've had with President Trump, we've been able to secure the release of a New York City college student who had been detained by ICE. We've been able to move forward what has been a longstanding dream about the construction of Sunnyside Yard.

And we know we have a significant way to go, but these meetings do truly assist in that path. And to me, the question always is: how can we deliver for the city? How can we deliver for the people of the city? And so having a conversation about potentially building 12,000 homes, about the importance of our Haitian neighbors here in this city, are conversations that are worthwhile to have.

And to the first question, this was part of a conversation I was having with the president, and I invited the president to come to Gracie Mansion. And he had also remarked to me in prior conversations about how many memories he has of this as a home for prior mayors. And I thought it would be a good location for a continuation of the conversation of how to deliver for the people who are being priced out of the city.

q.t:
Back to Sunnyside Yard. Twenty-one billion was the number that you all put out before. Is that something you actually think that the federal government will put forward? Did you talk about the kind of dollar amount?

And then also, this is the kind of thing that can get kicked down the road. Are you able to give us any kind of timeline of when you would like to see actual movement on the Sunnyside Yard project?

a.t:
We are sincerely interested and committed to this as an idea, which is why it's been the focus of the conversations I've had with the president, not only in this meeting, but also in the prior meeting at the White House. And again, what we're talking about is something very rare in our city. It's the possibility of constructing an entirely new neighborhood.

And again, it's only possible with federal partnership because of not only the scale of funding required, but also the authorization in constructing a platform that would then serve as the foundation for about 12,000 homes, about 30,000 jobs, and it would be transformative, not only in terms of working people who could create this, but also, and be paid enough to be able to afford to live in the city, but also working people who could actually live in a neighborhood that today is, is a train yard.

[Crosstalk.]

q.t:
I just want to know what went into this meeting. Did you reach out to him? Was this part of your conversation from the last time? And what did you guys do inside? Did you show him around? Did you show him what's new? Did he test out the bidets?

Then also, I just had to ask as well, did you guys also discuss federal funding when it comes to the counterterrorism funding for the NYPD and the missing funding? Hochul had said that she was hoping that you would talk about it.

a.t:
We had a wide-ranging conversation. It extended from a conversation around the importance of our Police Department. It went to TPS. It also extended to Sunnyside Yard. And to the first part of your question, I appreciated not only having that conversation with the president, making the case on behalf of New Yorkers. The president also has many memories of Gracie Mansion. He's been here a number of times.

I shared with the president also that I recently learned that he actually got married in the Blue Room at City Hall, which is where many of us spend a lot of our time with press conferences and Q&As.

And with the president sharing the historic nature of this building, not only as it has been home to mayors since Fiorello La Guardia, but also that it has so much of the history of this country. There's a cannonball from the Revolutionary War; there's a fireplace from the residence where Aaron Burr died after his duel with Alexander Hamilton. So, that is all a part of this building as well.

q.t: Mr. Mayor, can you tell us, you know, now [that] he's not here, so what was your reaction to some of the things he said up there, specifically about TPS? What was the conversation about TPS? Were you in there with Stephen Miller? What was his and Susie Wiles' thought on TPS, a big issue that's happening in this city?

a.t:
So, I appreciated the conversation. It was a productive conversation. Stephen Miller was not a part of the conversation. It was myself, the president, Susie Wiles, my chief of staff, Elle Bisgaard-Church, and what I made the case about is just how critical this is to so many New Yorkers and how I hear about this not just from those New Yorkers, not just from their families, but also from their pastors, from developers, from executives in health care and hospitality.

Especially when we're talking about Haitian New Yorkers, we are talking about one of the most critical communities in our city. And when we're talking about the status, we're talking about something that can either deliver or deny stability in their lives and the lives of those who love them. And so, I made very clear this is a priority for me, a priority for our city, and I appreciated the consideration.

q.t: For both of you then. Mr. Mayor, the president said that he hopes that you'll be a great mayor. I wonder what your thoughts are about that? Also tell us what the conversation was around TPS and immigration overall. And also, a question for the president, what made you think about today's, I guess, discussion in your time with the mayor that made you think he was going to be a great mayor or that you hope he's going to be great when you've had so many criticisms for him in the past?

a.t: You know, I'll leave it to New Yorkers on your first question to make their judgments. On your second question, as the president said, I shared my very strong opinions about how we can keep New Yorkers safe, how we can keep immigrant New Yorkers safe, and how important immigrant New Yorkers, especially Haitian New Yorkers, are not only to the fabric of our city, but also to our city's economy, to so many of the industries that build our city and the stability that is in the president's hands. And I appreciate the conversation that we had and the consideration to that end. And you had your third question for the president.

No, I certainly hope he will be a great mayor. You have to understand, I want what's good for New York. I want what's good for the country. So, if I had a choice of having him be a bad mayor or horrible mayor, I don't want that. I want him to be a great mayor, and he certainly got potential, got great potential.

[President Trump exits.]

[Crosstalk.]

q.t: How do you feel? Will you change anything?

a.t: I feel strongly about a lot of things. I feel strongly about taking care of people. And that's what we do. We're doing a good job of it.
Thank you, Mr. President.

Thank you very much. Thank you very much.

[Crosstalk.]
Sorry, just before you go, the president is saying he can answer a couple more questions.

q.t: Do you want to talk about TPS? A lot of New Yorkers are here on protected status and it's been removed.

a.t: Well, the mayor feels very strongly about it, I can tell you. And he did bring it up. But he feels very, very strongly about it.

q.t: Thank you. Mayor, to you first, what's your response to President Trump banning outlets from the White House grounds? Did you challenge him at all about this in your meeting with him? Historians and legal scholars have called it textbook authoritarianism. And, Mr. President, are you banning outlets like MSNOW, CNN and Politico in order to distract from the Iran war and high gas prices?

a.t: I told the president that we're going to have all of the members of the press here on the lawn. And that is something that I believe in, is everyone, no matter the opinion or the critique, that we engage.

It's interesting because they said they were going to boycott me, but they never boycott me. So, I wasn't very worried about that. Look at all that press.

But, no, I'm not — I'm only doing it because I think the press also has an obligation. And, you know, I won in a landslide. I won the election in a landslide. I've done great things. I've done a lot of great things. I've settled eight wars. We have the best economic numbers for the country in the history of our country. We have $21 trillion pouring in. The biggest number ever, any country, was $3 [trillion].

Nobody's ever done what we've done. I never get anything positive. It's always negative. Even having to do with the war. We've done so well. We have total — Look, they're not going to have a nuclear weapon. Let me just put it that way. And they're not doing well. They're not doing well.

In fact, I had meetings on it today. They're doing very poorly. You would think that an outlet would write at least reasonably well, but never. If you look at CNN, it's fake news. If you look at MSNOW, I don't even know what MSNOW is. I guess it's the MSNBC, what it used to be, or MSDNC, as some people call it. That's Democrat National Committee.

But it's just biased news. And I think that these outlets have an obligation to be fair. And if they're fake news, I really think I have an obligation not to allow them into another very special house. This is a special house, Gracie Mansion. Well, the White House is the most special of all houses, I have to say. And I don't even think the mayor would argue with that.

And I think I have an obligation not to let fake news [in]. They're very bad for the country, very bad for national security. So, I have that obligation. So, we'll see how it works out.

q.t: So, Mr. President, you spoke about Sunnyside Yards. Are you committing to supporting that project? And it sounds like you also talked about affordability. You have dismissed that in the past. But that is one of Mayor Mamdani's key agenda items. So, did you talk about affordability? And is there anything you can do for affordability for New Yorkers?

a.t:
Well, I know a lot about affordability because I did that housing. I did many, many low-income and moderate-income buildings over the years and had great success with it. It really was very important.

I would think that Sunnyside would have to have a component, at least a pretty substantial component, of exactly that. So, yeah, we discussed that. If you do Sunnyside, I think you're going to have to have that kind of a component.

q.t: Mr. Mayor, Mr. President. This is the first time that a sitting president has visited Gracie Mansion in decades. Mr. President, on the way here you posted that this is one of your favorite places in the world. Why is that? And, Mr. Mayor, what did you show the president? What did he want to see?

a.t:
Well, I can say from my standpoint I love New York, and this represents New York. This is where the mayor lived and continues to live. We were discussing it a long time ago when you first got elected. I said, well, are you going to move because you were maybe having some doubts about moving in because it is a little bit on the luxurious side.

And I said, when you're the mayor, you have to live there. And he's done that. And it was very nice inside, beautifully kept. But it's a very, very representative place of New York, a very important place.

We appreciate the president's commitment to the city. And today the president shared many of his memories of having been to Gracie Mansion before, having been out here as well on the lawn. And we appreciated the conversation of how we can work together to deliver a lower cost of living for New Yorkers.

q.t: Mr. President, Mr. Mayor, there aren't too many Democrats who would roll out the red carpet for Donald Trump. You did that today. What tangible results, achievements could you point to from your relationship with the president?

a.t: You know, one of the focuses of the conversation the president and I have been having is about the possibility of building more housing here in New York City. We've spoken about Sunnyside Yard. And it's a real pleasure that, just today, we've agreed to set up a new level of that conversation between our housing and operations team at City Hall and the White House team. Because what we're speaking about is 12,000 homes, 30,000 jobs, the prospect of an entire new neighborhood in a city where housing is the number one cost. And I appreciate the president, his interest in this, and we also know the president not just as the leader of the country but also as someone who has built quite a lot of housing here in our city. I don't know, Mr. President, if you want to add anything.

Well, I can tell you that Sunnyside is a big job. I've been watching that for 35 years. Everybody has wanted to do something with Sunnyside Yard. We met at the White House a couple of times. But we met at the White House. The mayor brought that up, the possibility of doing Sunnyside Yard.

It's a very — I would say that was a very federal-oriented job. You're going to need a lot of federal approvals and probably some federal money to do it. But it's always been a great location. I owned a building in Sunnyside. It was a great building. I know it very well. So, when he mentioned Sunnyside Yard, they've been talking about developing that for 50 years. So maybe they have a shot at doing it.

q.t: I'm wondering if next week you plan on meeting with President Trump, [inaudible], or any foreign dignitaries while they're here for the general assembly?

a.t:
I will have a few meetings that we're in the process of setting up at this time that we'll share more details about soon.

When it comes to the president, we continue to have a conversation about how best to deliver for the city, and that is a conversation that has been done in person, it's been done over the phone, and it will continue so long as either of us have the ability to deliver for this city. Thank you.

q.t: Are you expecting protests like every day, is one day—

a.t: Yes, we're definitely expecting protests every day. I can tell you we're expecting multiple protests every day, and we will get you the number of permits and organizations that we've worked with so far.

q.t: Is there any estimates to how many groups have asked for permits?

a.t: Do we have the number? Marcia, we can get that to you, how many have asked so far?

q.t: I wanted to follow up on the idea of the demonstrations. I wonder if, first of all, any of these organizations that are planning demonstrations have had to get permits from the NYPD, and also are there going to be demonstration areas that they will be limited to so that they will not be able to get directly near the UN or directly near the Israeli embassy or directly near Gracie Mansion, where tomorrow there is going to be—

a.t:
So yes, we work very closely with organizations that facilitate protests, both on permitting, on logistics. Most of that work is done through our Community Affairs Bureau, which is actually the people who are on site often first, with those groups helping to facilitate First Amendment activity.

As I mentioned in my remarks, there will be frozen zones, as there are every year, where vehicles cannot access and pedestrians cannot access, but we are not planning anything for this year that is out of the ordinary, i.e., different in terms of those frozen zones than what we've done in years past.

q.t: I wanted to ask you about the demonstrations, specifically when Prime Minister Netanyahu is here. Can you speak about what that day will look like in terms of protests, what —if you need to make contact with some of those organizations, [inaudible]. And on the flip side, in terms of [inaudible], with those demonstrations, how much of a challenge does that present when you have [inaudible]?

a.t:
So, the NYPD, as you know, handles thousands of protests and demonstrations each year, and there is no organization better trained to facilitate First Amendment activity. As I mentioned in my prepared remarks, obviously every year around the UN General Assembly time we do see an uptick in the amount of protest activity. And this year, I do not expect to be any different.

So, the NYPD is prepared to work with organizers of protests and facilitate First Amendment activity. And as always, we have no tolerance for violence or destruction of property or breaking the law.

q.t: As a follow-up, maybe, so private students [inaudible] going to land in Newark, apparently not at JFK, is that a security decision or should we read something into that? And then secondly, does the presence of the prime minister, President Trump and the President of Iran, all within the same couple of days, how does that add to the complexity or perhaps [inaudible]?

a.s: Deputy Commissioner Rebecca Weiner, Intelligence & Counterterrorism, NYPD
a.t:
So, each movement of each head of state or foreign minister or dignitary is coordinated based on logistics, and you shouldn't read anything into any particular movement at all except that these are all collective decisions to maximize security for everyone.

And also remember, 200 dignitaries from 200 countries coming here, moving around the city presents a big coordination challenge. Every year for the last 81 years, there have been geopolitical hotspots whose governments have come to New York City, presenting just that sort of issue. So, this is no different.

Last year was the 80-year anniversary, and there was a lot of turmoil around the world. The whole point of the UN is to try to work through that diplomatically, and as you've heard from our commissioner and from my colleagues here, as well as the mayor, we do that to keep people safe, no matter who you are, visitor or resident, no matter what sort of instability is happening around the world. In New York, you come, you talk about it and you move around the city safely, and we keep the city resident safe as well.

q.t: Mayor Mamdani, this question is for you. So, ahead of the planned protests next week, has anybody from the NYPD asked you to maybe cool down your rhetoric when it comes to Israel or Netanyahu?

a.t: The conversations that I've had with the PD have been purely on standard preparations for this event, as well as standard preparations for keeping New Yorkers safe. And I am fully confident in our police department's ability to do so, and I'm fully confident in their ability to do so each and every day, even outside of the General Assembly.

q.t: My question for the mayor is similar. You've asked New Yorkers to be patient a lot of times this year, you asked them to be patient to close fifth avenue, sixth avenue for the World Cup, etc. [Inaudible] you've correctly pointed out to many of them it's traffic [inaudible]. Many New Yorkers we've spoken to wonder, why is it worth it? Why is the UN General Assembly paying for them worth it? What would you say?

a.t:
We're proud to be the host of the United Nations General Assembly, and we're proud because what this event represents is also a recognition of the fact that we are all part of something larger than ourselves. We are having countries from across the world come here, and I think as you've heard it from many who've come to this podium today, it is in the hopes and the spirit of international cooperation.

Now, my job as the mayor is to ensure that the impact to New Yorkers is as minimal as possible in terms of their ability to go from point A to point B, and we will never be satisfied with what we are delivering. We'll always look to make it a little bit easier each and every day.

Today, I come to you on the day we've filled in our 200,000th pothole. So, it's making sure the streets are smoother, people can move across them, and I think to what both I and the commissioner have also is that people — encouraging people to use mass transit in this time. Because it is going to be serious gridlock over the course of those days.

q.t: Commissioner, from Televisa Univision, New York did very well when it came to the World Cup. As far as security, but that was a different sort of event. It was an event that united people of the United Nations, a very different tone. Perpetrators might want to send a message. What would be your biggest concern right now? Drones, would it be land? Biological warfare? I don't know, we're talking about AI lately, what would you say is your biggest concern right now? What would be your message to New Yorkers?

a.t:
Yeah, I think that we just spent a lot of time laying out everything that the New York City Police Department does and is doing, particularly next week, to secure what is the largest event of the year, the United Nations General Assembly. You will see a full deployment of New York City police officers and all of our specialty teams. And that deployment is designed to keep New Yorkers safe, but also to address any threats that we might see.

My message to New Yorkers is please remain vigilant, not just next week, but always. If you see something, say something, tell a police officer, call 911 or call our counterterrorism hotline at 1-888-NYC-SAFE.

q.t: Mayor, the students at Ramaz and some other Jewish schools are planning a prayer vigil outside Gracie Mansion on Friday morning to talk about their support for Israel and for Bibi Netanyahu. I wonder if you have any plans to go out and talk to them and explain your concerns and your views and hear what they have to say.

a.t: I welcome them. They can have a vigil, or I've heard some describe it even as a protest. Whatever it is intended to be, they have the room and space to do so outside of Gracie Mansion. I think that at the time that they are there, I will probably be somewhere else across the city.

q.t:
I'm Henry Beebe-Center with Streetsblog. In your Vision Zero Reimagined statement on Tuesday, you said we should not have to wait for another family to lose a loved one before we make a street safer.

But another family did indeed lose a loved one on Canal Street last week, where DOT has a safety plan but has put it off until next year at the earliest. And the Bedford Avenue bike lane remains unprotected despite constant danger to cyclists whose families might be next. So, why are you making them wait?

a.t:
So, these are conversations that are ongoing within our administration. We take very seriously the importance of delivering street safety and, frankly, to do so in a manner that develops a network across our city. And we also know that while we are proud of the fact that the number of fatalities has decreased since the time that Vision Zero was announced more than a decade ago, that we will not rest until that number is zero.

That number continues to be more than 200, and that is why yesterday we announced a whole suite of initiatives that we are going to be taking, and that is also going to be complemented by a streets plan that we will be releasing soon.

q.t: I'm so sorry. Thank you so much.

a.t:
No worries. I just wanted to make sure that I knew of the same thing that we were talking of. So, our Law Department is reviewing this lawsuit. And we are fully committed to transparency. And we're working to return FOIL requests in full accordance with the law.

And then on your first question, you know, I have made very clear about my views, my thoughts, my assessments. Also, when it comes to the UN General Assembly, my focus is ensuring that our city remains prepared to host representatives from across the world to keep New Yorkers safe. And I think also to ensure that we're able to both address the global conversation that is happening here in our city and the very local concerns that New Yorkers have about traffic and their ability to get from point A to point B over the course of that time period.

q.t: Your deputy mayor, yeah, Ana Maria Archila.

a.t: She's the commissioner for International Affairs.

q.t: The Manhattan Institute filed a lawsuit looking for your administration to turn over records related to your deputy mayor and a meeting with the Iran UN ambassador. It didn't end up happening, but just what is the delay for these records? Why not turn them over?

a.t: Sorry, I think — you're referring to the commissioner of International Affairs or deputy mayor?

q.t: Just to follow up on Hannah's question, just if you could explain exactly why — I mean, obviously I know that you're not a fan of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. Why did you choose not to attend any protests this next week? And did you have any conversations with the president about potentially any protests? And then, I have a second question for you as well.

a.t: You can ask the second one as well.

q.t: So, Benjamin Netanyahu is going to arrive in NYC next weekend. Can you tell us if you're planning to protest his arrival? If not, are you encouraging others to do so? And to follow up on that, has the NYPD expressed any concern to you about the scale of protests, planned protests, things like that?

a.t:
I do not have any plans to attend any protest at the UN General Assembly, and I have also been in touch with our PD in general as we prepare for the UN General Assembly. Right now, there are no expected threats that we know of, and we [continue] to be confident in being able to deliver safety and security for New Yorkers.

To New Yorkers, I have never encouraged them to protest. What I have always told them is that they have the right to do so in the city. We respect that right. And this is a city that is proud of the Constitution, proud of the First Amendment, we'll continue to do so.

q.t:
So, then City Council posted today that they are going to have an oversight meeting about regulation of AI. They've invited the Anthropic CEO and the OpenAI CEO.

Wondering if you'd be open to meetings with those CEOs as well and if you've had any other further reach out than just your calls for saying that there should be more government regulation. Have you spoken to President Trump about it or any other officials?

a.t:
These are conversations that are ongoing internally within our administration of all the different steps that we can be taking to reckon with a question that is on the forefront of Americans' minds coast to coast.

And when it comes to the City Council's announcement, I do welcome efforts by the Council to ask these kinds of questions, to probe these kinds of companies, to explore the role that the city can take in potential regulations.

And yes, I'd be open to those meetings, and frankly I think that what we are really looking forward to is not just having individual meetings, frankly, but to have a policy that can address the scope and the scale of the questions that are in front of us.

q.t:
I have two questions, both on the EDC.

[Crosstalk.]

You appointed Lina Khan as chair of the EDC in July. Do you expect her to have more prominent role than past board chairs? Is the role and responsibilities of the chair going to change in any way? And my second question, are there any other new projects that we can expect the EDC to take on soon?

a.t:
So, what was the last part of it? New projects you expect them to take on? Okay. I'm very excited by the fact that we have Lina Khan as our board chair, and she has showcased a drive, desire and ability to deliver for working people across this country for many years at a national level and has also been instrumental even just as one of the co-chairs of our transition.

She will help to develop that vision, and I'm also very excited about the leadership of the head of our EDC, Tony Shorris, who has just recently started and is an integral part of ensuring that we are able to not only deliver economic development for New Yorkers across the five boroughs, but also economic justice, and that this be a city that isn't just one that is thought of as the wealthiest city and the wealthiest country in the history of the world, but also one where we can address the fact that one in four New Yorkers are currently living in poverty.

q.t: Like, in other words, it's 10 minutes. Tell us when they get warned, when they need to start leaving.

a.t:
Yeah, so there's external signage that has the 10 minutes. You also walk in, there's a sign that says 10 minutes. Audio plays, it welcomes you to Throne, tells you it will close the door behind you. It's playing in the back.

It then will tell you it's a 10-minute limit. At five minutes, there's music actually playing throughout, which is also a behavioral science technique in deterring loitering. It's nice music if you're in there for three minutes, maybe not that great if it's 30 minutes.

At five minutes, the music breaks. It says, "Hey, you're halfway there," very friendly. At eight minutes, it will say — it stops and it says, "Hey, your use is coming to an end. Make sure you're prepared. The door will open at 10 minutes." The music comes back on.

At 10 minutes, there are flashing lights. The audio comes on. And this is both in English and Spanish for all of these indicators. It says, "The door — your time is up, the door is opening.” The door’s opening. That extends for about 30 seconds. So, if you are still pants down, we're not gonna open the door on you. But then the door does open.

And again, as I said before, that has proven to be a very effective safety mechanism as well when people are having a medical emergency inside, which thankfully doesn't happen that often, but can. So, does that — thank you.

q.t:
[Inaudible] your whole name and spell it for me?

[Crosstalk.]

a.t:
The other piece is the accountability. In the design, we've used a lot of behavioral science to give people nudges. So, in the same way that when someone's waiting behind you in line in a bathroom situation, you might take a little extra minute, make sure you didn't dribble on the seat, wipe anything up.

The same thing holds true here when you enter with your device. And so, we're able to, if somebody is smoking inside, actually send a warning saying, “Smoke was detected during a use associated with your phone. If this happens again, you may risk losing access.”

What we see over time with over 2 million uses is that only 0.2 percent of people are repeatedly misusing the restrooms and getting restricted. We also have a path to get access back, but that is also a critical piece of why we're doing that.

q.t: Following up on the homelessness question, if you're homeless and perhaps you don't have a cell phone, [or] you don't have a charged cell phone, maybe you didn't, weren't able to connect with some, a provider to get a tap card. Maybe the — it's off hours when the nearby tap card locations are closed. I can imagine there being a barrier and I'm wondering, since it seems like the doors do open eventually at the end, why is there a kind of a need for an electronic entry system at all?

a.t:
I think one of the key parts of this, and we've heard this, is the feedback loop for New Yorkers to provide of the cleanliness of the unit, of the use of the unit, and that actually triggers a response in terms of it being cleaned faster and sooner.

So, that's very important for us, because you heard it from Henry, who's, I think, indicative of many New Yorkers, at one level sympathetic because of what they've had to experience and another level also skeptical because of what they've heard. And we need to make sure that we can address those needs while also being able to address the concerns around it.

I think one of the other critical parts of this is to have local partners within a 10-minute walk of these Throne Labs — is a critical way such that it's not just those with phones, but also those who have tap cards, and that that card is something that can be used to get into these bathrooms.

I don't know if there's anything else — okay, all right. It's a great name, by the way. It's an incredible name, I don't know—

[Crosstalk.]

I don't know if it's worth adding, but the ability to track the number of uses is also how we get to those service levels of saying that it's going to be cleaned every 10 to 15 uses.

Because you have to understand how frequently it's being used. Here in New York, there's so many people, some areas are more dense than others. We want to make sure that that maintenance and cleanliness operation is up to par with what we expect from public restrooms in the city.

q.t:
And my other question is, what happens if you run out of time? Does it just — can you reset the clock if you're in a bad situation?

[Crosstalk.]

a.t:
Yeah, I think balancing publicly accessible private space and misuse — it's a balance. So, if there is a need for more time, unfortunately, there is not a way to extend. We are working on a way to do that for people with existing mobility challenges or issues that are ongoing. But for now, no.

But our strategy is really just informed consent. So, there's signage on the outside about the 10-minute limit, on the inside, audio and visual, and then there are warnings throughout the use that are telling you you're at five minutes, eight minutes, 10 minutes, and then you even have a little bit of a buffer at the end when you know it's really getting serious. So, thank you.
To also just say succinctly that this is not a place to scroll on your phone. I know that many people do that. This isn't one of them.

q.t: Police precincts.

a.t: Police precincts? I'll get back to you.

q.t: If the police will let me use one, I'll usually try to get in there. Are those public?

a.t: Which ones?

q.t: So, if I could follow up, I just wonder what the next step of sewer socialism will be.

a.t:
You know, I think the next step is, what are the issues that people are dealing with in terms of their quality of life. We've seen New Yorkers come forward to say it's the pothole on their block — that's a priority for us. We've seen others come forward and tell the Council member, the Council member [has] brought it forward of, "I need a place to be able to take my kid when they need to go to the bathroom." That's the priority for us.

Anything that a New Yorker is struggling with in their day-to-day life, that's a priority for us, because we want to show that City government can help you live a better life in this city, and for far too long New Yorkers have been rightfully skeptical of that.

[Crosstalk.]
What's your favorite public bath in New York City?

q.t:
So, Mr. Mayor, I know that this is only a pilot for 17 public restrooms, and I know that Sandy Nurse wants 2,100, but will all the restrooms that you do after this be like this, the modular units, or are you exploring other options as well?

The reason I ask the question is that these are fairly big, and you have to find enough space to put them in. And the question is where you would find it. Does it have to be public space? Will it be on a street, in a park, at an intersection? Do you have to take public property to do it? Will you put it in NYCHA? What are the things that you're looking at in order to expand this? And will it always be these modular units or will you look at other options as well?

a.t:
We're going to be looking at all options. Just to give you one example, over the time that we've been in office, we've also opened an automated public toilet as well. I had made an announcement, I think, as this Council member had referred to in the early days of the administration, and that very site actually just opened up its automated public toilet this week. So, that's one example of a way to do it. The modular restrooms are another example of the way to do it.

Frankly, Marcia, I'll be honest, I don't think that there's a shortage of places that could accommodate a public restroom. The interest and demand is so high. And when you look at these, what is so exciting about them is that they do not require what most restrooms require in terms of the connection to so much of the infrastructure of our city.

And also, the cost that we're talking about, 17 of these — and I think the deputy mayor of Operations can correct me if I'm wrong — 17 costs about what one public restroom has historically cost in New York City. And that is part of why we have not built that many, because we've seen the cost of these restrooms just escalate year after year.

q.t: Can the general public have access to City Hall [bathrooms]?

a.t:
I think that everyone should be able to use every bathroom that is, you know, within public access. I'll get back to you about the specifics of the City Hall bathroom.

What I will say is that for us, part of the reason that this is a pilot is we want to evaluate the results of this. We're hopeful, and what I would love to see is that at the end of this year that we can see the success of these 17 modular bathrooms and then, as the Council member said, build this into our larger vision.

Because we're a city of 8.5 million people, and we need to have enough public infrastructure for people's day-to-day needs. And I think, especially when we're thinking about New Yorkers who work outside as well as parents who are taking their children around, they shouldn't have to have that panic or have to look for a Google Maps list of different businesses that you can get into to use their public bathroom. And I think that there are too many New Yorkers who have had to deal with that, frankly.

q.t: City Hall.

a.t: There are a number of them.

q.t:
And mayor, my second follow-up was Mayor Adams had a much broader announcement, frankly, a couple of years ago promising public resources and immediately after people had trouble accessing many of those public bathrooms up to and including City Hall.

So, what is your commitment to the existing public infrastructure, and should anyone be allowed to use the bathroom in City Hall without having to, you know, get ID'd and jammed up by the cops?

a.t: I haven't thought about the bathroom — so which bathroom specifically?

q.t: I was just wondering about the enforcement aspect to this because although I empathize, as the father of a 6- and 3-year-old, [with] having more public bathrooms, I've also covered instances in other places where modular-style public bathrooms have resulted in drugs, prostitution and homeless encampments, so I'm wondering how you're going to combat that here.

a.t:
So, I really appreciate the question because so much of the way in which Throne Labs have set up these modular bathrooms is specifically geared toward the kind of outcomes that we want to see. So, there are a few things that I'll just rattle off and then feel free to come up and add some additional details.

One thing that is critically important for New Yorkers to know is that every single unit is cleaned by a real person and is done so on average every 15 uses or fewer.

The other is that these are bathrooms where there's, you know, you start to have flashing lights after a certain point to encourage people to get out of the bathroom. Because, again, the average time of using a public restroom is, I think, somewhere below four minutes, about three and a half minutes or so. And so, the kinds of things that you're speaking of is typically a much longer use of time in the bathroom that doesn't actually need to be accommodated by this. I don't know if you want to add some details.

And I'm Jessica Heinzelman, co-founder and COO of Throne. The other thing is after plenty of warnings, as the mayor's talking about, with acknowledgement that the time is up, the door eventually will open, letting that user know well in advance.

And that's actually saved lives in other locations where someone is having a medical emergency, contrary to your traditional public restroom that has a door that might stay locked for hours until maintenance comes along and knocks.

This actually provides access to an individual where people can walk by and see. In some cases, our cleaners have showed up and been able to help somebody immediately. And all of our staff will be offered training on Narcan as well.

q.t: By the way, did you ever put the bidets into Gracie Mansion?

a.t:
Yes, they're all there.

[Crosstalk.]

q.t: Mayor, second quick question is, does 17 on top of the 1,000, does that really make a dent when the goal is 2,000? Are New Yorkers going to notice this?

a.t:
Brother, I'll tell you that when you need one, if you can find one, makes a difference. So, 17, yes, it is an important first step toward, you know, you heard from the Council member about a larger vision. But to us, this is also what it looks like for a City government being responsive.

I mean, I can tell you the time when I discovered the public bathroom in the Times Square subway station was an incredible moment for me. And I hope that many others have that same moment when they discover these 17 Throne Labs across the five boroughs.

q.t: Thank you. I have a couple of quick on-topic questions. Number one is, can you talk about the barrier to entry since either a phone is required or a tap card that someone would have to pick up? Isn't that keeping out the same homeless population that others just spoke of?

a.t:
So, one of the reasons why, when I began my remarks, I also began with acknowledgement of the World's Borough Bookstore is that we are partnering with a lot of local institutions that are going to be passing out these tap cards so that people can actually have a physical manifestation of them.

And that is going to be a critical part of ensuring that this is something for all New Yorkers. I'll also just invite Throne Labs CEO to add some additional details to that.

a.s: Jessica Heinzelman, Co-Founder and COO, Throne Labs
a.t: Thank you. The additional benefit of having the phone access is to also be able to hear from people using it so that we're able to get cleanliness ratings immediately as well as any feedback. That goes into our systems, generates tickets so that can get out there quickly. And then we're so thrilled to be working with a number of the local partners. There is going to be signage on each Throne with the address and location and hours where tap cards are available within a 10-minute walk.

q.t:
Actually, I'm on-topic as well. So, when it comes to enforcement, you know, you've spoken a lot about how you guys are going to crack down on drivers and when it comes to that super-speeder bill, but are you guys also looking at potentially installing more speed cameras places in order to ramp up enforcement?

And then you said a lot of the details are going to come out later in your transportation commissioner's plan. When is that going to be released again? And is there — are you going to be holding another event? Thank you.

a.t:
That will be released soon, and yes, that will, much to Max's chagrin, come with another event. And I think to your first question, for us, it's about how do we hold those who are violating the law accountable. If it's a New Yorker who's buying an e-bike that goes at 35 miles an hour from one of the dozens of retailers, we want to hold that retailer accountable, stop them from selling that e-bike. If it's a small number of New Yorkers that are repeatedly found using ghost plates and speeding and operating their vehicle recklessly, then yes, it's the utilization of the super-speeder program.

Again and again, we have seen far too often a response to horrific tragedy across the city, as if it is simply part of the cost of doing business here. And we can never grow numb to families who are shattered. You know, just as we were switching to off-topic, a mother from Families for Safe Streets looked at me and pointed at a photo of her child and said, "It's his birthday tomorrow." And they will not be able to celebrate that birthday.

We heard from a 12-year-old speaking about how he never met his older sister. This is what we have tolerated. And we are proud of the fact that, yes, the number of traffic fatalities have reduced since the launch of Vision Zero, and we are still speaking of fatalities beyond 200 every single year. So, we know that there is more work to be done, and we look forward to doing it. Thank you all very much.

q.t:
This is actually on-topic. Part of the plan looks at larger vehicles and how to discourage them, including possibly increasing tolls on them going to the city. I know you're just exploring that, but is that, I mean, I read that as maybe increasing congestion pricing for bigger cars. Is that something you're looking at?

And then also — sorry, second related question — another thing it looks at is bringing city control over self-driving cars. Do you have a vision for, like, Waymo's in the city in the future? Is that something that you think is going to happen during your term?

a.t:
My vision is for keeping New Yorkers safe and also of ensuring that we're protecting the livelihoods of so many of the drivers who have helped to power this city over many, many years.

And then to your first question, before I was the mayor, I was an Assembly Member in Astoria and Long Island City. And I saw a number of times where the presence of trucks on these small, narrow roads were ones that could have fatal consequences.

There was a woman who was actually killed riding a Citi Bike by a large-scale truck just a couple of blocks away from my district office. And so, yes, we are exploring every potential avenue to discourage heavier and larger vehicles because, as we've seen over the last few years, cars across our country have gotten much, much bigger, and sometimes they've gotten to a level of size where there isn't even a safety component; where the driver cannot even see a child walking across them because it's not even present in their windshield.

q.t: Two quick questions — good, thank you. One, just clarify for me if you can, sir, just out of the, you know, the safety policies here, what can technically be done this week or this — today or this month without changing state law? And then also my second question: we had a particularly violent week in the Bronx, some eight wounded. Just any reaction, sir, to the increase in violence?

a.t:
So, on your first question, some of the key focuses are continuing the actions we're taking and escalating the scale and the speed of them. So, for example, Sammy's Law is something that we've spoken about. Thus far, we've rolled out 215 miles per hour slow zones. We are going to deliver, by the end of this calendar year, 800, and then by the end of the first term, 2,300. That does not require any additional authorization.

Additionally, when it comes to super-speeders, we do not need additional authorization from Albany. We are now working with the Council and partner agencies to develop that legislation and that infrastructure so that the small number of drivers that are repeatedly violating street safety laws will be held accountable.

Beyond that, also moving from an approach of daylighting from sign-only to hardened daylighting. The importance of this is that we've seen that have the greatest effect and actually creating safety for New Yorkers.

So, these are a few of the examples of what we're pursuing right now. There are others like pedestrian zones. Those are going to be ones that we're going to expand and expound on in the street safety plan — sorry, in the plan that is forthcoming later this year with Commissioner Flynn.

And then to your other question, we are both proud of the work that the NYPD has been doing, as well as partner agencies, to drive down murders and shootings. And we will also never be satisfied until we completely eliminate crime in this city. And so, when we hear the news, as we have been over these past few days, of shootings in the Bronx, this will continue to be a concern from us, and how we can deliver on that — it's going to be through increased attention from the PD as well as work with our CMS partners.

q.t:
Well, these drops in enforcement by the NYPD on moving violations—

[Crosstalk.]
Why is that happening? Will you actually order your NYPD to step it up?

a.t:
Every single member of our task force, all the 19 members — which in our administration for the first time also includes the FDNY — are going to be partners in actually delivering on Vision Zero Reimagined.

And what that means is we're going to take a hard look at how best we can change behavior that we're seeing in violation of our street safety laws and then utilize that. That includes the PD; that includes the other 18 members as well.

q.t: Beyond a moratorium on data centers, what's some other specifics you would like to see?

a.t:
I think we need to see policies that have to do with the pace of development. We need policies that respond to the Hugging Face incident. We need to see ones that respond to the assertion from the head of Anthropic that the Hugging Face incident has occurred at every single AI company.

And we need to see an answer to these concerns that are shared by Americans from across the country, beyond, "We are in an arms race with countries from across the world." We're talking about companies that are bringing up the end of humanity as a possible outcome of this technology, and it has been a very flip response to that level of concern. And to your first question — can you repeat your first question one more time?

q.t:
I don't know if the NYPD official already left, but I have one off-topic and one on-topic, actually. The statistics that were just referenced that are going down on traffic enforcement from the NYPD, I'm wondering if you just have a sense of why there's such a steep drop and if you're going to actually order your NYPD to step up that enforcement. And then I have an off-topic as well if you want me to ask now or wait.

So, on something totally different, artificial intelligence. I know you said earlier in the week that you would like to see the federal government play a larger role in this. On some specifics, Bernie Sanders has introduced a bill that would create a nationwide moratorium on data centers. Is that something you would support? Is that the type of increased federal presence you would like to see?

a.t:
I think that's an important part of it. I don't think that that's the entirety of what we need to see from the federal government. Bernie has been an incredible leader in the conversation around artificial intelligence. What we are also talking about, however, is beyond data centers, the question of pacing the frontier, as it's been described over these past few days and weeks and months.

What are the federal government's policies to ensure that this rapidly advancing technology is going to be regulated as opposed to just simply determined through a profit motive or through the decisions of a few individualized companies that will or will not have an IPO sometime soon?

q.t:
So, my colleagues over at Gothamist have reported problems with ACE enforcement. Some of it is ghost plates, some of it's people just obstructing their plates. On my ride up here, from Crown Heights up Bedford, where there were not a single block of unprotected bike lane that didn't have at least two vehicles parked in the lane. There were about six traffic cops that I counted on that stretch. There were no tickets on any windshield wipers. And then turned down Grand where on at least two occasions I had to jump out of the bike lane; once I had to avoid a 53-foot truck, which has no business being on Grand.

So, I understand that there's a real effort to move to automated enforcement because it is — because it's unbiased. But I'm not aware of any kind of automated enforcement that can measure this, you know, exterior dimensions of a truck. And there are problems with ACE. It has not been as successful as some of its boosters would have hoped. So, how do we get from here to being able to ride in the bike lanes to this press conference?

a.t:
I think that it's going to take every single tool. That does not mean an exclusive reliance on automated enforcement. It also means a continued partnership with the PD to use those tools of ticketing when any violation is present. And I bike pretty regularly in our city. I see exactly the same things that you see. And part of it is, what tools do we still have that we haven't used under prior administrations that we can use now?

Part of this plan is also an identification of additional tools we need to develop through partnership with Albany. And that's what also is so important about having Assembly Member Emily Gallagher here, having Families for Safe Streets here, is because we know there will also need to be an agenda that enhances the tools that the city has so that we can get to that point where our streetscape is the envy of the world.

q.t: Do you like the behavior you see on the street?

a.t:
Do I like the behavior I see on the street? I think that there is far more to be done to ensure, no matter what mode of transit we're talking about, we're looking at an adherence to street safety.

[Crosstalk.]

q.t: Moving violations that they don't impact driver behavior. Was that your answer?

a.t: No, the point that I am making is that I do not measure success by an increased number of tickets or by an increased number of violations. To me, the judgment of success is by a change in behavior. I think these are important tools, but I don't think that they are all one-to-one. We have members of the NYPD here. If there's anyone that wants to add—

q.t: [Inaudible] I'm understanding your answer, moving violations for drivers don't impact their behavior? Is that what you've just said?

a.t: Sorry?

q.t: Just last month the NYPD issued 28 percent fewer moving violations than in 2019. I want to know why that's been tolerated under your administration. And then I have an e-bike question. Collisions, this is year-to-date compared to last year, collisions of e-bikes up 25 percent, but moving violations are only increased by 8 percent. It sounds like there's a tolerance there. And I want to know, since you told NYPD not to give out these criminal summonses, why that is a worthy trade-off. And as far as, I just want to say, you're saying the behavior has to change — the behavior is atrocious all around.

a.t:
And that's why we are here, because we know that there is still so much more to be done.
