And when it comes to what we have seen with e-bikes across the city, one of the key things that we've found in terms of some of the highest-profile incidents and crashes have been e-bikes that are going far beyond what is legal on our streets. And so, our focus has also been on how do we stop the sale of those devices so that that is not even an option.

Now, when it comes to the question of criminal summonses versus civil summonses, we were seeing a utilization of criminal summonses without any kind of an impact on behavior and creating a disparate policy for cyclists versus drivers. Our focus is for safety, and our focus is to ensure that there is no tolerance for any of these violations, no matter what your mode of transit is.

We know that close to 90 percent of all traffic fatalities are caused by vehicles in our city. We also know that for many, when they're talking of these near misses that Marcia has brought up, it comes from an e-bike going at 25, 30, 35 miles an hour.

q.t:
My second question is, some reporting earlier today from Streetsblog about the NYPD has shifted its enforcement to e-vehicles, to e-bikes, when we know statistically the number one danger for pedestrians, for cyclists, for anybody on the street are vehicles.

My question is, how do you get the NYPD to ramp up its enforcement of drivers who run red lights, who speed — even just biking here today, taking the alleged Grand Street bike path, completely blocked by trucks, cars, no enforcement whatsoever. How do you get the NYPD on board? Because much like other plans, we see this laid out and then the NYPD kind of shrugs.

a.t:
So, there's a few things. The first is that our goal here is not going to be measured in terms of the number of tickets that are issued or the violations, but rather behavioral change. And the NYPD is a partner in delivering that change. So too is the redesign of streetscapes across the city. We've seen, for example, one of the most effective ways at delivering increased bus speeds is not just from the ticketing of police officers, but rather from ACE, or what used to be called ABLE — automated ticket enforcement, as well as the redevelopment of the streets themselves for the creation of those busways and bus lanes.

So, we are looking at every single tool that we have and just know that for us, it is not enough to have delivered that streetscape. We then need to ensure that it's actually being utilized in the same way. And so, we are going to exhaust every single tool at our disposal.

[Crosstalk.]

q.t:
So, before you took office, we asked several people with advice for you. We asked Janette Sadik-Khan, who is the Department of Transportation head under Mayor Bloomberg, and she said, "Declare that implementation is the alpha and omega of transportation policy. You're not going to get credit just for press releases, only for projects on the ground."

So why are we here putting out yet another plan and not implementing or at a groundbreaking or at something that we know how to do because we've seen a lot of these plans? And I have another question after this.

a.t:
Two questions? Marcia's setting the standard. I appreciate it. What gives me joy of standing here is that I have stood alongside these very elected officials, these very advocates, these very agency leaders at groundbreakings over the course of the nine months that we've been in office.

Today is not a thing that should be celebrated in it of itself; it should be celebrated because of what it will deliver, and its success will be judged by what we deliver. Not the vision that we have, but rather what we can use that vision to actually get to New Yorkers.

And when I look at our DOT commissioner, when I look at our deputy mayor for Operations, I see individuals who know very clearly that that is how we will be measured, and that is exactly what they are looking for, is things that we can achieve in our time in office. And your second question.

[Crosstalk.]

q.t: If I could just follow up with another question. So, I'm also wondering, you know, you're talking about making these pedestrian zones. Could you give us an idea of what you envision as these pedestrian-only zones? Where will they be? Will they be in main thoroughfares? Will they be in neighborhoods? And what do you envision them to look like?

a.t: So I think that there is some of what we have said today that will be shared in greater detail in the forthcoming streets plan. And I know that the commissioner is hard at work at the development of that. I think what this also comes back to is looking at our city with a vision of how can we make this the safest place possible. And that also looks at places where the vast majority of people are currently pedestrians, and yet we haven't actually upgraded our laws — you know, whatever our guidance is — in those same neighborhoods. I don't know, Commissioner, if you'd want to add anything.

I think that's exactly right. You know, there's denser, transit-friendly neighborhoods of the city where they're already dominated by pedestrians, but the street may not really be designed to reflect that.

We know that enforcement is just one of the legs of the stool when it comes to safety. Engineering's another important one: how we design our streets. And so much of the way people behave does come down to sort of psychological cues. So, the more we can do to design an environment that encourages the behavior we want to — the more we'll see that behavior. Thank you, Marcia.

q.t: Mayor, on the way coming here, over three blocks on 57th Street, I noticed eight e-bikes, scooters and regular bicycles going the wrong way on a one-way street, going through red lights, weaving through traffic that was stopped so they could get around buses and cars. I'm wondering, since they seem to be very dangerous, what you're going to do to deal with that. Every New Yorker has a story about a near miss. And the question is, why don't the police arrest them or give them tickets? Why don't you put license plates on them to make it easier? There's a lot of danger on the streets just by the fact that they feel that they can go any place they want.

a.t:
Well, I want to make very clear that our administration has no tolerance for the violation of street safety, no matter what mode of transit that you're using. And when it comes to e-bikes, I first just want to use this as an opportunity to also give an update on that, to what you were referring to, Marcia, of New Yorkers who have their own stories; many of them also have to do with e-bikes that can go at far higher speeds than what is legal on our streets.

And I want to thank our Corporation Counsel Steve Banks for spearheading cease-and-desist letters that have been sent out. A number of retailers, in response to those letters, have agreed to stop stocking those e-bikes for sale that violate our laws. There have also been a number of productive conversations, including with Alibaba and Best Buy, to start to modify their sales, and they have indicated an interest in developing sales restrictions.

Now, beyond that, we do also have members of the NYPD that are here. NYPD members, what our goal is, is behavioral change. And so, I don't look as much as a goal to the number of violations that are issued, the number of tickets that are issued. What I want to see is a change in behavior. And what our NYPD also has, though, are the tools that, if they determine that something is reckless or dangerous or it is a violation of what is able to be on those streets, they can even go so far as to take that micromobility vehicle. And they have done so in the past.

q.t: Yeah, just any other proactive measures — if you're looking at any other towers in the area besides those tents.

a.t: So, I will just bring up our commissioner, Dr. Alastair Martin, to speak to additional details of the proactive steps.

Thank you, Mr. Mayor. So, first, let me just say that for the one individual who has passed, our hearts are with that individual's loved ones, their friends, their family. And that death represents to us all the more reason to really make sure that everything that needs to happen happens quickly, aggressively and effectively. And that's exactly what we're doing here now.

With regard to the cooling towers, the region that we're looking at contained about 20 different cooling towers. All of those, as you heard the mayor say, have been sampled, and over the weekend, every single one of the cooling towers that had a PCR-positive result [has] been ordered to do the full drainage, the cleaning and the disinfection of that tower. We have the vast majority of those that are done, and the ones that have not been done yet will be done by the end of today.

We're working to identify all the data with regard to the history of the monthly compliance with those cooling towers. But I'm proud to say that we've been on target with our annual inspections for every single one of those towers.

q.t: Is there any proactive investigation into other cooling towers in the area? And how often — I know there's this 30-day rule to review and inspect the towers — how much of that is being taken care of, and is there a database on that, that these are getting investigated and these are getting inspected every 30 days?

a.t: Sorry, the beginning of your question, could you say it one more time?

q.t: Legionnaires. Yes. What is the latest that the City is doing to investigate the Bronx outbreak, and are there any lessons learned from the East Side outbreak, and what are you doing differently?

a.t:
So as of yesterday, the latest is that 10 people have been diagnosed with Legionnaires' disease within this cluster. One New Yorker has tragically passed away, and we are heartbroken by this loss of life. We are thinking of their loved ones and sending them our condolences.

We continue to encourage any New Yorker who has experienced flu-like symptoms — be they cough, fever, difficulty breathing, and that they live or work or have visited the area — to contact a health care provider. In terms of the steps that we have taken, I want to assure New Yorkers we are moving aggressively to contain the spread. The Health Department has sampled all cooling towers in the area. They did so on Thursday within 12 hours of identifying the cluster. The community health outreach workers started to canvass the neighborhood the next day, on Friday. That continued through the weekend, and the initial screening test results were completed. And the orders to clean and disinfect 10 cooling towers were issued on Saturday. By the end of today, all 10 cooling towers will have been fully cleaned and fully disinfected.

And what we are doing is — there have been a number of new policies we have implemented, I think, as of about a week or two ago that we have announced. We are always going to keep pushing on the question of what more we can do, because this has been an issue that New Yorkers have had to deal with for far too many years, and we are looking to develop any kind of tool that can help to ensure that Legionnaires’ is something that we're able to combat.

q.t: Do you have any sort of timeline? I know the department versus Office of Community Safety is not totally in your control, but I guess does this give you any urgency to get things moving on that end?

a.t: The disbanding of the Strategic Response Group is something that I would separate out from a conversation around the Office of Community Safety. It is a conversation that I'm having with our police commissioner in a manner that we do it that can respect New Yorkers' rights and keep New Yorkers safe.

q.t: I'm wondering about your reaction to a recent lawsuit against the Strategic Response Unit of the Police Department alleging that overtime assignments in at least one of the units were distributed on a racial basis, and also that there was a supervisor in the unit to basically beat arrest numbers from previous times. I wonder what your reaction to that lawsuit is as well as that your administration is now in a position to be spending money and time defending these allegations.

a.t: I think those allegations are incredibly troubling. And this is the first that I am hearing of them. This is something that I will follow up after this press conference. I continue to believe in the importance of decoupling our response to terror threats from our response to the use of First Amendment rights. And that is a longstanding position and that is one that we will deliver on.

q.t: Do you have any position on using cash assistance in some of the pre-existing public charge rules? Do you think that that's appropriate? How do you think about this in a more general sense?

a.t: I think that the policy that the prior administration took was the correct policy of refusing to defend this in court.

q.t:
I have two questions. One is actually an on-topic from before. So, the public charge rule change is obviously in addition to existing rules, and this concept of public charge. I'm just wondering how you feel about that concept sort of philosophically, sort of taking aside whether it's legal and setting aside this latest change. Like, how do you feel about the concept of public charge and its use in immigration status?

And then, I wanted to follow up on Jesse's question: DCWP, you have a lot of federal regulatory folks in your administration; do you see a role outside of what you did in the Department of Education for the City to get into regulating AI?

a.t:
First, I just want to underline the importance of the federal government taking this threat seriously. Too much of this conversation has been dominated by concerns of profit or an international arms race and too little about concerns for humanity at large.

And we will continue to explore every avenue we have in New York City government, all while knowing that there needs to be greater leadership at the federal level. And then to your first question, what concerns me so deeply is that in a climate where federal immigration officials have shown no interest in law and order, despite that being their stated objective, you have an entire population that spans from those on visas, those with green cards, those with citizenship, those who are simply children of immigrants, being terrified at any and all immigration policies and rule changes.

And the decisions that terror and fear not only will lead families to take, but have already led families to take, [are ones] that will change people's lives for the worse for years to come. We're speaking about taking people out of Medicaid, of SNAP, of so many of the things that people rely on because they're lifesaving. And that to me is what is incredibly concerning, that this is, without hyperbole, life or death for so many.

q.t:
We've just come off the back of a couple of weeks of really scary news in the AI space. So just a few examples: AI agents hacking and covering their tracks, going rogue, AI researchers quitting, citing the potential end of humanity.

Also in New York City, there's warnings of AI taking masses of tech jobs of young people that have been training in this space. I feel there's a sense of fear in New York City. I know it's not something city government talks about frequently, but what is your message to New Yorkers who are feeling scared and confused about this information?

And then secondly, there's a City Council member who's calling for an AI Emergency Task Force to be started potentially in the mayor's OTI. Is this something that you could commit to?

a.t:
So first what I will say is, like many Americans across the country, the news coming out of this technology in recent days and weeks has been incredibly alarming. We are speaking about reports that, as you said, include suggestions that this could lead to the end of humanity. And whether it's the Hugging Face incident or it's the assertion from one of the heads of Anthropic that these kinds of incidents are occurring at every single AI company, we should be seeing a far greater response from the federal government on this issue, one that has the urgency befitting any conversation around the end of humanity.

And in terms of what City government is going to do, we are going to continue to explore all of the avenues we have to protect New Yorkers. When you speak about New Yorkers having their own concerns — recently, we made the decision to ban the use of generative AI from 2K through eighth grade, and that is an ongoing conversation within City government.

q.t: With the UN next week, just wondering if there's been an update yet on your security clearance. And then, speaking of the UN next week, any sort of message you have? I know that you had said that you would maybe hope that people protest the Israeli Prime Minister, Benjamin Netanyahu. Just wondering, you know, is there still a call to protest, and what are your thoughts?

a.t:
Thank you. So, I just want to be very clear. My prior remarks were that if people choose to do so, then they are able to because that is the law here in New York City. I continue to leave it to New Yorkers to make their own decisions.

When it comes to your question about security clearance, the process of my getting a federal security clearance is ongoing. It's moving within the typical timeline for receiving one. A number of senior administration officials have a security clearance at this time. The NYPD also regularly briefs me on intelligence and investigations that do not involve federally classified information, and we will continue to move forward.

q.t:
My name is Abu Taher, I'm from Time Television, and my question is, the Trump administration is saying, what about what they are doing, it's previous law, they are just executing the law, what is the answer of this?

And number two, the immigration, you know, the people who process the immigration for their families, they're imposing new rules, which is they will check the sponsor credit history. Which a lot of people are afraid about, that they cannot bring their families, does it include your lawsuit that this is also illegal?

a.t:
So, first, let me say that the difference between the 2019 rule versus the rule that we are challenging today, they did not allow federal immigration officers to have so much discretion. The reality is that the guidelines fail to even indicate what immigration officers should consider.

Two, with regard to the credit history of sponsors, that also is included in our papers as well, but it's important that individuals understand that this is really all about cruelty. Cruelty is the point. Having a chilling effect on immigrants is the point. Letting individuals know that they are not welcomed here is the point. Immigration animus is the point. The fact that you are different from everyone else is the [point]. And the fact that you're going to deny individuals who are sick and hungry and homeless benefits is just beyond the pale. And that's why we are seeking in the state of New York to vacate this rule. It is unconstitutional, illegal, and we urge the judge to make that decision before Friday.

q.t: Hello, Mr. Mayor. Well, I have a question. Have you spoken to President Trump about this? You have successful conversations with him in the past about topics that you have different opinion on. Have you spoken to him about this, and would you expect anything to hear from him?

a.t:
The president and I have an ongoing conversation around immigration policy. We've both been very clear about the fact that we have deep disagreements on that policy, whether it pertains to ICE raids or TPS protections or public charge.

This is a disagreement that continues. And the case that I'm making is that this is a rule that will hurt this city. And we all stand here united in our commitment to protecting this city, and we will do everything we can, talk to everyone we can, to ensure that we can actually protect New Yorkers.

q.t: Hi, I know you're telling people not to disenroll from benefits like SNAP. But assuming that people are afraid and maybe they don't sign up or maybe they do disenroll, is there a situation you think the city will have to step in to try to make sure that the needs are being met?

a.t:
We are going to exhaust every tool that we have to take care of New Yorkers. And I want to make very clear, when we speak about immigrants, we are not somehow speaking about a separate population from New York; we're speaking about New Yorkers. I myself stand here as the first immigrant mayor of our city in generations.

And we are going to exhaust every tool to fight this rule. We are also going to ensure that everything we can do, especially in response to HR 1, we are doing all with the knowledge that there is no city in this country that can make up, dollar for dollar, what the federal government is looking to cut in terms of services to those who need it.

And the argument that these kinds of rules will save the U.S. government money — it is money that we are going to have to pay at a later stage at a higher price because people don't stop getting sick. People simply will get more sick, and then the first time that they will interact with a health care provider will be at the emergency room.

And you look at everyone who is here, you look at public advocate, assembly members, state senators, city council people, advocates, the attorney general, all of us have spoken to health care providers who have told us how difficult it is for them to be working in an emergency room and treat it as a primary care doctor, because that is the world that we live in now.

And Steve, if you want to add to the legal issue.

Just very briefly, Melissa, it's a 100-page complaint, and it required 100 pages because there's so much illegality in the rule that that's what was required.

This is not just a repeat of 2019 when the City and State went to court and beat back a similar public charge effort. It's even more harmful and more extreme.

Read the complaint and you will see that the chilling effect is an illustration of the problem with the illegality, but on every one of those 100 pages is a legal claim that was strong in 2019 and it's even stronger now.

Yeah, just in regard to your question, it's in violation of the Administrative Procedure Act because it's arbitrary and capricious. There's no meaningful decision with regard to these rules.

Two, the agency has exceeded its authority. This public charge rule goes back to 1822, where Congress basically said that it only applies to individuals who cannot support themselves, not individuals who apply every now and then for public assistance because they fall on hard times. And you should not also equate public charge with dependency. This has nothing to do with dependency; this has to do with opaque rules and rules where you're giving so much authority to immigration officers to consider every and any public benefit, including school lunch.

q.t:
What is the city's backup plan in case you don't prevail? Can you tell us just a little bit more about what, if anything, you're planning in terms of helping people access food and or medical care?

And can you go into just a bit more detail, please, about your legal argument? And do you have to prove that there's a chilling effect specifically because of this rule? Is it about the chilling effect or about the people being entitled to the benefit?

a.t:
So, I'm first going to answer your question as to what actions we're taking separate from the legal steps. And then I'm going to pass it over to our Corporation Counsel, Steve Banks, to add some additional details there.

In terms of the steps that we are taking, this rule is set to take effect on Friday of this week. We are spending each and every day right now looking to communicate with as many immigrant New Yorkers as possible about what this rule does and what it does not do.

We are equipping a lot of our city workers with the information of this so they can also communicate this. And we've set up this hotline to ensure that New Yorkers have a place they can call so that they know who they can ask for this kind of advice.

Before I pass it over to our Corporation Counsel, I do just want to bring up our public advocate, Jumaane Williams, because we've spoken about the fact of concern for immigrant New Yorkers. He has been a leader in this issue and has also correctly described himself as the highest-ranking Caribbean official here in our city.

And we know that these kinds of attacks, we have seen them every single week, and we've recently seen them against our Haitian brothers and sisters. We're seeing them continue with a broader population. I just wanted to know, public advocate, if there's anything you wanted to ask.

Thank you, Mr. Mayor, and thank you to the AG. As a son of immigrants, you know, this hits home as the highest-ranking Caribbean official and Black elected official, this is his home.

Oftentimes the Black immigrant experience is left out, but having also represented communities, particularly high populations of Haitian and Haitian immigrants and Haitian descendants. This, I need the media to really understand the chilling effect that this has, and really drive home the fact that even people this may not affect are really feeling it. And so, with the combination of the raids that are happening, the combination of getting rid of TPS, and now people trying to wade through legal arguments they may not understand, parts of our districts are ghost towns already as people are no longer coming out and supporting their businesses.

And now to have to make the decisions of whether they feed their children or not. The purpose of this is cruelty. That's it, cruelty and fear. That is the purpose of all of these immigrant decisions that are coming from the Trump White House and absolutely nothing else, particularly to non-White immigrants. I want to be clear about that.

And I say that every single time Donald Trump has said the only people who need assistance are white South Africans. Everyone else is left to fend for themselves. There is nothing ever that helps with public safety. None of this helps with public safety, all this does is create cruelty and violence. And I know it was said it will cause people to die. I want to add it will cost more people to die because people have already died because of Trump's policies. Thank you.

q.t: The City and State were already going to have to grapple next year with changes to various benefits impacting citizens and noncitizens because of the “big Republican bill,” SNAP and Medicaid and the like. So, if you have to deal with that and this, are you just generally worried about the health and safety of citizens in New York, both immigrant and nonimmigrant, with these changing federal policies?

a.t: I am incredibly worried about the impacts that both existing law will have once implemented as well as this rule change. And at a time when we are facing the reality of being the most expensive city in the United States of America, to see the federal government pursue rule changes and legislation that will make hungry New Yorkers hungrier, that will make poor New Yorkers poorer, it is a slap in the face to everything that we should be doing in this moment, which is to make it easier for working-class New Yorkers to afford their life here in the city.

q.t:
Mayor Mamdani, you have said that all New Yorkers will bear the cost of this rule. Can you quantify that? How much does the City expect to spend on emergency services if immigrant families stop using them?

And then my second question is what protections, immediate protections, can the City offer these families, including protection of their personal data, immigration status and information if a judge does block the rule from going into effect?

a.t:
So, first and foremost, I just want to say very clearly that our intent here is not to win a temporary injunction. It is to stop the implementation of this rule entirely. And the reason for that is we know that this is something that will have devastating consequences for immigrant New Yorkers, far beyond just those who it technically applies to.

And a lot of the reason for that distinction is that we have seen a climate of fear for immigrants regardless of their status. I have a clear memory of going into a Dominican barbershop in Harlem and speaking to the barbers about ICE raids. And one of them turned to me and said, "We all have status, and yet few of us are showing up to work because they don't care who has status anymore when they're picking people up.”

And so we're talking about something that we know categorically does not apply to certain sets of New Yorkers, and yet we're already seeing evidence of those kinds of New Yorkers unenrolling from lifesaving benefits.

So, at this time, I cannot give you an exact cost to the City because we are trying to do everything we can to ensure that we not only stop this rule but also that we communicate to New Yorkers that are not technically affected by this rule to not take decisions that they otherwise cannot undo once they move forward with it.

That is why one of our points of advice, separate from our legal action here, is for any immigrant New Yorker with concern to call our Mayor's Office of Immigrant Affairs hotline. Again, that number is 1-800-354-0365. And we encourage every immigrant New Yorker with concerns to go to a trusted legal provider before making those decisions.

You've heard it not only from those of us in government, but also outside of government, of the kinds of concerns they're hearing. These are actions that will have devastating consequences for New Yorkers across our city.

q.t:
Wow. Mayor Mamdani is such a light. It was such a joy to share a space with him today. He is highly sought after. His time is limited, so we didn't get to get into everything I would have liked to. But I think ultimately what we should take away from this interview is that we can have — and I won't say a Mamdani, it's not just about him. Like I mentioned, Mayor Brandon Scott in Baltimore. I mentioned Mayor Brandon Johnson in Chicago and the things that they're doing. Every city has unique needs. They need a unique person to meet those needs. But when it comes to this sort of progressive and/or even, dare I say, leftist politic that we're wanting to see right now, we have to be the change we want to see in our neighborhoods. Like he said, to pick something that you're passionate about. 

But what I think a lot of people need to hear is that midterm elections is not just a switch. It's not going to turn everything back to normal. We're not just going to be back in, I don't know, good graces with government. We're going to have to repair a lot of the — you guys still bleeping stuff? — a lot of the [] that has transpired up until now. And so what that means is, I don't think we're still just waiting on November. I don't think we're just going to vote and hope that fixes everything. There are things people need right now. Because number one, people are being cut off their insurance right now. People are getting taxed higher. People are losing their jobs. The affordability crisis is increasing exponentially. And people need help right now. 

And if I can leave you with a message, Mayor Mamdani left us many gems, but if I could leave you with a message, we all have to be better neighbors. And I think that's the example he's setting in New York. He's encouraging people to be better neighbors to each other and showing up the same way with his team of city workers, the Mayor's Office and administration, even in partnership with Gov. Kathy Hochul. And leadership is top-down, and the people are a reflection of the leadership. So if you want to see your leadership change, if you want a Mamdani in your city, you have to be better neighbors. 

And some people may say, what does that look like? Some people are all over the internet showing us how to grow our own food, how to clean our own water. And there's a lot of things that can sound scary, people talking about potential power outages. There's a lot of knowledge amongst the populace. There's a lot of skills we can share. But I just really want to instill in people, best I can, these moments of crisis are not the time that we turn away from each other. It's the time that we turn toward each other. 

This, too, shall pass, you know? We'll see you next time on “The People's Brief.”
Everybody, I don't know, a master class in doing your job. Thank you so much again for your time. It was so nice to meet you.

a.t: Thank you. Nice to meet you.

q.t: As you should. I wonder what you have to say to people about your concerns coming up for the midterm elections. What do you think they should prepare for this, I don't know, how we should be moving as a nation? Everybody's going to see this.

a.t:
I think that I'm really hopeful that these are the midterms where we take back the House. And to me, that's not simply important from a political level. It's what that can mean for working people. When I'm thinking about the cuts that have come from Washington, D.C., under this federal administration, the health care cuts we're about to see, the SNAP cuts, these will be devastating for people. And so, if you have Democrats who have the House, then it means that there is actually a path to fighting back on some of these things. 

And so often politics, it feels like it's removed from the day-to-day. But what we're really talking about is people going to the hospital, people going to the grocery store. These are ways to make it that little bit easier. I think we've seen what that cruelty can look like from Washington. It's time to actually redefine what Washington can be.
Yeah. Thank you so much.
Very welcome.
This has been amazing.
Thank you so much.

q.t: Yeah. He calls himself a Southern Trump and he'll be everything Trump was in the South. He's already here. I don't know. We don't need that. Anyways, I wonder what you —

a.t: I got "Baby Shark" playing in my head.

q.t: I have one more question for you. This whole season is about making sure people know what they need to know and are thinking about what they need to think about heading up to the midterms. Me being in Atlanta, one of my biggest concerns is making sure people know that billionaires have no place in local and state government. We've got this man named Rick Jackson running against Keisha Lance Bottoms. He's got to get out of here. Calls himself “Baby Trump.”

a.t: Calls himself Baby Trump?

q.t: I had an MP3 player that I couldn’t plug up to the computer. LimeWire. That was my —

a.t: Guilty as charged.

q.t: Well, my parents never let me have one of those.

a.t: I had to check my privilege out here.

q.t: I think we're also super effective at bridging gaps with messaging from Boomer, Gen X and also Gen Z and the people. I don't know. I just feel like we're the middle sibling that just knows what everybody needs.

a.t:
Well, I mean, even if you think about the internet, we lived through a time where it wasn't our second language and we lived through a time where it was starting to become it. So there's at least some sense of what it looks like to live in both of those worlds.I mean, I think about, like, my first iPod. 

You remember that?

q.t: I also feel like, I think that's a general rule of thumb, but I feel like so much, even in that answer and the way that you move is so millennial-coded and the way that we show up and we're seeing a lot of millennials really shine when it comes to these primaries gearing up for midterm elections.And I just wonder what you think about what our experience may have made us prime for this time to be leaders.

a.t:
I think as millennials, we're old enough to have lived through the promise of the world around us and the contradictions. Like, we came of age during the financial crisis, during the Iraq war, came of age at a time when we were taught and learned the hard way that so many of the so-called experts who we could trust to steward our future were, in fact, ensuring that our past looked much brighter than what we were about to live through. 

And I think that also imbues us with a responsibility that we may have to be the ones who are part of writing that next chapter. And it's so exciting to see so many other millennials who are a part of what it looks like to do that and to just be one small part of it.

q.t: Okay. And I'm sure you've been asked this before, but what flipped that switch for you? What made you say, "I need to run for this position because I'm going to be the best person for the job"?

a.t:
You know, I think the biggest thing that frustrated me was how we were seeing the city have a skyrocketing cost-of-living crisis and a sense that the mayor could do nothing about it when, in reality, the mayor was exacerbating that cost-of-living crisis.

And that is what really pushed me over the edge: that it can be different. And if we just tell ourselves that this is what it is, then we're allowing it to get worse. 

And I want to try. I didn't think at that moment that trying meant that everything could work out. But when, you know, a friend of mine, Phara Souffrant Forrest , she always tells me, "Closed mouths don't get fed."
I know that's right.
And so, if you, you know, the only way you can succeed is if you're willing to try.

q.t: Yeah. How did we get here, though? So did you have any thoughts that you'd be running for office, what, nine years later?

a.t: I did not think I was going to be mayor nine years ago. When I was getting my milkshake back, I wasn't like, "Just you wait. I'm going to be the mayor in nine years." No, I did not have that thought.

q.t:
I use — I'm a poet. So, I write a lot of things by hand and just my notes and things. And that's also exercising my brain in a way. But I think what this also points to is that this is why you always need a team to do the things that you want to do. And I think so often when people talk about you, they talk about you as the focal point. And I don't renege on my statement, you are still a star. But you also put emphasis on all the people that help you push any of these things forward. 

And I heard you earlier speaking to our director and you said that you used to be a PA. And so does that give you any sort of perspective on what it's like to just making sure you're treating your team members fairly and all the things?

a.t:
I think it gives you a perspective of a different vantage point. And also just how critical every single role is to the outcome. As a PA, my job was mostly like, "Get this milkshake, get this juice." But I would also motivate myself knowing that if I gave this to someone, it would make them feel better, they could do their job better. 

And there is so much that it takes to do this kind of work in City Hall. And too often when it works, it's framed as if it's a reflection of just one person, when, in fact, it's a reflection of a process and a team.I could not be doing this without this team. And that's also something that I would just offer to others. You shouldn't compare yourself, one individual to another. You should compare the people that you're building around yourself, because the collective is actually what's going to deliver it for you.

q.t: Absolutely. I'm a writer. I'm a writer. So, I literally have to put all my things down and schedule out time in my day to just sit in front of my notebook and even — and just wait until my brain declutters.

a.t: Do you write or do you type?

q.t: Yeah. Yeah. Force yourself to be off. I think choosing self is a part of resistance as well. And just choosing time to unplug is a part of resistance as well. But I think people are looking for maybe a get-out-of-jail-free card or just an apathetic perspective to want to just completely let it all go. But if we want things to change, we have to be actively engaged.

a.t:
And I think, yeah, if your brain is broken like mine, sometimes I have to motivate myself in strange ways. And one reason why you should also take time to turn off is that that's when you can actually think. That's when you can reflect. 

If you're just living at this speed, you will never get the time to actually dig into the depth of something. And you don't know the ideas that come to you when you're running or you're biking. Or even if you're just — I know there have been times where it's like, I don't want to stop looking at the work I have on my phone. But sometimes when you do that, you can actually resolve the question that's in front of you.

q.t: How do you shut off. And I think it's so hard. And what I hear you say in the response to my question is that I think, unfortunately, in this moment, we have to be on so much. We just kind of have to be on so much. But what you do is you try to find agency and holes and time.

a.t: And force yourself to be off.

q.t: It means I'm working all the time. So, when I asked you, I genuinely was trying to understand just —

a.t: How do you shut off?

q.t: Correct. What's my sign? I'm a Capricorn.

a.t: What does that mean?

q.t: Get a load of this guy. Anyway, lucky in all the ways.

a.t: She is. And I think the other thing that's really lovely is the people that I work with, you actually look forward to seeing them every day. You look forward to coming into the office. And I know that's — I mean, that's not always been my experience when I've worked. And to have that here, it's because you have a shared sense of purpose. You know why you're doing this. You're doing this for the people outside of City Hall. And that's the other thing of why bike, why take the train, why walk, why get out of this building is because too often it feels like politics is just inside these buildings. Caring only about the concerns of the people inside the buildings. It has to be about outside the building. What's your sign?

q.t: No, I just mean, of course you're showing up for everybody. That's all —

a.t: I don't know enough about astrology, so I didn't know if that was, like, a prompt.
No, no, no.

Yes, I'm a Libra. I was born October 18th. And I will be honest with you. One thing, biking is something that gives me peace of mind because you can't do anything while you're doing it. And so often now, you feel like you have to be multiply productive. You know, like, you're on your way somewhere; you can be doing something as you do it. When you're biking somewhere, you just have to focus on getting there. And that is something that clears the head. I did just have a chance to take a week off with my wife, and that was lovely.
She's so beautiful, by the way.
Isn't she?

q.t:
Well, thank you. I wonder, you mentioned just for everyone, it's hard to receive all of the bad news, all the news we get in general, and it can be overwhelming. I can imagine knowing what's going on in the world is overwhelming for you but also having to hold the position that you have. 

I also see you outside riding bikes. You're with the people doing the things. You're at Rikers spending time with people there. What do you do to take care of yourself? And do you take time for yourself? What's your sign?

a.t: My sign? I'm a Libra.
Okay. Shoot.
Oh.

q.t: So, I want to ask you, I'm a firm believer that everybody who is skilled or knowledgeable in politics shouldn't just be expected to run for a position. I think we should also model being informed citizens. And while I'm doing all this talking about phenomenal mayors across the nation doing amazing things, I still feel like there is a responsibility for citizens to be engaged. And so, I wonder what advice you would give to people who want a Mamdani for their city. What type of environment should they be cultivating to have that type of leadership be able to thrive?

a.t:
I think one is, find what you're passionate about. Sometimes it feels overwhelming because it feels like you have to care about everything in order to care about anything. And what I would say is, if there is something that you are particularly passionate about, let's say it's public transit. Let's say it's libraries. Let's say it's parks. Pour yourself into that because that is something that you can start to put together a sense of, okay, this is what I want to see. This is what I have in front of me. These are the obstacles. 

Because with the scale of things in our world today, it can feel so overwhelming, where it feels like, you know what, it's better to not be engaged. And what I've found in my own life is the way that I've found purpose is focus, focus and specificity. 

And so, if you're in Atlanta, I would say, what's the thing that you see as what City government could do more on? And picking that, starting to think about what that life could look like, and then pushing for that, that gives room for others to step up. 

Because there are a lot of people who are waiting to do something, but they're worried that they're alone in thinking about it. And even if just one other person steps up and says, "You know what, that's my concern," you start to feel like, I'm actually not alone in this anymore.

q.t:
I know I'm from Atlanta, but I would like to call you mayor while I'm here. I hear you, but I'm still kind of stuck on just how much you've been able to achieve and get done. And I love the way that you speak about these things because it feels like I'm talking to another person who experiences government. Like, you want to model a way that you would want to live. 

And just getting back to the red tape of it all, you push so hard to get these things done. And I know it's not just you, your team, city workers, even partnering with the governor to get things done. What is the impetus for you to keep going and to push to get these policies?

a.t:
I think that the biggest thing is to deliver for people. A lot of times politics has felt like a hobby that only some people can afford to have. And I want politics to be something that people understand that can make their life better. And so, we need to do that for people to believe that it's possible. 

And one of the things that, when you do this work, you come up against is understanding that there's a rationale that you hear in politics. It doesn't stand up to when you're talking to someone outside of it. What I mean by that is I'll ask, "Why do we do this?" Sometimes the answer I'll get is, "Because we've always done this." 

When you tell someone why you can't pave their pothole, they don't care if it's the same reason you could have given them 10 years ago. They want to know how and when you're going to do it. And so, some of this is just pushing and pushing and pushing past the "We've always done it this way" to get an answer that actually makes sense. 

Because it feels like we have a different language in politics. We have a different — and a different framework entirely. And it needs to be one that actually mirrors what working people are worried about in the city.

q.t: I love that. Mayor, can I call you mayor?

a.t: Please.

q.t: I'm so glad you said that because you're actually making me skip ahead a few questions, but I think this is a great segue. Speaking of universal child care, speaking of all the potholes, speaking about the way that you have tackled the junk fees and subscription fees, even fees for small business owners, I think the way capitalism works, it's convinced a lot of Americans that they have to just make more money in order to achieve a better quality of life when, in fact, there are government structures and entities in place to make sure it's provided for them. So, I wonder what you think the socialist-style of leadership is going to reveal to Americans over time or even short term?

a.t:
My hope is to show that there are things that no one should be priced out of, and dignity is one of them. We understand that at a certain level in our country when we're talking about libraries or we're talking about public schools, but for too long we've only said it in words when it comes to housing or when it comes to child care. 

We believe that it's okay that the market will set the price and if you can't make it, then that's what it is. I don't think that in the wealthiest city, in the wealthiest country in the history of the world, we should have one in four people living in poverty. And to me, that is not a reflection of whether or not they're working hard enough. 

New Yorkers work so hard every single day, but it feels like the harder people work, they're still stuck where they are in their life. And we want to make it such that there are certain things that every New Yorker will have as a part of their life and that this is a city where the harder you work, the better you do.

q.t:
It's really phenomenal to see the way he's transformed the way they're handling crime and just young people and community in general. And we need so much more of that. [We] got Mayor Brandon Johnson also sharing with you and standing up to these corporations. He's doing things like calling for a general strike. 

So the people are doing the things, but I feel like too often or for too long, so many constituents have felt like they've been met with the response, "Oh, my hands are tied," or "There's too much red tape." So how much do you suggest other elected officials can also do their [] job?

a.t:
I think I'll say one of the most important things I learned was that nobody owes you their support. Nobody owes you their faith or their trust. You have to earn it. And so that means that when someone tells you that they don't believe that City government can actually deliver for them, your job isn't to debate them. It's to deliver for them. 

And I think that's something that we've found more and more people starting to believe that City government can be more than what it's been because, finally, the things that they've looked at in their own neighborhood [and] their own life and said, "They can't do this. How can I believe them on that?" We're fixing those things. 

And to me, if you want to deliver universal child care, you have to pave the pothole. If you want to show that we can actually make the most expensive city in the United States of America affordable when it comes to housing, you also have to open the park. It's all of these things together.

q.t: You're getting all the good things everybody else wants. I would say, though, of course you're not alone in your stardom in terms of being a mayor. We've got Mayor Brandon Scott out in Baltimore really transforming the way —

a.t: He did some incredible — he continues to do incredible work on public safety.
Correct.
When you look at the statistics, it's really — it speaks for itself.
Yeah. For sure.

I had the privilege of speaking to him in the months leading up to taking office. And one of the reasons that I wanted to have that conversation was just looking at what he's been able to usher in. It's been quite something.

q.t: Yeah. And I feel like we see it. We feel it reverberating, like, off the screen. The culture or the climate feels different in New York. Everybody feels happy and go-lucky and just, you know, you guys won the championship. You're the mayor —

a.t: 53 years.

q.t: What's it like to do your [] job?

a.t:
I want to say shout-outs to all of the city workers because, yes, I work hard. They work very hard. We have more than 300,000 city workers. And so, when New Yorkers wake up, they go outside, they see the pothole paved. More than 191,000 in the last nine months. That's a city worker. 

And so doing my job is also the privilege of leading that workforce. It's a very difficult job, but it is also the most fulfilling job I could ever imagine because when this job works, it means you are making someone's life better. And I don't think that there's anything better than that.

q.t: Thank you so much. I'm going to jump right in. I'm going to cut to the chase. You're a star. I know you're a human being. You have your own flaws. I've even seen you be on the receiving end of some emotionally driven and high-charge feedback and frustrations from your constituents, but I've also seen you handle that with grace. And the way you show up for your city is so refreshing and inspiring. So, I want to start with a question I feel like everybody everywhere across the globe wants to know.

a.t: Wherever you want to go.

q.t: Hello, everyone. Welcome back to another episode of “The People's Brief.” I'm your host, Lynae Vanee, and today we have a very special guest, someone who we feel is everybody's mayor, but he's only officially New York's mayor. Please welcome Mayor Zohran Mamdani.

a.t: It's such a pleasure to be here. Thank you for having me.

q.t: Question for you regarding a primary race that happened last night in Rhode Island. There was a Democratic Socialist candidate, David Morales, who won against a Democrat in his primary. Wondering if you've had any overlap with him, and then also just sort of continuing the storyline questioning of Democratic Socialist candidates winning their primaries. What does that sort of say about the party and your reaction to that?

a.t:
I think it comes back to what I've said before, which is: what is the Democratic Party, if not its voters? And we're seeing that the voters across this country are eager for not only a change but also for a vision of something that we are fighting for.

And I've spoken a lot about childcare this morning. I've often couched it as the second driver of the cost-of-living crisis. The first driver is housing. And the little that I do know about this soon-to-be new mayor is that one of the central issues in his race was around rent stabilization and around the importance of delivering on affordability not just as a goal, but as a result, and what we've seen is that his constituents agreed with exactly that.

q.t: Because every mayor has said exactly what you have said, with some changes, and it hasn't changed. Anything specific that you've been doing?

a.t:
Well, I think one thing I want to credit the team on is that there is a willingness to exhaust every option in front of them and an unwillingness to accept something as a longstanding problem and therefore part and parcel of a school year.

And so, in the conversations that we've been having, these are conversations about the procurement of additional buses, the conversations about the training of additional drivers, and the conversation about how we ensure that our goal isn't just the vast majority, but it is to meet the needs of every single student.

q.t:
These are also education on-topic, sort of. The first is about there was reporting that the English test scores for third and fourth graders had really declined over the last year. I know the chancellor isn't here, but I just wanted to get your take on what more the DOE can be doing to improve these test scores. I don't know if it's related to the literacy changes.

And the second is about a school bus shortage. This happens every school year, it seems like. There's delays and shortages, particularly for students with special needs, who have no other way to get to school. I just want to know what more you think the city can do. It's every single year, just like any first-day-of-school photo op, it seems like there are issues with busing, and it seems to affect the students who are most vulnerable. So, I just wanna get your take and what more will you be doing for that?

a.t:
So, on your first question, Katie, we are continuing to support and increase our funding of New York City Reads and Solves. We think that that is critical in not only the question of literacy but also in response to the question of these scores.

And, to your second question, you know, every day is an opportunity to do more for the children of this city. And we will not accept that just because something has always been the case, that it will always have to continue to be the case.

When it comes to our buses, we are doing everything we can to ensure that every single student is able to get to school. For the vast majority of them, it means a bus route. For some of them it means prepaid rideshare cards as well as OMNY activation.

And we are also working at addressing this for what you described it as, which is a long-term issue. And that comes to conversations with union partners as well as within New York City public schools to ensure that as we get further into our tenure, we're not looking at the continuation of these kinds of issues.

q.t:
It's kind of still on topic, but going back to the payments to the providers, you know, I know you mentioned that everybody's getting these bridge loans that they've been seeking, but I guess are you frustrated that it came to the fact that they have to get a bridge loan?

You know, the way it typically works is they get a portion of their contract disbursed to them at the beginning of the year to allow them to do all of the setup that's required. These are people who don't make a lot of money [and] are often running these programs out of their homes. Is it frustrating for you that they're now in this financial position?

a.t:
When we are talking about these kinds of providers, I think you are absolutely correct that they deserve not only recognition, but a real sense of appreciation from all of us for the incredible work that they do and the difference that they make for families across the city.

And as you said, sometimes we're speaking about centers, sometimes about home-based providers. And I was both proud and surprised to have apparently been the first mayor to visit a home-based provider earlier this year. And many New Yorkers turn to them because of the cultural and linguistic fluency that they have and can offer.

And when it comes to our goal, it is to ensure that we are registering every single contract. We have registered over 500 thus far. And also, that we provide these loans in the interim, in the process of that registration, so that no provider has to wait on registration to be able to access those kinds of funds. I am fully confident in our team in continuing that work. And also, we know that this is going to be a critical part of delivering universal childcare and we are looking forward to it. Thank you very much.

q.t: I wanted to ask, with the first day of school and obviously the 9/11 anniversary tomorrow — with the 9/11 anniversary tomorrow, the Ccouncil is expected today to pass a resolution calling on Albany to pass legislation essentially to update the school curriculum around the 9/11 anniversary and aftermath. I wanted to see, do you think there are gaps currently in what New York kids are learning about 9/11 and the aftermath, and do you support the resolution?

a.t: I definitely support any resolution towards ensuring that we live up to the statement of “never forget.” And we know that for many, many New Yorkers now, they were born in a world where 9/11 had already happened. So, it wasn't a personal experience as it was for so many of us. And I also want to credit the 9/11 Museum for the incredible work they do in providing that kind of education, [and] also in providing a number of modules for educators across the country to teach their students exactly that.

q.t: For the mayor and governor, are there any plans this year to start to clear the waitlist of over 25,000 kids waiting for childcare vouchers, which is the thing I hear most often from providers — is what the city and state could do to kind of immediately reduce the burden. And then on procurement reform, how do you square the effort to speed that process up with the new review that's now going to be required for ed tech contracts to make sure they comply with the new AI limitations?

a.t:
I think that it is not only possible but necessary to be able to do both. And you heard it from the chancellor, one of the focal points of this proposal is one-business-day turnaround. So, it's not the fact of less review; it's the fact of a more rapid response.

And it is critical because in New York City, especially, time is money. And we see too much time being spent on delays that, when we look at where they come from, they're actually coming from within City government, and it's time to actually bring that to an end.

[Crosstalk.]

First, I just want to appreciate the governor for the funding that was provided allowed us to continue offering the vouchers that had been promised in years past. That is critically important to ensure that we can continue to deliver for those families who have come to rely on that. And also, we've been able to take away the cost of a number of those vouchers as well that we've seen were being charged to a number of lower-income New Yorkers.

And the conversations will always continue. The governor has supported childcare before I was in office and continues to be a leader on that. But our focus right now is how do we continue to steward that program and better deliver for families. I don't know, Governor, if you want to add.

No, the voucher program is a real lifesaver for families. When I first became governor five years ago, the income threshold was that if you earned $57,000 or less, you would get a voucher, which would help cap your cost for childcare at about $15 a week, which is quite extraordinary. But I knew there were many families underserved. That number is about $115,000. So, when you increase that, many more people are eligible — over 125,000 more kids — and we had to have the money to match that.

So, we did help the city earlier this year outside the budget to fill the gap that was created. So, we're trying to keep up with it. I know how important it is. And so, we're continuing to be committed.

Again, $12 billion on healthcare — I'm sorry, on childcare — five years ago was a fraction of that. So, we've been heavily, heavily, heavily investing $4.3 billion [in] this year's budget alone. And so, I'm committed to it, the mayor's committed, and you can count on that partnership for many years to come.

q.t: My question about, in terms of this is, you know, and we've seen families in the past have left New York, have left public school. But now we're offering this tremendous opportunity. Looking into the future, how does keeping families in the New York City school system help to fund the school system? Because what we've seen is a lot of families that leave, and then that means schools are not funded, and then we end up with underfunded schools in neighborhoods such as this. So, can you talk a little bit about what this is doing so that hopefully in the future we might see a school system that has more funding?

a.t:
You know, I think it's an incredibly important point, which is how do we ensure the flourishing not just of each individual child, but for the system as a whole. And that is why today we didn't want it just to be an announcement of the first day of school, though that's incredibly exciting, but also coupling that with an announcement around procurement reform. Because the better that we can steward our public school system, the more faith that New Yorkers will have in that system.

And again, this is not a debate that we want to win on the rhetoric that we use. It's a debate we want on the results that we can deliver. And that's what we're looking to do, and that's why I have full confidence in our chancellor, because we have a vision of delivering excellence in our public school system, and it's all the more possible when you have a partner like Governor Hochul who looks at these children and sees the potential of our city.

q.t: Numerous providers still tell us that they're waiting on money. What can you tell them today about how soon they'll either get their loans or payments from their contracts? And also, given these delays and the known structural issues with these contracts going back years, do you wish you had waited a year to implement 2-K?

a.t:
I think it's critically important that we both address longstanding issues in our New York City Public School system and advance an agenda that makes it more affordable for families to stay in the city. You've heard it from the governor, and you've heard from me as well that so many families are being pushed out of the city, out of this state because they can't afford the cost of childcare. This is going to be transformative to that end. And for any provider that has reached out for a loan, we are turning those loans around in five business days. We have registered over 500 contracts, and when it comes to those loans, we've actually dispersed more than 300 thus far.

These are interest-free loans that we have also dispersed alongside the supplying of first-day-of-school supplies for a number of providers that may have needed it, and I want to also just say thank you to our chancellor and to New York City Public Schools staff who have been working around the clock to make sure that they're available for any and all concerns.

[Crosstalk.]

q.t: What have you learned from the rollout of 2-K this year for 2,000 kids? 10,000 is a big expansion for next year. What have learned from how that went when it comes to things like paying the providers, which obviously a longstanding issue, but are you hopeful that you can do that a little bit more smoothly when you're scaling up? And I guess how do you get parents excited about this? I know plenty are, but there was a lot of effort to get people to apply. How do you get them confident in the program that it's going to be an option for them next year?

a.t:
I think that the best way to win the trust of parents and earn their faith in this program is by delivering. And we've already been able to read the stories of so many parents who are now able to join the workforce because of this program, who are able, you know — I think the governor and I met a parent at our last announcement together who told us that now they were actually able to go back to work and what it was going to mean for their family and that they had found a placement at a center that was, I think, three blocks away from their home. Although that might feel like 12 blocks when you're walking with a toddler.

And what we also know, and whether it's at Mamá Tingó or wherever else across the city, the demand is far more than 2,000 seats, and that's an opportunity for us to scale this up not just to 12,000, but to always ask ourselves, how can we make this the program that New Yorkers deserve?

Because the governor has long said that our families are her fight and childcare has been her focus. And when we talk about cost-of-living crisis here in New York City, childcare is the driver after housing. For a family of three to afford childcare, just for a single child, $334,000 is how much they're supposed to make a year. That is far out of reach for most New York families. We have to be the difference there. I don't know, Governor, if you want to add anything.

No, we share the same priorities in that a lot of people talk about how New York City is very expensive. So, we're chipping away at those pressure points. And even when I was in other parts of the state talking about a universal four-year-old program, the average parent has to pay for private pre-K programs about $16,000 to $18,000 a year. So, I had two kids in a preschool program. I wasn't a working mom. It didn't add up.

So, when we can lift that off of parents when they're doing the calculation, “Can I afford to stay in the city that I was raised in, that I have a great job in, but life is getting so expensive” — and we take that stress point, that financial burden off of them, all of a sudden it becomes, “Yeah, I can afford to live in New York City.” And that's exactly what we're driving for, as well as to the employers who should be listening to this. When you're trying to recruit the top talent from around the country — and we are the No. 1 destination for recent college grads — we want those college grads, when they start a family, to say, “I can finally stay here.” And that's the scale of what we're talking about here. That's why this is so transformational.

q.t: I did want to check in on the waitlist for 2-K. Last we spoke, there was a — 2,000 children were selected off of a lottery of 5,700 applicants. Did that ever move? Did any families get into the program who didn't get an offer initially?

a.t:
So, you know, one of the first things that I heard this morning was even just at Mamá Tingó is that there's more than 100-person waitlist or 100-child waitlist, rather, for two-year-olds. And schools have now started making offers off of the waitlist. So, that number is starting to move.

And we're excited because, as you've heard the governor say, this is something that is for 2,000 seats this year, 12,000 seats next year. And we are excited to keep working together because what we're talking about is something that is transformative.

We're talking about families not having to pay $20,000 a year at least for this kind of childcare and for the chance of a child like Luna or Lunita to be in a classroom alongside so many other children whose lives are now going to be transformed.

q.t:
I have a question for Deputy Commissioner Weiner. Can you tell us a little bit about the threat picture, where we are right now, being as one of the anniversaries of 9/11? Can you talk a little bit about whether or not we are safer today than we were back then, and so why and what is the rationale for doing so?

Deputy Commissioner Rebecca Weiner, Intelligence and Counterterrorism, Police Department: The threat is quite different from where it was 25 years ago. It's decentralized geographically with the rise of al-Qaeda and ISIS affiliates globally. It's diversified tremendously ideologically. Now we're not primarily dealing with al-Qaeda or even al-Qaeda-ISIS, but a proliferation of threats coming from conspiracy theories, grievances, nihilistic violence, far-left, far-right, anti-government [and] all of those things.

It's a much more individualized and idiosyncratic threat, which means that we have to be on our toes. A lot of the tripwires that we established in those early years post-9/11 had to be altered, and that's just what we've done here at the NYPD, working with partners. We have to be forward-leaning and very much everywhere, all over the place, to confront this new, modern 2026 threat, which is exactly what we've been doing.

Commissioner, I know you don't normally share the size of the appointments, but I am curious how this year's ceremony compares appointments-wise to previous anniversaries, as well as other large events, like, say, New Year's Eve. [Inaudible].

a.t: So, as you've heard me say, in preparation for so many events this year, we have amped up or increased our deployments for large events this year, particularly since the start of hostilities in Iran. And so, yes, our deployment this year at the World Trade Center for 9/11 will be larger than it has been in previous years, as will be our deployment this year for the High Holy Days at shuls and yeshivas and Jewish cultural institutions, just based on the realities of the world that we live in today.

q.t: [Inaudible] 15,000 signatures on a petition demanding a criminal investigation of events before, what was known, what happened during, including Mayor Giuliani, who had never really clearly said where he was at the time of this event and what he knew, and then what happened with the poison air – which was my idea, I was going to use that term, you used it for me. The poison air that people died, 10,000 people died. Who's going to go to jail for this?

a.t: When it comes to criminal investigations and district attorney's decisions, I will leave it to those attorneys to make that determination. I don't know, Gale, do you want to–

I mean, the great news, as you heard earlier, is the Department of Investigation can do their investigation, and they can refer to the district attorney if appropriate. And they've done that in the past and they could do it now.

q.t: To you and to anyone else who wants to answer this, was this a cover-up?

a.t: This was multiple mayoral administrations refusing to release documents that New Yorkers were owed. And we would not be here today were it not for the dogged tenacity of all those on this stage, in this atrium and beyond, who have refused to accept no for an answer, who have refused to accept any variety of technical justification that in the end was simply an attempt to deny New Yorkers what they were owed.

q.t: We're wondering if there's an assessment of how much it could cost, because under previous administration that was always the claim, right? "We can't release it because it's going to be so expensive."

a.t: You have to look behind those claims and understand what's real and what's not about potential future litigation, and that's the result that we've gotten to today.

q.t: Do you think he lied, though?

a.t: I leave it to New Yorkers to make their judgments, and what we want to do is finally allow them the documents that they have long been demanding.

Look, as I said before, we're very focused on making these records available to close this chapter on the City having documents with information and not providing it to New Yorkers.

Might there be lawsuits in the future? There have been lawsuits to release the documents. Could there be lawsuits relating to the release of the documents? Sure, but that's not a reason not to release the documents.

q.t:
Maybe one for the corporation counsel and one for you, Mayor. Under [the] previous administration, the argument has long been that these records can't be released because of the fear of how much this could cost the city in legal settlements. Do you have any sense of how much this could actually end up costing the city in legal settlements, if there's a ballpark dollar figure?

And then for – I can wait with my second question if that's –

[Crosstalk.]

It sounds like you're saying Rudy Giuliani lied. Given that that's the case, do you think he should stay away from Friday's memorial service?

a.t: I think that the focus of memorial services should be on the New Yorkers who were killed that day, their families, the survivors, the first responders. I don't think it should be on politicians.

q.t: How do these documents specifically help folks who are not enrolled yet enroll? What evidence does it provide?

a.t:
My hope is, just like Melissa's question raised, is people will think about where they were then and what these records show about what they were breathing then, and it provides knowledge to all New Yorkers, but particularly those that were in the affected zones. And this is an opportunity for people to specifically see what was the air quality while they were over there.

[Crosstalk.]
We're just gonna have a couple people add in.

q.t: Is there one document that stands out in your mind that has a particularly damning quote?

a.t: I think the ones that are the most damning in my mind are not the ones that are communications among people, although they're certainly the Harding Memo and the memo in relation to Congressman Nadler's concerns. To me, though, they're the ones who show the test results and show the knowledge of what the air quality was.

q.t: Steve or Mr. Mayor, can you take us through two or three of the smoking guns that were uncovered in these documents that hadn't been known before today? And second, how specifically does the release of these documents help expand the number of folks who could be eligible for VCF or whatever?

a.t:
I mean – depends how you define smoking gun. There are a lot of documents that clearly indicate what so many speakers today have talked about, which is that there was information known about the prevalence of carcinogenic materials, whether it's in a particular building, whether it was general air quality.

On some level, those things have been known, but actually seeing them and having the specificity, I think sheds light on what was known then. And there are more documents that we'll be reviewing and we'll be putting them up, I think, with that same view to make sure that people can see with particular knowledge what it is that people knew at a very time when the city was reopening.

You know, residents that were left, as Congressman Nadler sounded the alarm, left with, you know, rags and mops to clean asbestos out of their homes. Those are the kinds of documents in this first tranche that you will see.

q.t:
Mr. Mayor, do you have a sense of how many people have not signed up that could be eligible, what that is? I know personally, Michael Barasch can tell you, I interviewed him once a long time ago, 15 years ago. I was a reporter who covered the early days of the 9/11 health, and even when I developed 9/11-related illnesses, had no idea that it was linked. And, you know, so you have to wonder what a typical civilian who doesn't know anything about this. What do you think in terms of the exposure? I know it's a federal responsibility.

And separately, maybe Steve or Ben, you could answer. Are there other documents that should be released that are still not, say, from other agencies, the Port Authority, other documents that you believe hold more facts that we don't have access to yet? Thank you.

a.t: I think I would first just say thank you for sharing your story because in doing so you also give others courage to understand that they too are a part of exactly what we're speaking to. I'll be frank with you that I think the number of those who are eligible but have yet to enroll, it is a staggering number. I don't have an exact one.However, I know that City government thus far has not even tried to the fullest extent of its ability. And that's going to change moving forward. Steve, I don't know if you have additional details.

Thank you, Melissa. I would just add that in looking at the documents just in the first tranche, there are some federal EPA documents, and as we go through other documents there may well be documents from other agencies, and hopefully that will shed light on New Yorkers' interest in seeing what non-city agency records may or may not show.

I'll add just one thing. The borough president recently wrote to Governor Hochul asking Governor Hochul to do the same thing that the city is doing. And I don't think the borough president has got a response.

And obviously I think Congressman Nadler, you know, the experience with the EPA, the federal government probably has a lot of documents as well. The interactions with, at the time, the Giuliani administration – much of them had to go through the Pataki administration to go to the Congress. So, there's a record somewhere.

q.t:
Aside from the importance of truth and transparency and government accountability, all of which are extremely important, what else do you think we might learn from these previously undisclosed documents that we didn't already know?

For instance, is there anything new that you're seeing that could change the way we look at 9/11 medical illnesses, either medically, scientifically, that could change our understanding of exposure? Or what illnesses might be linked to exposure that day? And then I have one more question.

a.t:
You know, I think with 170,000-plus documents in the portal today, and as Steve mentioned, many more tranches to come, I think that there's going to be a lot to learn from these documents.

I also think beyond doing the right thing, beyond making it easier for New Yorkers to make clear their eligibility for this fund, it is also important that those who faced such sustained pushback for years finally be told by the City of New York, "You were right.
