You were right to push. You were to demand." And that the city is finally catching up to that.

And I also just want to thank people on this stage, because the tenacity to fight for something over 25 years in opposition of any kind of administration, it is remarkable. And I truly think that you have done the words "Never forget" proud.

q.t:
My second question for you is, you know, now that these documents are out, I just wonder if you think that the legacy of some of the leaders – I know you said the blame can't be pinned on a single person perhaps, but I wonder if this opens up a need for perhaps revising the legacy left behind by the previous administrations, namely the Rudy Giuliani administration, you know, and their immediate response to the attacks and the recovery, but also the Bloomberg administration and how they handled, you know, everything that came after.

I think the legacy that they have is that they responded and, you know, America's mayor and the reconstruction of the city. Do you think that legacy needs to be restudied, knowing what we know now?

a.t: I will leave that to New Yorkers to make that judgment.

There's another problem that the legislation does not address. When we wrote the legislation, we had to make arbitrary limits. We limited it to nine – you know, it had to be below Canal Street. You could have said 14th Street. The poison certainly wafted into Brooklyn, but because we only had Charlie Rangel said $4.5 billion dollars to work with, we wrote those limits.

We also had to limit it to people who are in the area between September 11th and May 30th of 2002. We know that there were people, for instance, who went back to work in the municipal building after May 30th, and the municipal building hadn't been cleaned up. And it was very dusty. And a lot of the people who went to work then, there, have certainly – have come down with many, many different cancers.

So, this is a problem. It's not under the purview of the legislation we passed, but this is a problem that we're gonna have to deal with somehow.

q.t:
You were just making this point toward the end of your last answer, but I want to ask you again, just kind of talk about how the city is expecting that more people may be eligible for the resources that are available.

For so long, rightfully, the focus had been on first responders, but today – everyone here today mentioned the people who lived downtown, students who continued to go to school, the people who were there who just went back to work. What's the expectation about how many more people could come forward? And then I have a second question.

a.t:
I would say it's not that more people may be eligible, more people are eligible. We know that more are eligible than those currently enrolled. We know especially for those who lived in the area but have yet to receive the kind of sustained outreach. And it's not for a lack of trying of some of the city workers who have frankly also been heroes.

You know, when I was at this meeting, there was a man who told me that he was called six times before he finally said, "Fine, I'll join the fund. I'll come to H+H nd I'll have my meeting." And he said, "Why do I need to do this? Because I am so healthy. I am in great shape." And then he talked about how within a year, two years after, his body started to deteriorate. And he was so thankful that he had doctors who knew exactly the kinds of 9/11-related health consequences that he should come to expect. And he was able to fight that complication off.

And so, this is going to be something that we finally provide support to so many on this stage who have been doing it without City government support, and also to make it very clear that to anyone who lived in that area, if they are developing any kinds of health complications, they should understand that there is potentially a relationship between the horrific terror attack of 9/11 and what they are currently going through.

q.t: Very quick follow-up, either for you or Steve Banks, does this – I know obviously this is intended to help people get the services that they might be eligible for. Does it also create the possibility of legal risk for the city? Could people continue to sue? I know you're settling this suit.

a.t: I fought City Hall for a lot of years. This is my second time in City Hall. If you're in City Hall and afraid of taking action because somebody is going to bring a lawsuit, you're probably not going to take the action [that] needs to be taken.

q.t: I just want to follow up on Katie's question. You know, it looks through – from my read of these documents, like city officials under Giuliani and under Bloomberg definitely knew that there were increased levels of asbestos and benzene, other carcinogens. They reported that to the EPA. You said trusted officials lied. Who specifically are you referring to? Did those mayors lie? And if so, could you just kind of say specifically – I know broadly we're talking about lied about air quality – but what did you see or get briefed on in those documents that show they lied?

a.t:
You know, I think – I wish there was a limited number of people who misled the public, that I could describe them in just a few names. But the truth is that, as we have heard, this goes across a multitude of those that New Yorkers have trusted. And we are here to release these documents today because for a long time New Yorkers have known the truth and yet they have been unable to see the truth in any document that's been presented to them.

Even when we speak about the Harding Memo, for example, this is the first time that the city is releasing the memo. This is the first time that we are putting forward documents that so many on this stage and beyond have fought tooth and nail to get any kind of a glimpse of.

And it does come back a lot to the question of air quality. It also comes back, as we heard from Congresswoman Maloney, to the fact that our federal representatives had to fight relentlessly over years without being able to get the support from the city to underline what the consequences were for so many.

And I recently met with a number of New Yorkers who lived in the area around Ground Zero. I met a young woman my age who was at school at the time. And we are now going to use every tool we have to reach out to those who may be eligible to be a part of this fund, but who for too long haven't even been spoken to about this. And, you know, you heard it earlier, there are people – you said people came from Mississippi?
From every congressional district.

From every congressional district, we have New Yorkers who don't know that they could be eligible for this fund, leave alone those who don't live in this city. And so, today is a long time coming and also now our focus has to turn to how do we reach out to every single person to ensure that we have a truly accurate sense of what the consequences are.

q.t: Has there been any consideration to the fact that there could be some documents hidden in these things that were never really spent on?

a.t:
Absolutely. I would never want to take your opportunity, Ben. We're going to look at everything that we've got, and if we can't find things, we'll look for other things. Ben, happy to –

[Crosstalk.]

Just to be clear, it wasn't just the Adams administration, every administration has resisted this actively. The Adams administration just did it badly. And the only other thing I would say is, yes, Steve's right about the documents, but ultimately, I think what you have to remember is the DOI investigation that Gale got, the speaker and the mayor has funded, that hopefully is going to answer any questions, because they can talk to people. They're the equivalent of a prosecutor.

I mean, they're really the reason why the Adams administration produced the 68 boxes, because once the City Council passed the DOI investigation, they sent out a missive to every agency: Produce your documents. And then three weeks later, the Adams administration informed the court they found 68 boxes that they had lost because they had carpeting problems.

So, I think that that's really – the real issue is the documents are one thing, but the DOI investigation is really going to hopefully answer the question.

q.t:
I have two questions. The first is, you know, many mayors before you lied, either obviously or just in the case of maybe former Mayor Adams prevented these documents from coming out. I wanted to get your take on the idea that a mayor and the many people who worked for those mayors willfully misled the city at a time when there should have been unity.

My second question, which maybe is a little bit more wonky, former Mayor Bloomberg and many of his staffers, it was reported that they used Bloomberg.net servers for a lot of their emails and messages, and not all of them had made it over to the municipal archives. I don't know if there's a possibility that there could be more documents within these emails and other things that were on the third-party server, and if there is a chance there could be 9/11-related documents there and if there was any effort to get that?

a.t:
So, I will answer your first question, and then I'm going to pass it over to our Corporation Counsel to add some details for the second question.

I think for the first, I just want to echo what so many have said on this stage, which is that today's announcement is a testament to everyone here, to having persevered through mayoral administration after mayoral administration after mayoral administration after mayoral administration.

And we are doing this today because it is the right thing to do. And we are doing it because, as so many have said, "never forget," there have also been many who have willfully prevented the release of these kinds of documents. We are talking about more than 170,000 documents that are live on this portal as of now. We are talking about a universe in the millions.

And I want to also just say thank you again to the partners on the stage, to Ben. Because the release of these documents is not simply a blanket release of every document that we may have and therefore people do not even know if it is relevant to their concern. Rather, what this is, is a release of documents, having worked with advocates on this, that are related to the very search terms that so many have been concerned about. Search terms like asbestos, search terms like cancer.

I think you've heard it here, but we are now at a point where so many more New Yorkers have lost their lives as a result of 9/11 health-related consequences than were killed on that day. So, just once again, thank you to everyone here for all that you have done to make this day possible. I'll pass it over to our Corporation Counsel.

As the mayor said, there are documents after documents after documents that we're going to be reviewing. And we're doing it together with the 9/11 Health Watch. We'll be meeting regularly. And if we start to reach dead ends, we'll be collectively looking at those dead ends and figuring out how we can go around them.

You've got a tireless advocate over here in Ben Chevat. I think in my past, I wasn't too shabby as an advocate either, and we were really going to be focusing on how to get the answers that New Yorkers have been waiting for 25 years.

q.t: I wanted to follow up on Politico reporting about your somewhat of an endorsement for AOC's presidential run. Do you agree with the petition you signed that AOC is the most viable Democratic candidate for 2028?

a.t: I think that the congresswoman would be viable no matter what decision that she makes, and I think she would make a good whatever it is that she wants to pursue. Thank you very much.

q.t: I wanted to quickly follow up on the influencer's line of questioning. If you could just say what the corrective action was? Was it just that the messages were set to not disappear? Or was there any other action taken there?

a.t: Yeah, so once we learned about this particular instance from the reporting, the corrective actions that we took included reminding staff to disable disappearing messages. As I mentioned before, we do have a regular schedule of training and retraining for all staff on a number of concerns and matters, including this sort of thing, specifically compliance with record retention laws, and so we will continue with that program as we've been doing since day one. That's another part of it. And, of course, because we learned recently from the reporting that was done, we will continue to look into this matter to see if any other corrective actions need to be taken here and generally.

q.t: It's not the same thing as journalists. I don't get any money from a company to push a product, but sometimes influencers do. So, I don't think you can equate a journalist with an influencer in every case.

a.t:
I want to be very clear: The fourth estate, journalists, are a critical part of how we not only engage with the city that we love, but also how we are held to account by the city that we love. And I think the point that we are trying to share is that it is important for us to utilize every possible avenue to reach out to New Yorkers. And when it comes to those interviews and engagements with content creators who use, whether it be Instagram or TikTok or whatever social media platform that it may be, that is always premised on the topic at hand and never contingent on some kind of a contract or anything of that nature.

[Crosstalk.]

q.t: I just wonder if you have any ethical concerns about it, given the fact that you could be using influencers that are accepting money to do other things. And does that cross an ethical line that gives you pause?

a.t: We are always striving to fully comply with all legal requirements. I will pass it to my chief counsel to speak about additional details of that.

And thank you for that question as well. No different from journalists, some of these social media influencers, depending on the platforms, are also subject to disclosure requirements. And so, the sorts of platforms that we're talking about typically will have disclosure requirements to the extent that they are in any way beholden to outside corporate interests, they will disclose those.

As the mayor has said, from our end, these are not paid relationships. We are disseminating information in ways that are calculated to reach a maximum number of New Yorkers, the same way we disseminate information in spaces like this one.

q.t:
I just want to follow up on this whole issue as well because there are experts who are raising questions about the use of influencers because sometimes influencers may not be paid by New York City, but they're paid by other organizations to do the things that they do, and they question the ethical position of that, given the fact that they could be paid to do other things.

And as a follow-up to that, I'd also like to ask you whether any influencers have been paid as subcontractors from any City agency and if that's something that you think is appropriate or inappropriate.

a.t:
I think we've seen in the past that City agencies have contracted a wide variety of people as an attempt to get their message out. When it comes to our City Hall, we have never contracted an influencer or paid an influencer for an engagement or an interview with me. And I think to your first question, Marcia, what I would say is that we are always available to speak to New Yorkers about the topic at hand, and we are looking for as many ways as possible to get that information out.

And to us, the question comes back to: Does this serve a New Yorker? And I think it just goes back to 2-K. We want to make sure that we can look back at an outreach period and say we did everything we could. And if we find that even one parent could find out about this through a radio jingle, then you know what, we have to do a radio jingle. If we find that one parent [could] find out about it through an Instagram video, it's worth doing an Instagram video.

I mean, recently we made the decision to make videos in multiple languages about the 2,000 tickets we gave away to high school students for free for Broadway plays, and what we found is by utilizing social media we were able to reach far more people about the work that the Theater Development Fund does than if we had said this isn't something that should be considered.

q.t: You know, influencers don't have all the oversight that maybe some journalists here have. I mean, why go to them to disseminate something? Some people may see this as propaganda coming from your administration, versus actual information that traditional forms of journalism —

a.t:
You know, what I would say is we send the same information that we send out to a press list about an announcement that we're making — for example, about 2,000 seats available for free 2-K for the first time in New York City, here's how New Yorkers can apply. That's also what we want to share with influencers. And I think that, you know, even the term, frankly, is one that it doesn't keep up with the way that so many are engaging with media, are consuming media.

I mean, just recently, one of the most significant developments we've seen in the NBA, a $30 million fine that's being levied onto the Clippers, is a result of Pablo Torre's investigation. And Pablo Torre has been described as someone who exists out of the traditional media. So, I think that these, to me, are examples of why we should be engaging with our press, as we do. We should be engaging with anyone who a New Yorker might listen to or read.

q.t:
I'm going to follow up on that same topic. You have an Office of Mass Engagement that kind of already does this. So, I'm just clarifying, I guess, why you would need this army of influencers when you have this Office of Mass Engagement.

I also wanted to ask you — there was a scathing letter from the monitor when it comes to Rikers and what's going on there. They accused the Department of Correction of not cooperating and not being transparent. I'm wondering, do you still, you know, why would your administration not be cooperating with a court-ordered, mandated overseer of Rikers, and do you still have confidence in the ability of the head of your Department of Corrections?

a.t:
Thank you for these questions. I would say first and foremost, I have complete confidence in Commissioner Richards and his commitment to this work. I actually was just with him right before this as we were together on Rikers Island to commemorate the service and the sacrifice of DOC members on 9/11, close to 25 years ago. And when it comes to the monitor's letter, we are addressing those concerns, and our administration is committed and continues to be committed to working closely and collaboratively with both the federal monitor as well as the remediation manager to improve our jail system. And one of the things that that means is keeping lines of communication open, sharing information transparently and taking the steps necessary to deliver reforms.

And to your first question, what I would argue is that we need to take every step that we can to connect New Yorkers with the information about how City government can help them in their lives. And the New York Times that actually reported on a mother who had found out about 2-K because a friend had forwarded her an Instagram video about it.

So, what we're talking about here is the importance of knocking on New Yorkers' doors to let them know about their rights as tenants, informing New Yorkers at their bus stop about how there could be faster, as well as also reaching out to as many people as possible to communicate everything that our City Hall is looking to do for the people of this city. Because we do not want to say that only one medium is one by which a New Yorker should consume the news. However they consume the news, we should be there and be engaging with them.

q.t: Is it safe to assume that this staffer received training and authorization to have Signal on her phone?

a.t:
So, all City Hall staff are receiving training and retraining on a number of obligations, including ones having to do with the Freedom of Information Law and the rules that apply to the retention of City records. And we do that on a periodic basis. We do it on a repeated basis. And we will continue to do that.

Again, here in this instance, as soon as we found out from the reporting, we took immediate corrective steps, and we'll continue to look into this. And, of course, we'll continue with our program of training and retraining.

q.t:
I wanted to ask you about a Times story today that looked into the influencer issue, and they found that this Signal chat — at least one of them that was being conducted with influencers — was set to automatically delete messages. So, I know I asked, or my colleague Madina asked you the other day about whether this had been complying with record retention laws. So, I guess my question is, do you have a sense of how that happened that these messages were being deleted? It seems like they should have been preserved. Was this chat authorized by Legal Counsel, and were these people trained?

And then my second question is — They asked for the budget and list of influencers, and City Hall didn't give this information to them. So, can you tell me why you're not releasing that info?

a.t:
I'll just start by saying we know that our responsibility in City government is to ensure that New Yorkers receive updates about services, whether that's how to report a pothole, whether that's to sign up for a 2-K slot or how to file a 311 report. And I am proud of the work that our team has done to connect New Yorkers to those services, to keep New York informed, to reach New Yorkers across neighborhoods, mediums and as many languages as we can. And to be crystal clear, because I know that there's been some confusion in some reporting about this: City Hall has never paid a content creator or an influencer for an interview or an engagement with myself.

And as I said earlier this week, our administration will always strive to comply with all legal requirements, including those that relate to the preservation of city records. And if we find that there are any departures from what's legally required, my administration will look into it and immediately take corrective action. I'd also like to just invite up our chief counsel, Ramzi Kassem, who can add a few details to your question.

Thank you, mayor, and thank you for that question.So, there is no citywide blanket ban on the use of Signal or other apps like that. At City Hall, our policy is we have a general rule and then, of course, we have exceptions. The general rule is that City Hall employees should use the apps and the messaging apps and the communication apps that are downloaded by default on their devices and that they should come to my office if there is a need, on a team-by-team basis, to use any other app like Signal or WhatsApp or TikTok.

And so, based on that assessment, we would authorize the downloading of that application, but subject to rules and restrictions that ensure compliance with all city rules, including record retention rules. So that means for an application like Signal that has many useful features — I mean, encryption is not unique to Signal and WhatsApp. iMessages has it as well — but for an application like Signal, large group management, other useful features may be helpful for a particular team at City Hall. So, we would authorize it, but specifying that you have to disable disappearing messages to remain in compliance.

Our practice from the start of this administration has been to train and retrain City Hall staff on all these rules and restrictions. When we learned about this incident from reporting, we took immediate corrective action. And, of course, we will continue with our practice of training and retraining all staff to ensure full compliance with city rules and regulations.

q.t: I wanted to ask about the Racial Equity Plan. Obviously, it's passed the executive budget, but November plan is coming up. How much is it going to shape this upcoming middle of the budget?

a.t:
I really appreciate this question. The Racial Equity Plan is something that is critically important to our administration, and what it also outlines is the specific areas where we think we can make a real difference to what has been a legacy of a lack of equity in our city. Whether we're talking about maternal health mortality, whether we're talking about unemployment, whether we're talking about housing, these are all examples that see. And even when we speak about our foundational focuses of building affordable housing, of faster buses, of universal child care, the impacts that these also have. And finally, we made it very clear that this is an all-of-City-government approach that has to include every single agency, and so that will be something that informs our budget as we get into it.

[Crosstalk.]

q.t: So, would you encourage people to come out and celebrate?

a.t: Yes, I would encourage everyone to come out and celebrate. And as you heard from the police commissioner, as you've heard from deputy mayor for Community Safety, you can come as early as those moments are to join the celebrations and really be a part of something that makes the city so special.

Thank you for that question. It's very important and it's paramount on everybody's mind. One, I think because there is no agreement with civil enforcement, we don't have as much information as we might have. And then two, I think it's tactically difficult for them to do some of the things they have been doing, which it may actually make it safer here.

But two, the last one is, I don't want to say there's no reason to fear any day. I don't think there's any more reason to fear to come out on Labor Day, and I think the fact that we have the mayor that we do, the police commissioner that we do, the elected officials that we do, we're going to do everything in our power to protect everyone that's here. And so, we want everybody to come celebrate, it might be a moment of reprieve in a very, very tough time.

[Crosstalk.]

q.t: My question really goes into the fear some people have been spreading that there might still be ICE on the parkway for people who are undocumented or status insecure. So, I'm curious to know how the NYPD, the rest of the city's infrastructure might handle a situation where, you know, there might be some sort of immigration enforcement.

a.t: So, the NYPD does not engage in civil immigration enforcement, period. We do not coordinate with ICE.

And what I will also just add is that you heard it from the public advocate, and also before I was acknowledging elected officials — we also have our City Councilwoman Crystal Hudson, who is here alongside us.

We are all united in what this parade is, which is a celebration of the Caribbean community, without which so much of what we love about New York City would not be the city that we call home. And this is going to be a weekend, this is going to be a Labor Day, where each and every New Yorker has the space to celebrate that.

And I also just want to make my own position very clear is that ICE's actions, while they state their motivation is that of public safety, do nothing to advance that. They are a cruel agency. They're one that I believe should be abolished, and they are one that has created a real sense of fear and terror across the city, across immigrant communities.

q.t: I have a question for the police commissioner and for the public advocate. For the police commissioner, could you just highlight the differences between NYPD enforcement this year and last year? What's changed? And then for the public advocate, you alluded to some tense moments during preparations. I'm just curious if you can elaborate on what you meant by that.

a.t: For the NYPD, it's a very similar plan to the plan that we used last year. There are some different barrier configurations that we are testing out this year. We've upped the number of cops that's deployed. Basically, between J'Ouvert and the West Indian parade, Sunday night all through the day Monday, everyone in the NYPD is working. So, we have a larger deployment, and we also have different things going on with our drones, but those are the three major differences.

I know everyone's shocked that I had some tense conversations involving PD. That's a shocker. But really, I think when you're having conversations around safety, having conversations around culture, people play different roles, and so there's obviously gonna be tension on how much of which role do you want.

But everyone came to the conversation — everyone, including PD — [asking] how do we make this as safe as possible, and how do we make sure people are able to celebrate their culture as much as possible? And I think those two things grounded everyone.

I think WIADCA and J'Ouvert City International welcomed additional law enforcement and their tools. They definitely want to make sure that the Office of Community Safety, deputy mayor behind me, and the Crisis Management System have a larger role as well. So, I think everybody came with their tools, and we figured out what is the best plan to go forward.

And I think we'll also agree, like right after this, you don't wait as long as we normally wait to have the conversations so that we can even improve upon it. But the time issue, I think, was a big one. We found addressing the time at J'Ouvert City International really helped. So, I think there's a lot of focus in how do we get this thing started on time? Can we get it started even a little bit earlier and make sure that it gets ended on time so that we can, you know, some of the elements that sometimes happen toward later on won't. But I think it was no different than any kind of conversation you would have had with a negotiation happening.

q.t: There's been some rumors, usually online, but some in the community are a little worried that you guys want to possibly cancel the parade in the future in favor of smaller parades throughout the year — like we've seen Independence Day, Flag Day. I just want to know if you can lay the rumors to rest that that's not being considered.

a.t:
No. We are excited for this parade this year and for every year.

[Crosstalk.]

q.t: So, I have two questions. So first, can you speak to what made you decide to go with a one-year moratorium versus the two-year moratorium that parents and advocates were asking for? And then separately, with respect to your recent reporting on your network of influencers pushing city initiatives, have your lawyers cleared your government staff to use Signal to communicate with these influencers? And how can it be legal under FOIL laws, given that Signal self-deletes?

a.t:
So, with the first question, we wanted to make sure that we are putting forward a policy that both is fulfilling our responsibility to students, to parents, to teachers and giving us a time period to evaluate the results of this policy. If we find over the course of this year that this policy needs to be extended, then we will extend it. If we find over the course of this year that there are amendments that need to be made, we will amend it.

All of it will be driven by the results that we are seeing, the feedback we are receiving from principals, from teachers [and] from students. And again, too often, many of these larger-scale policy decisions are not being driven by those kinds of factors. They are being driven by questions of profit. They are being driven by an attempt to be as quick as possible.

And yet we know that the responsibility we hold is an immense one to our students. And we have to ensure that we are confident in whatever policy we're putting forward. This is a policy that we are confident about. We will revisit it at the end of this one year.

And then to your other question, we also know that New Yorkers get their news in a wide variety of ways. And it is our responsibility to ensure that we communicate information from City government directly to the people of this city, whether that means to all of you, to TV, to radio, to social media, to content creators and so on and so forth.

And my administration will always strive to fully comply with all legal requirements, including those that relate to the preservation of city records. And if there are any departures from what is legally required, my administration will look into it immediately and take corrective action. Thank you.

q.t: And just a real quick follow-up. So, for students with disabilities, does it have to be in their IEP, written into their IEP? Or can teachers use some discretion for students with disabilities?

a.t: So, it can be in their IEP. It also could be in their 504 plan, which is an alternative non-IEP support. I think if there are other assistive technologies that they think would benefit students either with disabilities or students with 504 plans, they can discuss that with the IEP coordinator at their school.
And I think one final important point that we've heard in engagement, if it's an assistive technology that can help them to communicate with their parents, for example, that also would be allowed.

q.t: Can you just list some of the examples specifically of the exemptions for students with disabilities and I think English language learners? What are some examples of the kinds of tech that can be used in these cases?

a.t: So, one, I'll just underline that some of these exemptions are also to adhere to state law around what we have to provide to a number of specific sets of students. I'll just bring up our senior adviser, Ailish, to speak to that.

So assistive technology is a core part of a student's individualized education plan. So just a couple of examples you could use. Students with ALS or severe cerebral palsy may use eye-tracking software. So that's where a camera is watching their eyes so they can type; students write whole papers using that eye-tracking technology.

So, in that case, they'd be exempt from the screen-time limit, right? So, we wouldn't say 30 minutes or 45 minutes for those students. They would have all the time they need in order to meaningfully participate.

For English language learners, the DOE has created an ERMA-approved app called “Hello!” App that supports the translation between students and teachers and between teachers and students' parents to support that ease of communication. That would be an example of an exemption there.

q.t: I just want to make sure; do you have a list now of what AI products are being used in schools? Because that didn't exist earlier in the summer.

a.t: We have cataloged a list of those that will both be discontinued and the five that are allowed to be used.

q.t: I wanted to follow up on Morgan's question about enforcement. She asked about the students. She asked about the teacher's union. Is there anything in enforcement here that would hold teachers accountable for what's being used in the classroom? And my other question is really just about what is being used in the classroom. We heard during the City Council hearing earlier this summer that the central was collecting what exactly are the AI products that are in schools currently — is there a list going out about what's going to be revoked now? What does that look like?

a.t:
Yes, there is a very clear set of specific guidelines for our entire public school system. And as we said earlier, we are discontinuing the use of close to 40 different products that were in use in prior years that did have AI at the heart of those products.

And the point of that is also that in putting forward a comprehensive policy like the one that we are putting forward today, we are finally creating a policy for the entirety of our public school system, whereas prior to that, it was operating in the absence of central guidance around that.

So, we are putting these forward. And when it comes to the question of enforcement, we trust that our teachers, our principals [and] our superintendents will be abiding by this. And the reason we have been so specific is because this is where we have our confidence for what is beneficial for our students.

When we're talking about these core five pilots, we're talking about pilots that at a maximum a student could engage with for 45 minutes in a week. And when we're talking about the close to 40 educational tools that were previously in use, we're talking about ones that did not meet our standards. But the specifics of those tools will be sent out.

Just to speak to teachers for a second, our guidance to teachers hasn't changed. It stands where we were in March, where teachers can use AI products [for] teacher-facing for planning. They can't use it for grading and assessment and so on.

q.t: And is there any reason why the union wasn't here today?

a.t: No, I think this is a policy that has a broad coalition behind it. We've seen, I think, just this morning that the head of the National Union, Randi Weingarten, issued a statement of support as well.

q.t:
I'm just wondering how you guys plan to enforce this rule in classrooms? Will there be some sort of punishment if students do decide to use artificial intelligence?

[Crosstalk.]

a.t:
As with any of our policies, our implementation is going to begin with those who know our schools best, our principals, our superintendents [and] our teachers. And as you've heard, whether from Assembly Member Simon or from State Senator Brisport, while we are speaking about the technology of today, we are also speaking about transitions that teachers have faced in years past.

Whenever there's been a shift, teachers have had to be at the forefront. And I remember when I was in school, it was Google Books and Turnitin.com. These were at the forefront of those conversations. And so, we trust that teachers, principals [and] superintendents will be there. And what we also trust is that if there is any conversation about the procurement of education technology, it will go through our new New York City Public Schools procurement systems.

And that comes with an adherence to a rigorous set of criteria that is looking at the privacy, that is looking at the efficacy, that is looking at ensuring that these tools are actually beneficial for our students.

q.t: I have a question about the strength of this policy. There's exceptions that are outlined in it. There are — you mentioned several times; it's just a one-year moratorium. What should parents expect? Could these be loosened next year, or is this sort of the foundation going forward that K through 8 is going to have these strict limitations, or could there be a loosening of this next year or in the coming year?

a.t:
What parents should expect is that we will make our decisions not with the profit motive in mind, but instead with the fulfillment of our purpose, which is to teach our students, to ensure that they can grow, they can learn, that they can question and that we are making evidence-based decisions.

One of the things that I mentioned earlier in my remarks is studies. So often the studies that are put in front of you that showcase the beneficial aspects of generative AI for our youngest students happen to be sponsored by the companies that you would then contract with to provide those same students those kinds of tools. We want to ensure that we are actually providing tools to our students that we know to be beneficial, as opposed to tools that we know to be profitable.

q.t: And then one follow-up for the chancellor. Can you just reiterate the ban on cellphones or how that's being used in the classroom or personal laptops, things like that, and if that's been changed at all in this new policy?

a.t: So, there's no change to the cell phone ban. As you know, that's a statewide ban, and we've done really good work with that. We saw a huge increase in conversations happening, certainly at recess and in the cafeteria. And so, the only thing that is impacted by this is for K to 2, for 2-K to 2, there will be no one-to-one device use. And our recommendation is 30 minutes for grades 3 to 5 and 45 minutes for grades 6 to 8.
And Matthew, just before you ask also, I'm just saying to any of the electeds who'd like to step forward and respond to any of these questions, please also feel free.

q.t: Just building off of that, can you talk about how the course of the year, talking to different teachers in different classrooms at different ages, what is their reaction to this? Is it positive, or are they hoping to — there are AI elements and things that may not be as public, like using a chatbot or things like that. I guess, are they confident in being able to teach and learn and be able to do what everything they need to do as well, if these are being limited?

a.t:
I think what we've heard time and again, no matter who we're speaking to, is the importance of the teacher-student interaction. We are seeing artificial intelligence become more and more a fact of life, and there are conversations across the country where people have put forward ideas that this could perhaps replace that interaction. We want it to be very clear that it is not going to replace that interaction here in New York City Public Schools.

And what we have also heard is the importance of protecting childhood, and what I mean by that is allowing students the opportunity to ask questions, allowing them to engage, allowing them to fail in whatever it is that they might be doing so that they can learn from that.

I even think back on the advice that my father gave me when I was going to college. He didn't instruct me to go after one particular subject. He told me, anywhere that I felt excited by learning, those were the kinds of courses to take, because my job was to learn how to learn. And I think in many ways, that's what our job is also, to ensure that students still have that possibility in front of them.

q.t: Cheating.

a.t:
Oh, yes. So, this is something we've actually been obviously dealing with for quite a few years. The idea around this policy is to make sure that we get to limitations. I think we ought not to forget that last year there was AI usage in our school. This policy seeks to limit that and seeks to expand our teachers and our understanding of how to combat the external use of AI when it's used at home.

So, we'll be continuing to support our teachers in that way. But I will tell you, the ongoing conversations with our parents is really important. As we've seen with our cell phone ban, this sparks really strong conversations about best practices and how we manage our students at home.

q.t:
This addresses AI use in schools, but there's a problem with students using AI at home, right? I mean, let's be real. They're using it to cheat. They're using generative AI to write for them, to answer problems. I mean, is there any tools we can give teachers to combat that, to spot writing that's been done with AI?

And then I just have one separate, more specific question for the chancellor. I guess I'll just ask you now. There's been a lot of complaints from students about the OMNY cards. Can you talk about why they're not being offered OMNY cards for express buses and commuter rail? And also, they're being deactivated Aug. 31, which leaves a gap before the start of the school year.

a.t: Let's take the OMNY card question first. That is a very big topic in DOE and with so many of our students. And we are in a partnership with the MTA on OMNY cards. We are considering a pilot that is going to make a lot of those OMNY cards digital. We are considering many ways to make them more durable, which is one of the things our students complain about. And so, this is an ongoing conversation. As the mayor said, I've been engaging directly with young people on this, and we're working very closely with MTA to get to a process that's going to work long term for young people.
On the first question, do you want to add anything [about that]?
What was the first question again?

q.t: Mr. Mayor, back in March, this was obviously already a hot-button topic in education, but the DOE's plan for AI on its website listed things that, at that point, the school system was okay with AI being used for; things like brainstorming, organizing, refining communications, translation. I'm curious how involved you were directly with how we went from that to this today.

a.t:
I want to credit Chancellor Kamar Samuels for leading this process [and] his team, for ensuring that we did not confuse speed with progress. And the announcement that was made earlier in the spring was intended to be the beginning of a conversation. As we heard from Assembly Member Jo Anne Simon, even today is not the end of that conversation; this conversation will continue.

However, the intent of it is to deliver for our students, and we cannot do so without also hearing the reflections from parents, from students, from educators, in the time that followed that announcement, where we intentionally looked to carve out time, forums, platforms for us to engage with that. Today is a reflection of that, and it's a reflection of Chancellor Kamar Samuels' leadership.

q.t:
So, I was hoping to get some more information about the, I think it was the 38 contracts you said where you're going to disable some AI functionality. Does that include some of these big citywide contracts like Amira, the reading tutor; or Google Gemini, which is built into many students' Chromebooks; or even HMH, the big reading vendor, which has some AI capacity?

What does it look like to disable just the AI part of that when it can be pretty deeply embedded in the product? Are you canceling these contracts? And then, going forward, what can principals expect about how you're evaluating software that they're considering purchasing?

a.t:
I think at the core of your question is our priorities. It is all too easy to inherit contracts, to inherit approaches and to say it's simply what it is now. And we wanted to take a step back to actually evaluate our responsibility to the nation's largest public school system, to the students who come every single day, to the teachers who make it possible and to the families who entrust us with that responsibility.

And one of those responsibilities is the privacy of these students. Another responsibility is to ensure that we're actually teaching these students to learn, to grow and to ask questions. So yes, we did disable more than 30 of these products that were previously in use. I'll just call up Ailish, our senior policy adviser, to give some more additional details to that, she can provide that.

a.s: Ailish Brady, Senior Advisor for Education
a.t: To your specific question, yes, AI products, including those embedded in Tier 1 curriculum where the AI can be turned off, will be turned off. So that includes Amira and any HMH products you mentioned. If a product cannot have the AI turned off, then that will be taken off the board entirely in our schools.

Just one additional point before we go to the next question, which is that we have a rigorous set of standards that we are going to apply for any educational tool. And we do not care how big that company is, how profitable it is, how long we have been working with them. They need to meet the same level of standards. And if they do not today, that doesn't mean that we won't work with them to get there, but it does mean that those standards have to be followed.

q.t: Now Mayor Mamdani told me that what he learned from talking to firefighters is their belief that the duty to, quote, "Never Forget," is not only a personal responsibility, but a collective responsibility to learn about those who were on duty that day and who were killed.

You know, Marcia, when he talks about being nine years old, and I've spoken to so many young people — My daughter was 10 that day. Such a formative time of your life and troubling, too, because you don't really understand, but you do understand. And yet, he seems so moved by everything.

Well, he told me that what happened was that people in his class had fathers who were working in the area at the World Trade Center, and they couldn't get through because there was no communication. And the fear that they would never see their parents again was palpable.
You can tell it really made an impact on him, and the emotion was evident on his face 25 years later.
It’s a different side of him we don't really see, but he's obviously moved.
Great interview.
Yes, Marcia, wonderful. Thank you so much.
So, what would you tell the 9-year-old about this city 25 years later?

a.t:
That it is still the city that he loved. It is still the city that was his home, and now that I have the privilege of being here for the 25th anniversary and ensuring that it's a day about those that were stolen from us and the legacy that they leave behind of what it means to love and lead a city.

[Interview ends.]

q.t: You know, the number of people who have died of 9/11 illness has now surpassed the number of people that actually perished on that day. I wonder, as mayor, would this inform your response if there were another attack?

a.t:
I think that it shows the responsibility thatCity government has to continue to not only remember, but to be there to support these families.

One of the decisions that I made this year was to allocate tens of millions of dollars so that we would create a portal where New Yorkers could search through City government documents to see what all the City government knew at the time. Because as you've said, now the number of New Yorkers who have lost their lives since 9/11 has surpassed that of those who were killed on 9/11. And so many of these New Yorkers are ones who made the decision to run towards Ground Zero. And for that, they have suffered medically, and the city should be there for them.

q.t: You know, when you talk about somebody looking for their loved one, it gives me chills because I talk to so many of those people who are looking for their son or their relative, and I wonder, when you hear those stories, what's your response? What effect does it have on you?

a.t: It breaks your heart because it shows you that, as much as people try to measure the darkness of that day in statistics, we have to remember that we're talking about families whose lives were shattered. We're talking about people who are often described by their profession but remembered for the fullness of who they were to every person in their life.

q.t: You've chosen to visit these firehouses privately so that you could meet with people in small groups. It must have been very emotional, and you must have heard stories about how it affected them. What was your takeaway from those meetings?

a.t:
It's incredibly emotional because you are meeting firefighters who — some of them have memories of that day; others have joined this work because of that. You know, I met a man whose father was killed on September 11, and in honor of his father, he joined the Fire Department.

I went to Rescue 3 in the Bronx, where I learned of a brother who spent days searching for his brother, refusing to leave until he found his brother and then eventually joining the same rescue company. This was Danny and Tommy Foley. And you go to these firehouses, you see that "Never Forget" is something that they have lived up to, not only in the fact that you can look around the firehouse and you can see, etched sometimes in chalk, the names of those who were reporting that day, but also in the testaments that they have built to those that we lost, and in the knowledge that what we lost were not just New Yorkers, but also people who were willing to give everything they had in service of a city they loved.

q.t: On Secretary Mullin’s presser, which you called both a distraction and BS during this press conference, he says that they've arrested 2,100 criminal illegals who were here. I'm quoting him. Do you have any knowledge of these people? Are they, in fact, criminals, have committed crimes, is just their paperwork out of order? And is it fair to call it BS if, in fact, these are criminals who were here?

a.t:
No, no. There is no way that that number constitutes people who have committed crimes the way we consider a crime a crime in New York State. They consider anybody who crossed the border a criminal. So don't fall for that. That's what I'm calling out. Do not fall for that. There are different statistics, and I can get them for you. Sometimes it's four out of five people who are being detained as criminals have no criminal record at all, zero. Their crime is being here. Their crime is being a healthcare worker in Brooklyn. Their crime is being a pizzeria worker in Nassau County. Their crime is being a high school student. Their crime is their existence in the Trump administration's eyes. And I'm not buying that. I'm not buying that. 

 

Especially those like Venezuelans who came here [and] walked through the door with a legal document that says you are welcome here, the Haitians and others, people from Afghanistan. Temporary Protected Status meant our government said you can come here. And now, all of a sudden, you take that out of their hands, and now they're criminals? I encourage the press to question that as well.

q.t: Beyond the abstract, does it mean budget lines cut, people laid off and why is no one from the NYPD here?

a.t: As the mayor of the city, I'm here, and I represent all of our departments in doing so. And in terms of the tangible to the PD, this is a cut that will then impact our ability to have bomb squads here in New York City, at the level that we have today.

a.s: Christina Farrell, Commissioner, New York City Emergency Management
a.t:
Hi. So, on emergency management, to start with, 110 of our staff members are funded through the Urban Security Initiative, and those are obviously across all of our departments. Many reporters have been in watch command. You've seen the work that Notify NYC does, the wireless emergency alerts that we send out when we have any type of man-made or natural disaster. Much of that is funded. 

 

We do many large exercises, as Commissioner O'Leary said, with the state, with all of our partners across the region, including other states. We did that for the summer. We do that for hurricanes. We do that for terrorism and other things. Looking at the city's stockpile, looking at our logistics program, every bit of emergency management is funded through this money. 

 

And if it doesn't come, we're working with management and budget in the city with dishes, but there will be serious impacts on the way that we prepare New Yorkers and how we manage large-scale emergencies.

q.t: Mayor Mamdani, do you want to talk about what this means for the NYPD in practical numbers?

a.t:
This is the kind of funding that supports certified bomb squads across the entirety of New York State, and also here in New York City. And it is funding that affects NYPD, FDNY, NYCEM [and] emergency preparedness across the board. And that is what is so galling about this, is we're not speaking about money that could be used to some potential benefit. 

 

This is exactly the kinds of operations and equipment that are critical, and they are critical on a day-to-day basis. And we've seen our departments utilize these to life-saving effect. You know, Commissioner Farrell, if you just want to come out here and share a little bit from the perspective of NYCEM of what this actually looks like.

q.t: So will you go today to — I don't know where the press conference was, but I don't know if you're going to go —

a.t: If he's got a check, I'll be there.

q.t: For Mayor Mamdani, I see that no one from the NYPD is here. I don't know if it was a scheduling thing, but if you want to talk a little bit more about what the lack of this funding means, does it mean layoffs from some of these units within the department, and what that actually means? And I know for the governor, you're inviting him to come here. Would you go to where the secretary is to demand the money, or do you—

a.t: I'll go anywhere to pick up a check.

q.t: But they're making it clear that you are not keeping New York safe because you are creating these policies that are in favor of immigrants, according to them, illegal.

a.t:
And as a respected member of the journalist community, I'm sure you asked them the question: Have you looked at the statistics that show New York is safer than it was two years ago, three years ago, four years ago? So, New York is safer. So, I encourage all of you to not buy that argument that this is keeping New Yorkers less safe. 

 

And I will stand up for the immigrant community. Again, [I’ve] been crystal clear. You commit a crime; we don't want you here. And I also have to say, our policy is that if someone has committed a crime, they go through the criminal justice system, they're prosecuted, they're convicted, the victims get justice, [and] the person goes to jail. 

 

We notify ICE that these individuals are about to be released, and they should be deported. That's always been our policy for decades. You know what? Sometimes they don't even show up. ICE doesn't even do their job. They don't care. So, I'm not buying what they're selling here, and I don't think you should either.

q.t: Governor, that was 10 months ago, and we've seen an uptick on cases of deportations and detentions of Venezuelans. And because of the situation that we've given more leniency to immigrants with these new policies, do you think that's a reaction from the federal government to that? And would you change any of your policies to get these funds in order to keep New Yorkers safer?

a.t: We're not aware that there's a connection between our policies and these funds. They're just withholding our funds. These are properly allocated funds from the House of Representatives and Congress.

q.t: The tweet you mentioned where he promised to be there.

a.t: No. We have been in communication with the Department of Homeland Security. They know they owe us this money. And so instead of walking around about rotten apples and talking about all this BS, we're about apple pies. We like apples here in the State of New York. We support that. And also, he ought to come over here right now and deliver that check. That's what I'm waiting for.

q.t: So just to clarify, no conversation since the tweet?

a.t: Which tweet?

q.t: A question for the governor and the mayor. Can you give us any sense of conversations you've had with the president about this? And, Governor, have you enlisted any help from maybe the state's GOP congressional delegation, people with relationships in the White House and Congress? And the same question for you, Mr. Mayor. Have you had a conversation with the president about this?

a.t:
I called the president when they withheld $187 million. And I said, "Mr. President, I'm going to do a press event." I said this a while back. "I'm going to do a press event and say that you're defunding the police. Is that what you're going to make me have to say? Because you are defunding the police." And within a couple of days, he tweeted that, "I'm proud to restore the money." That has been a promise that is broken. He needs to restore it. 

 

And shame on the Republican members of Congress who know we're dealing with this. They're aware. And they never ever use their voices to speak up on behalf of keeping New York State safe. They're too busy running around saying, I hope — I'll watch my language — a lot of lies, a lot of lies. And again, the media has a special role here in this environment. When we're telling you the truth, you're hearing it not just from me and the mayor, but the commissioner of Homeland Security and all the law enforcement is standing behind me. 

 

Are they saying that they're not telling the truth? Because I'll stand with law enforcement any day of the week over what we're seeing out of the Trump administration, which is to deflect from what's happening with the war in Iran, the fact that prices keep going up, the fact that they've broken every other promise. 

 

This is a long litany of broken promises from the Trump administration. And it's about time they know that Americans are paying attention. They want to be protected. And shame on you for withholding this money and not delivering it to me right now, 10 days before we honor those lives that were lost on 9/11.

q.t: [Inaudible] also said because New York City has a sanctuary city policy, that’s one of the reasons also that he is here today.

a.t:
I'm not sure how much more there is to add to what the governor has said. I think specifically to respond to that, I don't know how you describe a record low of murders and shootings as being anything other than something that should be celebrated. 

 

And we are proud as New York City to be a city that has sanctuary policies. These are policies that used to be defended by Democrats and Republicans alike. These are policies that were introduced to ensure that every New Yorker would feel comfortable coming forward to report crimes as well to local law enforcement. And as the governor said, we have long had a set of more than 170 serious crimes that if anyone were to commit, we would be in contact with the federal administration about. 

 

What we are seeing, however, from ICE is an attempt to criminalize the very fact of being an immigrant. And we are seeing a terrorizing of immigrants across our city and, frankly, across our nation that has left so many, regardless of their status, in deep fear about even leaving their home. 

 

Not that long ago, the governor and I were here standing on this stage alongside other leaders from across New York City and New York State speaking about the importance of extending TPS to so many New Yorkers who have now been stripped of it. Because we know what we're really talking about is jeopardizing the ability of hardworking New Yorkers to continue to live and work in this city. We want this to be a place where that can be the case. We're not seeing that from federal policy.

q.t: Governor and Mr. Mayor, if you could respond. So, as you mentioned, Mullin is in the city right now doing his own press conference. My colleague is there, and he said that basically, Mullin is saying that both of your administrations have made the city and the state less safe, specifically citing the 287(g) agreement. Wondering what your response is to that, and do you think that that is one of the reasons why they're also withholding this federal funding?

a.t:
Well, once again, they don't understand facts. The facts would confirm that crime has gone down in all the major categories. So, we are not less safe. We are safer. There's not been a 287(g) agreement in New York City ever. So, the fact that the crime is going down has no bearing on whether or not we told other counties that we don't want you focused on being immigration enforcement officers, civil immigration enforcement officers, for ICE — an $87 billion agency — when you need to be focused on solving local crimes, preventing local crimes. 

 

So once again, they're wrong, absolutely wrong. And if there are cases where there are individuals who are in this country undocumented who are involved in crimes, we always have and always will make sure that we cooperate under those circumstances, always. We are not a sanctuary state for criminals. I cannot say that more often. So, I encourage the press to ask them why they're lying. Mayor?

q.t: And where are they sold, and who made them?

a.t: You know, I love it. Just go out there. Shout-outs to MJ. That's really lovely, man. Thank you.

q.t: MJ — you have truly made people like him happy. You know, as they get older, to see that there are people who are actually — maybe there's a chance this old American experiment could turn out OK.

a.t: Shout-outs to MJ. Shout-outs to the bootleggers who sold him those three T-shirts, because that's one of the things I also love. I've never even seen some of the T-shirts people have worn here. I'm like—

q.t: Thank you. You guys, this is Mayor Mamdani. We got our sit-down. We got our talk. Thanks to his team and his staff for carving out time.
Thank you, guys, we really appreciate it.
Zohran, thank you, man. Thank you for your work.

Before we go, I promised my dad, my 79-year-old father in Maryland — reformed Zionist to pro-Palestinian freedom person that he's become over the years. But more importantly, someone who just admires great politicians, a guy who's holding Bobby Kennedy's legs on the back of a convertible in the '60s, who walks around Chevy Chase, Maryland, wearing three different — he has three different Zohran shirts. He wanted me to tell you he worries about you, he prays for you. And he just — I'll be honest, as my wife can attest — he's just obsessed. Just — you have, there are lifelong, like, you know, hippy-dippy people who like, they just—

a.t: Shout-outs to your dad, man.
His name is MJ.
Shout-outs to MJ.

q.t: Does that office have power to prevent sales or just give them legal help?

a.t: It's more about proactively providing them with legal advice. When it comes into the actual accountability for someone who's engaging in deed theft, that's through partnership with the district attorneys. And they're also taking it seriously.

q.t:
And the last thing, and I'm glad you brought up maternal health and Black women, because there has been this narrative that's been attempted to shape, not only about the DSA, but about Mamdani with regard to the Black community and their focus on the Black community.

When I first met you, we — you, me and Ras Baraka and a bunch of Black men met in Harlem to talk about your commitment to the Black community. And I think — so first part of the question is how much of that is someone trying to shape a narrative about you and the DSA with regard to the Black community? And then is there work that needs to be done by the DSA, yourself as a mayor in New York City, to embrace priorities for the Black community?

a.t:
There's always more work to be done, for me, for everyone. And the reason for that is we're talking about the very New Yorkers who have been pushed out the most from this city, right? Whenever I talk about raising taxes on the wealthiest, people will respond with what is generally a myth of capital flight. But the flight that's actually happened: 200,000 Black New Yorkers have left the city in the last few decades.

There are so many people who will still tell you they're New Yorkers, but now they live in South Carolina. They live in other parts of the country because they couldn't afford to live in this city. And you can feel that in neighborhoods across the city; you can feel that in classrooms across the city.

And so, for me, it's — always ask yourself, how has this city left people behind and how can we actually start to show up? So, we're talking about maternal health; we're talking about the mortality rates that are disproportionately affecting Black women. We also have to ask ourselves: how do we start to build housing that isn't just increasing supply but also is increasing affordability within that supply at the same time, while delivering the strongest tenant protections this country has ever seen. And then also asking yourself, how do we do similar initiatives for stability for homeowners? Because a lot of Black homeowners — especially older Black homeowners — have had to deal with the scourge of deed theft.

So, we went out and created the first-ever Office to Prevent Deed Theft. This is an office that will actually proactively go out there to talk to our aunties and uncles who are being taken advantage of by people who know that they want to pass their home onto their next generation and are instead going to be signing their home over to someone they've never met before.

q.t: OK, on children and parents, I was very happy to see the headlines about your doula program. And I know the doula program started under Adams. So, I read about that, but tell me, what's different?

a.t:
Well, I think one of the key things is we also want to look at what was working in prior administrations and then build on that. Sometimes there's a temptation where if you have criticisms of a past administration, you say everything they were doing is something we wanna throw out and we wanna restart it again. We want to ask ourselves what's actually working here.

The doula program is an example of something that is important. And also, these are the kinds of approaches we need to take if we're serious about combating maternal health and mortality that we're especially seeing for Black women across New York City. We have to be approaching it in this kind of a multifaceted way.

q.t: As a parent, it was such a breath of fresh air to hear about your 2-K program. Where are we at now? And I know it's only in certain areas, but can we expect it to be citywide?

a.t:
Yes, you can expect that. We are rolling out 2,000 seats of free childcare this fall. So, when school opens, that's with 2,000 seats of free childcare. And that is so exciting because we're talking about free childcare, which means that a family doesn't have to pay $20,000 a year for that same seat.

Next year, we're going from 2,000 seats to 12,000 seats. So, we're gonna be expanding the neighborhoods that we're present in with this. And then by the end of year four, we will be for every single child in New York City that is two years old will have free childcare.

q.t: But you think that the timetable is a 10-year timetable?

a.t: I think that's the maximum.

q.t: And for those of us in the city, the difference is Van Wyck was a state thing. This is a city thing. While you're on the job, we can constantly badger you about what's gonna be done—

a.t: Badger me!

q.t: I was 8 when they started — I'm 51.

a.t: You could have like a T-shirt, right? I know that the state is hard at work on the Van Wyck.
OK, so that's a state thing.
That is a state thing. But my last — the last update I've received is [that] we're looking at completion this fall.
Oh, OK.
That's not bad; that’s something.

That's the last thing I was told. And I know there are a lot of people who are not going to believe that until the day that that is completed. And I do not begrudge you that.

When it comes to the BQE, we're talking about the one section that is City-controlled. And that's what's so important for me is we have autonomy over this one section. So, it's up to us. It's a responsibility on us. I can't say, “You got to go ask this person or that person.”

And this is one of the areas where it's safe right now, but that's really being tested because we're talking about a BQE that was designed for 50,000 cars that now has more than 100,000 every single day, not to mention the much heavier trucks that are on the BQE.

So, we're talking about a timetable of over a decade where we will be able to sustain that level of car traffic by creating a temporary bypass so that those cars, while we're doing these, while we're overhauling the BQE, this central part, do not have to go onto local streets. That they can actually be on an adjacent, temporary highway that can then bring them back onto a BQE that is functioning while we make these kinds of changes.

q.t: Where we at? And what is the truth? And then walk us into your plan with the BQE, which looks like it's about to be Van Wyck-[adjacent].
Is that what they're saying?
Well, no, because even in your video, you were like, "All right, guys, this is going to be hard. It's going to be long. There's going to be some rerouting," like, you know.

a.t: I wanted to be straight with people. So, I think — I'm glad you brought up the Van Wyck because, to me, you know, like when my friends talk to me about the Van Wyck, it's almost like a marker of time.

q.t: Yeah, but he isn't in the cigar lounge, just like my man, Eric Adams.
So, real quick on that, broken things and accustomed things being broken. Van Wyck Expressway.

a.t: Come through.

q.t: That's the czar. And you didn't have to pay someone another salary and add someone to the payroll—

a.t: You know, it's, for us, the question is just: how do we get to the outcome? And a lot of times it's a conversation around the outcome; it's not actually getting you there. We just want to put the trash in the bins.

q.t:
Just going to go put — yeah, if you put the trash into the container, [you’ll have] less rats.

[Crosstalk.]

a.t: That’s the czar.

q.t: Because to really think about why is there trash out on my street? Like, with what people pay for their apartments. They walk outside, and there's just garbage out on the street. You're just saying that there'll be 6,500 containers. You know, I'm gonna try not to throw shade. We were waiting for some changes over the last few years. There was a rat czar. There was all kinds of things.
I was gonna ask you, the rat headlines have gone. Like, I don't even see rat headlines.
You don't have a rat czar, do you?

a.t: No, we're just going after them.

q.t: Yeah, it is. That is that exceptionalism.
Glamorize dysfunction.

a.t: And some of it is just a way to survive, right?

q.t:
Well, and your ability to articulate that and continually, no matter the onslaught, redirect and focus people on what matters, I think contributes to the success that you're seeing in the job, right?

And that was one of the reasons we wanted — been kind of on you and your team so hard to get our opportunity to sit with you was because we're very excited, man. We're very excited that we're living in a time where people get to see someone really give their all to try to make things work.

Because so much of the culture of New York City is accepting the way things are, accepting corruption, accepting broken things; “Ah, man, this New York City, ain't never gonna happen. It ain't never gonna—

a.t: You glamorize.

q.t: You will cry. You will cry. But thinking about it, I haven't thought about this in a long time. I remember I was going to BMCC. I lived in Inwood. I was about to catch that 1 train. And then I just remember the — everyone on the platform freaking out. And I just didn't understand what was happening. And my phone didn't work. So, I remember everyone was like, "Go home." I went home and turned on the television. And I was like, I just couldn't process it. I couldn't process it. But I haven't felt that feeling. I haven't been — I just remember crying because I was so scared. But I recommend you do go to the museum because it is powerful. It's very powerful. And you will shed a lot of tears.

Well, and seeing the attempted — because it's bizarre — the attempted negative narrative of trying to attack you for being a part of the 25th as the mayor of the city, or individuals in New York City or wherever you are on social media, acting as if people from all backgrounds weren't affected on that day or lost people on that day or whatever — is so, I guess bananas is the only, that's how, like—

Well, not to mention then the secondary trauma that then happened for Muslim New Yorkers and Middle Eastern New Yorkers of all backgrounds who looked a certain way in the months and years that followed. It led to a really horrible time of Islamophobia. So, in addition to like the immense tragedy that all Americans felt, you then had a group of people who not only were dealing with their own tragedies because their people were lost and they lost people but now are being villainized because this is what we tend to do. And that is sadly not something that has changed.

It is something that we sort of lived in a bubble and pretended like things were better for a little while, and we'd all come together. And sadly, in 2026, it does not feel like anyone is together at this moment. Are you able to just, like, ignore the ridiculousness of people suggesting anything about your place as someone who is the ultimate servant to the city?

a.t:
I think I always bring myself back to what the point is, what my job is; and it's to serve the city, and it's to ensure that the day is one where it's not about me, it's about the city. This was an attack on the city. And when you go to that museum, and you see all of the different New Yorkers coming from all backgrounds, all parts of our city, and you realize that what this day should be about is a commemoration of them, of their families.

And I look forward on the 25th anniversary, I will be there at the event as I was last year to commemorate those who were stolen from us, and in all of the events around that. Because what we — when we're talking about the fear that you felt, that was something that so many New Yorkers felt. And at the same time, there were New Yorkers who felt that fear and ran towards the towers to try and save people.
Save lives.

And when I went into these firehouses and they were explaining to me that the names that you're seeing on the wall, some of those people were supposed to be at home. It's hard to comprehend that. Talking about somebody who had just finished a 12-hour shift is a change of shift, and they choose to get back on the truck. That's what sacrifice looks like; that's what—

q.t: I was actually on the air, but I wasn't in New York City yet. I was in Portland, Oregon, actually. And I was actually doing the news. And I was like, “Yo, some idiot” because it wasn't known that it was a passenger plane. Like, it was just kind of like, yo, somebody, a plane ran into the World Trade Center. Like, it's like, I thought it was like Cessna, some individual person, whatever. And that's at 6 a.m. And then you just start to get information. And I was on the air that day until like 2 o'clock in the afternoon, just reporting the news, trying to get updates, understanding what's taking place.

a.t: Have you guys been to the museum?
Yeah.
I have.
I actually haven’t done the museum.
You should go.

q.t: So obviously there's a ton of noise around everything you do. And we're pretty transparent about this. Most of it, to me, a strong percentage, is just rampant and in-the-open Islamophobia, in my opinion. 9/11 is around the corner, and it's 25 years. This is obviously a big deal for New Yorkers. Ignoring the noise about your involvement, we know that obviously you'll be doing all the things as mayor that you should be doing and that you wouldn't miss it. What does the 25th anniversary of 9/11 mean, and what is your personal 9/11 story? Like, you were a kid in Morningside Heights at that time, right?

a.t:
I think for me, the 25th anniversary, it's a moment for our city to come together to grieve what was one of the most horrific attacks our city has ever seen. And we know that the focus of that day should be on that day and on the families and the lives that were forever changed by that day, lives that were shattered.

And we also know that for many, that day never ended. And what I mean by that is that we are now in a place in our city where more firefighters have lost their lives since 9/11 from 9/11-related health complications than on 9/11.

And I've had the privilege of visiting a number of firehouses across New York City where they sent firefighters on that day, some of whom were scheduled to be on, some of whom would just finish their shift; they were supposed to be going home, and they said, "I'm going."

And they still have etched in the wall the names of those who were reporting for duty that day.
