And that, to me, is what the day has to be about, honoring that sacrifice, honoring that service, honoring those families and knowing that this moment is a moment that has to be a solemn one and really recognizing that and being there as much as we can for the entire city.

And my memories of the day: I was nine years old, and at that age, you don't fully grasp the horror of what it is that we're talking about, but you do have a sense that something horribly wrong has happened. And my memory had more to do with the sense of panic amongst those in whom I would never see it, adults, teachers and people who were in the hospital who had no way of grappling with what they had just learned.

Early dismissal, everyone going home, a student knowing their parent was in Lower Manhattan that day, trying to find out if they're okay. That's also the panic, is the sense of, where are my loved ones? And this is a city where so many people's loved ones were killed that day. What are your memories?

q.t: You need to develop a nickname, your Little Flower nickname, you know what I mean?

a.t: Yeah, 5’ 11” Flower.

q.t: And they called him a socialist; they called him all types of names when he was trying to do things for the city.

a.t: Called him everything, man. One good nickname was “Little Flower.” It's a great nickname. It's also a great coffee shop in Astoria if you ever wanna check it out.

q.t:
So, it sounds like, you know, because part of my convo on the air and with our team is always like, “Yeah, start has been great, but that close has to be equally, like, you got a —” And that is often, you know, and I'm sure from you studying politics and I'm sure you think about that, like, to the degree of like, can we sustain the momentum, the trust, the, you know, the energy?

Because I'm sure, I mean, look, when you walked in, I was like, "Yo, bro, you all right? Like, you're doing a lot. Like, you good, my dude? Like, how are you keeping this up? Right?” And then I was reminded you're 34; I'm 51. So you'll be all right. You'll keep pushing them, guys.

But on that note, yeah, the close, man. Like, are you even able to look out that far, two years from now, three years from now? And what are some of the things that you want us to be paying attention to, to pressure-test, like you're saying, to be a part of the community that's like, "Nah, bro, this can be better. You said X, Y, Z. How do you, how can we help with that pressure test?"

a.t:
Well, I think there's two things. I'm a big soccer fan. And in soccer, when a team takes a lead, there's a lot of different approaches that they can take. One of them, and we saw this in the World Cup, is when people try to just sit back and protect the lead. They kind of give up everything that got them to that point, and they just wanna hold it. And you start to feel the pressure just build.

I use this as an example; I leave it to New Yorkers to judge how we're doing. If New Yorkers believe that we've had a good start here, then our job is not to then say, "Let's not screw it up." You have to keep going. You have to keep pushing. Because if you get into that kind of mindset, where you wake up in the morning and you're trying to not make a mistake, then that's going to paralyze you from any of what you actually have to do.

I want us to be so much more than simply managers of the way life is. I want us to make life better for people. And that means going beyond trying to not make a mistake. And it also means that when you make a mistake, you have to move beyond the ego of the fact that it's been made and ask yourself, ‘Why did this happen? How does it never happen again?”

And I think to you, the thing that would be most helpful is how do we keep pushing ourselves to be as ambitious as we can be? You know, I believe New York is an exceptional place. I also believe we sometimes suffer from something in New York politics called “New York exceptionalism,” where we say, "Oh, if that worked there, it can't work here.” This is New York. We're different."

And in many ways, what you're actually doing is just justifying mediocrity by trying to say that it's a fact of life here in New York City. But I want people to be looking around the world, looking around the country and saying, "Look at what's working over there. Look how we could start to think differently."

I mean, one of the key things that is a focus for us when we're thinking about quality of life is trash, garbage disposal, right? We are now gonna be rolling out more than 6,500 Empire Bins so that we're going to stop seeing black bags of trash out on the street in the way that we grew up associating with New York.

And it's like, what are the other things that we've come to accept as if they're a fact of life when, in fact, they're not a natural state of being; they're a result of political choices. That's the thing to me where I'm always wondering, and sometimes it's not even looking that far; it's looking at our own history. Because I'll tell you, when you look at mayors like La Guardia, you look at what their ambition was, you look at how far we've strayed over the last many decades in how we've constrained our thinking.

q.t:
Yeah, I think one of the most refreshing things about your administration and the people — and shout out to your team, by the way — is the transparency on social media. You guys do an exceptional job, because we see for the first time things getting done, period. And it's super refreshing.

I mean, one of my favorite things to see is when people have been shouting you out, like, "Hey, mayor, there's a pothole right here," and boom, it's fixed the next day, or that week. We've never seen anything like that before. Tell me about your strategy. Did you specifically say, "This is something I want to do?"

a.t:
Yeah, I think first, I just want to start by saying what you said, which is shout-outs to the team, because so often in politics, it's what we call the principal that gets the credit, right? It's the politician at the heart of it. We're talking about a city workforce of more than 300,000 people who are out there, and they are grinding and they are delivering for the people of the city. When it comes to potholes, we have paved over 191,000 potholes in these first eight months. And a lot of this comes from the feeling that we have as an administration, which is that there's no problem too small, no task too big for us to tackle.

And as much as I talk to New Yorkers about the importance of the kind of sweeping, ambitious vision of universal childcare, for example, we also have to deliver on the smallest problems in their life. Because if you leave a pothole on someone's street, they will look at that pothole and say, "How can I trust City government to do anything bigger than this if it can't even do this?"

And it's the same thing where anytime government is failing someone, that's where they are losing their faith in even believing in government. That's where they're telling themselves, "Let me just get as far away as I can from government."

You know, there are people who feel like my job is to make as much money as possible so I never have to rely on government, because look at what it looks like right now. My job is to win that trust back and not do it by browbeating someone, but by delivering.

q.t: Yeah, up to like one inch per hour, and we're getting three inches per hour or something like that.

a.t: You know, and this is also what the other side of the climate crisis looks like in a quality-of-life, day-to-day aspect of it all.

q.t:
Did you see the people online that — remember, people were making videos, like, "Oh, nice work, Mamdani, look at this." You know, you got Michael Rapaport walking down the street [saying], "Look at this." And I'm like, what do you people expect?

If there's three and a half feet of snow on 87th Street between Broadway and West End, and then a truck comes through and plows that, and your car was there, you may have problems with your car. But, like, do you ever get caught up in these sort of unrealistic expectations, or are you able to go, "These people know this isn't reasonable."

a.t:
I think you have to separate the noise from maybe, you know, the person you cited, to good faith, right?And I think that's the thing: you can never confuse the two where you tell yourself, all critique is bad faith, all critique is noise. If you do that, you make your world smaller and smaller, and you start to just tell yourself that everything you do is right, and you can never end up there.

And so distinguishing between the two, a lot of that has to also do with the team you put around yourself, people who are willing to go beyond just saying yes to you, willing to push you as well. And I think what, you know, what we also realize is with the climate crisis, these kinds of storms are only gonna get more intense. They're only going to get worse. And so what may have worked in the past is going to have to be changed now, because the scale of snowfall is at a specific level.I mean, we talk about the rain. We have a sewage system built for rainfall of a hundred years ago. That has intensified.

q.t: No, your whole life, you've never seen anything like that, right?

a.t: It was in a long time. It was like since I was watching NY1 waiting for my school to pop up on the list of which—

q.t: Do you remember after that, because for people who are not watching this, not in New York, we had snowstorms back to back that were unlike anything in my entire time living here, probably you, too.
Yeah, they were calling them 10-year storms. Yeah, in my 20 years.

a.t: Usually that kind of language is hyperbolic. “Yeah, it's like 10 years.” I'm like, “Oh, it is a 10-year storm.”

q.t: What was the first, like, “Holy [], I'm mayor,” moment?

a.t:
I mean, in the first week, there were two five-alarm fires. Then we had the first snowstorm that we'd seen at that scale in a long time. And then we had the first blizzard in more than a decade.

And it was just — I remember this one moment where someone was like, "Yeah, so typically the way that City Hall accounting works is we allocate the amount of money that we've spent on snow removal in the last few years as the amount that we'll have now." And we didn't really have any snow to a significant level last year.

I was like, "So what do we do?" And you just realize that you have to come up with a plan in the moment as quickly as you can and then be willing to just pressure-test every single part of it. Because a lot of what — I mean, you guys know this, working in any job, there's the rationale in the job and then the rationale in the world outside the job.

But there are things that make sense to people who are working there, and then when you step out of it, you explain it to a friend of yours, and they're like, "I don't know what you're talking about." And one of those things is, "This is how it's been done." A New Yorker does not care if that's how it's been done, if it's not working. And so one of the key things is pushing past a rationale of, "We do it this way," to say, "Why do we do it this way?"

q.t: I mean, just stay right here with the glazing.

Right. Just keep glazing. Just live in the glaze. But I do just want to salute you, man, because I don't think anybody can remember a time that a mayor started and was attempting to be so transparent and making it easy for everyone to follow along and understand.

Also not being afraid to, like — look, you know, the billionaires and the people who run media want to shape things the way they want to shape things. And thank God for social media and the way you carry yourself. You're able to make sure that your story doesn't get lost and the way you want to tell your story doesn't get lost. Is there anything that you feel like in the first six months you could have done even better, though?

a.t:
I think you have to look at every day as being one you can be better at. And I don't mean that like flippantly. I just mean that sometimes there's such a desire to categorize things in wins and losses that you forget the fact that you have to push yourself every single day.

I mean, that's one of the things that I love most about New York City is that the hunger for being as good as you can be is part of what makes people New Yorkers. And for a long time, it's felt like that's only been true in certain sectors, but not in politics. It's felt like we have a culture of exceptionalism in the arts, in sports, in finance, in whatever it may be. But in politics, it's just like mediocrity is accepted simply as what it is.

And so, for us, it's that even when you think you've done a good job, you know this thing is going to happen again, right? Like, you don't just get one of these crises or one of these events. I mean, one of the first things that I learned is that this job is, in many ways, it's like you are facing bigger waves than you've ever faced in your life, and that that wave will end and another one will soon come.

And so just as important as what you're doing in the moment is what we call an after-action, where you meet after the issue has left everyone's consciousness and people have moved on to the next issue. How do we make sure that our response to this isn't just repetition, but it's pushing yourself? Because to me, in that example, [that] is how you find if you can actually keep up the pace with New Yorkers.

q.t: So, we wanted to, you know, first salute you for having an amazing beginning to your, you know, mayoral run. It's pretty unanimous for people who live in New York City. We'll get into the negatives and the narratives and all of those things.

a.t: You don't even have to go there.

q.t: Do you feel they found it all, though, by now? That's the question.

a.t: Yes. Yes.

q.t: Oh, my God. Do you have moments when you're, you guys are in bed with your wife, and you're like, "Babe, look what popped up?" And you're like, "Oh, my God."

a.t: Some things you expect, some things you do not expect.

q.t: Now, how did you feel when it started to go viral, and you saw a young you. Like, how does that feel?

a.t: It's a funny thing. Because you feel like you're in a different part of your life. But the way that the internet works, all the parts of your life collapse. And then you also look back on yourself of how I used to enjoy when other people's — you know, you'd be watching, like, Timothée Chalamet's high school performance. This is great. And I'm like, “I shouldn't have even watched that.”

q.t: I feel like I've seen your chest too many times because of that video.

a.t: Imagine how I feel.

q.t: Half Jewish, half Christian. Full Muslim name. Peter Elliot Rosenberg.
Yeah, I'm not gonna give you my whole government, but my middle name is Yolanda.
Laura Yolanda Stylez.
Yeah.
Yo, real talk, though. I know we didn't plan to start here, Laura, but do you wanna share why you don't wanna give your full name?
I just don't want people in my business. That's it.
It's a real thing.

That's what it is. I don't wanna get — I wanna protect my family. It's a real thing.

Mayor Mamdani:: It's understandable.
And the reason I bring that up is because people are all in your business. Ugandan rap videos have become a thing.

a.t: Everything.
Everything.

q.t: You're talking to Glaze Monster No. 1 right here.
Ladies and gentlemen, the sit-down has happened. Ebro, Laura [and] Rosenberg here at City Hall. We have Mayor Mamdani. That is Zohran Kwame Mamdani, a.k.a.—
Are you giving him full name?
Yeah, that's the mayor of New York City.
Show respect.
Listen, we can't just let them weaponize his name. We gotta also celebrate his name. You know what I'm saying? We gotta do that.

a.t: Do you guys have middle names?
I'm Ibrahim Jamil Darden.
Salaam alaikum.

q.t: We are accused of liking you too much, a.k.a. glazing. So there's gonna be references to us glazing throughout the convo, all right?

a.t: Glaze away.

q.t: Well, I hate to plug a competitor, but I believe Gothamist has reported on it. It's tough for you. I was off last week.

a.t: Working for Gothamist last week, I see.

q.t: Some transportation advocates have put forward the idea of tolling drivers on the city-owned section of the BQE to help pay for the reconstruction project. Is that something you've heard about? Is that something the city's considering?

a.t: It's not something that I'd heard about or considered until this moment, but do you have an outlet where I can read more about it?

q.t: When were you first aware of the challenges and the issues that could in some ways delay and mar this major initiative?

a.t: I think we've known that when we're talking, as you had mentioned earlier, the kinds of contract delays that have been endemic in City government, that's something that we've been attuned to, and the need to overhaul that overall. When it comes to the specific concerns that some providers were facing, last week as we became aware of this, we have now put everything that we have to ensure that we are resolving all of these concerns in time for the first day of school.

q.t:
I have two questions for you. The first is about the 2-K rollout, which I know you and the chancellors announced today that there's going to be a, quote, "whole-of-government" approach. I'm just curious: why did it take a week before school starts — well, a week and change — with lots of reporting about the delay in payments for this whole-of-government and this $43 million investment to begin? I know that there's always been issues with nonprofit payment, but I just wanted to know if it took that long.

And the second question is, my colleague Greg Smith wrote a story about an African burial ground in Elmhurst that's owned by an Episcopalian church in Queens. The pastor wants the site to be landmarked, and he wants the city to buy it. I don't know if you've seen the story and if you have any thoughts on that.

a.t:
I haven't seen the story as yet, but if you send it to the press team, I'll be sure to read that.

[Crosstalk.]

And then on your first question, I just want to be very clear that the delays that we are discussing are unacceptable. And ever since these were identified, we have been working around the clock to both ensure that they are fixed for the upcoming school year and also that they are fixed in general. Because, as you said earlier, some of these are also reflective of an issue that has plagued City government, not for months, but for years. And what we are talking about is rebuilding the capacity that has been severely decreased over the last few years of staff who are charged with both setting up and maintaining our early childcare system, as well as increasing headcount and putting systems in place to ensure that we're overseeing these contracts and actually expediting the process by which they are registered.

As you mentioned, that is going to be done in tandem with a $43 million investment that specifically hires 200 people to address these kinds of critical gaps, but also overhauls the entire system as it pertains to contract registration and communication with early childcare providers.

Now, I also just want to take this opportunity to address that in the time since we've all last spoken about this issue, we have reached out to every single early childcare provider, and we have done so while also sending emails, as well as making over 800 calls to ensure that every organization hears from us directly. Since last week, the team has counseled over 50 providers who had expressed any kind of concern. They have all been connected with loans, as well as with additional supports.

We have also tripled the number of staff who are working to process contracts. Any provider who has applied for a loan by today and has submitted a complete application will see their loan processed by the end of the week. We are also continuing to process these requests on a rolling basis with a rapid turnaround time, and also any provider who requests supplies by this Friday will receive them before the first day of school. And we will also continue to process those kinds of requests on a rolling basis.

q.t:
Two public safety questions for you. The first is that a nurse was killed on Third Avenue and Sunset Park over the weekend by a hit-and-run driver. There have been six pedestrians and five cyclists killed on Third Avenue since 2014. Do you have a plan to speed up the safety work that's been planned there by the DOT for several years? And how are you going to address that spate of traffic violence?

And the second question is, in one week, we have J'Ouvert and the West Indian Day Parade. Every year, there's a debate over how much security the parade and J'Ouvert sort of merits. Can New Yorkers expect to see more security, the same amount, and are you going to be marching in the West Indian Day Parade?

a.t:
I will be there at the West Indian Day Parade, and I was proud to be there last year, and I'll be proud to be there in the years to come.

When it comes to security protocols, we're going to do everything we can to keep New Yorkers safe. This is a day where so many New Yorkers come out to celebrate, and it's also a day where we have seen acts of violence in the past that we want to make sure are not a part of what it means to celebrate this parade.

And when it comes to your question on Third Avenue, we have seen tragic hit-and-runs across the city over the past seven days, and they underscore the importance of Vision Zero, and they underscore our administration's commitment to ensuring that New Yorkers can get to where they're going safely, no matter if they're biking, walking, driving or riding public transit.

And when it comes to Third Avenue specifically, we are going to be moving forward with the redesign of Third Avenue that had been stalled for quite some time. We will have more information soon.

I do also just want to say that we, all of us here at City Hall and, frankly, across the city, are keeping the victims' family in our hearts, because these are horrific, horrific hit-and-runs that we've seen over the past week.

q.t: And then just really quickly on Mulgrew and the UFT—

a.t: Those conversations are ongoing. They are productive, and they're reflective of the fact that we are aligned in the recognition of the critical work that paraprofessionals do every single day and have been doing for quite some time. And that our issue with the legislation was more on the question of its legality as it was written. And so, I'm hopeful in those conversations, and I know that they're ongoing.

q.t: Well, do you feel like the message of the RSS would resonate at all in New York City? Do you feel like that's something that, you know, voters and New Yorkers here would be receptive to?

a.t: No, I think if it did, then I wouldn't be the mayor.

q.t: Do you have any reaction — I know you talked before this RSS rally at MSG that happened on Saturday. Do you have any reaction to just what was said there, and if you think that message resonates at all with New Yorkers? And Brad Lander, the congressional candidate you endorsed, was heckled by some people there over his positions on Israel. What would you say to those hecklers?

a.t: I haven't seen what that heckling was. What I would say is that I was proud to endorse Brad in his run for Congress, and I think that he will be an incredible champion for this city, and I think that he has put forward policy proposals that are reflective of our city's commitment to human rights. And then to your other part of that question, what do you mean by what was said there?

q.t: Last week, I spoke with Mike Mulgrew about the paraprofessional bill, and he had suggested that negotiations were improving because you personally had gotten involved in this. I'm wondering if you can give us any update at all or kind of characterize what types of solutions you're talking about with the UFT? And then I had a question after that.

a.t: Go for it.

q.t: You and the Council member have said you expect thousands of restaurants to participate in this. Do you have a more specific estimate on how many — who might join? How many more might join? I think there's only 1,600 restaurants right now in the program.

a.t:
What I can say is that what we've found, we heard this from the Council member earlier, is that the prior administration's policy and rulemaking had led to a significant majority of previously participating businesses opting out just because it was too expensive to be a part of. I don't have additional details as to the specific number we expect, but it will be an increase from what we're seeing today. I don't know, Council member, if you want to add.

[Crosstalk.]

q.t: There were four bills passed in this package. The other ones have to do with the scheduling of payments and violations for sanitation and enclosing cafe sidewalk sheds in the winter. Do you support those as well? I know you're only signing this one today.

a.t: Yes, those will be lapsing into law. One of the key reasons to sign this legislation into law was not only the scale of the impact that this legislation will have on thousands of small businesses and restaurants across New York City, but also the fact that if it was to lapse into law, then it would create a lapse in service that was actually being delivered.

q.t: For providers in the immediate who are looking like a Sept. 10 opening is not possible for them, they can't pay their teachers, they can pay their custodians to open the schools, they can afford the meals that they have to give the kids mandated, what is a solution? Because right now it seems like the bridge loan is the only solution. A lot of them have not seen a response yet for their application for a bridge loan.

a.t: We have made this very clear that this is a top priority internally, and New York City Public Schools will be pursuing that, whether it means the registration of those contracts expeditiously or it means the provision of an interest-free loan, because these providers should have all the resources they need to start school and start providing what, frankly, is an essential service for so many families across the city.

q.t:
So, from City & State yesterday, I was the one who reported about the discrepancy in the funding for 3-K and pre-K. So, in my experience while speaking to these education providers, a lot of them expressed a lot of concern about the idea of universal 2-K because under these conditions of them not getting their, you know, payments on time, and a lot of them spoke to me about regularly receiving late payments, almost a month late.

And so, they said they spoke to you in February and kind of discussed their concerns regarding pay parity and how a 2-K rollout is supposed to go forward under this current condition of not being able to get properly funded for 3-K and pre-K.So, under these recent experiences, I guess what would you say about your impending 2-K rollout?

a.t:
First, what I want to say is thank you to these child care providers because they are such a critical part of what even makes universal child care a possibility in our city. And in that time that I spent with them, what I also heard from them was the importance of the city being responsive to the variety of needs that they have.

We made the decision to invest tens of millions of dollars in additional funding for a better contract for many of these providers because they hadn't seen an update to that contract for many years, while a lot of their costs had been going up. We also made the decision to create a grant fund for child care providers who are in need of immediate financial assistance, and the absence of that could force them to go under.

And this is all a reflection of the fact that we don't have this child care system without these providers, without these child care workers. And we're also not going to accept what has been the standard from the city over the last many years of these kinds of delays. And that's why this is a top priority for us to both fix this for now and fix this for the future as well.

q.t: So, what would you want to say to the people who erroneously got some of these tax bills for second homes, and do you have any plans on extending the exemption?

a.t:
You know, we've extended the exemption deadline to Oct. 6, and again, if someone does not appeal by that time, they can still appeal to the Tax Commission until early next year. However, we're confident that with a little more than a month and with this newfound information that that should be a requisite amount of time.

And to any owner who has additional questions, what I would always say is that we are here to answer those questions, whether that is through the Department of Finance, whether that's through calling 311, whether that's going in person at a business center. Our job is to answer those questions. Our job is to make this process as easy as possible.

q.t: But were the letters saying that they'd be exempt from the tax always part of the rollout, or did that come following the court?

a.t:
The letters that are being sent now as a result of early access to the 2025 income tax filings, that is a reflection of the new information we have and letting New Yorkers know if they haven't started an exemption process that they don't have to because we have the requisite information now.

[Crosstalk.]

q.t: Building off of Dan's question, also in the filing, it says that there's going to be approximately 4,000 property owners who will receive a letter informing them that they won't be subject to the tax. Was that always part of the initial rollout, or was it always the plan to send people the letters and then they would have to file for exemption themselves?

a.t:
The plan always was that we wanted to give New Yorkers enough time to ask any questions that may come to mind, to appeal for an exemption, and that is part and parcel of why we hired dozens of additional civil servants to be able to actually reach out to those New Yorkers to field those kinds of questions, and that we changed the business center such that they could actually accept any questions in person wherever they were in any one of the five boroughs.

And so, yes, there have been a number of New Yorkers who have filed for exemptions. We have about 3,000 of which have been accepted thus far. And we will continue that process until Oct. 6. And then after that point, if New Yorkers still want to appeal an assessment, they can still appeal to the Tax Commission until early next year.

q.t: And really quick, secondly, City & State is reporting that some childcare providers have not received the advance funding from the city and DOE ahead of the first day of school. And they're having to take out loans and dig into their own pockets in order to be able to open on Sept. 10. Do you have any explanation for the delays, or when these providers will be able to see those funds come in?

a.t:
So, this is something that is a top priority for our New York City Public School system, is to put significant additional resources toward the registration of these early childhood education contracts and to ensure that every single provider is ready for the first day of school. And that both includes whether their contract will be registered or whether they will be provided with an interest-free loan.

[Crosstalk.]

q.t:
Okay, so, completely different topic, but right now the NYPD is searching for Jesus Acosta, who's wanted for a robbery and murder in a bodega here in the Bronx. He was also connected to a homicide in Brooklyn. The Bronx DA confirms that he has five local arrests, and there's also reports showing he was paroled in April after a 10-year sentence for a subway shooting.

Do you think that there should be more harsher penalties to keep people with records like this behind bars, or should there be more coordination with the state and local courts in order to ensure people like this aren't getting out on parole and causing more mayhem in the city?

a.t:
I think, first and foremost, we know that when the NYPD makes something a top priority for them, it is something that they put every single resource that they have toward it, and I'm confident in their abilities of being able to find him. And what this speaks to is the importance of public safety. And to me, every day is an opportunity for us to do more.

We're proud of the fact that we're reducing shootings and murders to the lowest levels in recorded history in our city. And we also know that there's always more work to be done, especially as we're speaking about this in the Bronx, where we know in recent weeks, we’ve seen the kinds of shootings that have torn families apart and, frankly, entire neighborhoods that are still shattered by the loss of the young people that [have] been stolen from them. So, this will continue to be a top priority for us.

q.t: Just to follow up, why were these estimates so wildly overestimated when you were starting with a pool of 26,000 potentially covered properties?

a.t:
So, by my last count, I think we sent out less than 20,000 ‘you may be subject to’ letters. I think it was about 17,000 or 18,000. And at the time that we sent those out, we did not have access to the 2025 income tax filings. That is something that is typically released in February of the next calendar year. The state has now provided us with early access to those filings, and that's what's informing these three categorizations of the letters

[Crosstalk.]

q.t: The city's court filings on the second-home luxury tax, it seems like the number of covered properties is dwindling by the thousands and getting closer to the 5,000 homes affected that a former city finance commissioner estimated. So, tell me, why do you see the numbers dwindling so fast, and what does this mean since your budgets assume years out, you're going to get $500 million each year?

a.t: We continue to be confident in that assessment of what the annual revenue will look like. And what we see right now is that we have three categories of properties that we're going to be sending out letters to. To your question, two of those three categories, one of them is to properties owned by a corporate entity like an LLC or a trust where the Department of Finance does not have sufficient information on a primary residence holder. That applies to about 6,400 households. Then the third category is properties where the Department of Finance does not have any 2025 tax returns that would indicate whether or not this is a primary residence holder. That amounts to about 4,400 households.

q.t: So should co-chair Gustavo Gordillo step down after lying to The New York Times, lying about his job to get a full-time gig with DSA and failing to support union workers?

a.t: You know, the D in DSA stands for Democratic, and I leave it to the organization in its own voting of who it is electing as its leaders.And I think what we've seen with Gustavo and what we're seeing to any others who are in the fight for a fairer, more affordable New York is that their focus is on making this a city that everyone can belong to, and I welcome anyone who's committed to that.

q.t: My second question was about Congressman Hakeem Jeffries. You spoke about him yesterday. You said you continue to support him for speaker. But I wonder if you have thoughts on the fact that he met with Jared Kushner in recent weeks. I wonder if you have thoughts on that strategy and if you've spoken to him at all about how Democrats should be strategizing ahead of a potential majority after the midterms.

a.t:
I don't have many thoughts on that. What I would say is that I continue to be in regular communication with Congressman Jeffries. And it's a communication that is always built on: how can we deliver for this city? How can we deliver for New Yorkers? It's something that both of us care very deeply about.

And when it comes to what life looks like after the midterms, one, I hope that we would be celebrating taking back the House. And two, I would always hope that, at that point, we are articulating very clearly what we are standing for.

We know for quite some time that we are standing up to a federal administration that is taking cruel and punitive action against the ability of many working-class Americans to afford their day-to-day life. But what is our agenda that we're fighting for? And that is something that we are looking to make clear here in New York City. It's an agenda for those who have been left behind. It's an agenda for those who work all day and still don't have enough money in their pocket to pay for their groceries.

And I'm excited at seeing the number of Democrats who've been elected in primaries, whether it's Claire Valdez, Darializa Avila Chevalier, Brad Lander, others, and now that we could bring that, hopefully, into a majority.

q.t: Two very separate questions for you.First, I wonder, you probably want to talk about this new initiative with the U.S. Open and making tickets more affordable and available to New Yorkers. And then I have a separate question.

a.t:
Well, yes, we're very excited that today we announced that we have secured 1,000 discounted tickets for New Yorkers to be sold at $100 a ticket. They will go on sale tomorrow at 10 a.m.And any New Yorker who lives in our city, all they will be required to do is provide their ZIP code. They can buy a ticket for themselves and one other lucky person. It'll be first come, first serve, pun intended.

And we're excited about this because part of the beauty of living in our city is also the exposure to some of the greatest sporting events across the world. And the U.S. Open is one that so many New Yorkers have fond memories of, and yet what we've seen is, like with many sporting events, the cost has continued to increase, and many New Yorkers feel as if they don't have a chance at being a part of something like this.

So just like we secured 1,000 tickets for the World Cup at a discounted price, we've done the same with the U.S. Open, and our mission is: how can we bring as many New Yorkers as possible to be a part of such a wonderful event?

q.t: And then my second question, Julie Menin, I believe yesterday was asking the city's Transportation Department to restart these talks around age verification for Citi Bike riders. I know your administration has intervened earlier this year in blocking, I think, biometric screening. So I'm just wondering where you stand. Do you think there should be stronger age verification for Citi Bikes?

a.t:
You know, the prior administration had reached out to Lyft in support of this as a measure, and when we came into office, we were informed of a number of the risks that would come with the implementation of this, risks that include the handling of data of minors in New York City and also questions as to the efficacy of this kind of data in asserting what the actual intent is of this program, whether it's age, what have you.

And so I continue to have that skepticism after having been informed about those critiques of this kind of a program. And I think what we've seen in the last few weeks, the last few months, is that when it comes to a lack of safety with e-bikes, a lot of it is actually derived from the purchasing and sale of e-bikes that are clearly in violation of New York City law.

And so one of the things that we have done is send out these cease-and-desist letters that have now taken effect to the more than 40 retailers who are found to still be selling e-bikes and e-scooters that are clearly operating at speeds that are not legal in the city.

q.t: I wanted to follow up on Holly's question. Just wondering, do you see unaffiliated voters as potential supporters, or are they a political threat? And then I have a second question.

a.t:
I see anyone who is registered to vote as a potential supporter, and frankly, anyone who lives in our city. And as the mayor, my job is to respond to the needs of everyone, no matter how they feel about me or whether they voted for me or whether they voted at all.

And when I'm running for office, I'm looking to speak to everyone. We're speaking about open primaries, but I'm also someone who ran through a competitive general. And that is the moment in which you speak to anyone regardless of their registration.

And, you know, earlier we were talking — I think Holly had mentioned outreach to Trump voters. I think by the end of the election, one in 10 voters who voted for Trump in New York City voted for our campaign.

And so, to me, it's not about classifying someone as whether they are with you or against you. It is about asking them, what is it that you're looking for from city government? What are the struggles you're facing in your life, and what are the ways in which we can actually help you with that?

q.t: On a related question, actually, you know, now that a couple of weeks have passed, do you have the tally of how many TPS recipients the city had to part ways with, and can you tell us what particular agencies were most impacted?

a.t:
We can get back to you on the exact number. What I can tell you is that these were city workers across a number of different agencies, workers who performed vital service to the city. And it's just one part of why I have spoken with the president directly about the importance of extending TPS for Haitian Americans, for Syrian Americans, for so many who have now been deprived of that status.

We are also talking about a status that was created with the intention of shielding sets of people from having to return to home countries that were deemed to be unstable. And when you look at the conditions in Haiti today, the idea that we would send Haitian Americans back in this moment, to me, is a betrayal of what TPS actually stands for. And we continue to call on the federal government to change that decision.

q.t: I wanted to ask if you are aware of any changes to the city, any changes to city policy that have resulted from the federal changes to work visas for international job applicants, H-1B in particular. The Trump administration last year, so before you took office, obviously implemented a $100,000 fee for employers for each visa they've sponsored. That's affected workforces all around the country, hospitals, nonprofits. Do you know whether it's affected City government at all?

a.t: Not off the top of my head, but we will get back to you on that question.

q.t: Should the rally be canceled, though, at MSG this weekend?

a.t:
I don't support the rally, but I don't know if the city has any jurisdiction on canceling a private event.

[Crosstalk.]

q.t: Since Lindsay, I think.

a.t:
Since Lindsay. And so what that showed to me is that it is possible to bring more New Yorkers in. It's not a question of the rules that you set up. It's a question also of how you want to engage with them. So that's how I navigate that question.

And then, you know, I also stand here as the first Indian American mayor in our city's history, and my mother's family is all still in India. And the vision of India that I was taught by my family and the one that I grew up being very familiar with was of a pluralistic society, of a secular republic that believed in the belonging of each and every person who was from India.

And it has been incredibly troubling to see the rise of a movement that is predicated on an exclusionary vision of any country, frankly. And so it is one that I find myself in deep opposition to, not only as an Indian American, but also as the mayor of a city that believes deeply in the belonging of each and every person, no matter their color, their creed, their religion, their faith, wherever they're from.

q.t:
Well, just during your campaign, I feel like the whole ethos was about expanding the electorate. And you made that video that went viral and got so much attention about reaching out to Trump voters before too many people were taking your candidacy seriously. And then you did make inroads and expand it, getting more people involved, getting more people registered to vote.

So, I just wanted to press you a little bit on how that squares now with opposing open primaries, which would allow these — I think it's more than a million unaffiliated voters — to participate in that part of the process.

a.t: I think that our campaign showed that the current system is not incongruent with getting more people to participate. And in fact, it comes out to the way in which you build your campaign, the way you reach out to people and also if you are encouraging more and more people to register, to change their location of registration to where they actually live, and also that they actually have a home in whatever political coalition that you're building.And at the end of the election calendar, I think we received more than a million votes, which was the first mayoral campaign to receive that, I think, since the '60s it may have been.

q.t: Okay, question about the RSS. The Indian right-wing paramilitary organization is planning to have a rally this weekend at Madison Square Garden, and there are protests against this rally, including one right now, I think, at City Hall. Shahana Hanif, Brad Lander and Lincoln Restler have all called for it to be canceled. Opponents to the rally cite the RSS' treatment of religious minorities in India. That's something you've spoken out about. So just wanna get your position on that. And then I also have a question about open primaries.

a.t: You can give me that one, too.

q.t: I wanted to ask about enforcement, you know, what happens when these cases are not back in court after five days, and what sort of conversations have you had with OCA about how to give guidance to their judges on these new rules?

a.t: I first just want to thank and acknowledge OCA for all of the work that made today possible. And I think it's worthy of a round of applause. We know that this is the right thing to do. There is still a lot of work to actually follow through on it. And that is what OCA and so many others in this room are making possible. I'll pass it over to a member of my admin to speak additionally on that question.

Yeah, so just to be very clear, when we first sort of brought this idea forward, recognizing that we had cases like you see on the easels here that have been delinquent for months and months and months, and talking to all of the Legal Aid attorneys and also to the attorneys within HPD who litigate these types of cases, it was clear that we needed sort of to speed this up in order to not extenuate how long tenants are suffering.

Again, to the earlier question, we give a notice of violation. Our door is open. If landlords want to get compliant, they certainly have an avenue to do that in partnership with HPD. So, this is really about those landlords who have been warned, have been noticed, have been issued violations, and just continually refuse to comply with the law.

We are very grateful that the Office of Court Administration acknowledges how serious an issue this is and has now established a very clear timeline so that tenants will not have to wait for justice indefinitely.
Thank you, and just before we move over, I just want to introduce State Senator Kavanagh to share some words on this.

Thank you, Mr. Mayor. Just a very brief — sorry I'm late; I had a subway mishap. But I really did want to be here because, you know, we've spent a great deal of time and energy trying to address the housing crisis of this city, in the state, across the board, using all the tools available. We have shored up our rent laws and our laws that protect tenants. We've added good-cause eviction tools. We have invested enormous amounts of capital both to create new housing and to stabilize and secure the housing that we have.

We added changes to our regulatory system that the city continues to work on to remove obstacles to producing new housing [and] to converting commercial buildings to residential housing. And just this year, we added some protections, working with the Manhattan district attorney to go after landlords who deserve criminal prosecution for their harassment of tenants.

But there's been one stubborn problem that has resisted change and reform for a long time, and that is a situation that all of us in elected office hear about all the time. It's a building, a multifamily building, where the property owner is unable or unwilling to maintain the building in a way that keeps it habitable, that keeps it livable and that keeps a decent place for people to live.

So that means tenants then spend a long time living in terrible conditions, often displaced from their homes for long periods. The solution is very much making sure we can adjudicate these cases promptly and get redress for the tenants and get people back into their homes.

So, I wanted to be here to thank the mayor and his all-star team, his all-star housing team and Judge Ally and Sloan and all the people at OCA for coming together and addressing this.

This is a rare collaboration where the city and the courts really roll up their sleeves and try to sort out a difficult problem. So, this is great news. I look forward to seeing the fruits of all of this work. Thank you.

q.t: I'm wondering if you could talk about how you differentiate a truly negligent landlord from one who, you know, says they simply can't afford to replace the boiler or replace elevators because costs are outpacing revenue.

a.t:
What we are talking about today are some of the most severe cases. We're talking about cases where a third of the building is facing some kind of a serious violation [and] cases where we have elevators broken down. And when it comes to the law, everyone has to follow it. And for far too long, that has somehow not been understood when it comes to housing in our city. If a landlord is not able to follow the law, then they should not be a landlord of that property.

And what we are talking about are things that have incredible consequences for New Yorkers. At one of the Rental Ripoff Hearings, I sat across from a tenant who showed me a video of one of her neighbors having to carry her disabled child up the stairs because that elevator was broken.

We’re talking about seniors who live on the 10th floor of a building. How are they supposed to get up there or get down from there? And these are things that do not exist in isolation. And what I mean by that is every so often, I'm standing in front of the press corps and our cameras, and I'm talking about a heat emergency. I'm talking about the cold weather that's coming. And we are trying to reach New Yorkers wherever they are. These are the kinds of things that also intensify the isolation of those New Yorkers. We have to make sure that these laws are actually being followed.

q.t: I will get it for you.

a.t: Okay. Thank you.

q.t: And just one more question. There's a bill in the State Senate that would introduce another Housing Court subpart for, I believe, buildings with sub-10-unit buildings and affordable housing buildings for eviction cases specifically. What's your stance on that bill? And does anything that you're announcing today kind of feed into that push for more efficiency in that specific process?

a.t: I think we're going to get back to you on that bill. Do you have the bill number?

q.t: Quick follow-up question about 7A. By some estimates, there are only about two dozen active administratorships right now. If things speed up and, you know, things go as seemingly the plan is to have more administratorships and more transfers of management happen under 7A, are there already organizations, for-profit [or] nonprofit, lined up to take on that role? Is there a backlog or a vetting process that's already in the process?

a.t: So, yeah, it is, in fact, right. We have some 7A administrators right now who are serving, but we also have a process by which we can take in new administrators, so we are not limited to a specific list, and we very intentionally keep that open on a rolling basis so that as we need more, we can meet the demand by prequalifying responsible management companies and receivers who can step in.

q.t:
I have a question about one of the types of legal actions here. The HP action, which is trying to compel landlords to do repairs, is also a tool that's used by some NYCHA residents to compel repairs. And they're sometimes also forced to relocate because of repair issues.

I'm wondering if this pathway will also be open to NYCHA residents to use to accelerate those types of court cases. And if so, is this initiative about not only keeping private landlords accountable, but also forcing the city's housing agency to respond to what is a large backlog of repair needs?

a.t: You know, I think just to first lay out very clearly that one of the critical parts of our housing agenda is delivering for public housing residents who have for far too long been overlooked and left behind by government policy. And one of the key ways that we've sought to do that is through the allocation of a multibillion-dollar housing plan specifically for public housing and then also looking for additional ways that we can make targeted investments beyond that. One of the early investments we made was in heat pumps in the Rockaways to transform a specific NYCHA housing development. I'll pass it over to our deputy mayor to add some additional details there.

a.s: Deputy Mayor Leila Bozorg, Housing and Planning
a.t: So, I think as we evaluate the types of HP actions that this would apply to, NYCHA will be included in that.

q.t: Do you have a sense of the volume of cases that will be eligible for this path given past caseloads, and to what extent is this change necessary for the 7A program in Fix the City? Like, was the 7A program as part of the Fix the City initiative possible without this change? Like, to what extent does the pace of that rely on this change?

a.t: You know, it is hard to give an exact sense of how many New Yorkers will be impacted. However, we do know that these types of cases, the ones that we've listed earlier, are exactly the ones that tend to be the most complicated to resolve. And the extended timeline that they have taken historically, as well as the backlog that it creates, it not only means consequences for those New Yorkers who are bringing these cases to this court but also ramifications that extend beyond that for the entire Housing Court system. I'm going to pass it over to our deputy mayor for Housing and Planning to speak to a little additional detail on 7A. Oh, actually, we'll have Commissioner Dina Levy come up.

Yeah, so on the 7A question, obviously this is a tool that HPD has had for many years, but one of the challenges, particularly in these very difficult cases, is that the time it takes to remove a really seriously delinquent owner in order to get in responsible management means that the buildings continue to deteriorate, getting more and more expensive. Ultimately, the city needs to come in and repair them, so this will be a huge tool that we will layer with other tools to really pursue those landlords who are willfully negligent in managing their buildings.

q.t:
Last week when the 911 system went down, nobody knew about it for — the outage went out for seven hours. No one found out until The New York Times released an article that night. 

I guess City Council members are now trying to call for an oversight hearing, not just looking into what exactly happened, but why your administration didn't say anything, not only to the press, New Yorkers. But during those seven crucial hours, nobody told New Yorkers who were desperately trying to call 911 that their calls might not be answered because of this outage. 

I just want to know exactly why your administration decided to not tell New Yorkers when this was happening.

a.t:
So, our first order of business when being alerted as to the issue with the call system was to resolve the call system, and that was the focus. And after what we found is that a significant number of the calls that were coming in over the course of that period of time were being rerouted to another part of the 911 system. And there were about — there were fewer than 400 calls, unique calls that were not connected. 

And so, over the course of the time since that was resolved and as it was going through the day, the work was being done to do everything we could to reach out to New Yorkers directly to ensure that we could provide them with whatever service was necessary. 

Because again, this is one of the most critical parts of our city's infrastructure. And we have identified that this was from a Motorola software update. And now we are looking to take all of the steps we can to ensure this does not happen ever again.

q.t:
So, two questions. I first wanted to just get your reaction to TIME's reporting on Hakeem Jeffries meeting with Jared Kushner. What do you think of Jeffries potentially being Speaker in light of this? 

And then my second question is, it's now two weeks until the first day of school, and there's still no AI policy, and principals aren't supposed to buy new tech until there is one. So, can you just give any update on that? Will it be coming in the next few days? I know this is a stressful issue for schools.

a.t: It is an issue of immense importance to us in the administration, and it is an issue that we will be speaking to soon. And to your first question, I continue to support Congressman Jeffries and his bid to become the leader.

q.t: So, three cyclists were killed by hit-and-run drivers last week, and one pedestrian was killed by a hit-and-run driver this weekend. Do you still support Vision Zero? And if so, what will you do to end these preventable crashes?

a.t:
Yes, I still support Vision Zero. I still support any initiative that we have to reduce the number of crashes across the city and to ensure that there is no longer a hierarchy of safety based on what mode of transit you're using. Whether you're a pedestrian, a cyclist, a driver, a public transit rider, you should be entitled to the same level of safety. 

And so, one of the things that I've spoken to with my deputy mayor for Operations, with our DOT commissioner, is how do we implement the changes to the streetscape that also understand the ways in which we are either incentivizing or disincentivizing safe choices made by New Yorkers. 

And so, a lot of this is actually delivering on the protected bike lanes that we have seen forgotten over many years in our city, as well as delivering more bus lanes and busways and bringing the first bus rapid transit corridor to Flatbush by 2030. 

These are all different steps that we're taking to address this. However, as you said, it is something that is immensely concerning, because we're talking about fatal consequences and families whose lives are irrevocably changed.

q.t:
Okay, and on Legionnaires', Mr. Mayor, on Friday, I reported that the Health Department is now saying that they don't expect to have the results of the source testing that they're doing, the genome sequencing to try to determine the source. Originally, the Health Department had said August, then they said late August. Now they're saying mid-September, which means it'll come after the Sept. 2 hearing that's scheduled with the City Council. 

Do you still anticipate your team testifying before that hearing, and do you expect a more difficult hearing on the Legionnaires' outbreak because those results will not have been in, or is it going to be an easier hearing for you because we won't know the source?

a.t:
You know, I think the Council has a role to play, and it is in conducting those kinds of hearings, and our job is to ensure that we're answering and delivering for New Yorkers when it comes to Legionnaires'. I'll get back to you specifically on the genome sequencing question. What I will say is that the cluster has been closed. It's been about five weeks since the identification of a new case. 

However, we know that Legionnaires' has been something that has afflicted our city on an almost annual basis, and we are looking at ways to ensure this is something that we deliver on for the weeks and months and years to come, but I do appreciate the question.

q.t: Okay. You mentioned here for the Parks announcement, you mentioned peace amidst the chaos. So, I wonder how much peace amid the chaos does a mayor actually get on vacation? Can you give us a sense of how many calls you had to take? What was the — did you get any middle-of-the-night phone calls or when the 911 system went down, for instance? And then I have another question.

a.t:
You are checking in with your team on a regular basis, not just only in the event of a crisis. And then obviously, if there is anything that comes up that demands your attention, you have to be there. You have to have some kind of cell service. 

But the peace of mind is also just a time to reflect and a time to rest. And I think it's also part of what we want for every New Yorker, that they also get time to actually step away from the day-to-day. And I'm incredibly appreciative of my team, who ensured that the work to deliver for the city continues unabated.

q.t:
I have two questions. Regarding the last-minute changes to the Brooklyn Democratic Party proposed by Assemblymember Bichotte Hermelyn, what are your thoughts on that, and have you talked to Julio Peña? 

My second question is regarding the paraprofessionals lawsuit. Your team has said they're currently in talks with UFT President Mulgrew regarding an agreement on the para pay. How have those talks been going, and how has the relationship with Council Speaker Menin been affected following the lawsuit?

a.t:
The relationship continues as it's been, and the talks have been productive. And they've been productive because we have a shared understanding of the critical role that paraprofessionals play in our public school system and in our city. And we are looking at ways to permanently address this inequity. And that's the subject of those conversations. 

And then to your first question, I very much oppose these proposed changes by the current Brooklyn Democratic Party chair. I oppose them because they are an attempt to circumvent the will of voters, and what we should see is a Brooklyn Democratic Party that is a reflection of what New Yorkers want to see in their home, as opposed to a representation of so much of what has led New Yorkers — and Americans — to become disengaged and disaffected with politics at large. 

[Crosstalk.]

q.t:
Two questions. One, my colleagues reported last week that a 911 call center in the Bronx went down overnight. Can you speak to what specifically caused that and what's going to be done to prevent those kinds of outages in the future? 

Second question, can you share any tidbits about how you spent your time upstate? You were spotted in Leeds and at, I think, a grocery store, Tops, buying roast chicken, I was told. Can you share anything about what you did, what you read? Is it still "Gods of New York"? Any tidbits.

a.t:
Yes, I bought two roast chickens at the Tops supermarket at Coxsackie. I also went to Casa Susanna in Leeds. I had a lovely time, and it was — it was very restorative, and I also stayed in touch with the team on a regular basis to make sure that all was always going well. 

And on one of those issues, you know, when it comes to the 911 calls, the issue has since been resolved, and the system is running normally. And again, what normally means is that every 911 call is being connected and responded to by a call taker. That's been the case since the issue was resolved. 

In terms of your question of how this happened, what we've identified at this time was an early morning software update by Motorola that created this issue. And that issue was then resolved by the morning of the same day, and we are now taking steps to ensure that that never happens again.

q.t:
I'm sure you did. I wanted to ask you: one of the leaders of the New York City DSA is facing questions about his background, his work history and where he lives. I wanted to know, you know, for you, somebody who comes from the DSA, do you still stand by him? And do you think that what has come out about him undermines the credibility of the movement that the DSA is about affordability and trying to keep people here, especially because his home is in Bed-Stuy, where a lot of Black New Yorkers are having to leave because homes are being bought up and are just unaffordable? 

And then the second question is, while you were away, the hearing on the pied-à-terre rollout happened. Before you left, you seemed to hint that your officials would be at the hearing, saying that you were confident in their ability to answer the questions despite the lawsuit that was ongoing about it, but then the day before, they didn't show up. 

So, I'm just wondering, you know, do you think that New Yorkers deserve to get answers from your administration when it comes to this rollout? And did you know at the time, the Thursday or Friday before — I can't remember — that your administration officials weren't going to show up at that hearing?

a.t:
So, the reason to not attend that hearing was on the basis of the legal consequences of doing so, because we are in the midst of a legal case on this very question. And so, we know that the hearing last week was explicitly focused on the very issues that are at the heart of that case. 

And we didn't believe that it would be in the legal interest of the city to send a senior representative. However, we did send a written statement from Commissioner Lee, and we also did inform the Council that the commissioner would be available to take any kinds of questions after Aug. 31 because by that point, there would not still be that same question of the legal concerns. 

And to your first question, look, I think anyone who is focused on delivering a more affordable life for the people of New York City, a fairer life for people of New York City and, frankly, of those of the world, should be welcomed into this work. And that's what I see so many doing, and that's the kind of initiatives and efforts that we continue to encourage.

q.t: How was your trip? Can you tell us where you were?

a.t: You know, I can tell you, I went to an incredible Georgian — sorry, an incredible Uzbek restaurant called Alons — I know, sorry. I saw the T-shirt; it says, "Cool Georgian Dude," and it just threw me. I don't know where he is now. He has the dog with him. But it was a lovely time upstate. Bounced around, missed the city, missed you guys, happy to be home.

q.t: Disruption you're going to cause by the construction, you know, the fact that you're going to have to build that overpass or whatever you call it, and will there cause it — will there be a disruption to local communities?

a.t: Yeah. So, the plan does require a bypass, a four-lane bypass at the level just below the promenade. Previous proposals had put that bypass on the promenade, which would have been quite disruptive. We feel this proposal does lessen the community impacts of prior proposals.

q.t: My second question has to do with your decision to take on the reconstruction of the BQE and the amount of money it's going to cost. Are you hoping to get federal funds, or do you think that you'll be able to pay for it out of the capital funds that New York City already has?

a.t: What we have announced today is something that will be done through city funds, and that is something that we have put forward because the cost of inaction is, frankly, too high. Every year that the city does not act on the BQE costs the city at least $160 million. And there have been many administrations that have understood the importance of this. We want to be one that also delivers on the fix to this central part of the BQE. I'll pass it over to our deputy mayor of operations to add some additional details.

As the mayor mentioned, this program, we aren't anticipating having any federal funds, and that enables us to advance this project on our timeline with our design, our scope and having complete control over our community benefits. So, it's a benefit to the program to be issuing those federal funds.

q.t: Is there anything that you can do to help these bodega owners who feel that they're going to be losing money?

a.t:
Absolutely. What we can do is continue with our approach citywide of looking for ways to cut costs and cut the regulations that so many bodegueros, as well as grocery store owners, have to jump through in order to do their work. 

And what we found through our OPEN Task Force is already the identification of more than 50 potential changes that target things from the current necessity of having two different licenses to sell hot food and cold, dairy, frozen dessert, as well as the kinds of things that make it harder for bodegas to both sell items outside of the store and inside of the store.

q.t:
First of all, Mr. Mayor, I thought I'd apply to be the chef at Gracie Mansion. 

[Crosstalk.]

So, two questions. The first one is this. A group of about 15 minority groups that represent bodega owners are filing suit to stop your city-run groceries. They say that your city-run groceries, and I quote, are "a direct assault on minority businesses by a mayor who claims to be a champion of the disenfranchised poor and working-class New Yorkers." How do you feel about that? They feel that they're being disenfranchised? And what's your response to their suit and their attempt to stop your city-run grocery stores?

a.t:
I continue to be fully confident in both the legality and the importance of our initiative to deliver five city-run grocery stores, one in each borough, to the people of our city. We are talking about a reflection of a cost-of-living crisis that has seen grocery prices increase by about 30 percent over the last few years. And we're also talking about delivering five city-run grocery stores in a city of 8.5 million people that has more than 1,000 grocery stores. 

And we've seen, in fact, with Essex Street Market in Manhattan as well as Moore Street Market in Brooklyn, a model where the city has subsidized groceries and it has not had a negative effect on bodegas around them or on grocery stores around them. And I'm confident both in the legality of this, that will stand up in court and the importance of delivering it —

q.t:
I mean, you're their landlord, so can you get some free tickets for people who want to go? I don't care about tennis, so I'm not asking for myself, but for other people, like — 

 [Crosstalk.]
It's happening right now, and there's been lots of coverage of how much more unaffordable it is this year, so is there anything you can do for this session of it to—

a.t: That's something we'll get back to you on.

q.t:
And quickly, my second question is about the U.S. Open. I know, Mayor Mamdani, you've made affordability one of your core issues. When it came to the World Cup, you gave away tickets. The U.S. Open, which happens on city-owned parkland that gets taken over for the U.S. Open for a few weeks out of the year — and generally, the public can't access a lot of the borough's largest park. It's more expensive than ever. They've reduced the number of Fan Fest tickets. I think they even reduced the number of cheaper tickets to favor more expensive tickets and then tickets given by sponsors. 

Is there anything you would want to do to make the U.S. Open more accessible to regular New Yorkers? And would you ever want to revisit the current deal that USTA has with New York City so New York City and particularly Queens actually makes more money if it's going to be more expensive and more unable for the average New Yorker to attend? Would you want to find a way to make New York City be able to actually better financially benefit from it? And particularly Queens.

a.t:
You know, I think we never want to accept the premise that something has to be unaffordable when it comes to a sporting event that is part of what so many love about our city. Some of my favorite memories as a kid growing up in New York City are going to the qualifiers for free before the [U.S.] Open began. I remember when I bought a grounds pass — I think it was $50 bucks for day one — and I know that that number has skyrocketed over recent years. 

So, we are always going to look to ways to make these kinds of events more accessible to everyday New Yorkers. That is not something that will be limited to the World Cup. And the reason for that is that it is a moment that can really open so many kids' eyes to the wonder of a sport that they may not know before. And as you've said, it is happening in one of the jewels of our city. So that's going to be something that we continue to work on, and it is something that continues to be a part of our affordability agenda.

q.t: For, you know, a place like, I think, Knickerbocker Avenue flooded in Bushwick, is there a current project nearby there? Because that place floods a lot.

a.t: Yeah, and as we see these places that have more common flooding, we have our agencies take a look at the specific situation. Sometimes it's a larger catch basin there, and sometimes it's a bigger project, and sometimes it's a repaving that changes the grading. So, we have to look at each neighborhood and figure out exactly what it is that is creating that flooding condition and then attack that problem.

q.t:
It wasn't like I reported it out. You guys, thankfully, let me have an early look at it. I have two questions. The first is about — I know you were away for it, and I know it's a persistent issue, but with the deputy mayor of operations here, the really bad flooding we saw not too far from here, it was in Bushwick and other parts of the city and here in Queens. I know what we're up against with the sewers not being able to handle this much rain, but is there really nothing more that the city can do to help stop some of this flooding? 

I know we're supposed to clean up catch basins, but at a certain point, what more can the city do on that? And then I have a second question about the U.S. Open — I don't know if you want to hear it now or wait.

a.t:
Fighting off my curiosity, I'm going to go for the first question and then we'll come back to your second one. This is one of the foremost priorities for our administration because, as you said, yes, we know the facts of the context, which is that we have a sewage system that was built for the rainfall of a century ago and that the climate crisis has intensified and increased that rainfall. 

And also, it is not going to be the case that we are simply going to sit on our hands until the day in which the sewage system is entirely overhauled. So, we are exploring every single avenue that we have, whether it is from the installation of cloudburst technology to the use of permeable pavement to the question of floodable parks, parks that are actually built to absorb that kind of excess rainfall. I'll pass it over to our deputy mayor for operations to add some additional details.

Thanks. And I think we think about this thing in a few layers, right? We have the, you know, real-time event management, where we have our agencies out there responding, doing things like clearing catch basins and checking our highways and doing additional passes with street sweepers. 

And then we have, as the mayor mentioned, a number of sort of like midterm programs, investing $100 million in modernizing catch basins, all the cloudburst programs that we've done, the rain garden projects that we have to do much more of, and then we have the bigger, longer-term investments, like the $3 billion program that we're putting into place to build more stormwater and sewers in southeast Queens. So, we put all of that together to try and create a comprehensive strategy to manage the future of climate change.

q.t: I wanted to ask you about the drop in reading scores. The UFT president, Michael Mulgrew, has criticized the way the DOE has implemented its literacy program, NYC Reads. He says unless the city makes some changes, he's going to pull teacher support for that program. And then my second question is about the pied-à-terre hearing. Given the fact that there's this ongoing lawsuit, are you comfortable with your administration officials testifying in that hearing? Because likely everything they say will be pulled for that lawsuit.

a.t: You know, I have confidence in our administration officials being able to navigate what are often concurrent obligations, both whether it be to a hearing or to an existing lawsuit. I was asked earlier about Elizabeth Street Garden, and I said the other day that there are few things more certain in New York City than death, taxes and Randy Mastro suing this administration, and that is, again, where that lawsuit is coming from when it comes to the pied-à-terre lawsuit. And then on your first question, I continue to be confident in NYC Reads. And it is developed with the real findings of what's been effective across the country in mind. And we know that it is a critical thing that we equip our public school students with. We look forward to being in conversation with the UFT as we look to not only build upon the successes of the last few years, but to go beyond that.

q.t: 12 noon.

a.t:
Okay, so then we'll be sure to look over them, and I appreciate all of these different initiatives that are all looking towards the same thing, which is how to deliver safety and justice in our city, and that continues to be a focus for us.

[Crosstalk.]

q.t: Court Watch NYC is going to release the results of its research into the number and nature of arrests in the city. I'm not asking you to comment on their findings; they haven't been released yet, but you are in regular communication with the police commissioner. Are you confident that she is executing your vision for policing in New York City?

a.t: Yes, I would not have someone serving our city if I was not confident in what they were doing, and I look forward to the release of these findings. Do you know when they are being released?

q.t: I wanted to ask you: yesterday's Siena poll came out; the governor and her rival, Blakeman, are only 10 points different. I wanted to get a sense from you if you plan to either help the governor while she campaigns — you had very good favorability ratings in that same poll — and what that might look like. Also, next week when you're actually on vacation, the pied-à-terre hearing is going to be happening for the Council. I wonder if you plan that perfectly for that, and also wondering — Trump this week said that he is looking at ways for the federal government to get involved when it comes to pied-à-terre. What do you think about your maybe bestie or not, frenemy at this point, getting involved?

a.t:
I think I'll leave it to the president to share his own opinions on it. I continue to believe in the importance of a surcharge on secondary homes worth more than $5 million as well as our ability to implement that surcharge. And just to go back to the importance of it — we're here today talking in some ways about art, but in other ways also about affordability. And the importance of a tax on a secondary home worth more than $5 million is that it raises half a billion dollars, and that is money that makes our streets safer. It makes our schools stronger. It makes the city the world-class city that we all love and know as our home. And I'm looking forward to all of the improvements that we can deliver with that revenue.
