And then, Kelly, the first question, yes, I do support the governor in her reelection, and I will be making that support clear at every opportunity that I have. And I also think there is a very clear choice here between Governor Hochel and Bruce Blakeman. Yesterday, I was standing with Governor Hochul as she announced that she was going to invest more than $7 million in funding to ensure that there are no unaccompanied minors without legal defense in our city. The Trump administration had made a decision that would strip these minors of their legal defense. Now, if a New Yorker looks at what ICE is doing and they want to see more of it, they should vote for Bruce Blakeman, who has created his own militia in Nassau County. If a New Yorker looks at what ICE is doing and is shocked by the inhumanity and the cruelty that is in the very heart of that agency's operation, then they should vote for Governor Kathy Hochul.

My vacation timing — it was not about this hearing.

q.t: I wanted to ask you about the meeting that you had earlier this week with the rabbis. I just wanted to see if you would be open to sharing feedback that you got from them and your thoughts and feelings after the meeting and how you think it went.

a.t: Thank you for the question. You know, I had a candid and productive conversation with rabbis representing a wide swath of New York's Jewish communities and affiliations, and I appreciated hearing from them. My door will always be open to every Jewish New Yorker, and that is a door that is open not only to a conversation, but also to a commitment of what it actually looks like to deliver on the ideal of a city where not only is everyone safe, but everyone belongs, everyone is made to feel as if this is their home. And our administration has been taking steps over the last many months of enacting that, whether it looks like increasing funding for hate crime prevention programming by more than 800 percent, or expanding our City's Office to Combat Antisemitism to its largest ever size, while developing a first-in-the-nation municipal response to combating antisemitism.

q.t: I wanted to ask you about the Elizabeth Street Garden situation. Can you just explain why you didn't try to go to the state lawmakers who may have power to actually move housing forward on that site and how you square — I know you've talked about building housing on every available city-owned lot, and yet here's this situation where that's put to the test and you don't do that. And then I have a second question about the push for a $3 city bike cap. Are you interested in making that program more affordable? I know you're an avid user of the program yourself.

a.t: Yes, I'm a “Bike Angel,” I think is the term. Though I haven't won enough points to recoup anything. Sorry, there's a $3 push you were saying? I mean, we are always interested in making Citi Bike and cycling in general more affordable, but I'll take that back to the team. And then on the first question, I think a lot of this comes back to the fact that the first deputy mayor of the former administration, Randy Mastro, took steps that rendered it nearly impossible to move forward on the fulfillment of a vision of building housing at the Elizabeth Street Garden. And we have a continued commitment to building housing everywhere that we can, and that is also why, as we take steps to resolve this case with the developers of that original site, we are going to be building 180 homes not too far away, as well as more even at 100 Gold Street.

q.t: I was encouraged when the chancellor mentioned that there is a hopeful expansion to younger kids as well, because we know that early exposure is important. But when you speak about Broadway especially, I'm very grateful and excited to hear about all of the support for cultural institutions like City Center. Is there a plan to support a cultural institution of Broadway that is not a cultural institution, [a] building or organization, and to support the commercial theater that brings so many people to the city and really is of all New Yorkers?

a.t:
Just to make clear, you're asking if there's a plan to support commercial theaters beyond the CIGs. That's something that we'll bring back to the team. We'll have that conversation. Thank you.

[Crosstalk.]

q.t: Mr. Mayor, it's great to see you take part in the announcement for this program. We don't usually see somebody of your caliber standing here in front and center. So, thank you for that. But I did want to ask, is this a one-time-only program or is it going to be continued in subsequent years?

a.t:
This is the beginning. And what I mean by that is that we are going to keep asking the question of how we can be working together, and how we can ensure that it is oriented towards all of our children, right? Nobody loses in this lottery because everybody wins this membership. Some also win 2,100 free tickets on top of that. But whether it's this lottery or it's other ways, we are going to continue to both invest time and resources to make the arts something at the fingertips of every New York City student.

[Crosstalk.]

And before you go, if I could also invite Assembly Member Simone, Dr. Nantasha Williams and Council Member Brewer. If they want to share what the Broadway musical was that made it for them.

Thank you, Mr. Mayor. I grew up in blue-collar Queens of Maspeth, and I didn't even know what Broadway was, and I didn't see my first Broadway show until I was in college. Although I can't recall which was the first show, I remember my husband now, my boyfriend at the time, Jason, saying, “You've never been to Broadway? We have to go to Broadway more.” And seeing “Angels in America” and seeing how it reflected something that I am and what I grew up with and what I saw around me, and it moved me.

So, I hope this program will move a child in this city to see himself or herself on stage. I also wanted to be an actor too. My father, he just recently passed away, he said, “You're acting, kind of, right now as a politician.” I told my father, “I'm not acting, I mean what I say.” And he goes, “I am just kidding with you. I love you.” And I'll leave it at that. But thank you for giving me the opportunity to speak because this is going to be an amazing program and I'm going to fight for funding in Albany too to make sure every kid in this city can afford to see themselves on stage and maybe also one day act.

Dr. Williams: My mom took me to see “Cats.” And like, I remember slightly falling asleep, because it's long, but I remember the costumes. So, I would say that was my first Broadway play, but I feel like most memorable was “The Lion King” after that.
Do we have Gale Brewer who is here with us? Oh well, we lost her. She's off to see a play. Broadway News, please.

q.t: I'm wondering, was there a Broadway show that you saw as a kid that inspired you? For me, it was “Annie” at the Martin Theatre. How about you?

a.t: I remember seeing “In the Heights” for the first time and being blown away because Broadway is something that you typically think of as a portal to another world; and yet when I went to go see “In the Heights,” it was a world that I knew, but to see it on stage, to see it with the depth, the fluency, the talent [and] the art, it was incredible. Still sometimes wake up singing 96,000. And I think that I want that experience for every New Yorker. I want them to be able to see a world they didn't know and sometimes to see themselves as well. I mean, I remember also watching “Fela!” the musical. That was an amazing experience, you know, to see an African icon and his life on stage right here in Midtown. It was a beautiful thing.

q.t: I guess, what is your plan to increase arts funding and access — not here at the City Center — but within schools all around the city? Not just at specialized schools or art specific schools, but to ensure that there is — every kid in New York City can learn an instrument, have a librarian in their library and then also perform in a play. I don't know if the chancellor wants to hop on. He's hiding in the back.

a.t: I'll just underline one thing that the deputy mayor said and then pass it over to the chancellor for additional details. We were proud to work with the Council to deliver more than $320 million in funding for DCLA and for arts institutions, that's a record amount of funding. And the reason we wanted to do that is even in a moment where we faced a $12 billion fiscal deficit, it is always a moment to invest in the arts. And we also created, for the first time, a stabilization fund for cultural institutions that were experiencing either unexpected or an emergent need, because we also know that since the pandemic, especially with the cuts from the federal government, there are a number of cultural institutions that are struggling today, and they need help to just keep their doors open. So, I'll pass it over to the chancellor.

a.s: Kamar Samuels, Chancellor, New York City Public Schools
a.t:
Yeah, super exciting to be here and super excited to talk about the arts, because we know that public schools play such an important role in terms of ensuring that our kids know our city. For someone like me who moved here and grew up in the Bronx, I was amazed when I came to my first Broadway experience, and we want to make sure that schools ensure that all of our students are having that experience.

And so, I also have our arts director, Paul Thompson, here, who is a part of ensuring that our principals make sure that they have the knowledge and the skills to engage with our arts residents, because that's a huge part of ensuring that every child has an experience in elementary school art. And one of the cool things that I was talking to our folks at TDF about is ensuring that — what if we ensure that every New York City Public School kid in middle school had a Broadway experience, right? That is something that we're seriously thinking about, but really ensuring that arts is a huge part of our kids' lives and that they know our city is one of the things that we are truly committed to.

q.t: I know this is an initial rollout of 2,000 tickets, but what are your plans for expansion? And if you want to talk a little bit more— I know there's been some writing about, I guess, the role of a lottery system with equity, which is one of your kind of core tenets. So, do you want to speak a little more about how that is used that way? And we can experience and expect more of this, because with how many, maybe the chancellor can speak to how many theater kids there are in the city, and 2,000 tickets. And unlike the World Cup, it doesn't end. So, I don't know if there are plans to add more.

a.t:
A theater kid, I think, is subjective. This is but one example of what is going to be a long term commitment to the arts, to culture and to ensuring that every New Yorker sees themselves in arts and culture. And I think it's 2,100 tickets that are free for any high schooler across New York City. But as you've heard all of us say, anyone who applies to this lottery will then get that free membership for the next few months. And that's a membership that can really expand your sense of the city and of the world.

I mean, you just heard Deputy Speaker Dr. Natasha Williams speak about the Louis Armstrong Museum. It is an incredible museum. I only saw it after I became the mayor. And this is one of the places where any high school student who applies for this lottery could now go to see for free. And that's what's so exciting is that the arts are also a portal to a world that you never even knew existed, let alone one that you thought had room for you. And we're always going to be speaking to our deputy mayor, to our DCLA commissioner, to our MOME commissioner, to everyone who helps to lead this work inside City government and all the partners outside as to how we can make it easier for kids to grow up with a sense that Broadway is for them as well.

q.t: On the pied-à-terre lawsuit, the city has continued to implement the tax while it appeals the decision from Monday. But if the court ultimately rules in favor of the plaintiffs in that case, does that mean all this implementation work is for nothing? Is the city doing anything to prepare for that fact if they have to start from scratch? And also on Elizabeth Street Garden, did you ask the legislature after coming into office if they would at all be willing to explore lifting that designation?

a.t: I think we've been clear that the actions of the prior administration made it nearly impossible to proceed on that vision and proceed on it in a way that would be realistic. And when it comes to your first question, we continue to be confident not only in the importance of a tax on secondary homes worth more than $5 million in the necessity of the half a billion dollars it would raise towards making sure that our streets are safer, making sure that our schools are stronger, that our city is more affordable. And also, our Law Department has informed Mr. Mastro that it will appear before the Appellate Division Second Department on Thursday morning to address the stay and any other related matters.

q.t: Anyways — wanted to ask you two very different things, having nothing to do with what you just talked about. The Elizabeth Street Garden. Your administration is gonna walk away from the plan to build housing in the garden. How do you explain doing this given you promised last year that you would move forward with that plan? And then on a totally different topic, the City Council announced today that it's launching an investigation into prediction markets. I'm curious where you stand on the idea of regulating prediction markets? Do you think there needs to be more regulation on that in order to protect from deceptive marketing practices? And who do you think should ultimately regulate prediction markets? The state or the federal government?

a.t: I think to be direct, yes, I think there needs to be more regulation. I think it's an open conversation as to what each level of government should do. However, I don't think that we have seen the limits of that regulation as yet. And I appreciate, especially the attorney general, for having taken action on this. I think that was a couple of weeks ago. And on your first question, you know, it was in the campaign itself before the general election that I shared with New Yorkers that the actions of former First Deputy Mayor Randy Mastro made it nearly impossible for any future administration to be able to fulfill a vision of building housing on the Elizabeth Street Garden site. So, while we are working to resolve the lawsuit with the developers who are set to build upon that site, we continue to believe in the importance of building more affordable housing. And that is why we are going to be building more than 180 homes at 22 Suffolk Street and more at 100 Gold [Street] as well.

q.t: So, a group of organizations are conducting sit-ins at courthouses across the city to review arraignments and just watch in on them. They're saying under your administration, arrests for low-level arrests have remained high or even increased. They also cited data from the Mayor's Office of Criminal Justice that the number of arrests from January to June of this year exceeded 50 percent. They're kind of calling on you to address this and stand up to your campaign promises of addressing low-level arrests. I just wanted your response on this. They're supposed to be releasing their findings tomorrow.

a.t:
I look forward to the release of their findings, and I think that if I'm understanding your question correctly, if they're engaging in court watch and they're going to observe these kinds of proceedings, that's an important part of our criminal legal system. And I've made very clear that I don't believe New Yorkers should have to choose between safety and justice. We have to be able to deliver both of these things. And I was sharing earlier about some of the achievements that our administration is proud of when it comes to the fewest murders on record and comes to the fewest shooting incidents on record. And also, we know that every single day is an opportunity to do better. So, I look forward to the findings, and we'll review those. Thank you.

[Crosstalk.]

q.t: So, as of recently, as [of] last fall, the NYPD would go to conferences in Israel with the Israeli National Police. This past January, Speaker Julie Menin also mentioned that she would not stop plans if the council had plans to take these trips to Israel. Based on the recent comments that you have made against Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, does your — does the NYPD or the City Council have current plans to visit Israel this fall? And if so, do you think that your comments might cause a backlash on the reception?

a.t: I don't know what the City Council's plans are. They're an independent body, and I'll leave it to the speaker to answer that question. I can follow up with the NYPD to find [out] about those plans. I'll tell you, most of my focus today is Tremont Avenue busway, but I will follow up on that, and we'll let you know.

q.t: I want to ask you about something AOC said over the weekend that you probably heard in an interview, where she quoted Council Member Chi Ossé who once said on Twitter or X, “Woke 1 was crazy.” And she was talking about it in response to questions about whether the left has some sort of — during that time whether how she responds to some unpopular or controversial proposals on the left like defund the police. And I wonder what you make of that? What do you make of that statement, because you yourself have walked back [from] “Defund the Police.” Do you think Woke 1 was crazy?

a.t: Look, I think that each person has a responsibility to tell New Yorkers, to tell Americans when they're running for office, what they believe. And sometimes what you believe can change, it can develop, it can grow. And I know that there are some for whom they still believe in that. I've made very clear that I do not believe in defunding the police, that I will not be defunding the police. And that to me, delivering critical public safety also looks like working with our police department alongside many other partners. And we've seen over the first seven months of this administration what that can look like when we're talking about the fewest murders on record in New York City; the fewest shooting incidents on record in New York City. And that to me is how we measure a lot of our public safety.

q.t: So, mayor, everyone knows you campaigned on fast and free, and you have talked recently about [how] you still want to pursue free, but New Yorkers now understand that's not happening right away. But on the fast part of it, level-setting-wise, are these busways going to make buses fast or just faster from the slowest in the country? Because six minutes each way, there might be some New Yorkers hearing about this saying, doesn't sound very fast to me.

a.t:
You know, I think every day is an opportunity to do better for the city. The first thing we want to do is improve from where we are. As you've said, we're talking about a bus that at times is crawling at slower than five miles an hour. So yes, we have to make it faster. Our goal is to make it fast.

And what that is going to come from is not only the busways that we're speaking about, like the one on Tremont today, but it's also going to come at its peak from bus rapid transit. And that is an example of how we're going to utilize every tool that we have to make it such that these are not only achievements relative to where we were prior to this administration, but they are achievements in and of themselves.

q.t: So, we're very excited about this busway here at Streetsblog, but we also all know that a busway [and] bus lanes, they're only as good as the enforcement, keeping cars out of them. And NYPD data showed last week that the uniformed officers in the department only gave out nine bus lane tickets for parking in bus lanes across the entire city in a week. And I know that the NYPD is supposed to be a really big partner in the Fast Buses Plan. So, what do you have to say about that kind of effort, given how important they are to keeping bus lanes clear [and] bus stops clear, places like that?

a.t: I think, as you said, enforcement is critical to ensuring that our buses can actually travel at the speed that we are building the streetscape for them. In addition to NYPD enforcement, though, one critical part of this is also ACE and ABLE, and ensuring that we're expanding the number of miles across the city where we are able to hold those accountable who are deliberately trying to slow down our buses by being in those very lanes, oftentimes seen by consecutive buses. So, we will follow up on whatever enforcement that we can enhance. However, the importance of enforcement is not lost on us at all.

q.t: Mayor, you had the first bus town hall event last week. Are you planning on doing something similar in the Bronx for this, you know, bus rapid transit plan over here on Tremont?

a.t: You know, we are going to continue to engage with New Yorkers to hear from them of how best we can speed up their commutes. I'm going to pass it over to our Deputy Mayor Julia Kerson to speak more about the additional details on this.
Thank you. Yes, we will be kicking off community engagement here later this year.

q.t: Kind of along the lines of Evan's question, this station seems like it has ideal conditions with other stations; you know, the heat, where is it gonna go? In this case, there's municipal buildings where it's kind of clear what the path would be, but with more like private building ownership, would it be as easy to do this?

a.t:
I mean, [the] mayor and I were talking about this before we came out this morning. We are taking advantage of an existing underground connectivity and network that makes it easy to feed it. But the key is that you're actually capturing the excess heat, storing it and that is taking place here in this station complex.

And seeing how efficiently that can be done – how much heat we can store, how that reduces the temperatures in the stations – are two of the three big variables. There's obviously the piping network that will allow you to deliver it to adjacent buildings. But there are a lot of places in New York City where there's connectivity below grade. We all know the Con Ed steam network and so on and so on, and there are individual campuses like Rockefeller Center, which might be advantageous opportunities.

q.t: The DCAS commissioner mentioned that something about this station having an abandoned center platform was part of why this might work. Can you tell us a little bit about – and I know that we're studying the feasibility – but what about this station makes this something that can be used for the heat pumps, and are there some technological restrictions about where this can be put?

a.t:
Evan, I'm going to have to give you a bit of an 'I-owe-you' because somebody will get into that level of detail, but the way it's going to work is that they're going to do burrowing holes for geothermal right below the platform we are on, which is this unused center platform.

And we think that that's the most advantageous location relative to both the underground conditions and also the connectivity to the underground piping network that feeds City Hall and the other buildings that are served by this connected network. But for more detail on that, I'll have to ask someone to follow up with you.

q.t: I'm just hoping to get some more clarification about your conversation with the president. Did you speak with him before you issued that statement on Friday, and then just kind of trying to get in your head as well about why you decided to issue that statement on Friday night? It was past 5 p.m. It seemed like, from some talking to people, it seemed like it was a little hidden. Why not hold a press conference and maybe explain your frustration with this ruling?

a.t:
You know, I spoke to the president prior to that, and I made clear to the president, as I've made clear to anyone across the city, the vital importance of TPS. Again, TPS is something that is granted, also in recognition of the conditions of anyone's home country. When we are talking about the conditions in Haiti today, they are very similar to the conditions that led to the authorization of TPS. We are talking about a place that the United States government is recommending to Americans to not visit, even going further than that. And for us in this moment to tell Haitian New Yorkers who have made the city their life for years that they have to go back to that; it is terrifying to imagine what might be waiting for them there.

And we're also talking about Haitian New Yorkers who have been truly at the heart of so many of the industries that power this city – health care, construction, hospitality, city workers – so many different aspects that, without which, we wouldn't have the city that we have today. And we also wanted to make sure that we only took this action at the point at which it was legally required to do so, because this is not an action that we want to take in any which way or form.

And we also took this knowing that if we waited any longer, it might come to the detriment of those who hold TPS today, who might be able to find an alternate legal status here in New York City due to whatever other status that they also may enjoy. We've seen this before. For example, someone who holds TPS might also have a secondary student visa [or] things of this nature. We don't want to be hurting those New Yorkers' abilities to stay in the city.

q.t: And then secondly, I just wanted to ask if you have any update or any comment on the investigation into the boat crash near the Statue of Liberty over this weekend?

a.t:
I was heartbroken to learn about the tragic boating incident in New York Harbor that killed a young mother and her five-month-old daughter. And my thoughts are with the family and their loved ones as they grieve this devastating loss, and I know that many New Yorkers feel exactly the same way.

And I'm deeply grateful, as well, to the members of the NYPD and the FDNY who responded to this emergency swiftly and performed vital, life-saving work, which ensured that many New Yorkers' lives were actually saved in the process of that. Now, we will continue to update New Yorkers with any information as we have. That is what we have at this time.

q.t: And do you know how long that will take, the design work? Is there a timeline for that process?

a.t: I think a lot of that depends on what the findings are of the study, as Chair Lieber shared.

q.t: If this is starting in 2027 for the feasibility study, realistically, how long do you think that study is going to take? And when exactly would this all go into effect when people could actually feel a difference on the platforms?

a.t: So, we are actually aiming to confirm the geothermal feasibility by the end of this calendar year. And if it is found that it can be implemented, then the design work would begin early next year.

q.t: Do you have any regrets on the rollout?

a.t: You know, this is – we always know that with any new tax, there are more questions than there are answers. And we're looking to make sure that every New Yorker that is potentially affected – again, we're talking about 17,000 homeowners out of a city of 8.5 million – have all the information that they need, and we've extended the deadline for them to appeal to the Department of Finance to September 18. Again, if they do not appeal by that point, they can still appeal to the Tax Commission by March of 2027.

q.t: Wondering if you can respond to the pied-à-terre tax lawsuit that was filed on Friday. It's going to court today – how your legal team is working on that? And then also, do you have any regrets on how the rollout was done? And what are your thoughts moving forward on that?

a.t:
You know, there are a few things more certain in New York City than death, taxes and Randy Mastro filing a lawsuit against this administration. So, we look forward to vigorously defend our city's position in court as we have done so with the previous lawsuits that he has filed and I'm sure with the lawsuits that we will continue to file in the months and years to come. And we are confident in our position.

And that is a confidence coming from both the legality of the city's actions as well as the importance of a surcharge on secondary homes worth more than $5 million, a surcharge that will help fund safer streets, that will help fund stronger schools, and it will help fund the city that New Yorkers deserve.

q.t: When it comes to your pick for the city's Board of Standards and Appeals, obviously it seems that some Council members aren't as happy with the pick. How do you feel about that, especially seeing as you have housing advocates that are actually supporting your pick, and you also have people that don't necessarily agree with you that more so lean conservative that are siding with you this time?

a.t: I believe that we have made the best possible pick for this position. We are speaking about someone who has all the requisite experience to combat the affordability crisis and build the kind of housing the city has not seen for a long time. And we know that the absence of that kind of housing has led to an increase in rents across New York City. We are talking about a city that has not been building at its required level since 1961. I know the comptroller is very passionate about housing construction. I don't know if there's anything you'd want to add.

We're in the midst of a housing affordability crisis. We desperately need to build more housing, and you have a leader in John Mangin who has been at the forefront of some of the biggest successes we've had in zoning in New York City of the last decade. He was instrumental in City of Yes, which modernized zoning around the city. He was instrumental in the Charter Commission that's now gonna allow for expedited approval of desperately needed housing all over the city. I couldn't imagine a more qualified leader. I definitely have – he has my full confidence, and to me he is the kind of leader we need right now amidst this terrible housing shortage.

q.t: Over phone or by text?

a.t: I spoke with the president and made it very clear that this is something of immense importance to this city, to our economy and to the welfare of all those who call the city home. And also, that the president is the only person that has the authority to extend TPS or to grant the Deferred Enforcement Departure and that that is something that would be welcomed by many of us.

q.t: Directly?

a.t: Yes.

q.t: [Inaudible]... directly to Trump about this?

a.t: Yes.

q.t: I wanted to ask about something that happened on Friday with TPS for Haitians. What do you say to New Yorkers who saw you folding to Trump potentially and firing Haitians who work for the city who have TPS?

a.t:
So, when it comes to the decision that the city made, it was one that we were forced to make by federal law, and that was as recently decided by the Supreme Court to review the work authorization of Haitian TPS holders and separate from any employees who have not established alternate paths to legal work. Only President Trump has the ability to restore TPS or to grant Deferred Enforcement Departure to affected TPS.

And doing so would provide not only those TPS holders with the certainty of knowing that they can continue to work and live in the city, [but] it would also demonstrate an immigration policy that is just and a commitment to an economy that is flourishing here in our city.

Now, we are doing everything that we can to support recipients in a time of incredible instability. That means free legal consultations to assess eligibility for other forms of work authorization. It means assistance navigating health insurance. It means ensuring that every employee is connected with agency staff.

And what I will also add is that we are talking about communities, Haitian New Yorkers [and] Syrian New Yorkers, who have been critical parts of this city. Just the other week I was at National Night Out in Bed-Stuy at Restoration Plaza. I got on the train. As I was waiting for the train at the platform, a young woman came up to me and burst into tears as she shared that she was, in fact, a Haitian New Yorker who was on TPS. She was terrified.

This is something that is true for so many. And we are only taking the actions that we are forced to take. When it comes to what we want to see in this city and in this country, it is the extension of TPS. It is ensuring that these New Yorkers are recognized for what they are, which is New Yorkers, and that they are here; they are at home. I don't know if –

q.t: So, something similar was done in 2000 at Grand Central. How is this different? And is that still happening at Grand Central, the cooling system at Grand Central that was put in?

a.t: I'm pretty sure the cooling system in Grand Central is a very spotty kind of spot air-conditioning network that you experience when you're on the platform. So, this is a much more systematic and comprehensive approach that captures heat and stores it and transfers it in a way that Grand Central, as far as I know, that Grand Central initiative did not. I'll look at it, Sam, see if I'm wrong, but that's my understanding.
Yes, Sam, that air flows down from the terminal above, so it's an unusual situation [in] the commuter terminal.

q.t: This is what this one's for you, unless Janno has some really big thoughts on Summer Streets. You know, there's an op-ed in Streetsblog this weekend from a Manhattan Community Board member. He argued that instead of using police cars for traffic control and security, the city should invest in some kind of proven anti-vehicle technology that you could put barriers for security purposes. And since it would be kind of a bother to put up [to] do it for an entire weekend to make Summer Streets Saturdays and Sundays. Just curious if you have any thoughts on that if you've read the op-ed?

a.t: Summer Streets is one of the many things that we care very deeply about. It's also a day that so many New Yorkers look forward to, and each year has built on the successes of the last, so I will take those recommendations and I will read that op-ed.You were saying it's about extending the day, perhaps, to an entire weekend and adding in –

q.t: The question for both of you is, I know that this is preliminary, but just in terms of what potentially this could look like, how much cooler are we looking at, and what would be a success in terms of this station if the average is 96 [degrees] in the summer?

a.t: I'll tell you, when you look at the goals for even modifying temperatures in subway stations, to take it down by a few degrees would be a significant improvement when those temperatures peak in mid-summer. So, we're not projecting, Stefanos, exactly how much it would deliver, but we wanna see if we could get it down a few degrees. That would make the difference between total misery and merely sweltering on some of our worst days, and we want to make sure that we're just improving the environment. We're not going to create an office air-conditioned environment, but our goal is to improve it dramatically.

I think just to give you a sense, Stefanos, we are talking about a timeline where we are aiming to confirm geothermal feasibility by the end of this calendar year, and then design work, if it was found to be implementable, would begin as early as next year.

q.t: And for the both of you, if you'll pardon the pun, is this event proof that you guys are cool with each other? Because you weren't exactly on the same page when it comes to the free buses.

a.t: I think that the two of us are New Yorkers, and that means that we're never going to agree on every single topic that comes to us. What we do agree on is the critical importance of delivering for New Yorkers and making this public transit system the envy of the world. And I never thought I'd want to bring the heat of the Chambers Street Station into my office, but that's basically what we're talking about. And what we could see is a first-of-its-kind approach that could lead the nation. And that is in many ways what the MTA has done for many different decades. It's time to now bring that to 2026.
My response: I agree with the mayor.

q.t: Three years ago, you and Jamie announced a study of whether it was practical to potentially air-condition some stations. Is this related to that or wholly different, and what became –

a.t: Let's be honest, air conditioning is a big challenge in a system where you have so many openings. We have the vents. We have the stairways. We have all these other exits. It's really hard to create an enclosed environment to air-condition. We're still studying it, but this is in some ways a more promising approach, which is just to capture the waste heat, take it out of the system so temperature goes down and then use that heat to heat adjacent buildings in the winter. We love this idea, but we gotta study the heck out of it to make sure it works.

q.t: So, just as a follow-up, what would you like to say to strap hangers who are going to see – you hope – a big difference when they get off the subway at the station?

a.t: Here's the bottom line: You know, the New York I grew up in, the trains didn't come and they weren't air-conditioned. We have, even with the low level of investment in the MTA, we finally have a fleet which is mostly air-conditioned. We all know that it ain't perfect, and service is a lot better, so you get on an air-conditioned train faster and more predictably. Now we are attacking the third leg of that stool, which is to make the stations more livable. We know that this is no fun for New Yorkers. We're determined to do something about it.

I would just add that when we're talking about the heating costs, as you heard from the comptroller, it's $1.4 million to the city just to heat the David Dinkins Municipal Building. So, this has the potential to save the city money. It has the potential also to help us combat the climate crisis and to better the experience of riders across New York City.

We have; I think it's almost 20,000 riders who use this station daily. For too long, it has become synonymous with the use of this station. And I think what you're hearing from Chair Lieber and from so many others here is that we're incredibly excited to be writing a new chapter of our city and one that matches the ambition that we've seen in our city about a century ago.

[Crosstalk.]

q.t: Janno, I know that it's going to cost about $800,000 to do a pilot study. How much would it cost to expand this to all the subway stations if it turns out to be a workable thing? And the second thing is, how much would you save in terms of energy costs if you could heat all the municipal buildings down here?

a.t: I don't think you're looking for a second career, but I would say you asked all the right questions. Those are the questions that the study is meant to answer. How much did it cost to do this here, Marcia, where we actually have a network of underground pipes connecting City Hall and the other buildings? How much energy savings, what energy savings for the city, but also what is the benefit in terms of a reduced temperature for the subway station? So those are the questions that this is meant to answer. If we get good answers, you know we're going to be looking for other opportunities to deploy it elsewhere in the city.

q.t: Thank you, mayor, for providing this platform. My question is: What is New York City’s plan to ensure immediate access to drinking water during extreme heat events? Is the city considering water pouches, bottles or IV water pouches, their distribution at subway centers and parks, cooling centers, et cetera?

a.t:
I really appreciate this question, and I think you heard it from our DEP Commissioner that we do have the best drinking water in the world. And one of the most beautiful things about it is that this water is water that you don't have to purchase a water bottle to have. You can find it at a water fountain in your local park. Just yesterday, I was alongside a number of incredible Parks workers helping to bring to life a few additional water fountains in Prospect Park. This is work that is going to continue because we want to make it easy for New Yorkers to stay hydrated wherever they are.

And then you heard it earlier — when it comes to this heat wave, when it comes to heat indices of around 100 degrees — we want to encourage everyone to drink even more water than they would think they need to. It is important to stay hydrate in this time. It is important to take every precaution you can. We will have water available at our hundreds of cooling centers. We also have cool vans, which is a new approach that we've started, where these are mobile vans that have electrolytes; they have cold water; they have a place for people to cool down with air conditioning. They also have food to ensure that people are staying healthy. And that will be the case across the five boroughs. And it will also be the case that we have check-ins with older adults that are vulnerable to this level of temperature, because we know that every year around 500 New Yorkers lose their lives as a result of the heat. And we'd never want people to simply treat this weekend like any other. We want them to be prepared for what is very serious conditions and take every precaution they can.

Thank you so much. Thank you. All right. Do you have anything else, commissioner? Okay. Well, thank you all for joining us. That's all we have time for today on the question front. In a moment, one of our colleagues from DEP is going to come up and do a flood demonstration, but that's it for questions. Thank you. We're going to conclude the live stream. If you have more questions here in the room, feel free to come up to me or Ivonne, and we'll get those answers for you. Thanks again
Thank you so much.

q.t: [Inaudible] work together with the Trump administration in order to get finally these resources?

a.t: I think we have to be realistic as to what the administration's focus has been, what policies they've pursued, and always leave the door open in case there is a change of approach. We will never be above working with anyone if it can benefit New Yorkers.

q.t: So basically, I understand this proposal that the city has in order to try to prevent flooding. And since you invest more resources, the results are going to be better. So, my question is: Do you have any plan including the Trump administration in order to work together as a team to have more resources trying to make more benefits for people in these kinds of situations? Or so far, the Trump administration is not included in these kinds of plans?

a.t:
I will always look for any possible partnership, whether at the federal or state level, to deliver for New Yorkers. I will also be honest that while we leave that door open, what we have found instead when it comes to the federal administration has oftentimes been cuts to funding to programs that are incredibly important. Today, we are speaking about a heat wave, and we're also speaking about the health impacts of that heat wave.

If we speak about federal policy as it pertains to health, it's been a lot of very cruel cuts that have significant impacts on New Yorkers' ability to stay healthy in the city. And I know that that is a lot of what Commissioner Martin's work focuses on. I don't know if there's anything that you'd want to add, too.

Dr. Martin: Absolutely. Thank you. Our responsibility at the health department is to protect the health and safety of New Yorkers, and core to that is making sure that New Yorkers have health coverage they can rely on and depend on. And what we've seen recently, at least with regard to federal policy — I’ll give you a specific example of HR1 — attempts to chip away to undermine that sort of core, that bedrock that New Yorkers rely on.

We’ve seen it recently with cuts to the Essential Plan, which have meant that hundreds of thousands of New Yorkers now don't have access to reliable and affordable health insurance. And we're also concerned about the coming changes that will begin in January when these Medicaid changes take effect. But our role, our responsibility at the Health Department and across city agencies under this mayor, is to step in when the federal government steps back from its responsibility, and that's what you can expect from us.

q.t:
My name is Aisha Arain from [inaudible] NYC. My question was on language accessibility. So, we are based in Midwood, Brooklyn, which is an immigrant community. And like a lot of immigrant communities in New York City, a lot of its residents do not use English as their primary language on a day-to-day basis. A lot of the older residents aren't on Instagram; they aren't online.

If they call a hotline, will someone be able to speak their regional language? A lot of these older residents have medical conditions that are exacerbated by heat, especially. And they may be victim to some of those statistics that we were talking about earlier. So, are there any new initiatives or older ones that are in place for residents who do not have English as their primary language? Thank you.

a.t: I'll start, and then I'll pass it over to you. I think your question also highlights the importance of roundtables like this one, because we know that there are many New Yorkers for whom English may not be their first language. And the publications around this table may be the ones that they read; the radios may be the ones that they listen to; the TVs may be the ones they watch. And we want to make sure that there is no hierarchy of information based upon what language you speak in the city; that every person who lives in the city understands both the heat wave that we are speaking about, the ways in which they should prepare, and the tools that they have on offer. So, language access is critically important to us, also in the services that we provide. And I'm just going to pass it over now to NYCEM to add a few additional details to that.

Thank you, mayor. Thanks for the question. So, we absolutely agree. Language access has been, you know, a core tenet of our emergency public notification program since the very beginning. NotifyNYC messages — that program I spoke about earlier — are available in the 13 most-common languages spoken in New York City, and people can register. It includes American Sign Language. All of our messages have video with closed captioning. And then if people need a different language, they can call 311 and 311 has access to hundreds of languages through their translation service. And they can read the message to the New Yorker and make sure they get the information that they need.

q.t: I wanted to ask, as you know well, having represented Astoria and Long Island City, the outer boroughs as they were — You're looking at neighborhoods, by and large, that have been redlined and often suffered disproportionately because of disinvestment and neglect, and so they are hotter, they are more dangerous because of the heat and because of related circumstances. So, I'm wondering what your message would be to residents in these communities that feel that, in fact, they have been overlooked and that they're scorched — they are really in a bad spot. And what your administration specifically sees as an imprimatur to change that. What does it look like after you're done with this?

a.t:
I think the first thing I would say to these neighborhoods is: “We hear you.” We are speaking about neighborhoods in our city that have either been last on the list or not on the lists at all. And I think that the clearest way to show a recognition of that is to demonstrate a different course of action. And so, one of the critical parts of our response has also been investment. How do we ensure that we are investing the requisite amount of money to transform the material reality of these New Yorkers? You spoke of southeast Queens; we have a multi-billion-dollar commitment of investing in flood prevention initiatives in southeast Queens.

And when we're looking across the city, the different kinds of things we can do; it goes from porous pavement, to bioswales, to cloudburst technology, to any which way that we can both absorb more water as well as prevent the kind of flooding that we have seen become the norm. The other thing I would add is that I understand that it will take time to earn New Yorkers' trust in these neighborhoods, because when it was flooding in Hollis recently, and I went and I spoke to a number of homeowners, a woman told me that she has had to deal with this for 30 years. That's many different mayoral administrations; I would not begrudge her if it takes her time to trust this one.

And we are looking at everything we can do differently. You know, we procured flood kits that — I'm sorry, pump kits — that can actually help these homeowners to pump out some of the excess water that they have had to deal with. And that's now a part of our response strategy. And we are exploring a number of different ways in which we can turn the page on what's really been a story of neglect for many, many years.

[Inaudible.]
Yes, that it includes every single option that we have, absolutely. Thank you

The data for us, when we were looking at where we do deploy — for instance, our cooling centers at the health department — was pointing us in these very neighborhoods, in tree neighborhoods; places like Tremont and the Bronx and East Harlem and Brownsville, Brooklyn. And so, our cooling center deployment was very much focused on: how do we make sure communities that need these resources get these resources from the Health Department, as well as our misting stations, where outdoor workers and deliveristas are enjoying this resource and staying cool? Similarly, we used the data and the evidence to demonstrate where to deploy those resources. For instance, the misting station in Jackson Heights that I referenced earlier. So from our standpoint, the data is driving the deployment of these resources at the health department, as well.

q.t: A lot of our riders, they live in southeast Queens [and] central Brooklyn, and they rely on public transportation. And we see oftentimes during these storms that these subways are flooded. Any plans in place to work with the MTA to provide alternate transportation routes? And then, particularly, what we often see is that the ride-sharing apps have surcharges; [is there] anything in place there to prevent that during these storms?

a.t:
So, I — when it comes to the MTA, we have been having conversations with them as to all that we can be doing together to combat flooding. As you know, we have seen this in our city for years and decades, and we also know that it's not acceptable. And a lot of this is a legacy of sewage infrastructure that is more than 100 years old. And yet, we are looking at every single avenue we have to make it easier for New Yorkers to get around the city, because we know that no matter how hot it gets, no matter how cold it is, there are still many New Yorkers who have to get to work. And we want to make sure that this is as easy as possible for them.

Separately, a lot of what we see when it comes to flooding, we are looking to take as many preventative measures as we can. I'm proud to say that in large part, thanks to the incredible work of DEP, we have cleared over 71,000 catch basins in the seven months that we've been in office. We are talking about a period of time where a fourth of this year so far has been under a flash flooding advisory. And when we clear those catch basins, we know that that makes it much easier for us to actually ensure that the water is going into our system, as opposed to it being blocked from that because of garbage or whatever else you may have.

When it comes to the rideshare companies and the surcharge, you know, this is the business model that they have. [It] is one of surge pricing at different points. I would say that it is as good a moment as any to remind New Yorkers that yellow cabs do not have [surge pricing], public transit does not have these kinds of surge pricing, and these are exactly the places that if you want to find stable, consistent pricing, you'll still find them in the midst of these conditions.

q.t: The second question is: last year, former Mayor Adams proposed a pilot program to legalize basement apartments as a way to expand housing conditions. But we also saw tragic cases of residents living in the basement unit dying during flooding. So, what's your administration's plan for moving forward with these proposals?

a.t:
Our plan, first and foremost, is a plan about safety. How do we ensure that every New Yorker is living in a safe and habitable place? And one of the ways we do that is by bringing basement apartments up to code. And so, what we have done differently in our administration is we've actually invested more than $1 million in bringing a program to life for homeowners who want to ensure that they have a habitable basement apartment that they can rent out.

And the reason, as you've said in your question, is that there are many New Yorkers who already live in basement apartments. However, they are living in apartments that do not have all of the standards that would make them a healthy place. And then, in a moment of this kind of flooding, that is brought to bear. And amidst this, I also know that we can pass it over to NYCEM, but NYCEM also has specific messaging for residents of basement apartments. A specific messaging line [and] a specific chat that is looking to always ensure that New Yorkers know when they need to get out of that apartment, when they need to get to higher ground.

Because as you've said, April, we've seen in previous storms that a number of these fatalities have occurred in these kinds of apartments. I used to represent Astoria and Long Island City in the State Assembly during [Hurricane] Ida. That was some of the closest calls that we had, and we know that some people lost their lives elsewhere in the borough of Queens. I don't know if there's anything you'd want to add.

Thanks, Mr. Mayor. Great — I appreciate the question. As the mayor said, we do have as part of the NOTIFY NYC system, which we encourage every New Yorker to sign up for, and they can do that by downloading the app, through the App Store on either Apple or Android or visiting nyc.gov/NOTIFYNYC. We have a specific basement notification group, where we send out messaging to those that live in basement apartments any time that there is a flooding risk.

And I'll also just add that for the first time in the city's history, when we had two cases of high risk of flash flooding overnight, we opened up 51 [of] what we call safe locations, one in every City Council district across the city, to give New Yorkers who want a safe place to ride out the storm that was not their basement apartment, a safe place to go.

Thank you for your question. Just a reminder, we just want to get to as many people as possible. So, please just one question per person and also remember the microphones; they cannot hear you on the live stream if you do not have the microphone.

q.t: The first one is related to the delivery workers and outdoor workers because outdoor workers have to work during extreme conditions. So, I'm wondering what protections does the city currently provide for these workers, and are there any plans to strengthen those protections as the extreme weather becomes more frequent?

a.t:
Yeah, I think first, thank you for your question, because as you've laid out, there are a number of New Yorkers for whom their workplace is outdoors. And when the weather reaches this level of intensity — again — we are talking about a heat index of around 100 degrees. We know that the consequences for those who are outside can be serious. And to your question — yes — we are continuing to work on this. This was the subject of an executive order that I signed not that long ago, where guidance is being created across City government.

Even in advance of that, we have been sending out information to employers to encourage them to create plans for their employees who have to work out in the heat. And we know that there are many workers for whom the absence of those plans have real impact on their health. At that press conference where I signed the executive order, we heard from an airport worker who spoke about the fact that the heat index is one thing. Oftentimes in these workplaces, it is even higher because of the nature of the job. So, when he was loading bags onto a plane, I think it was at least designed to protect—

[Audio Drops].

—mayor signed to protect workers in these inclement weather scenarios. Our role in that is to help craft the health-related guidelines and criteria by which we at the Health Department will convey those guidelines to other city agencies and also use that as a model for the private sector here in the city. And I think there is an opportunity for us in the city to provide a model for other cities to do this in a way that keeps workers safe as well.

q.t: If it were me, they would kick my ass out. They'd say, “Get out.” Listen, I want to thank you for being here. And I want to tell y'all, you know, fear sells, but showing up and being in front of the people — that's more powerful than fear. And I want us all to be aware of that. That we have to see beyond, whether it's New York or Michigan, see beyond how they want to divide us. That's how they win. We can be in this collectively. Any final words?

a.t: No. I just want to say thank you for having me. And thank you all for being here because it is a choice of how to spend your time. And to have you all be here to ask these questions, to share your reflections and your experiences with me, it's something that I now get to take from this room and have be a part of the compass that guides this work. So, thank you all so much.

q.t: But there isn't one person that you feel—

a.t: I'm looking for somebody in their late 40s who's struggling with a cat [inaudible]...showing vulnerability, but also humility—

q.t: Because it can't be you, so like, is there anybody for like—

a.t: Ok, first of all, not me. I think we have a number of choices. I know that people are making their own choices, of whether or not they want to run. What I'm hopeful of is we're seeing a lot of examples of what it can look like to have that focus on the working person. People who understand that affordability isn't just something you say, it's something you have to deliver. And that in doing this, we're not running away from the Democratic Party; we're going back to what the party used to be. You think about FDR and La Guardia, you think about the New Deal; that's what the Democratic Party once was. That's what it could be again. And if we want to win, I think that's what we have to become.

q.t: People — if you could run for president, people would be shook. I mean, there's talk about this because this is somebody who could win. But I do want to ask you, is there anybody out there, if you think about this year called 2028, that's resonating with you as, “oh, they could be a pretty good contender for the Democratic nomination for president?” Is there anybody out there? It's just, as you and your wife are sitting back talking about life and politics, anybody out here that says, oh—

a.t: You're just sitting on the edge of Roosevelt Island right now, you just cast out. You're like, let me just fish!

q.t: You brought up a swing state, Michigan—

a.t: Oh, I’ve done this to myself. I see Jeff May smiling in the background.

q.t: So, before you go, I know you aren't going to answer, so I'm going to try.

a.t: Go for it.

q.t: The fear-mongering around it is just so interesting. But when you're engaging the people, it's obvious that it's about helping the working class. Outside of the labels, I don't care what it is, as long as it works.

a.t: And I think that's what I've heard from New Yorkers is, “I don't care what you describe yourself as, as long as there's room for me.”
Right.

And people have struggled in this city. So many of the people who helped to build this city are the ones struggling in this. And they are tired of bankrupt politics. Whether it's morally bankrupt or economically bankrupt or politically bankrupt, they want to see a government that works as hard as they do. They want a government that is as cautious with the way that it spends its money as they are when they're at the grocery store. And for too long, it's felt as if that's too much to ask.

And as much of a New York supremacist as I am, I also know that it's not just New Yorkers who are struggling with these issues. It's not New York that’s struggling with rent or groceries or childcare; It's people across the country. And part of the reason we also know that is that New Yorkers now live across the country because they couldn't afford to stay here. And whether you want to look at Michigan or you want to look at Denver or you want to look at New Jersey or New York, wherever you want to look, there's a hunger for a new kind of politics, and it's one where working people are back at the heart.

q.t: We have a few minutes left, but I want to ask the audience something. This is a predominantly Black audience. Is there anybody in this audience that is uncomfortable with socialism or democratic socialism? Raise your hand. You know, that's — it's so funny when I'm out here on these streets, and I'm talking to people. I know what the pundits babble and like, Bill Maher mentions you every Friday. He has an obsession with you. You would think you were one of his ex-girlfriends or something like that. It's crazy, but—

a.t: Not guilty.

q.t: Thank you for being here. And Brother Clay, I hope your leg is better. My name is Joan Warren. I currently live in Southeast Queens, but I grew up in Brownsville, Brooklyn, and I barely remember Major Owen, so thank you for taking me the way back. My question is, what measures would you implement to hold hospitals accountable where nurses are intentionally short-staffed while they are trying to take care of the community?

a.t: You know, our nurses do incredible work each and every day. And when I came into office, I met a number of norms about the office. One of those norms was when there's a labor negotiation, the mayor should stay out. And I looked, and I saw nurses who were picketing and striking for the right to earn enough to stay in this city and to have safe staff. And I remembered the quote, I think it's from Desmond Tutu. He says, neutrality in the face of injustice. [I’m] making a choice to paraphrase him. And I decided to go with Senator Bernie Sanders and stand on that picket line with those nurses and add my voice. Because as you have laid out in your question, this work — they are not fighting for luxury. They are not for things that would be nice to have. They're fighting for things that are necessary not just for their job safety, but also for the safety of patients. And it was incredible to see them and management come together to celebrate a new contract. And we celebrate the work that they do in this city.

q.t: How can New York City help mom-and-pop shops with marketing and visibility to offset rising rents and costs using Citi's assets?

a.t:
Well, first, I have to say, great t-shirt. Second, mom-and-pop shops are near and dear to me. They are some of what makes our city special. And especially in a moment where it feels like so much is being made uniform, so many parts of the city and the country and the world feel as if you can just cut and paste, there are these places in our city that you cannot find anywhere else. And part of this is when we have city resources, that we shine that light as you've said. Part of this is also asking small business owners, what's making it harder for you to stay open?

And what we heard from these small business owners is, yes, some of it's the fines and fees; some of it's also just the number of hoops they have to jump through. So, we had these task forces and these convenings; we recently came out a couple weeks ago and announced a task force called OPEN to help these small businesses and that we were going to introduce more than 50 regulatory reforms.

Some of these reforms speak to the fact that today, a small business needs to have a license to sell hot food and a license to sell a frozen dairy dessert. Makes no sense to me. And it's not just about the money that each license you have to pay for, but how many times you have to fill out paperwork and go to a new agency and go to the next meeting, and we want them to just be able to focus on their work.

And the second thing is, you know, some of these regulations are just arcane. There was a regulation that was limiting how much a bingo cash prize could be. It's like, I'm not going to get in the way of aunties and uncles playing ping-pong. This is not one of the city's problems. And so, I think it's asking, it's listening, and then it's acting on it. And we have a mom-and-pop czar, Delia Awusi, who's doing great work. But we're always trying to think about how can we shine a light. The last thing I'll say is we just had the World Cup. It was incredible. We had a lot of people come to New York City for the first time. We also wanted to make sure that, with all due respect to Midtown, they also went to other parts of New York City. And so, we started a $26 meal and deal, you know, a challenge really where we had small businesses sign up to offer $26 bucks to get a meal and a deal. And whether it was Xochimilco in the South Bronx, whether it was having tacos in Corona, we saw New Yorkers go across the five boroughs. And it was really a celebration of these mom-and-pop stores. Thank you for your questions.

q.t: She's right there in the front row. And I live in East New York. Many East New York residents take pride in maintaining their homes and investing in the community. How will your administration address neighborhood life and evaluate the impact that the concentration of homeless shelters has on a working community while ensuring adequate support for those experiencing homelessness?

a.t:
That's a great question, and it's a question that has empathy in it, and I appreciate that because sometimes on these topics, it's few and far between. I think first, we have to reckon with the fact that for many New Yorkers, investment in their neighborhood has sometimes come with a specter of displacement. People feel like, oh, I'm going to get a nice thing; it must mean that someone is going to come and enjoy this. And we have to show that we can deliver that investment for the people who live there right now. And earlier we were talking about universal childcare. The governor and I have been working together with leaders in the state legislature. We're delivering 2,000 free seats this year, 12,000 free seats next year for two-year-olds. End of year four? Every single two-year-old in New York City.

When we're starting that, we decide where do we want to begin this. And one of the conversations we had is, what are the neighborhoods that are either last on the list or not at all? And so, we made the decision that with these first 2,000 seats, we were going to start in the Rockaways, in Brownsville, in Fordham, in so many neighborhoods that we've seen economic need is so high and yet city investment is so low.

And second, when it comes to dealing with the homelessness crisis, we have to both deal with the short-term of it and the long-term of it. Long term of it, we have to build enough housing, ensure that it's affordable enough that people aren't being pushed out of that housing. Because we know that when rent goes up, there's a relationship with homelessness also going up, and when it comes to the short term, we have to have an analysis of fair, being fair with where shelters are placed and why we are placing them, why we need them.

And so, when I've had conversations with elected officials about this is why the city needs to open a shelter here, we talk about the fact that we are a city that's proud of the fact we have a law called the “Right to Shelter,” where every New Yorker has a right to a shelter. What that means is that we have to have a certain capacity for shelters, but then I also go back to my team, and I say, how do we make sure that in eight years I'm not picking up the phone to have the same conversation? How have we built enough housing so that it's not always just temporary, temporary, temporary, but it's also starting to move to the long term? And one of the things is it's just not enough to build housing at large; you also have to build supportive housing.

And for those who don't know, supportive housing is housing that comes with programming and clinical assistance and the kind of support that formerly homeless New Yorkers need to ensure that they actually get the tools they can to live a stable life. I think it was on Monday that I was in the Bronx at Casanova Residences celebrating the breaking ground with The Doe Fund of affordable housing, of which a significant portion is going to specifically be for formerly homeless New Yorkers, so we can get people out of shelters and get them into their homes. Thank you for your work.

q.t: I’m here with my 20-year-old daughter did not give me any grief when I said that we're going to see the mayor. She was like, okay.

a.t: Where is she?

q.t:
Well, I know one thing you do. You rock that Brandy “Full Moon” album.

[Crosstalk.]
Well, what about your favorite R&B New Yorkers? We got Mary, we got Alicia, we got Mariah.

a.t:
If it’s Christmas, I always say Mariah. Alicia Keys, she's just such a hometown hero, and I know that so many now, when we think of Alicia Keys, we think about “Empire State of Mind.” It was incredible having her at City Hall for the Knicks celebration. But I just think of so many memories of middle school and high school for me, and it's just to the soundtrack of Alicia Keys. It’s me just humming on the 1 train, “This girl's on fire.”

[Crosstalk.]

q.t: The rent is too damn high. [Inaudible]. You always appear positive and upbeat. How do you quiet the negative that comes your way online?

a.t: It's a very sweet question. We got to get you back to New York City. You know, I think one is just growing up in New York City. You are used to noise. And what you have to do is decide what you want to tune out and what you want to tune into. You can never just tell yourself, “I'm going to tune out all criticism.” Because then you might as well just stay at home and look in a mirror. You have to just understand when people are offering things in good faith, take it, take that criticism [and] take that reflection. And then I also just — I have to credit my grandmother; she told me from a young age that smiling was a good thing, that you should smile. And she would always encourage me to, and it just became a part of my nature. And It's easier for me to smile than to scowl, and I've been really lucky that New York City gives me so much reason to smile.

q.t: Roderick couldn't be here, but speaking of transportation, he said, what happened to the free buses? Is that still happening?

a.t:
That's still something we're fighting for. And, you know, I built a campaign with our team around the cost-of-living crisis. And one of the central three things that we would talk about in that campaign was making buses fast and making them free. And I've said that that's something we're going to deliver by the time that I'm done being mayor. And what we're doing right now is working on the fast. You know, we have buses in this city traveling five miles an hour. And I can tell you, there are times when you are walking faster than five miles an hour. I mean, I used to go to high school at Bronx Science in the Bronx. I would take the 1 train from 116 to 231st. I would get out; I would take the Bx10. I knew if I could see the Bx10 two stops away at the top of the hill that I could run and catch the bus.

And that is a good thing for me when I'm late, and that's a bad thing for the city. I should not be able to catch the buses if it's two stops away. And then we're going to keep working with Albany to make these buses free because you spoke about it just now; we're talking about the cost of public transit [being] three dollars. Disproportionately, the ridership of our buses is the most working-class ridership of any public transit. And what we found is that one in five of those riders are struggling to afford three dollars; we do not want people to be priced out of taking the bus. And so, we worked with the Council; we increased the eligibility for Fair Fares, which is reduced pricing for New Yorkers who make a certain amount, but we're still gonna keep working to make those buses free.

q.t: Do you have any policy plans to help working and middle-income New Yorkers earning around $120,000 a year? I know that seems like a lot, but in New York, it ain't nothing. And we're struggling, too. We're struggling too.

a.t:
I love the way you phrased this question because it speaks to the fact that what we used to think of as money that would be enough to build a good life, it is not the case anymore. After housing, the next cost for New Yorkers is childcare. You have to make $334,000 a year in New York City to afford childcare for one child. That's the amount that you have to make to be considered to afford it. Obviously, other people pay for it with making much less, but they pay for it at the expense of everything else in their life. So, $120,000 is still a struggle in New York City. And so, to me, I think there are a few things.

The first is we have to take a universal approach. And one of those approaches is when it comes to childcare. Universal childcare saves each family at least $20,000 a year. And we know that there are some families paying up to $40,000 a year, and this is for every New Yorker, no matter what their salary is — if they're making $120,000 or $60,000, because we know it's not enough to stay in the city.

The second thing is: how do we also ensure that the quality of what the city is delivering is so good that you will choose that city service no matter how much money is in your pocket? One of my favorite things about our city is the subway. And at its best, the subway is what everyone uses to get from place A to place B. Now, we have to deliver that excellence across every service, because when you do that, you also save people money that they would otherwise be spending on a private version of that.

And there's so much they can spend in the private market, but when it comes to things that are necessary for their life, when it comes to education, when it comes to libraries, when it comes to parks, let us deliver that standard of quality that New Yorkers know — actually, I can get the best thing, and I can get it for free.

q.t: So is the theory that if we build more housing, that will bring the rent down for the average person? Is that the theory? I mean, I know they'll call it socialism, but I know these landlords that charge $4,000 for rent; it's just egregious, it is disgusting, but it's private ownership, so you can't control that.

a.t:
Look, I think one is we have to catch up with demand, and what that means is you have to increase supply across the city. The other is we also have to ensure that we're holding everyone accountable because what we've seen is there are real estate portfolios that rack up so many different violations and tenants wait for so long that they feel like there's never going to be a recourse.

And I mean, I'm talking about a level of violation where there was a beehive found in the wall of one of these buildings, right, and if you do not address violations, it breeds impunity, and so what I'm so excited by is we can do all these things at the same time. Sometimes people have been told you either have to choose between protecting tenants' rights and building more housing; we're saying, it’s time to do it all.

q.t: I live in Manhattan; I'm a retired New York City worker. My question is — same as with the housing lottery — the rents continue to rise for the average New Yorker to afford. What are your plans to make the rents more affordable?

a.t: I love this question. First, I have to ask, what did you do for the city?
I work for HRA.

Oh my god. Well, I just have to say thank you, because before I was the mayor, before I was an Assembly member, I was a foreclosure and prevention housing counselor. And I used to work with working and middle-class New Yorkers who owned their homes and who were in danger of foreclosure. They were negotiating with a bank on how to get back into compliance with that mortgage, how to get out of delinquency. And HRA would be a place that I would go because there was the prospect sometimes of those families getting a one-shot deal, getting back on their feet. And I can't tell you how transformative it was for a family to know that there was actually a way out of that pain and that despair.

And obviously now as the mayor, it is a real point of pride to see the work that HRA workers do on a daily basis. To your question around rent and housing, we know this is the most expensive city in the United States of America, and we know that the preeminent crisis when it comes to cost is housing. So, there are a few things. The first is we want to and will build more affordable housing in the next 10 years than any mayor has in the last few decades. We've talked about 200,000 new affordable homes. Doing that alongside preserving 200,000 existing affordable homes and all of this while we build out the strongest tenant protections in the United States of America.

And the reason these things are important to go together is the longer you spend in New York, the more you will have the feeling when you see construction in your neighborhood asking, “Is that for me? Or is that somebody else? And am I going to be able to stay?” And the importance of making sure that the city is building affordable housing is that New Yorkers can know that there's room for them in that future as well. They're not just a part of the past. And we have to build more housing to keep up with the demand in the city.

We also have to make sure that tenants have their rights and those rights are enforced. Because I've met tenants who have shown me the kind of, you know, negligence that their landlords have made into a business model that is frankly unacceptable. On the first day of my administration, I went to an apartment building owned by a real estate group, and a mother showed me her apartment. She showed me the level of rust in her bathroom. Right outside of her bathroom were two of her kids, one of them in their early 20s. And I asked her, “How long has it been like this?” And she pointed at her kid, and she said, “Before he was born.” People have had to accept that, and they shouldn't have to any longer.

q.t: My question for you, Mayor Mamdani, was how would freelance artists who cannot provide documentation for each income join the housing lottery? And what goals do you have for your office of the NYC Department of Cultural Affairs to improve the lives of working artists? Because it's currently very hard for us to even engage with that office.

a.t:
