First, I want to say thank you for being an artist in this city.

[Crosstalk.]

You know, I talk about affordability a lot. Sometimes it is taken as if it is somehow separate from an agenda around the arts. And one of the things we have to ensure is that art is a part of life for everyone. And one of the key ways you do that is to ensure that artists can afford to live in this city. Because if you become such an expensive city that art becomes a luxury good, then you are depriving yourself of the magic of what art is.

And I don't want this to be a city where people come and go to museums to learn about what New York City once was. I want the city to be a living, breathing testament to what it looks like when art can flourish. And I’m proud we have a new commissioner at DCLA, and she comes from that world of how to integrate art into more of our lives.

I will actually follow up with her on the specificity of the question around freelance artists and Housing Connect, because in my conversations also with our Deputy Mayor for Housing and Planning, we've talked about the need to change Housing Connect because we have heard a number of frustrations from New Yorkers, and frustrations are an opportunity to do better. So, on both of those, I would love if we could actually get your number at the end of this, and we can follow up on that.

[Crosstalk.]

q.t: I'm a licensed clinical social worker, and I also served six and a half years in federal prison. And when you appointed Stanley Richards as the first formerly incarcerated commissioner of the New York City Department of Corrections, I was inspired, but I really wanted to know what inspired you to choose someone with that lived experience that had never been done before.

a.t:
First of all, thank you for your question and also thank you for the work that you do as a social worker. It is such critically important work now and especially in this city and in this country today. When it comes to Stanley, he is — that's one of the easiest decisions I've made as the mayor of our city. As you alluded to, he's the first formerly incarcerated New Yorker to lead the Department of Corrections. And we are speaking about someone who served time in jail and prison, and then spent years at the Fortune Society looking to help those who also served their time reintegrate back into society.

And what I so appreciate about him is that in every conversation I have with him, humanity is at the heart of it. Humanity for those who are serving their time, humanity for those who are working at those facilities and a recognition that it doesn't have to be a choice. And when I have walked through Rikers with him. When I have spoken to him about the necessity of closing Rikers, and we talk about the borough-based jails that would be built, he can sometimes point out to his own along the way. And that is — that is truly a place of leadership that I think only he could occupy. And it is a pleasure to work with him and to look to restore some more humanity to our city in the process.

q.t: There we go. Even with the Democrats, you don't all agree on every single thing.

a.t: If you have two socialists in a room, there has to be at least one disagreement.
Exactly.
That's what it means.
All right, let's open it up.

q.t:
Just quickly, is there anything of the DSA platform that's always being rambled on Fox News —

[Crosstalk.]

Is there anything specific to the DSA platform that you feel like, no, that's not really where I am? I mean, they always list abolish the Senate — this is Fox News — abolish the Senate, abolish the presidency, no prisons. Is there anything that you'd feel like, okay, that is DSA, but that's not where I stand?

a.t: I would say, especially when it comes to public safety, I've been very clear that we have our police force, we have prisons, we have jails [and] the purpose of these is also to ensure that we are delivering safety and justice hand in hand. And what that means is that New Yorkers need not choose between the two. And I am proud of our police department for their work in delivering the lowest levels of murders and shootings and even the number of shooting victims in recorded history over seven months over this year. And I also want to ensure that this is a city where New Yorkers know that that is not coming at the expense of justice.

q.t: So, I have one question that was emailed in that I want to open it up to you all. He couldn't make it here, but he had this question. “The DSA appears to be more of a white movement that focuses more on class than race. Mayor Mamdani focuses on race, but I don't feel welcome by the DSA. How is Mayor Mamdani working to make the DSA have a better racial lens?”

a.t:
Well, first I would say thank you for the question. And I think that what I appreciate about it is its criticism in good faith. And that's what we need more of in our politics. And I think to me, one thing I've appreciated about New York City DSA is that it has been one of the engines behind the creation of a new generation of Black and Brown leadership, the likes [of which] we haven't seen in quite some time.

When I look at other elected officials who I ran alongside, you know, I'm thinking about in 2020 it was Jabari Brisport, it was Phara Souffrant Forrest [and] it was Marcela Mitaynes. It was a number of us, and we see in every single cycle more and more of this new generation of leadership that isn't looking to rewrite history, but rather to honor the history that came before.

And I'll give you an example: one of my focuses has been universal childcare. Just earlier this week, we announced that we have received more than 5,700 applications for the first 2,000 seats of free childcare for two-year-olds. And in politics, there's always a temptation to describe everything as if it is your own achievement — it is you, you came up with it. The truth is, when we are advocating for childcare, we are also following in the footsteps of Major Owens. The truth is that when we're advocating for a city-run grocery store and tackling food insecurity, we're following the footsteps of Shirley Chisholm, whose initiatives helped to create SNAP and WIC.

And you see this time and time again. And so, I'm hopeful of what the future holds. And I also appreciate the questioner, and I'm sorry that they weren't able to be here, because I think that there is a desire to continue to both celebrate that history and showcase its continued applicability to the present challenges.

q.t: So, Karen Hunter, who here is the queen at Urban View, she said recently on her show, she says, "Zohran Mamdani is out there wrecking the machine.” Would you agree? Are you wrecking a machine?

a.t:
First, thank you, Queen Hunter, for saying my name, for honoring it with that time. I would say that I'm looking to wreck complacency. And what I mean by that is, there are a lot of questions that you can ask when you're in a position like mine, and the answer will be, “This is just how we do it. This is just how it's been done.” And that's not enough anymore; it's not enough because it hasn't been enough for New Yorkers. And what has been so exciting is seeing the leadership of civil servants. There are more than 300,000 New Yorkers who work for the city. And they go in day in and out, performing, frankly, acts of heroism.

You know, recently we had the old Pfizer building, structurally unsound in Midtown. A lot of New Yorkers saw it as they were looking up and wondering what was going to happen to this building, where one of the beams was buckling. There were civil servants who went into that building, not knowing how sound it was, to assess whether it was safe. And I had the privilege of welcoming them to City Hall from the Department of Buildings, from FDNY, and just saying thank you. And to me, what's so exciting is when we push on this, “that's how it's always been.” We have the voice, the efforts, and the initiative of hundreds of thousands of New Yorkers who've been waiting for the opportunity where they could show how it could be. And that's what's so exciting to me.

q.t: I love that, I love that. I asked Darializa this, who of course won in New York 14, and I want to ask you this similar question. I know Kamala Harris has reached out to you; Barack Obama has reached out to you. With Darializa and yourself during your primaries, there were comments that came up when you guys were critical of them. And that's all water under the bridge because they've been very supportive of you. But I'm curious to know, now that you are no longer the outside looking in, and now that you're the mayor of the wealthiest city in the world, and you have experienced, in my view, similar racism and xenophobia that Obama experienced and Kamala Harris. Do you have a different perspective or a different level of empathy for them? There were certain things they couldn't do because they were being blocked, and Congress wasn't working with them, and all of this hatred coming their way. Do you have a different view of what it was like versus before when you were the outside looking in versus being in this history-making role now?

a.t: I think you definitely develop an appreciation of the kind of pressures that people are functioning under, especially the pressures around those that you love. And I think it was Toni Morrison that said the function of racism is distraction, and you are constantly faced with this choice. When you face this barrage of xenophobia, of racism, it’s: do you want to grant it your time? Or do you want to focus on the work that you came here to do? And it's not going to always be the same answer, but when you look at President Obama, when you look at Vice President Harris, you also see them having to make that decision in real time every single day. And every moment that you have to face that decision is a moment you could have spent doing the work that you came there to do. And it’s truly been a pleasure to be in conversation with President Obama, to have spoken to Vice President Harris, and to recognize all that came before. Because in that recognition you also have a better understanding of all the work that still needs to be done to come next.

q.t: So, what's something that you've been able to do these past seven months that surprised you that it was so easy to get done, that made you say, “Why didn't anybody do this before me?”

a.t:
You know, there are a lot of caricatures of New Yorkers. We know them. Some of us, we revel in them. We're in a rush, we're rude, we're always going somewhere. There's another part of it where people say that a lot of us have left hope behind; that it's something that we might have had in the past, but we can't find in the present or in the future. One thing that has surprised me is how willing New Yorkers are to believe if you give them a reason. And that reason doesn't always have to be the biggest thing you can think of. That reason can sometimes be the pothole on their block. Now, I remember going to Rochdale Village in the final days of the campaign and to the transition before I was in office as the mayor, and an older woman in the back of the crowd put her hand up, and she asked me, “Will you honor the promise that was made to me?” I’m thinking, I wonder how big this promise is, you know, who said what, when, how much is this going to cost? I asked her, could you tell me a little bit more? She said it was a promise that there would be a speed bump, and it hasn't happened for decades.

And I bring that up as an example that when people lose their trust that government can do the smallest things, that's when they lose their ability to believe that it could do the biggest things. And one small thing that I'm proud of is, you know, right next to City Hall, we have the Municipal Building. It was renamed after our city's first Black mayor, David Dinkins, who is an icon to me and to so many others—
Who was a Democratic Socialist.

Who was a Democratic Socialist. He was the first one. I walk in that path. And there's been a little bit of a secret almost amongst city workers, city bureaucrats, city politicians, that if you want a really great view of New York City, go up to the cupola of the municipal building. And I had heard this from a few people. And one idea that came up in a conversation with the team was, why not make this a place where every New Yorker can go? In a time when it feels like everything costs more and more money, what if we had beauty as a public good in the name of David Dinkins? And so, one thing that we did was we put in the money to refurbish that cupola and make it a place where any New Yorker can go for free to see a view of the city that rivals even that of the Empire State Building.

q.t: Absolutely. Thank you so much. So, I wanted to start here. I know you're fighting for all New Yorkers, but just talking about Black New Yorkers for a minute. In the 2024 primary, you struggled with Black voters, but you've turned that around, and your approval rating of Black voters is extremely high. And I think every Democrat needs to hear this. Outside of affordability — because a lot of folks say that — what has been your strategy? What has been your execution to make sure that Black voters feel seen, heard and acknowledged? Because Democrats at large are struggling with Black voters right now.

a.t: I think that the first step is a recognition that you have to earn people's support; nobody owes you their support. And with that has to come a little bit of humility. The first question that was often asked of me when I was introducing myself in the mayoral primary was, “Who?” Because most New Yorkers had never heard of me, and why would they have? I was a State Assembly member representing Astoria in Long Island City, and I was going out to a church in Southeast Queens, and I was speaking to them in a race where they had heard of a number of other candidates either for months, years, sometimes even for decades. And introducing myself, sometimes it meant taking those early steps again and again, but always understanding that you have to prove why people should believe. And yes, a lot of people talk about affordability, and it affects everyone across New York City — we also know it doesn't affect everyone in the same way. In the nation's most expensive city, right here in New York City, the median household wealth of a Black family is less than $3,000. We have seen over the last few decades 200,000 Black New Yorkers pushed out of this city. And so, when you are coming up against that history, you also have to understand why people might be skeptical of someone saying that things could be different; because people have said it for quite a long time, people have not delivered it for almost that same period of time. And so, now what I see as the opportunity of governing is the opportunity to earn that trust. And I never begrudge someone that they may not have it on day one. It's my job to earn it on day two, day three and every day after that.

q.t: Obviously you are not new to this, but can you peel back the curtain a little bit on how you screen for that with 400,000 people [inaudible]?

a.t: So, as I mentioned, we will have a large number of officers at the parade, but as has been our pattern, generally most nights of the week, but particularly on summer weekend evenings, we do an enhanced deployment of officers and our gang and gun teams in the locations where we know that violence has historically occurred. And those enhanced deployments at the right times and in the right places is what I believe has been a major contributing factor to the unprecedented low numbers we're seeing in terms of shooting incidents, shooting victims and homicides in this city. Sunday will be no different. Thank you.

q.t: Commissioner and mayor, I was wondering if given the events two weeks ago in Bronx, is there a specific concern about gun violence and gang violence?

a.t: So, we're always concerned about gun violence and gang violence. And what I think that you are referencing is some gun and gang violence following the Bronx Dominican Day Parade. And so yes, we will have enhanced deployments of our teams that deal with guns and gangs, particularly once the parade concludes, to ensure that we do everything we can to avoid those issues this weekend.

q.t: And how effective has that been?

a.t: In 2024, at some of our parades, we had issues with people jumping over the barricades, and so the double moating really came out of those issues that we saw. And what the double moating does is it gives our officers more of an opportunity and time to make sure that that route remains clear of unauthorized people.

q.t: I have a question about the set-up of the parade — you talked about — one of the things you mentioned was encouraging parade goers to stand behind the barricades. So, for this parade, like was implemented in previous years for the Caribbean Day Parade, will there be a moat [inaudible]?

a.t: Yes, we are going to do a double moat at this parade and that is becoming standard for basically all of our parade routes where the roadway, the width of the roadway, can accommodate it. So yes, you will see that again this year at this parade, just as we did last year.

q.t: Thank you so much, mayor, for letting me have this time with you.

a.t: Please — it's been a joy. Thank you all everyone and to the hater who said that it was prerecorded: 6:32 in two seconds, come on. Have a great evening, everyone.

q.t: Let's see, here's another question for you, [Livestream Username].

Mayor, what would you like to see if you could look into the future to the end of your second term — we're talking way in the future here — that your administration accomplished for the LGBTQ+ community of New York City?

a.t:
I'm gonna first touch wood, as we are seven months into the first term. But if I were to accept your premise, I think a few things. I want this city to be one that is affordable for queer New Yorkers to live in and for queer people to move to as well. Because we celebrate our city as a place of incredible queer history and we also want it to be a place where that history can keep being written. Because so much of this city, it feels like the stories that we love about it are stories that might not be able to be told today because those icons would not be able to have afforded life in the city. And we know that queer New Yorkers are facing disproportionately high levels of poverty and unemployment. And that is but one example of what happens when we aren't taking action on this.

I think the other part of this is to ensure that we're using every tool at our disposal to both protect queer lives and also advance an affirmative vision of what queer life can look like in the city. And I've found that so much of those ideas can actually come from listening as opposed to lecturing. And I look forward to doing that for the next, you know, three and a half years and hopefully beyond that. So, thank you, thank you so much. This has really been lovely. Thank you so much Bernie for being a part of this.

q.t: Mamdani, along with your work to help lower cost of living, what will you do to help the homeless population?

a.t:
That is a lovely and important question. When we were talking about housing, like the conversation we were just having, one of the critical parts of it is also building housing for those who are both currently and formerly homeless. Just recently — actually, I think it was on Monday of this week — I was at Casanova Residences in the Bronx where we were breaking ground on a number of supportive housing units for formerly homeless New Yorkers. And for those who don't know, supportive housing is housing that also comes with the kind of programming and support that helps people not only stay in those homes but also ensure that they have all that they need to live a productive and a full life.

And it is critically important that we build all of these different kinds of housing in our city because to be frank, we haven't been building enough housing since 1961. We started at that point to reduce the amount of housing we were building; and as much as we are the biggest city in America — if we don't grow as a city, we die. And so, what we need to do is to ensure that we go back to the early days when we could build the Empire State Building in 13 months and not what we've seen over the last few decades, which is an ever-dwindling sense of ambition when it comes to how much housing we can build in the city.

q.t: I have another question from you. This is from [Livestream Username].

a.t: Hello!

q.t: And I can relate. As a radio person, everything had to be to the exact second. So that’s one of the reasons I have a watch that tells me exactly what the time is. So, I know. And again, to prove we’re live: 6:28 and fifty seconds. Beep.

a.t: Ten seconds ahead of me. Okay.

q.t: You got to have the exact time. You have to be in so many places.

a.t: Okay, I have to tell you something. I'm a little bit nuts, and I set my watch to like three or four minutes ahead.
Okay.

And I thought that would make sure that I would always be early. And instead, it has wasted so much of my time in trying to calculate what the actual time is. Because I'm looking at it and I'm like, “X minus 3.5, where are we right now?” So, I've recently admitted defeat and I have set the time to what the time actually is. Currently 6:28, 24 seconds on the dot. I recommend you all do the same.

q.t: Okay, I think — oh we have another question for you.
What watch is that sir?

a.t: This is a Casio watch, given to me by my wife. And you can find this pretty much anywhere.

q.t: —is it hits a lot of areas that are very important in my life over my lifetime. So, for instance, it goes to the World Trade Center. I worked at the Port Authority, so that was their headquarters. It goes, it stops at Christopher Street; Sheridan Square; Stonewall, which obviously has a lot of personal importance to me; it runs under Broadway. And as I talked about some of those experiences, I get to be part of Broadway through that. So, all of those things make the number 1 train to me — and it was part of the original subway system, by the way. When they first opened it in 1904, that was one of the original lines of the New York City subway.

a.t: It is one that is also a bit of a nostalgic pick for me, but I'm gonna go with the 9 train.
Okay!

For that real heavy dose of nostalgia. So, I used to live by 116th Street, and so it was the 1 [and] 9. And those are the trains that I grew up with when I first moved to New York City. I was seven years old. And that's how I really remember those early, early days.

q.t: I would have to say the 1 train. And the reason I say that—

a.t: Please.

q.t: And we've got another question for you. This is from [Livestream Username]. Mayor, can you tell us more about how you're planning to build more affordable housing.

a.t:
Yes, I can. Absolutely. So, as some of you may know, we've made a commitment to build 200,000 affordable homes over the next 10 years. And recently, we actually went on a double-decker bus tour of the Bronx because what better way to see the Bronx? Come on, you've got to get on a double-decker bus. Which is actually the first time I've ever been on a doubled-decker bus in New York City, because usually, you don't move around the city that you live in as a tourist. And double-decker busses are primarily for tourists, but it was great. Very close to the stop signs. And the reason we went on that bus was to bring to life something called the LIFT Tracker, the LIFT Report. Now this is a report about the city-owned pieces of land that we have where we can build affordable housing. And we saw three different sites. And these were sites that were designated as sites for affordable housing, some even up to eight years ago, and yet they look as they did then.

There's been delays, there's been the kinds of inaction that for too many people have come to typify local government. And what we showcased is that thanks to the work that we've done through our SPEED task force, through our LIFT Report, these are the kinds of places where we're going to be delivering new housing. It's going to be on places that are currently vacant. It's gonna be the transformation of a library into a library that has affordable housing built on top of that library. And we're gonna be able to do this by also cutting delays by up to two years, because the big question for us is, how can we move at the speed of this city? Because we know that working people — especially those who know Bernie's voice — are ones who never have an extra minute to waste. But for too long, it's felt as if City government has nothing but time to waste, and we're looking to make it clear that those days are coming to an end.
Sounds good.
Yes.
Sounds great.
Yes, yes, yes, it does. So, I have a couple more questions.
Sure.
What is your favorite subway line?

q.t: Yes. And I feel that in my life, I have been the person who has a lot of privilege. And I want to be able to do what I can to improve life for other trans people.

a.t: Pay it forward.
Yes, exactly.
Well, I think you're very much doing that.
Thank you.
And I think it's just a beautiful example of the fact that this is what home looks like and feels like. And to that person who asked that question, you too are at home.

q.t: Thank you, thank you. And as we're going down Fifth Avenue and I'm sitting in the back of a convertible, to hear people cheering for me gives me enough energy to go on for a whole [another] year or longer. Those kinds of things are just amazing to me. And that love is really something that I want to return. I want [to] do what I can. I — You know, there's that quote from the Spider-Man movie about, I think, you know, to one who's been given much power comes, you know, much responsibility.

a.t: From Uncle Ben.

q.t: Given the current wave of anti-trans rhetoric in the country, how does Bernie manage to keep her energy so bright? How does Bernie manage to keep her head held high? She's such an inspiration. Thanks a ton, and much love from a fellow trans gal.

Well, I would say that a big part of that for me has been the love I've received back from New Yorkers. That has been so affirming and encouraging to me. You know, I talked before about — I wasn't sure what this was going to be like when I started my transition. I had no idea that I would feel such an outpouring of love from New Yorkers. I was one of the grand marshals for the New York City Pride March in June. And—

a.t: Congratulations.

q.t: Mayor Mamdani, what are goals you have set for New York City a year from now?

a.t: Okay, I will give you two goals. Goal number one is that I witness Bernie performing the announcements live on the holiday train. I want to make sure that I actually do that. Goal two, just earlier this week we announced that we had actually met the demand for the 2,000 free childcare seats for two-year-olds. We had about 5,700 applicants and we're rolling out these first 2,000 or so seats later in the fall. A year from now, our goal and our commitment to New Yorkers is we're going to go from 2,000 seats of free childcare for two-year-olds to 12,000 seats of free childcare seats for two-year-olds. And so, by this point next year, we will have finished the application process I would expect. And the reason this matters is we are talking about the subway. One of the beautiful things about the subway is that for many New Yorker it feels within reach. Childcare is something that doesn't because the average cost of childcare in our city is $20,000. That's considered a good deal in New York City. Some parents are paying up to $40,000. So, when you are able to deliver universal childcare for two-year-olds, you are saving those parents anywhere from $20,000 to $40,000. And we're starting with 2,000 families this year. The goal, the commitment is to deliver that for 12,000 next year.
Wow, pretty impressive.
You know, that’s like — trying to do the math. How many subway rides into $20,000? Don't ask us, do not ask us. Okay, I've got a question from [Livestream Username]. Question for Bernie.

q.t: It's been amazing to me. We have another question.

a.t: Please.
From [Livestream Username].
We hope that's how to pronounce your name. Let us know in chat if that's not.

q.t: What was it like coming out as a trans woman?

I think for most trans people, that is one of the scariest moments in your life because you're not really sure what this is going to be like. You have your hopes and dreams of what it's going to like. But you don't know what it's gonna be like, until you actually do it. And it's a little awkward when you're doing that transition because again, you have so many years of experience living in one gender and now you're switching to another gender. In my case, I figured in that first June, which would have been June of 2023, that there would be some local interest with the local media because I was a known voice for New York. But come July 1, after Pride Month was over, we would go on to other things.

I was shocked that the interest continued, not just within New York City, but nationally and even internationally. That I was doing interviews with media from Germany, Brazil, Japan, all these places were interested in the story. And I think even one of the more surprising parts of it has been something that I never anticipated that suddenly I've become part of the Broadway world. And I don't mean on the 1 train underneath Broadway. It started a couple of years ago when Lin-Manuel Miranda asked me to be the voice of the train announcer on the Warriors album that he had created. Of course, an iconic New York movie that he recreated into a concept album that's now being brought to Broadway. And that has led to other things. Well, first of all, to work with Lin-Manuel Miranda was outside of any concept of possibilities that I had had. But I ended up doing with Cat's, The Jellicle Ball; I was a guest judge for that. [I] did a music video shot on the subway. So, all these kinds of crazy things that have been going on.

a.t: I think a lot of that is also a reflection of the fact that you and your voice are a part of the tapestry of our city. And it's a city that means so much to so many of us. And it's a joy to be able to engage with that, especially when there's a lot of modern life that feels as if it's mechanical, that feels maybe even that it's automated. And then to have a living, breathing person who was this voice that gave you instruction, that gave you some clarity in a moment. You know, as I was saying in the beginning, there were times when we'd hear your voice, we wouldn't have a train time, we wouldn't have cell service, we wouldn't have any other way to know. And then there it was. And I'm so glad that you are living these multiple lives now, whether it be in arts and culture, MTA. It's amazing.

q.t: Can you tell the stream about the $15 million for gender affirming care for transgender New Yorkers?

a.t:
Yes, absolutely I can. Thank you very much, my friend, for asking this and thank you very much for your advocacy on this issue. You know, we know that here in New York City, one of the many things that we're so proud of when it comes to our city is that we have been a haven for queer people across the country and across the world. And it's part of our city's history and it's a part of what so many love about this city.

And we also know that this is a moment in time where we have a federal administration that is deeply hostile to very existence of queer people, and especially trans people. And so, we made a decision earlier this year when we put forward our budget, to invest $15 million to start to deliver gender-affirming care for trans New Yorkers. And this is part of a larger commitment to the health and wellbeing of trans New Yorkers, both by creating our first ever Office of LGBTQIA+ Affairs, headed by the incredible Taylor Brown. Which is finally giving a home to the needs of queer New Yorkers in a way that hasn't been done before in City government.

And also, by registering our opposition to the federal government's attempt at being able to gain access to the private medical records of trans youth right here in New York City. And so, these are a few of the ways that we're standing up, but I thank you for your advocacy and for leading the way.

q.t: Guys, if you're going to pre-record, you got to not make it so obvious.

a.t: [Livestream Username], you just committed a live crime live because you accused us of something that's not true. If we were pre-recording, could I do this? I could. But could I mention your name and then respond to you? I could not. So, still struggling with chat and streaming but not pre-recording. Not yet. That's when we get really lazy with it. But there is a question here for you. [Crosstalk.] Oh, a question for me.

q.t: Indeed, every type of New Yorker is on the subway.

a.t:
That's the dream, that's the dream. And I know we have a few people from chat who are asking a couple of things. I think this one is for you. 

[Crosstalk.]

q.t: And maybe your funniest. Maybe they're the same thing.

a.t: You know, I used to struggle with claustrophobia. And you may recall 2017 was called the summer of hell.
Yes.

Where we were at a peak in terms of train delays [and] stoppages. And that was exactly the time where I was living in Morningside Heights and commuting to Bay Ridge. So that was about an hour and a half each way, I would take the 1 to the 2 to the N to the R. And it was on the end, typically right before Atlantic Avenue, that there would almost always be a stoppage in the tunnel.

And in those moments, I would start to feel this just like creeping paralysis and this anxiety reaching a fever pitch. And in these moments, something that would always calm me down is if I could strike up a conversation with somebody on the train. And you know there's a caricature of New Yorkers and that we are in a rush, that we are rude and all these things that people say about us. But in that moment of need, I just found so many people, whose names I have now forgotten, who were willing to give me one, two, three [or] four minutes. As I would say, “Hi, I'm Zohran. I'm struggling with some claustrophobia. Would you mind just talking to me about anything?” And then we'd have a conversation.
Right.

And that's the generosity of spirit that I so love about our city and about our subway system. Which is that it is also an example of a public good that at its best is so good, that no matter how much money is in your pocket you choose to take it because it's the way of getting around the city.

q.t: Well, I want to add, since we're talking about subways, what was your favorite New York City subway experience?

a.t: Wow. My favorite New York City subway experience.

q.t: So that was a lot of fun.

a.t: I can relate to that feeling because when I hear you speak, it's the same moment of recognition that this person lives and breathes among us and that we're here together in the same space. Oh, please.

q.t: Oh, I've done, you know, some charity events where, you know the so-called voice of God off stage and you're announcing somebody and then I'll switch to the subway voice and that always gets a reaction. In fact, at your inauguration, I had the opportunity to introduce myself at the beginning and I said my name and that got a little applause but then I said, and I'm probably the voice you better recognize as saying: “Please stand away from the platform edge.” And then the crowd really recognized who it was.

a.t: Oh my God!

q.t: So, we are on the subway car and—

a.t: I want to be there this year.
Okay.
I will have to follow up with you. You're doing this live?
Yes, we do it live.
Have you ever done announcements in your MTA voice for non-MTA things?

q.t: And people just eat that up. It's a wonderful experience to be.

a.t: Is that planned? You do it with the MTA or you two choose to do it?
We just choose to it together.
Oh my God.

q.t: And my colleague, who voices some of the subway announcements, Charlie Pellet. So, he and I — Charlie is the guy that says: “Stand clear of the closing doors, please.” And he and I will do live announcements on the train.

a.t: Wow!

q.t: I think my favorite is around the holidays every year in December, the New York City or the New York Transit Museum runs the holiday train, and they bring out these old subway cars from the 1940s and earlier. And people dress up to fit the time period that those subway cars existed.

a.t: That’s incredible.

q.t: Yeah, I can imagine that would be very difficult, but also heartwarming at the same time.

a.t: I think it shows how even in a city of 8.5 million people, even in the biggest city in the United States of America, we are a part of something bigger than ourselves.
Yes.
And as tempting as it is, and easy as it to feel alone in such a big place, there are also these moments where we feel like, actually, we're together. And I have a question for you as well.
Okay.
Which is, what is your favorite New York City subway experience?

q.t: But what I want to ask you is, what are the things that you discovered as mayor? What was most difficult? What's been most surprising for you?

a.t:
I think the most surprising for me has been that even in a city like ours, where all of us are in a rush, many of us have been hardened by the difficulty of life in the nation's most expensive city, but how willing New Yorkers still are to believe in a better tomorrow if you just give them a reason to. You just have to show people that there's a reason. They should open up their hearts [and] open up their minds. And sometimes that reason can be the pothole that you just paved on their block. Sometimes the reason can be that they just got an offer for free universal childcare for their two-year-old for the first time in New York City history. Sometimes that reason can be that they're a worker who just got restitution back for having been taken advantage of by a bad boss. And sometimes it can be that you've just got help setting up a tenant union.

And I think that all of those things, it's a reminder that in a world that can so often feel as if there isn't much reason for hope, that in fact, people want to. They're just looking for a reason. And I think to your question of what's the most difficult thing, I would say there are times when I meet people, and I'm meeting them in the worst moments of their life. I am meeting them when they have lost someone very dear to them. And when you hear the grief in their voice, it is a heartbreaking thing. You know, I recently went to a funeral for a young man, and I spoke right after we prayed together, and I then was saying goodbye to the family and his youngest brother; he gave me a hug, and he didn't wanna let go.

And that moment when a 10-year-old is tugging at your clothes to try and remember their brothers — it's an incredibly difficult thing. And I think that we also know that while the world moves on from the tragedies of the week before, the families never get to. And that means the city also has to be sure that we're there for them. So that is some of the difficulty that comes with this and also the opportunity, though, to be there for these families in those moments.

q.t: Oh, my pleasure. And I think I finally thought-out last week from that.

a.t: Yes, it was incredibly cold. To all those who remember, I had every conceivable heat patch on my body. It was unbelievably cold.

q.t: A little over a half year ago. I think I have finally—

a.t: Thank you very much for having done that.

q.t: I was the announcer at your inauguration—

a.t: Yes, you were.

q.t: Usually though, people will specialize in a particular — some people will specialize in audiobooks, for example, or some people will specialize and doing commercials. So, you have a lot of different things that people will do. Now, I want to ask you a question.

a.t: Please.

q.t: Oh my God, diva teach me your voice acting ways. So, Bernie, if I can translate that: What tips can you give to an inspiring voice actor?

I think the best thing to do is just to practice. Because you have so many different opportunities. There are lots of different types of voiceovers. For instance, there are people who do characters for cartoons. There are people like me who are announcers. There are people who do a variety of different things. So, all of those are good training for things that you might eventually want to do.

a.t: And do people who do announcements sometimes do cartoons, for example?
Yeah, they can.
Is it flexible?

q.t: What's for dinner?

a.t: The one place of certainty. You know, I think we have a number of people who are here on the chat.

q.t: I’m the voice — if you call the Port Authority or if you call PATH, you will get my voice answering the phone on those.

a.t: Incredible.
So that was—
So, they knew you from your work?
Yes, exactly.
Wow. That is incredible.
It was a lot of fun.
Well, I truly meant what I said, which is that your voice is the sound of home.
Thank you.

It's an incredible thing to meet you, because it also, as you said, so many of us — I mean — even to know that it is a person — you kind of just hear it as the voice of authority. You know, life is what that voice is telling you. This is how far the train is, this is where it's going. Sometimes you would hope that voice could tell you more. What else is there?

q.t: I had done some announcements on the voice — for instance — on the AirTrain at Newark Liberty International Airport.

a.t: Oh my God.

q.t: Well, I had been working during part of my career for the Port Authority of New York and New Jersey. And I worked in this agency called TRANSCOM that brings together all of the regional transportation agencies in the Tri-State area. And of course, that included the MTA. So, I got to know some folks from the MTA. And when they needed a voice, this was many years after I had left the Port Authority, they remembered and reached out to me and said, “Hey, we've got this new project. We'd like to use your voice for that. Would you be interested?” I said, “Sure, that sounds like fun.”

a.t: And so, at that time, what had you done for the Port Authority? A similar kind of announcements?

q.t: Yes, it was over a thousand. Because especially with numbers, we went from 1st I think to 259th, so every number like that that we had to do, every subway station. So, there was a lot of stuff that I had to record.

a.t: And how did you hear about this opportunity?

q.t: Right, the computer has to put it together because there are so many variables about how long it will be, which train is it — express, local — which direction. There's a million different variables.

a.t: How many words do you think you recorded for the MTA?
Over a thousand.
Wow.

q.t: Because you're talking in just little segments. So, when I did the recordings, we were recording things like “Uptown,” “Downtown,” “Bronx bound.” And then the computer puts it all together. So, you have all these different little segments and that's why it sounds the way it does, that there's a pause between each little word or phrase.

a.t: Because it's not recorded at the same time.

q.t: It was something that, again, with radio, I just kept on working at it. In some ways, I still work at it to try to perfect it, but it was something I worked on. Doing the subway announcements, though, was a little bit different from your typical voiceover or radio gig.

a.t: How so?

q.t: Well, for me, I think one of the funniest things is I'm standing on the platform, and I'll hear one of my announcements come up. And no one has any idea that the person who just voiced that announcement is standing right there with them. It's a form of anonymity, but celebrity at the same time. You're in both worlds.

a.t: It's incredible. How did you — to the point that you just said, the voice that you have for the announcements, it's not the same voice that you are living with on a day-to-day basis in the way that you're living in the world. How did you develop that voice? How did you decide that that was the voice you wanted to have for the announcement?

q.t: Generally, not. You know, the funny thing is that people don't recognize. And there's sort of a different voice that I use when I'm doing the announcements. So, they don't necessarily associate that voice with this person.

a.t: What is it like for you to be on the train when you hear — when you heard your own voice?

q.t: Well, the MTA started in 2009. I was still doing radio at the time. A lot of radio people do voiceover and back and forth. So, I started that in 2009, and it was something I had no idea how it was going to blow up in terms of so many people recognizing my voice.

a.t: Did you ever have it on a day-to-day basis, someone who would know you as the voice without being able to quite place it?

q.t: Well, for me, it started with radio. I fell in love with radio in about fifth grade and decided that I wanted to be on the radio. When I talk to young people, I tell them, radio back then was kind of like the smartphone of today. It was where you got your sports scores, your headlines, your weather, your time checks, little bit of everything. You got that from the radio since we didn't have smartphones. And I started practicing my voice by reading the newspaper out loud in my basement, and it turned into a career in radio.

a.t: That's incredible. And when did you move from radio to the MTA?

q.t: I wanted to ask you, though, just about his victory. He did especially well in higher-educated, higher-income areas, whereas his opponent picked up more support from more low-income parts of Detroit, rural areas with a lot of working-class residents. What do you kind of make of that dynamic, given that El-Sayed very much campaigned on a working-class-centered message?

a.t: I will leave much of the assessment to pundits. What I will say is that when you are facing $60 million in outside spending, you are facing almost what feels like surround sound across a state where people are hearing a message about you again and again and again. And to win this race as someone who is not currently holding elected office? It is a testament to what he ran on and also the way he ran the campaign. And I think I saw somewhere that he held more than 500 in-person events across the state of Michigan. That's the kind of work it's going to take to ensure that we are winning in November. And I truly give kudos to him and to the team that he built around him. I think the message of money out of politics, money in your pocket, Medicare for all, is one that even New Yorkers can relate to. Thank you all very much.

q.t: So, not totally closing the door on maybe going to Michigan?

a.t: I'm here right now.

q.t: So, with El Sayed’s victory, this is maybe the biggest potential prize for the American left in November now. Do you plan on formally endorsing him, maybe even going to Michigan to campaign?

a.t: My focus thus far has been on New York City, and what I will tell you is that I know that many New Yorkers were incredibly excited at the results. I tried to stay up until it was called, but then I eventually called it a day. But I do wish him the best.

q.t:
Ras Baraka was [inaudible]. New Yorkers are in there, we understand. What can be done? What can you, as mayor, or Attorney General James to join in with Mikie Sherrill

[inaudible] to bring accountability to that private jail facility?

a.t: I think, first and foremost, we can add our voices to the fact that Delaney Hall should be closed. That is something that you have heard from a number of elected officials. And yes, you're right that when I was a candidate, I was outside of Delaney Hall after Mayor Baraka was arrested and detained. And this is just one symptom of a federal administration's approach to immigration enforcement that has foregrounded cruelty and inhumanity. And I do believe that ICE should be abolished. I do think that there should be humanity back at the heart of the way in which our country conducts immigration enforcement. And what we are seeing is that these are not intellectual debates; these are conversations that have fatal consequences if we continue with the kinds of policies that we're seeing the federal government pursue.

q.t: We have another death in Delaney Hall; it happened in custody, a person that was chronically ill apparently. I know you know that area when you were, I guess, in the assembly—

a.t: Ras Baraka.

q.t: More inspections — I mean, I understand the office piece, and that's important, but this did kind of — like whoa, one out of 10 buildings we visited, there was a problem?

a.t: There are going to be more inspections and I also had the honor, frankly, of welcoming a number of those DOB inspectors and FDNY members to City Hall who went into that building and to thank them for their heroism, because it is truly a heroic act to go into a building that we all know is structurally unsound and do the work necessary to safeguard it.

q.t: I wanted to follow up on the DOB report that was issued late yesterday following the Pfizer building. Inspectors went out and checked out 180 buildings tied to various contractors that may have been responsible for the buckled beam. They found about 10 percent of those — 19 of the 180 — required either partial or, in one case, a full stop work order, so about 10% percent. You find that many stop work orders when you go out and do a concerted effort — should the city, in general, be doing more inspections of more buildings?

a.t: We are going to continue to do these kinds of inspections because the safety of New Yorkers is paramount. Now, of those 180 inspections that were conducted, there were none that were deemed to be an immediate public safety threat to New Yorkers. However, as you said, there were some that required a partial stop work order, and some that required a full stop work order. And what we've also found, because I know in conversations that we've had about this in the past, there have been questions raised as to, is there a specific concern that should be had about office-to-residential conversions. And in these inspections and in our work assessing the landscape of our city, since the issue was raised with the Pfizer building, we have not found a reason to be concerned with those conversions innately.

q.t: Mr. Mayor, I have two questions for you. One is about the pied-à-terre tax rollout. Are you looking for potential property tax fraud, and what will you do if you find evidence of it? And then my second question is, I'm wondering if you've seen reports about a number of retired paraprofessionals here in New York City who were informed by TRS this summer — these are people who are on disability pensions — that their pensions have been miscalculated, some for 10, 12, 15 years, and were informed that their pensions will now be cut in half and are being asked to pay back a portion of those pension that they have been receiving for this entire time. What are your thoughts on that? What can the city do to help these [inaudible]?

a.t: I think on your first question, the point of this period is that out of the 8.5 million people who call the city home, the Department of Finance assessed that 17,000 households may be subject to the pied-à-terre surcharge and issued them a “you may be subject to” letter. They have until September 18 to appeal that assessment to the Department of Finance. They can do that either directly to the Department of Finance; they can do it by calling 311; they can go into one of the in-person centers in every single one of our five boroughs. And the point of this is to make sure that only properties, secondary homes of non-resident New Yorkers that are worth more than $5 million, are the ones that are being subject to this tax. I know there are some New Yorkers who bought their home and put it in a trust, others who bought their home and put it into an LLC, and therefore the City just wants to make sure that this is a primary residence holder. To your second question, the City is one of many parties when it comes to the stewarding of these pensions. And to my knowledge, the law department has come forward and identified this as a mistake that took place over many, many years, and the need for us to be in legal compliance to correct that moving forward. We are going to keep a close eye on it and make sure that we're following up.

q.t: You've obviously been outspoken about change in the Democratic Party. Is he the type of candidate that you see as the change of the Democratic Party?

a.t: Yes.

q.t: Following up on that, I just wanted to ask you [about] the characterization that some are making, calling him “Michigan's Mamdani.” Have you had any conversations with him? And then also, what do you take away from that comparison in your similar things that you ran on?

a.t: You know, I have had the privilege of speaking to Dr. El-Sayed a few times. What I will say, and this was years ago, once when he came to New York City, he can lift a lot more than I can, and I think that that is, we should give him his respect in that way. I don't think in any way this man is a “Mini Mamdani.” I also think that what we're talking about is someone who has shone a light on the importance of public health and healthcare in our country for years. And I am proud to be part of a movement of politicians and candidates who are looking to put working-class Americans back at the heart of our politics, and that's our focus here in New York City, and just from what we're seeing in Michigan, it looks like that's what Michiganders want there to be their focus come November.

q.t: I want you to hear what he said. He said: “There is an urgent question facing America, are we going to maintain our status as the world's greatest superpower and beacon of liberty, opportunity, and security, or allow radical Marxist Democrats to destroy the very foundations that make us the envy of the entire world?” Then he has a new paragraph, “Democrats now openly express disdain for America and embrace the failed, dangerous, deadly path of communism. We must take a stand and fight to protect the greatest nation in the history of the world from being overrun by Mini Mamdanis.”

a.t: That's a lot of characters. He must have the pro account. I'm assuming that's in response to Abdul El-Sayed's victory yesterday evening. And I think first I'd just like to congratulate Dr. Abdul El-Sayed on his victory. He ran a campaign where it was best described by his words of, “money out of politics, money in your pocket, Medicare for all.” And if those simple commitments and beliefs are what drives Representative Johnson to these kinds of conclusions, I think it shows you how deeply out of touch the Republican party is with the concerns of working-class Americans, because what we have seen is, despite him facing more than $60 million in outside spending, he was able to prevail with a focus on a cost-of-living crisis and the way in which healthcare is exceedingly out of reach for those who have helped to make this country what it is.

q.t: So, I saw this X post from House Speaker Mike Johnson coming off the win of the progressive candidates yesterday, but did you see it? Because if not—

a.t: I have not followed his X [account].

q.t: If, in a year from now, I go on Amazon and buy an illegal e-bike, like how would the city know? [Inaudible] tapped into my Amazon, or Amazon is going to be forced to send that your way?

a.t: This is going to be done through active monitoring of these retailers and what they are selling. It's not the question of what you are making an individual purchase of; it's the fact that these are being stocked and sold. And a lot of times we're talking not just about passively stocking these items; we're talking about active advertisement that is targeted to New Yorkers. This is something that every retailer should know. I would argue that many of them do know it and they are still operating outside of it because they have not yet seen enforcement. What they're going to see now is enforcement.

q.t: Following up on the question about Crystal Hudson's legislation, Transportation Alternatives has also expressed support for banning the sale of e-bikes that can exceed 20 miles per hour. Do you support that legislation, and is there any way for you as mayor — can you unilaterally do something to stop the sale of those types of bikes today?

a.t:
I think the first thing we can do is enforce the laws that have already been passed and what we're talking about — the different incidents, whether we're talking about Gabrielle or whether we are talking about the Queensboro Bridge — those are vehicles that should not have been on the road as per laws that had been passed years ago. And I look forward to whatever the City Council wants to put forward. We work with them as partners in this. Our question is always: “What will keep New Yorkers safe?” And right now, the enforcement of these laws — that's our focus, because that's something we can do in the next few weeks. So, we can do it with immediate action. We look forward to seeing what the Council puts forward as well.

[Crosstalk.]

q.t: Do you plan to drastically expand the bike lane network?

a.t: I believe that we need to improve and expand the bike lane network. We need to ensure that every single New Yorker can travel around the city safely, no matter their mode of transit. And that is something that has been part of the conversations I've had with our DOT commissioner from the very beginning of our administration. We want to ensure every New Yorker can get around the city safely and never has to doubt whether their mode of transit is impacting their safety in that moment.

q.t: The other question is, do you have plans to drastically expand the bike lane network? Because it was first introduced by Bloomberg before e-bikes were even a thing.

a.t: Sorry, could you restate the question?

q.t: My first question is, do you support any kind of legislation that would require e-bikers to be registered or licensed with the state?

a.t: I think the focus of today is tackling the root causes of what has led to the loss of many New Yorkers' lives. When it comes to registration for e-bikers, I do not believe that that would actually improve street safety, and that's not an approach that I believe we should move ahead with.

q.t: In January, Council Member Crystal Hudson introduced legislation to ban class three e-bikes, which is the e-bike that Gabriel was riding last week. Why go this route for online retailers instead of banning them entirely?

a.t:
I think first and foremost, we are looking at a wide variety of avenues of how to take action on this issue. And that includes working with the Council on legislation that has been introduced prior, as well as on the legislation that was recently introduced. We also cannot afford to wait. We cannot afford to wait because we know the consequences of this are fatal for New Yorkers. And what we have seen is that this has been the law for six years. And these companies have willfully been violating that law.

What use is a law if it is not being enforced? And what we are going to do now is start to use every tool at our disposal to enforce this law and to ensure that whether you are a company that many of us have never heard of or the companies that we know are the wealthiest in the world, that you will be held accountable to this because New Yorkers' lives are at stake.

q.t: Is it not possible to do that? To force them to?

a.t: Everything is possible, and so we're looking at the possibility again of a recall. But at this point in time, it's all about enforcement and compliance with the law, ensuring that New Yorkers are safe.

q.t: This question is for the attorney general. If you want to also answer the question, mayor, that's fine. We're talking about safety here, right? So, is there a legal remedy, perhaps for these companies to be forced to issue some sort of recall and, you know, have these customers return these devices and perhaps get their money back? Since we have so many out there on the streets. Can you force them to do this?

a.t: So, there are so many recommendations that have been made. As the mayor indicated, the first step is compliance. And so, we issued an advisory — a warning — and then they will have until August 18. And then we will ensure compliance through injunctions. And there will be a number of inspections. We will — again — the whole of government; we will work very closely with corporation counsel to ensure that individuals know the law. And we will also be looking at whether or not the $2,000 fine is adequate. Whether or not we should increase it, but it's important to understand that it's $2,000 per infraction.

q.t: I wanted to ask, why give them a grace period if they're already breaking the law? What makes you think that they will, all of a sudden, because of today's announcement, follow the law? And also, the $2,000 seems really low for Amazon, a billion-dollar company. Many of these companies are in the billions of dollars. $2000 doesn't seem like it's going to make a dent to them.

a.t: You know, I think what we've seen is that once we bring the actions of these kinds of retailers and companies into the sunlight, it becomes far harder for them to defend what they are doing. I'm going to bring up our corporation counsel to speak a little bit more about the specifics of it.

I don't know, Kelly, when you get a letter that says stop, and you don't stop, then you're liable for all the things that the law gives us the ability to do, which includes seeking injunctions and stopping people from continuing the conduct. You're right. For a very large corporation, $2,000 isn't that much, but facing an injunction to comply with the law is enforcing the law and protecting New Yorkers. In terms of giving them two weeks to come into compliance, that seems to me, as someone who's litigated against government a lot — giving someone who is out of compliance with the law an opportunity to cure their non-compliance seems reasonable. And for those that don't cure their non-compliance, then the full force of the law is what they'll face.

And I want to echo something that Corporation Counsel Banks has just stated earlier, which is that the point of this is not the collection of fines. The point is compliance. We want every single retailer to be in compliance. Our dream is that by August 18, we are not collecting a single fine because every one of these 42 companies is now in compliance. The most important thing here is that New Yorkers are safe. And I can tell you that being on the phone with Gabriel’s mother, the heartbreak that she felt then [and] that she feels now, is one that no New Yorker should ever have to deal with.

q.t: What about the stores in New York City? These vehicles are already in stores in New York City, so is the City going to do inspections in those stores to make sure that they're no longer carrying these types of vehicles?

a.t: The inspections that we are going to be carrying out are not simply online; they are going to be across all methods of sale. And again, I just want to echo what the DOT commissioner has said. This is not that complicated for these retailers. If they are selling an e-bike that can go faster than 25 miles an hour, that's illegal. If they're selling a stand-up scooter that can go faster than 20 miles an hour, that is illegal. If they are selling a moped that does not have a vehicle identification number and a license plate, that is illegal. These are quite straightforward when it comes to the laws, and yet we've seen the willful violation of this. But to your point, there's going to be inspection and accountability no matter what the method of sale is.

q.t: In the meantime, though, what can purchasers look out for if they're not super familiar with the rules? I know you're doing, obviously, public outreach today, but when you're buying a bike or a scooter, is it obvious in the listings on those websites that they're exceeding the rules? Are they marketing it that way? And also, how will the city know if they are complying?

a.t: If who is complying, the retailers? First and foremost, that they are not selling vehicles that go beyond the legal limits of speed and wattage. And what we found in some of this advertising — by and large, companies are not informing New Yorkers that these are beyond the illegal limits. It's not, here's a way to get around the law; it's, here is the quickest way for you to get to where you want to go. And I'm going to pass it over to our DOT commissioner to go into a little bit more detail as to what those limits are because that is one guideline for New Yorkers. And as you've said, you know, this is a cease-and-desist period until August 18. After that point, these companies are going to have to deal with our corporation counsel. And we also know that this is an issue that has been of immense focus [for] our attorney general as well.

Yeah, and I would echo what the mayor said, that at the end of the day, the most efficient way to get compliance is through the retailers. That's a much smaller universe. Of course, we also want to educate consumers, and at DOT, with our partners, we've been putting out a lot of material. You can see one example here next to us, right? This particular one is geared towards the retailers, and it's a very simple decision tree of: Does the e-bike go over 25 miles per hour? Does the scooter go over 20? There are also some limitations related to either the weight or the power of the motor of these devices. And it's not that complicated. I think for retailers, it should be pretty clear. For buyers, it's a little more complicated, and that's why we're focusing on the retailers. But education is one big piece.

q.t: But technically, the surveillance of all of this online activity — what's the mechanism for that? You know what I mean?

a.t: Well, the first mechanism is we put them on notice that we know that they're breaking the law. We're requesting that they meet with us and lay out how they're going to come into compliance with the law. If they meet with us and lay out a plan for compliance, great. If they don't, we will go after them in terms of fines and enforcement.

And I'll just add one thing, Melissa, before you go, which is that sometimes when we are taking these kinds of actions, we're speaking about companies that many of us may not know the names of, companies that may register themselves in a new name every other week. Today, we are speaking about companies like Amazon, Best Buy, Wayfair, some of the largest retailers in the country, and that they have been operating outside of the bounds of the law is something of immense concern to us and to New Yorkers.

q.t: So, let's talk about what happens after August [18]. How does the state or the city ensure that compliance and is able to monitor all 40 of these retailers to be able to determine how many fines will be assessed per sale? What’s the method?

a.t: So, we are talking about a maximum fine of $2,000 that will be issued up to that amount for each individual infraction. And what we have seen in the past in the issuing of cease-and-desist letters is that you get immediate compliance for a number of those actors who are then alerted to what the fiscal cost would be of operating outside of the bounds of the law. And then there is the need, as you've alluded to, for regular monitoring of this. I'm going to bring up our corporation counsel to add to that.

Good morning. If we get to the deadline and everybody complies, that is a great result. If people want to not follow up and comply, we'll take legal action. That could include fines; that could include bringing litigation to stop the advertisements that are resulting in people purchasing things that they think are legal. So, it's a two-fold approach. Give people an opportunity to conform their conduct, and if they don't, we will take action.

q.t: There's a lot of conflation out there about what is an e-bike, what's an e-moto, a moped, you know, how is the city going to let people know like what is a legal device and what isn't — and also, you know, that has to do with some of the backlash against e-bikes.

a.t: I think first and foremost, we're going to go after those websites and retailers that are willfully selling illegal vehicles to New Yorkers. It should not have to be up to each New Yorker to know every single line of New York City law. We know the law very clearly. These retailers know the law very clearly, and if they don't, they have two weeks to learn it before we start to hold them accountable with up to $2,000 per individual infraction. And again, what we are asking them to do is follow the law that has been the law for more than five years. And yet they continue to violate it, not in a marginal way — we're talking about vehicles that can go sometimes more than double the legal limit of the speed. It's not one or two miles over. And they are doing this because they know that there is money to be made. However, as you've heard and seen from the attorney general, from the DOT commissioner, for us here, the most important thing is how to keep people safe, and it means taking action when we're seeing e-bikes that are going close to 40 miles an hour, stand-up scooters that might even be eclipsed at 50 miles an hour. These are not things that will keep New Yorkers safe, and we are going to hold those retailers accountable.

q.t: What were the parameters for choosing the 42 or over 40 retailers?

a.t: I think first and foremost is who is actually selling these kinds of vehicles. We're talking about e-bikes that go beyond the legal limit of speed; we're talking about scooters as well, stand-up scooters that go beyond the limits of wattage; and we're also talking about the mopeds that do not have VINs that are actually available to be seen by the naked eye. I don't know, Steve, if you want to add any additional details to that.

q.t: So, will there be an on-street enforcement aspect of this? I know you're talking about going after the sellers, but there's also a lot of these devices that are already on the streets. Will there be some sort of action by NYPD, because I know they are able to kind of seize and take away these devices?

a.t: So, this is the first step of what is going to be a continued focus when it comes to ensuring that we keep New Yorkers safe. And as you said, that first step is going to be the issuing of cease-and-desist letters to more than 40 online retailers. And you've heard this from the AG, you've heard this from the DOT commissioner; there are a number of New Yorkers who think that they are buying legal vehicles when they purchase these, because why would they think otherwise? And what we have found is these are some of the largest retailers in the country. And we are going to hold them accountable. They have until August 18 — I believe that's the date — until they have to comply with this. And after that point, it's going to be up to $2,000 per individual infraction. And as we continue to focus on this work, we will let New Yorkers know what the next steps are. For now, this is our focus.

q.t: Yes or no on the raids? Are the raids going to continue, do you think?

a.t: I think we're going to see a different direction when it comes to the kind of leadership that this new sheriff is going to bring.

q.t: I just wondered if you had any updates on the sheriff and his legal bills, whether the City is going to pay them. And then also a question for your new sheriff, Sheriff Raymond. Do you want to see him crack down on merchants selling weed without licenses in the city in the same way that Miranda did?

a.t: I want to see our new sheriff uphold that office in a manner that also inspires the trust of New Yorkers across the five boroughs. And I think what is truly inspiring about his journey is that it has been one of trying to create a bridge of trust between law enforcement and those that it serves. And especially in a moment like we are in today where so many Haitian New Yorkers are living in a permanent state of anxiety given the question of TPS, I am proud that we are seeing in his appointment the first appointment of a Haitian American to a top law enforcement position. I do apologize; I have to get back to you on your first question about the question of legal fees.

q.t: Are there legal modes or sort of uses that you think shouldn't be legal?

a.t: I think my first focus, frankly, is that which is already illegal, how to ensure that no consumer is duped into believing that that is an appropriate way to be moving around the city, because it is hard for New Yorkers to keep up with what is legal or illegal if they're able to buy it online, and our work is how to insure that each of those New Yorker knows this is something that's permitted, this is not, and the reason it's not is because it's not safe.

q.t: There's a suite of bills being introduced or announced today in the City Council cracking down on e-bikes and motorized scooters. Julie Menin's announcing that in a couple minutes, I think. It's a whole list of things that would crack down on faster e-bikes that are currently legal. I won't go through the whole list, but I'm curious if you've talked with the Council or Speaker Menin about those proposals and if you stand anywhere on whether these kinds of modes of transportation should be further regulated.

a.t: I'll wait to see the specifics of these proposals themselves. What I will say is having spoken to the mother of the young man who was killed while riding on an illegal e-bike, my heart just breaks for her and for all the families who've had their children stolen from them as a result of this. And as I and others have made clear, that bike is one that should never have been on our streets. And it is critically important that safety is something that each and every New Yorker has, no matter what mode of transportation they use. And that continues to be a focus for us — is how can we ensure that's the case as well.

q.t: I was out with sanitation officials this morning putting these stickers on cars that don't move for alternate side parking. This was done away with in 2012. It's back now. Gale Brewer was out sticking these stickers on cars. What do you think of this? It's an effort to get people to actually move their cars.

a.t: I think that it's critically important that the sanitation department be able to conduct street cleaning. And whenever I've seen the hardworking men and women of DSNY, the question is always, how can we make their jobs easier? If this does that, then it's something that I support.

q.t: I wanted to get an update from you on where things stand with the bill that the Council passed recently to give one-time payments to the paraprofessionals. The UFT president recently said that he would wage an all-out war if you didn't back the bonuses. Can you give a sense of where you're at, if you're planning to veto the legislation, or what's next on that?

a.t: I think, first and foremost, the paraprofessionals in our New York City Public School system do incredible and critical work, and it's work that should be appreciated and recognized when we're talking about what makes it possible for families to live in this city. I also believe that conversations around compensation are better left at the bargaining table, and what has been told to me in terms of a legal analysis of this bill is that it is a violation of the Taylor Law. And that continues to be the assessment that I am privy to.

q.t: I wanted to ask you about a tragedy that happened over the weekend in the Bronx. A mother and a grandmother were arrested for allegedly starving an autistic 16-year-old boy to death in their care. The Administration for Children's Services had closed a case into this family about two years prior to his passing, and the mom had also pulled him out of New York City Public School two months before. So, my question is, are you going to be calling for a probe into ACS's role in this case? And do you have any information about how this slipped through the cracks, especially since he was pulled out of public school?

a.t: So, I know that this has been a focus for ACS and for our commissioner, and I'm also deeply appreciative of their efforts when it comes to the brother of the young man who was killed and ensuring his safety in this time. Our focus primarily is on that question of safety, but it is a conversation that continues internally.

q.t: Are you concerned about offending or limiting people's contributions in the future because you've removed everyone on this board? Is there a way you'll try to keep those people involved?

a.t: I think we always want everyone who is interested in the future of our city to know that there's a place for them in the conversation around that. And as we create a new board, it's not to say that the old board doesn't still have a place in helping us think about what can come next.

q.t: I know that you've said you wanted to take the Mayor's Fund in a different direction and involve more community organizers and labor union leaders, etc. What message are you trying to send in removing the entire advisory board from the Mayor's Fund? These are corporate leaders who have shown willingness to volunteer their time and also an ability to tap into a vast network of wealth to help raise millions of dollars for the priorities of past mayors, including universal Pre-K, by the way. And so, I'm wondering, why not keep them around and ask them to help with initiatives like this one today, 2-K for instance? Is this a rebuke of good corporate citizenship, and are you putting ideology over practicality?

a.t: I think, first and foremost, we have a real appreciation for the contributions of these business leaders to the health and vitality of our city. And what this a reflection of is simply a commitment to a new era. And that is something that I've spoken of at large, but also specifically when it comes to the Mayor's Fund, we announced in April the direction that we wanted to take the fund with, and the creation of a new advisory board is an important next step in that. That will be a board that will bring together those who have achievements like the ones that you've listed, as well as those who oftentimes have not been at the heart of conversations of how philanthropy can build upon the work of public goods and public dollars. What I will say is we've already seen in just seven months multi-million-dollar contributions to the Mayor's Fund, specifically, as you said, with the goal of delivering universal childcare in mind.

q.t: That analysis happening now, or—

a.t: That's something the governor said. That is a focus of coming forward.

q.t: The governor mentioned an independent cost analysis. Is the City working with the state on that? Do you have timing for when that will come out? And do you have a sense if the $9 billion figure is more in the ballpark than the previously estimated $6 billion?

a.t: I think, as you heard from the governor, it's only right that we do an independent analysis and ensure that we have our full capacity being committed to having an assessment of what the cost is and what the scaling is.
