I will tell you that our focus right now at this time is actually on delivering this free childcare to families of two-year-olds across our city, and we're excited that in just a little — not too long from now, we're going to see families who can benefit from this. It's going to scale up to 12,000 seats, and we're going to continue to always do the work to ensure that that can expand out so that every family can have free childcare for two-year-olds.

q.t: Mr. Mayor, during the campaign and since then, you've talked about the need to raise taxes on the wealthy, on high earners and on corporations, in large part to fund universal 2-K. Do you still see the need for that or is it possible to fund 2-K going forward without increasing taxes on the wealthy?

a.t: I think the most important thing is that we fund programs like this. And what has truly been an incredible experience is having a partner at the state level in Governor Hochul, who is committed to that outcome. It meant that we could allocate $1.2 billion with just over a week of being in office. And I think in a city, in a country, in a world, frankly, where it seems that prices are only ever going up, to finally being able to tell families that the price of this one thing that they cannot live without is going down, it is something that is really at the core of what government should be doing. And it's only possible with partnership, and I'm very thankful for the governor as well as our leaders that we have here at the city and the state level for making that possible.

q.t: The 12,000 seats next year, will they be in every school district, or will they be limited to certain school districts?

a.t: We are going to expand across a number of school districts. They will be in every single borough. And as we know, Staten Island is a single school district. And we're going to be announcing that over the course of the next few months as to where that expansion will be, because I think what is always in mind for us is we want to be able to deliver this to every single parent, and we've said that by the end of four years that every single two-year-old will have a seat.

q.t: Well, first of all, I'm wondering, because you had 5,700 people apply, what were the qualifications, or what were the priorities that you gave in selecting the 2,000 people that actually made the cut? And what would you say to the parents who didn't make the cut about what they can look forward to in the future? And then I have a few give us more details about the funding, like where will you raise the money for next year's 12,000, and for the ongoing years, will you have to take it from other parts of the budget?

a.t: So, I'll go across the two questions. The governor made a two-year commitment in a funding stream of $1.2 billion. So, that allowed us to start with a program that would offer 2,000 seats this year and fund us through the expansion of that to 12,000 seats next year. Now, you've heard Senator Liz Warren describe childcare as infrastructure, and I think it's an apt characterization; because in order to provide these kinds of seats, we also have to do the work of ramping up the infrastructure so that we have the capacity. So, 2,000 seats this year, and then we're going to have seats in every single one of the five boroughs next year. And the reason we can do that is because of the incredible work at New York City Public Schools as well as through our office to support childcare over the course of that time period. Now, on your first question, as you heard from Emmy, and I think Emmy it might be worth just going through once more, priority is given to families who are in district who their child is already, you know, attending the school at a younger age. We also have a number of families who are applying who have siblings enrolled in that same school. This is always geared with the ease of parents' lives in mind. We don't want to have parents who have to drop off one child over here and then go to another neighbor to drop them off over there, but I know that Emmy will add additional details.

When families applied to 2-K, they have the opportunity to list up to 12 options on their application, very similar to the way our 3-K and Pre-K processes work. And then we, on the back end, work to match families to their highest rank choice pending availability. As the mayor reiterated, priority is given to families who live in the district, families who have a sibling at the program or who are continuing at the program. And then it's essentially a lottery among families who are in each of those priority groups. We know that there are so many families who want access to these seats and we wanted, as the mayor said, to make the process as easy as possible. So, all families had to do to apply was provide their child's birth date and their address. And then we worked to match families based on the priority structure. And then again, essentially a lottery where not all families could be matched. Families who applied to 2-K and did not receive an offer will be automatically placed on the wait list for any program they ranked on their application. We will be reaching out to families in the coming days to support them through that process. And as we are able to make wait list offers ahead of the first day of school, we will be in touch with families, and we are also working to add some additional capacity to meet some of the need. But we know this is why we need to continue growing the program.

q.t: So, there was a new study out that says that the childcare program is going to be much more costly than initially suggested, that it could cost up to nine billion dollars. I'm just wondering, what exactly is going be the strategy to ramp this up and to keep costs down? And then for Governor Kathy Hochul, just wondering will the state continue to fund this program? Is this just kick-starting or will the state be expected to fully fund this program for the years to come, especially when it expands?

a.t: So, I'll just begin by saying that when I acknowledged earlier the partnership with Governor Hochul, it's a partnership that began at the very beginning of this administration. On day eight, we stood together in Brooklyn announcing that the state would be committing $1.2 billion and that was funding that not only allowed us to offer these 2,000 seats this year, 12,000 seats next year, it also ensured that we had funding to fix the issues that parents [had] identified with 3-K. Because we'd heard from many parents that as much as they had dreamed, like Sandra and Fred, of being able to walk three minutes or maybe ten minutes if we look at the rocks to their school, that too many parents were being forced to go miles away from their home to find that childcare. And so, that funding helped us also resolve those issues while also providing funding towards vouchers. And we've always said that the goal here is to make it affordable to raise a family; because the question is not about whether this will cost money, it's a question of who will pay that money. And what I mean by that is that today, we have families across the city spending — as the governor said — between $20,000 to $40,000 a year to raise their child in the nation's most expensive city. And this is an initiative that we are working on, not just for the short term or the medium term, but the long term, to make it easier to raise that family here in New York City.

We plan to do an independent verification of the actual costs required, not just an outside study, that's how we operate, so I want to make sure that the media understands that. And in my budget this year, we've allocated $4.5 billion for childcare, as the mayor outlined, substantial amounts of that coming to the city, but also trying to expand to areas that have been underserved across the state of New York. I am committed through the program next year. I can't commit future budgets at this time. But I can tell you right now, I'm excited about the growth of this. This is just the very beginning. We know there's a lot more families to be served. We'll serve them in a way that we can afford. But I was proud to make the allocation we did within the confines of our existing budget this year and make commitments for next year as well.

q.t: Is there a deadline that they have to accept the offer by to be — you know — possibly a seat going to somebody on the wait list.

a.t: Families have to accept their offers by the end of August, we can get you the exact date.

q.t: So, you said there's just over 5,700 people who applied for this program, but there's only 2,000 seats. Can you explain how you narrowed down which families would be selected for the program? Was it based on income, location? How did you decide who would be getting these first 2,000 seats?

a.t:
Yes, so as we have always said, this first year would have 2,000 seats of free childcare for two-year-olds. And thanks to the governor's commitment, we would be able to expand next year to 12,000 seats in total. And as you said, we received about 5,700 applications for these 2,000 or so seats. And that means about 3,700 are on wait lists while we were able to grant admission to about 2,000 of those families. I'm going to pass it over to our executive director of the Office to Support Childcare, Emily Liss.

Emmy Liss, Executive Director, Office of Child Care So among the applicants — in order to determine who received those placements — we go through a priority structure very similar to the way children are admitted to 3-K, Pre-K, kindergarten and beyond. So, the highest priority went to children who have siblings or continuing students at programs with families who live in the 2-K districts being prioritized as well. And families when they applied were able to see what that priority structure would look like. So, the majority of our applicants — our families receiving offers there — are children who live in the districts that were prioritized for the expansion of 2-K, as well as the families who may have a sibling or [are] continuing at the program where they were headed.

q.t: On the pied-à-terre tax, I wanted to check, so the city sent out 17,000 letters, is that it? Will the city be sending out additional letters? And then how many exemptions have been filed so far? Have you guys received any back? And then why not utilize the Office of Mass Engagement to try to make sure that people are checking their mail, are making sure that they're getting these notices and know what's going on?

a.t: So, the assessment of 17,000 properties potentially being levied with this surcharge, that is the maximum number of properties. And now the process is on engaging with New Yorkers to see whether those who filed their property in a trust or in an LLC are in fact also primary residence holders of that same property. We have been engaging with a number of New Yorkers — we can have the team follow up with you with the exact number — already, just in the time since that first letter was sent. And that engagement will continue through September 18 with the Department of Finance, and again, if a New Yorker does not engage after that point, they can still appeal to the Tax Commission until March. And right now, what we are doing is investing in civil servants across the Department of Finance as well as OATH. We know that a lot of New Yorkers have long associated those agencies with any questions that they have with their property taxes. And so, what we've done is whether they're calling 311, whether they are calling the Department of Finance directly, or whether they are going in person into a business center, that they are all able now to ensure that they can help New Yorkers navigate those conversations. And we're thankful for the work of those civil servants.

q.t: Summer Streets kicked off on Saturday, and a lot of people who were there noticed that there was expanded police presence. Streetsblog reported a story on it; they say it's unprecedented, the number of police cars they saw blocking intersections. And many people said it really interfered with their experience of what Summer Streets is meant to be. I wanted you to speak to that — and it's also, I want to point out that that’s not the only type of community event where we've seen expanded police presence. It's also been reported that there are more police now at street festivals. What is the rationale behind that? And then I have a second question on Janno Lieber's comments that your talk of free buses has contributed to more fare evasion. Can you comment on that?

a.t:
You know, I think, Janno and I will always have a difference of opinion and that's fine, because here in New York City we learn how to live with each other, no matter how many differences of opinion we have. And the place of agreement that we have is how to make the slowest buses in America fast, how to them worth the time that New Yorkers pour into them when millions of New Yorker get on buses that sometimes crawl as slow as five miles an hour. Now when I was in high school, I went to high school here in the Bronx at Bronx Science, and to get there, I would get on the Bx10. And that bus went so slow that I knew if I could see it two stops away, I would be able to run and catch up. And that's not a good thing for a city when buses are that slow. Now, when it comes to making buses free, it is something that I continue to believe is important, because what we are talking about is a cost-of-living crisis in this city where one in five New Yorkers struggle to afford the fare at $3. And we know that that is only going to be exacerbated the longer this cost of live crisis goes and we never want a New Yorker to be priced out of that.

I am thankful of the work alongside with the Council, and we have our Council Member Justin Sanchez here, looking to ensure that we're increasing the eligibility for Fair Fares in the interim, which I also think is an important program. To your first question, I will follow up on the reporting around summer streets. I'm not yet aware of that article from Streetsblog. However, what I would say is, we want to ensure that New Yorkers are safe in all of these moments and we also want to ensure that New Yorkers can enjoy themselves and celebrate. And that was also one of the real focuses that we had over the course of this summer, and we most recently saw it during the World Cup. But thank you for highlighting the article and I'll be sure to follow up on it.

q.t: This morning, the NYPD put out their crime stats for the month of July. They said the Bronx is leading the city with a 12.5 percent drop in major crime, but with just in the last few days, there was a double shooting on Friday where an 87-year-old woman was shot in the face. This morning a 50-year-old man was shot to death in Van Nest. How do you kind of reconcile these numbers that the city is touting that crime is down when the reality is not of that on the streets? How do ensure that people in the Bronx actually feel safe when these crimes are happening on their streets?

a.t: I think first and foremost, so long as there is crime in the Bronx and there is crime in New York City, it means that there is work for us to do. And we can acknowledge and appreciate the incredible work of the men and women of the NYPD in reducing crime and also know that there's still so much more work to be done. And I will tell you, as someone who went to see Kai's body with his family at that viewing, I can never look at the heartbreak that that family is going through and say that the work that we have done is enough. There is always more work to be done and there always will be more work to be down until every 12-year-old can ride a bike to a bodega and ensure that they're just enjoying summer as every New Yorker has the right to.

q.t: Do you have any regrets about how it was rolled out? I mean, it was supposed to be something that you thought would help raise money for the city and instead you have people who are really angry.

a.t: I continue to believe that the pied-à-terre surcharge will raise $500 million on an annual basis. And the importance of this tax is that it is one that will ensure that our streets are cleaner, that our city is safer, that our schools are more supported. And what we are also doing is embarking on something new in New York City where we are ensuring that we are assessing the primary residents of homeowners in homes that are worth more than $5 million. And we've sent out 17,000 letters. And now from that, we’re receiving engagement from New Yorkers to assess what the final number is. The thing we did not want to do was levy this charge without giving New Yorkers a period of time where they could engage with the city. And now that's this period of engagement.

q.t: Mr. Mayor, I want to follow up on the pied-à-terre tax. I wonder if you have any regrets about the way this was rolled out, because you have a lot of people who are angry that they were, first of all, that their information was public anyway. But, secondly, they have been long-term residents of the city. They don't, they feel they don't have to prove that they've been living here since they've been living here all their lives. And do you regret the rollout? Would you have done it differently? And what do you want to say to these people who are angry?

a.t:
I think first and foremost that I understand the concerns New Yorkers have, especially when it comes to a new tax, and as we know that new taxes typically present more questions than they do answers. Now when it comes to the property tax role and the “you may be subject to” letters, I do also want to state that there has been both a willful and an unintentional conflation of both the property-tax role and these letters. The property tax roll, as you know is something that the city releases twice a year annually and has been doing so for decades, frankly, if not longer. This is a tax role that was released that had more than 900,000 homes on it. And we know that the pied-à-terre surcharge is for secondary homes of non-resident New Yorkers. The city sent a letter to 17,000 homeowners; that is a fraction of the number of homeowners in New York City and a fraction of the number of people who call the city home — an 8.5 million.

And in that letter, it stated that this is the process by which you can engage with the city to ensure that if you do not believe this to be an accurate assessment of your property, you have the time to appeal this assessment. And so, whether New Yorkers are gonna call 311 or they're gonna call the Department of Finance directly, or also now if they want to go directly to a business center in person, we want to make sure that they have all the resources necessary to that.

q.t: I actually had an on-topic question and then I'll ask you the off as well. My first one — great segue from the previous question about the LIFT tracker — last week, some Harlem residents sued over one of the projects that's actually on that tracker, 1727 Amsterdam Avenue. They believe their healthcare services are gonna be lost due to an affordable housing project coming there. I wonder, you talk about communities of color not being pushed out, Black New Yorkers leaving the city more than any other. Why not rethink that project if so many community members and officials don't want to see that project go forward in the form that it is right now? My separate question for off topic is, you extended the deadline for the pied-à-terre, I guess people to file for the exemption. I wanted to know why you obviously did that because there's been so many complications. I'm wondering, between the complications for the people that are filing for the exemptions and the work that your staff is doing, how do you see this tax even coming to fruition when there's so many complications early?

a.t:
So, I'll answer the first question and also bring up the deputy mayor for the specifics on the property that you mentioned. I will first just say that it is critically important that we build more housing across New York City. And the reason for that is the absence of that housing construction has been one of the factors that has pushed so many New Yorkers out of the city. As you alluded to in your question, the cost-of-living crisis, it affects every single New Yorker. The effect of it, however, is not born evenly. We've seen Black New Yorkers disproportionately hit by the impact of this crisis. We've seen 200,000 Black New Yorkers be pushed out of this city in the last few decades alone. And we've also seen that reflected even in the population of Black children and teenagers; from 2010 to 2019, our city's population went down by nearly 20 percent.

And so, one of the top priorities that we have as a city is how do we build housing that can ensure that Black history isn't just something that we celebrate in New York City, but it's something that we can also ensure can keep being written in New York City. Because one of the times that I saw a pastor in Harlem was when I met him on his way to the airport, I asked him where he was going and he told me he was going to meet a parishioner of his in South Carolina. Because now that's where she can afford to live. And I think that building more housing, especially whether it be in Manhattan, in the Bronx, in every single one of five boroughs, in Harlem. It is critical to ensuring that we can meet that, but I'll pass it over to the deputy mayor on any specifics.

Deputy Mayor Bozorg: On the specific project you named, yes, litigation has started. You know, that is a project that has been in the works for a very long time, many years, and there has been a long community engagement process. We of course want to continue to work with the community and hear their concerns. But there are health services that are both coming back in that project, as well health services and health investments that the Council member secured through the land use process that are investments we are making nearby. So, there is a shared goal of continuing the healthcare services that the neighborhood needs while also building this much needed 100 percent affordable project that has been long in the making. But we'll of course continue to work with the community and of course now through the litigation process as well.

And just to your second question, Kelly. Yes, we have extended the deadline to September 18. And the point of this period of time is precisely so that New Yorkers — the 17,000 homeowners who received the “you may be subject to” letters — have all the information they need and also have the time to be able to inquire with any questions, as well as appeal any assessment of their property as being one that would receive the surcharge. Again, this is a surcharge for secondary homes of non-resident New Yorkers that are worth more than $5 million. We've also made the decision to hire 24 additional civil servants across multiple city agencies precisely to be engaging with New Yorker on this question. Again, if a New Yorker does not appeal this by September 18, they still have until March to appeal this to the Tax Commission before this tax is actually levied.

q.t: I wanted to ask a little bit about the SPEED Task Force and the EO that you signed early in your administration. A lot of people on stage said that this was a long time coming, this specific project. Were there any specific aspects of the SPEED initiative that got things out of a gridlock, out of a place where they were not moving? Any permits that were kind of stuck that were able to be expedited through that initiative? And how does this go hand in hand with any LIFT initiatives happening in the area? I know we took this bus tour of a different part of the Bronx, but I was looking at your new tracker — there seem to be City-owned sites surrounding this. Is this gonna be kind of a hub for development in both of those areas, and can you go into that?

a.t: I'm glad that you brought up the bus tour, because what we saw on that tour were a number of sites that had been announced years ago. I met the borough president right before I got on the bus and she mentioned to me that as part of a rezoning that she won when she was a Council member, 2018 Jerome Avenue, she secured one of these sites. It's eight years later and you can go to that site, and it looks very similar to what it was in 2018. And so, I think the point of this is to say that the issue of expediting construction is not specific to any one location; it is an issue we are seeing across the five boroughs. And we never want to be able to look at a site and say that we are contributing to the delay of the building on that site. So, I am so thankful for the leadership of our deputy mayor in identifying any which way — both within city government, but also in terms of state law — that we can be expediting this, because that's a big reason why we lent our voice to the fight for SEQRA reform, because we had identified SEQRA reform as being one of the factors that was delaying construction times up to two years. And that is simply not acceptable in a city where we haven't built enough housing per demand since 1961. I'm gonna pass it to our deputy mayor for additional details.

I'll note just a couple other things specifically that came out of the SPEED Task Force and that we'll continue to work on. The SPEED Task Force, of course, looked at from environmental review through lease up, the different stages of the process and things we could do to speed up pre-certification, financing and the lease-up process. So, things like adding $1 billion to the budget for supportive housing — that's gonna allow us to finance more and more quickly. But the SPEED Task Force also named a couple things specific to the process of getting formerly homeless households into housing faster. One is a pilot that's called MATCH, that's really allowing developers to work directly with shelter providers to make referrals faster and easier. That's something that we're rolling out this fall. And then there's another piece looking specifically at the homeless placement process. We're introducing new technology to make that process — again, this is in the set-aside process — make that process just move faster. Those are two parts of the process that providers, both supportive housing providers and shelter providers, have told us there have been real bottlenecks. So, it's really a range of pieces across the development process that SPEED is gonna help with for projects like this.

q.t: There are roughly 100,000 people sleeping in City homeless shelters. Your administration released a housing plan in May that sort of touched on that, but I'm curious if you expect to release a separate blueprint kind of focused on how you're planning to address homelessness and bring down that shelter population. And then relatedly, does the city need more homeless shelter space in addition to housing?

a.t:
I think, first and foremost, we know that the preeminent crisis in New York City is that of the housing crisis. And we know the homelessness crisis is one face of that. And what makes today so exciting is that we are building not only housing that currently homeless New Yorkers, as well as those at risk of homelessness, can live in, but that we're accompanying that housing with the kind of services that make it possible for those New Yorker to transform their own lives. And we are doing this alongside an allocation of more than $5 million in the recently adopted budget, where we are putting money towards a cross-agency task force that is looking to bring vacant supportive housing units online quicker so that we can ensure that we are meeting New Yorkers’ needs as quickly as we can. I'm gonna pass it over to our deputy mayor for housing and planning to speak to your broader question as well.

Deputy Mayor Bozorg: Yes, so as the mayor noted, supportive housing is a huge prong of our broader housing plan. And as the Block by Block plan noted, we are increasing the funding, not just for supportive housing, but for all affordable housing, much of which has a 15 percent set-aside for formerly homeless New Yorkers. So, the plan itself is increasing exponentially the homes that will be built for formerly homeless New Yorkers. We are also working in partnership with Deputy Mayor Arteaga and the Department of Social Services and other partners on a broader homelessness blueprint that will be issued later this year. So, it's a little bit of both through the housing plan as well as strategies that will live outside of the housing plan.

q.t: Hi, I wanted to go back to the pied-à-terre. Do you agree with the way that it was rolled out? You know, many people would say that it shouldn't be on them as homeowners that believe that their properties weren't supposed to be the ones in that catch net, and it should be the city going with the scalpel versus this huge broad approach. I mean, what would you have wanted them to do differently?

a.t: To be clear, these “you may be subject to” letters were sent to 17,000 homes out of our city of eight and a half million people. And I nevertheless understand the concerns of some New Yorkers in opening these letters because I know that a new tax often offers more questions than it does answers. And what we are doing in this process is the work that is necessary to ensure that this tax is only levied on secondary homes that are worth more than five million dollars. Now, some of those homes are obviously secondary homes; some of them are homes that are registered as a trust or as an LLC. And this outreach is to ensure that they are occupied by a primary residence holder. And whether New Yorkers want to call DOF or the Tax Commission or 311, we are ensuring that various aspects of city government are prepared to engage in this so that we can actually be in a conversation with New Yorkers about this tax. That's all the time we have for today. Thank you all very much.

q.t: So, Black Lives Matter released their own audit today in which they claim that there are about 1,600 active NYPD officers with at least $100,000 settlements. If that is the case, should those officers be reinvestigated? And what would you like to see from the police commissioner in order to bring that number down and, you know, cost the City less money?

a.t: I think the first thing I'm going to do after this press conference is actually to review this, because it's the first that I'm hearing of it. What I will say is, something that Commissioner Tisch and I share is a belief that New Yorkers need not have to choose between safety and justice. That is paramount to us, and we're proud of the fact that we are delivering some of the lowest crime in New York City history when it comes to murders, shootings and shooting victims. That continues to be the lowest in recorded history here in our city. We also know there's far more work to be done to ensure that we're delivering that public safety on a daily basis, and that'll continue to be our North Star. Thank you for raising it, though.

q.t: Hi Mr. Mayor. I wanted to ask, you know, these three sites that you guys have been talking about today. The financing seems to be, I would just say, creative, but different than more than other ways. Is that because developing housing in the city continues to be a struggle? And then my other question is, among these hundred locations, are any of them being prioritized for communities that have long been needing housing?

a.t: I would say that that is generally a focus for us of how to build more housing, especially in neighborhoods that have been denied that kind of affordability. Just the other day, I was at a library in Brooklyn with City Council Member Alexa Avilés, and we were celebrating not only the 100th tenant union that was formed as part of Partners in Partnership, but also the fact that at that very library there was to be 100 percent affordable housing being built on top of it. Which I think is the first affordable housing that's going to be built in that neighborhood in quite some time. And when it comes to the financing approach, we are going to explore every option we have in front of us because creativity is going to be a necessary part of ensuring that we are finally building enough housing for the greatest city in the world because what we've seen for far too long is — it's been since 1961 that we've had a recognition of what we need to build to keep the city growing to its fullest potential.

I'll just add; every community needs affordable housing in New York City, and some have been producing more than others and so there is certainly going to be an effort to kind of figure out how to merge the Lift Task Force work with the broader work we're doing through the Fair Housing Framework to identify areas where we know we need to be expediting the creation of housing and specifically affordable housing. So, it really is a bit of both. Everywhere needs more housing, and we need to capitalize on the resources we have, but we will also be targeting areas where we feel like not enough housing has been built.

q.t: Was it always the intent of the executive order to include existing projects in the 10,000-unit count, or do you expect the LIFT Task Force to eventually identify enough new sites to build those 10,000 units that were named in the executive orders?

a.t: I think part of our focus is on how to expedite long-standing sites that have either been dormant or have been delayed, and how to ensure we can actually deliver on them so that we go beyond renderings and move into reality. I'm going to pass it over to my deputy mayor to add any additional details.

a.s: Leila Bozorg, Deputy Mayor for Housing and Planning
a.t: It's both about identifying the sites we're working on and how we can ensure that we speed them up and be transparent about it with the public. Folks are often asking where are public sites that we can use for housing. So, there's a transparency element to what we're working on and know today. And then we have also and will be identifying new sites to meet the targets laid out in that executive order, about identifying sites to build an additional 25,000 over 10 years. So, it is truly both.

q.t: I have a pied-à-terre question. I want to know how many people are being hired at both DOF and OATH in connection with processing pied-à-terre tax, I guess, where it applies, and what exactly are the new positions they're hiring for at those two agencies?

a.t: 24 people are being hired across both of those, and the focus of their hiring is to engage with New Yorkers who have questions about this process. And one of the reasons that we started this process at this point is to ensure that New Yorkers have the requisite amount of time to engage with city government before the levying of this tax. And so, for New Yorkers who have questions for the Department of Finance, they have until the end of next month, and then that period continues when it comes to the tax commission until March. And what I will also say is, I understand the concerns that some New Yorkers have, and they are facing, and I know that a new tax typically brings more questions than it does bring answers. And right now, we are working around the clock across multiple city agencies to ensure that we are engaging with New Yorkers about how we are going to be delivering a tax on secondary homes worth more than $5 million.

q.t: Are you waiting for his office to come back to you, or is there something that you and the governor can present to the president to advance it?

a.t: It continues to be a conversation.

q.t: What is the status of the Sunnyside Yard project? Have you and the president continued to have conversations about that?

a.t: It continues to be the subject of conversations, and the reason it's something of importance to us is that it holds the potential to deliver on more than 10,000 new homes, as well as delivering more than 30,000 jobs. And when we're looking at our city, one of the things that is most finite is land. And so, the opportunity to turn land, which is currently a railyard, into somewhere that housing could be built, is one that we're always going to be interested in talking about. This will be a long-term conversation given the scale of investment required and the scale of commitment, and part of that is the reason why this idea has been an idea for frankly close to a century, and now we're doing the work to try and make it into a reality.

q.t: And then with these city-owned lots that have been identified, does the admin have an idea for what portion should go to housing, or is it all supposed to be housing and then, you know, notch down from there if things are ineligible for like a new development like that?

a.t: Generally, our focus is on housing, and the reason it's our focus is that we are seeing people priced out of the city on a daily basis, and wherever opportunity we have to build more housing is one that we're going to take.

q.t: I'm wondering if — I know you're talking about speeding this up, do you have a benchmark of like how much time on average you'd actually like to shave off? I know that it can depend vastly based on projects.

a.t: I think we've set the goal of 200,000 affordable homes to be built by the end of 10 years. That will require a pace we have not seen in City government for quite some time. We are doing that alongside taking the measures that will also unlock private development alongside public development. And so, the SPEED Task Force — we've seen estimates that can cut what was a two-year wait into six months. Also adding our voice to efforts at the state level like SEQRA reform, which have a similar impact in cutting down that wait time. I don't know, deputy mayor, if there's anything you'd add.

I'll just add that, as the mayor noted, there's a series of reforms we're introducing, things like capitalizing on the SEQRA reform that the state passed that we've committed to enabling us to cut the pre-certification timeline from two years to six months. But some of the other reforms that we're using and introducing through the SPEED Task Force; through use of things like ULURP; through use of things like our fast track. We're hoping to cut down another, you know, at times it can be another 6 to 18 months that we're able to cut down, depending on the specifics of a project.

q.t: So, what efforts are you all taking to not only make sure that the community is aware of what's going on, but that that prioritize in getting affordable housing?

a.t: You know, it's a great question. I think one is that the community has helped to shape what these developments are going to be. You know, the second site that we just saw was affordable home ownership. And that's something that we had heard from the community when it comes to that specific site; it was a point of importance. In the first site that we saw, we hear often from NYCHA residents about their hopes for what housing could look like in their own neighborhoods. And I think you heard from the deputy mayor that that site is going to be one that's not just built on NYCHA land but will also have housing for current NYCHA residents. And that is critically important, that those who have borne the brunt of government neglect can now also be the beneficiaries of government investment.

q.t:
In plain terms, what do you see on this tour that reflects what you think you're bringing to these projects, which predated your administration, but you're promising to speed them up. I heard deputy mayor—

[Crosstalk.]

In plain terms, can you talk about what you're bringing to — picking up on what you were talking about before. What are you adding to these projects to make them come together?

[Crosstalk.]

a.t: I think one of the things that we are taking away from this tour is both what it will look like for this housing to actually be built, how it would transform places that you might not even blink at if you were walking past. And that is a reflection of the fact that there's a lot of land across the city that is not being used to its fullest potential to keep people in this city. And I think when we talk about when these announcements were first made, we're talking about multiple mayoral administrations ago, and now is the possibility — through the LIFT Task Force, through the SPEED Task Force — to start to actually make what is currently, you know, overgrown grass and trees into a place that can actually house New Yorkers. And it's going to take an all-of-the-above approach. In some places it's going to be a place that is fenced off; in other places it is going to a library that currently exists and transforming it into something that is not only keeping New Yorkers well-read, but also well-housed. And that is part of a partnership that we're proud to have with the New York Public Library system, and one that we believe still has far more units to unlock when we apply it across the city.

q.t: [Inaudible] local communities around these sites in addition to the agencies that might own them? I know community engagement is part of the process in a lot of these. I'm wondering if they're learning about them for the first time through this tracker.

a.t:
So, that's a really great question. Community engagement is a very important part of any housing development that we do prior to releasing a request for proposals. So, it is a multi-step process. First, in working with agencies to say, “I know this site is under your jurisdiction; is this something we can work together on to co-create housing and some other use?” That's about the question of, “Can we unlock this site for housing?” Once the answer for that becomes yes, HPD, EDC, the agencies develop an intensive community engagement process to work with folks to say, “This site's going to become housing. What do you need in your neighborhood? What are you looking for?” Often, what's produced then is something called a community visioning report that is attached to a request for proposal, so that respondents are responding specifically to the needs that communities have expressed through engagement.

And then, of course, the land use process has engagement as well, but the more intensive community engagement often is in that pre-RFP stage, and then there's touch points throughout the way once a site is going through a process to be developed. I will note, the time it takes to develop housing has made that community engagement process really challenging. You wanna engage a community before an RFP's released, but sometimes it's taking two, three, up to five years, even more sometimes, to actually finance that building. That's part of why our SPEED initiative's important; it's part of why the additional capital so that we can expedite the financing of these projects is important. So that so much time doesn't pass between that community engagement and when the housing is being delivered.

And I'll just add one final point on that, which is that right before we got on this beautiful double-decker bus, I had the chance to say hello to Bronx borough president, Vanessa Gibson. And she mentioned to me that the second site that we were going to was a site that she won in the 2018 Jerome Avenue rezoning. That site was won when the current borough president was a city councilwoman. And now, eight years later, it continues to look very similar as it did on that day. And that also speaks to what the deputy mayor is referring to when it comes to the delays that we've seen characterize a lot of our housing processes.

q.t:
I wanted to ask about one of the constituent concerns that was shouted here today about parking and one of the sites you mentioned at the beginning of the tour. The NYPD parking lot that was redeveloped in the East Village, you're replacing parking for NYPD on that lot as part of the redevelopment.

I'm wondering under what circumstances the types of lots that the city owned where there might already be parking or there might be city agencies or groups like the NYPD that might want parking, under what circumstances would you consider the city putting money into a project to replace the parking? Especially considering in your housing plan during the campaign you were against mandating minimum parking in new developments.

a.t:
So, I'll share a few words and then I'll pass it over to our deputy mayor. First and foremost, the importance of tackling the housing crisis comes from the fact that it is the dominant crisis in our city that is pushing New Yorkers out of the five boroughs. And you ask so many of the New Yorkers who now live in Connecticut or Massachusetts or Pennsylvania or Jersey City, and they will tell you that what pushed them to take that decision was because they couldn't afford the cost of rent in this city.

And what we've seen is that since about 1961, the city has not been building the requisite amount of housing needed to grow. And frankly, if you are not growing as a city, you are dying. And so, today's tour is both a reflection of the many different kinds of new housing developments that we are going to be investing in and a reflection of the fact that for far too long, new housing has only lived in a press release and not actually been able to be delivered on a timeline and where those who live in the neighborhood would also be able to enjoy that same housing.

So, today is about the housing we're going to be bringing online, as well as the work that we're doing within the bureaucracy of city government to speed up those processes so that housing can be built within the same lifetime of somebody who is currently being priced out. I'm going to pass it over to our deputy mayor to add anything.

On the specific question, you know, this is actually a huge part of the work of the LIFT Task Force is the partnership with other agencies to identify how do we work with you to have your needs met while also using a publicly owned site to help tackle our housing crisis. As I noted up top, we don't have that many very kind of easy, clean-cut vacant sites anymore to turn into housing. There are some, but they're dwindling. And so, it's upon us to look for other sites in partnership with agencies to figure out what can we do to meet both your needs and the broader housing crisis.

So, in the case of the NYPD parking lot, it's underutilized from a housing perspective and a zoning perspective. It's not underutilized from their perspective; it's critical parking for them. So, we work in partnership to figure out how we can do both. And that's the case whether we're talking about working with the libraries or working with other agencies that have parking. I'll just note in terms of the mandates, there's a big difference sometimes between mandating parking through something like zoning or your regulations and analyzing where parking is needed.

Often developers work to identify what is the actual market demand and need for parking in this area, to determine if parking should be part of that project. And things like the mayor has talked about and that we talk about in terms of zoning reform. The question is, should this be mandated in zoning or regulations versus allowing a project-specific sites or constraints to determine whether it's appropriate?

q.t:
Are those part of the hundred number?

[Inaudible]

a.t:
Okay, here on your right, this two-story brick building is our third and final stop. It's the Grand Concourse Library, built in 1959. Now, there's been a lot of discussion and interest in library and housing projects, and it's been great to see so much consensus form about the opportunities to co-locate housing and critical public services.

We already have a great example of some of these library and housing sites, including one across the Harlem River in Inwood. There are also others in work, including at the Bloomingdale Library, which our partners at the Economic Development Corporation are supporting with and the New Utrecht branch of the Brooklyn Public Library System in Bensonhurst, which we rolled an RFP out for recently. We are also, of course, excited to be working with our partners Tony Marx, President Marx, and the New York Public Library system broadly to identify additional opportunities.

Our work on LIFT also will be looking at other sites, not just the libraries, but other types of public services that we can co-locate with housing. EDC has been a key partner on some of these sites, especially in higher value neighborhoods where we want to cross-subsidize the land value to support with things like building new libraries. But this is an example of a site that will be 100 percent affordable and allow a new library to be built as well. This site has been designated to a development team and is getting ready to go through a rezoning process.

q.t: But you've identified them, those five sites?

a.t: They're in city ownership.

q.t: So, you're announcing — as part of this announcement today, you are talking about five RFPs that are being issued, but you are — you are announcing five new RFPs, but you are keeping what they are a secret? I'm just a little confused on that.

a.t: It's not that it's a secret, but there's a lot of work that goes into readying a site for public announcement, because all of these become competitions. So, we are identifying the 100 sites that we're working on right now, which include the six that we have announced since the beginning of the administration. And we are committing to an additional five RFPs per year, but we haven't — we're not naming which sites those are yet.

q.t: Okay, and so it's just five new sites today that the LIFT Task Force has identified?

a.t: The LIFT Task Force is going to be an ongoing task force, so since the day one EO, we've announced six new sites for affordable housing. We are also now committing to an additional five-per-year going forward.

q.t: Does it include previously Eric-Adams-announced, City-owned sites, like that doesn’t —

a.t: If they haven't closed on financing and our administration will be advancing them, [then] they will include those sites.

q.t: I'm still a little confused, so the previously announced sites are sites already in the works? Are they included in the 50,000 counts?

a.t:
Yes, so all the sites today are sites that have been previously announced but have not yet been completed. So, in our administration, we'll be working to close on financing or take them to the next stage. For the most part, close on financing. We're showing these sites as the types of City-owned sites that are examples of the models that we'll continue to lean into. In the first six months of our administration, we've already identified, and the LIFT Task Force has identified and rolled out about six new sites.

As part of today's announcement, we're also committing to an additional five RFPs per year at minimum for affordable housing on some of the additional sites that have been announced. The 100 that are now posted — we're now also announcing, of course, the tracker, which is the first time that we are publicly showing to everyone where these city sites are that we are working on for affordable housing. Those sites are going to be sites that are either between announcement and construction.

So, the five additional per year that we'll be announcing, we're not naming what those are yet just because of the process that we have to go through for working with local communities. We don't wanna contribute to over-speculation, but the 100 sites with 50,000 homes that will be on the tracker are all things that we've announced since the start of the administration or are working on in this administration.

q.t: [Inaudible] The program was stalled before; I wonder what's different now under this administration.

a.t: Well, it was stalled partially by the pandemic and then just needing to go through rezoning, but I think we are well past that, and as the deputy mayor said, the SPEED initiative and all the work that we've been putting into making sure we can go more quickly is now happening.

q.t: I guess you said it's going to stay permanently affordable because of that lease. I just wonder, then, how do families then build their equity if they feel like they're not going to really make anything if they're buying into [inaudible]?

a.t: It's a great question, and there is allowed — there is equity building. So first of all, it will be completely homeownership. So, the land lease is basically separating the improvement — the building — from the land. The land then stays under a ground lease that the Interboro Community Land Trust will own. As buyers move into the building and stay, they get to earn an amount of equity for every year that they're there. Usually, it's about two and a half or three percent every year. So, when they sell, they do make some equity. But it's affordable to the next generation. And the assumption is it's growing with incomes over time.

q.t: So, is the whole building [a] rental and [a] buyer?

a.t: No, no.

q.t: I was wondering, it seems like some of these projects, this one included, have been in the works for a while. For each of the projects today, [were] these projects actually identified by the LIFT force in January, or are they long-standing projects?

a.t: So, this one was identified prior to that, but as the deputy mayor said, delayed, primarily because we released the RFP at the time of — literally like a month before COVID. So, there was some slowdown on this one. And then also because of the rezoning, there was additional delay. But I think this one we knew about, but we haven't been able to get it going until now.

q.t: Can you say more about what it means for NYCHA [inaudible] public developer? [Inaudible].

a.t:
Yeah, in some cases NYCHA will be acting as a development partner. On Sol on Park, it's an example where they're using their tools to support the development in a way that benefits NYCHA residents. There's other examples where they'll actually be co-developers, participating in developer fee and cash flow splits. NYCHA originally built a lot of affordable housing in our city. They also built some of the Mitchell-Lama housing that exists in our city. So, we're really trying to lean into the role that a big public institution can play in building and sustaining affordable housing.

[Tour continues.]

Alright, we have arrived at our second stop, the future site of Claremont Houses. Claremont comes from the French words “Clair” (clear) [and] “Mont” (mountain), which refers to the vistas and airy hilltop vibe that used to characterize this neighborhood. This is a project that's been in the works for many years. The city actually first committed to build affordable housing on this site as part of the Jerome Avenue rezoning in 2018. As I mentioned earlier, part of our goals in this administration is to work to speed up the development of affordable housing everywhere we can. This is an example of a long-standing project that's hit hurdles, and we're going to be moving swiftly to get it to a financial closing.

Since the time that it was committed for housing, it's gone through an RFP and a rezoning to get to this point and all of its land-use approvals. That's the path that many of these public sites take. Communities advocate for it, fight for it to become housing, and then the city works to deliver. And this project is actually much more than just about keeping our word. It's also about finding opportunities for affordable home ownership projects everywhere we can. And this is going to be developed by a team that includes Habitat for Humanity and the Interboro Community Land Trust.

It's a project that's going to be financed through HPD's Open Door program, which, again, delivers affordable home ownership opportunities all across the city. And in our administration's first executive budget, we committed to doubling the amount of affordable homeownership opportunities through the Open Door Program. I'm now going to pass it to Commissioner Levy to say a little bit more about this project.

Thank you, deputy mayor. So just two quick things I would add. So, the point that the deputy mayor made about the fact that this project will be transferred to the Interboro Community Land Trust means that there will be a ground lease under the project that will keep this new development affordable permanently for generations of homeowners. So, you know, anytime a family goes to sell, they'll be able to earn a little bit of equity. But the next generation of buyers will also get the benefit of that really deeply affordable homeownership.

The second thing I'll say is that this is also going to be in the neighborhood where we are focused on the new Bronx plan, which is a commitment to go really deep in terms of housing quality and making sure that we are building all types of affordable housing as well as amenities throughout this neighborhood. So, we're really excited to be launching this first Open Door project in the same neighborhood where we will be doing a really deep dive into our Bronx plan. So, with that, we have questions.

q.t: Can you talk a bit more about how Transfer of Assistance works?

a.t: Sure. So, Transfer of Assistance is a tool through the Department of Housing and Urban Development, federal government, that allows NYCHA to apply. It's a tool, through the Rental Assistance Demonstration, to convert Section 9 assistance to Section 8. Those Section 8 units are converted into a project-based voucher contract that helps with the financing and underwriting of the new affordable housing project. But because those units are coming specifically from NYCHA residents, they will voluntarily apply to be part of the project. Those units specifically are for those NYCHA residents. That also allows NYCHA, for the units that convert over, to use their Faircloth Limit to then backfill the homes that folks are coming out of, with additional Section 9 assistance. So, we both enable a new Section 8 unit and a resident to live in a brand-new home, and we enable NYCHA to bring a brand-new public housing unit online. Yes, the NYCHA team is looking to use this tool, and this is part of our goal in supporting NYCHA to reboot its role as a public developer. We'll be using it both on NYCHA land but in partnership with owners of other land as well.

q.t: People are upset, right? Like, you get it? You get the anxiety?

a.t: But the only individual, so the individuals that are impacted are the ones that are going to be receiving a you-may-be-impacted letter, at which point we provide a number of resources to help those impacted respondents to get through the process to see if they do qualify or should be exempt from the surcharge because of one reason or another, being a primary resident because they are currently living there under a trust, or it could be a family member, maybe their parents own the property, and they are out of state but their child was living there, or it could be that we just didn't have the information because a spouse was deceased and the property was under their spouse and we just don't know whether or not the individual living there now is the property owner. There's a number of reasons why we might have a lot of these edge cases and we knew that it would, but that's why we have the committed resources to do so and help these individuals go through the process in order to ensure that only those impacted will be impacted. We have until the end of August, August 21 and August 24, for those to come to Department of Finance to show their residency or exemption. But we also have the Tax Commission, who is going to be taking these appeals all day through next March. So, we are trying to build in as much resources to help as many impacted respondents as we can to walk into the process and ensure that only those who are supposed to be surcharged are surcharged. Thank you, everyone.

I think we're always going to do everything that we can to ensure that we're communicating clearly to New Yorkers and I think that what we found thus far is when it comes to these letters being sent out, it is anyone that the city believes may be subject to the surcharge and now the work will begin to ensure if someone has registered their property in a trust or they've registered their properties in an LLC and they are in fact the primary residence holder there, that that is something that is communicated with the city. We've put the investment and we're putting in the time now to ensure that come next year, this tax is only levied on those who are non-primary residences that are worth more than $5 million. Thank you all very much.

q.t: I have a question for the mayor and the commissioner, and to the commissioner's point that there was a misconception, I think the misconception was on your agency. It says in the supplemental role: “This role includes those properties that may be subject to the surcharge.” Do you owe the thousands and thousands of people some kind of explanation for the anxiety it caused, thinking they might have to have a tax, and then have to go fight City Hall to prove they are exempt with information the city should already have? Where is the excellence in that in government that you've promised?

a.t: So, the website indicated that it is a supplemental role of all residential properties that may be impacted and all residential property is the only ones that are impacted. We didn't submit a supplemental roll for commercial properties or vacant properties. And so, we did exactly as we were mandated to provide an updated supplemental role of potentially impacted properties, which is all residential. And on the website, it indicates that that it is a list that may or may not include those impacted by the non-primary resident surcharge. I mean, so we—

q.t: About the pied-à-terre, “Pied-à-Terrorize the Rich.” You know, this misinformation was really spreading that the city had put out some sort of hit list against rich people. In retrospect, do you think there was a better way that the city could have rolled out the information around this tax and the tax list, there being kind of a public one and a smaller, more private one that we're unsure the number of. What can you say about that?

a.t: I think as I've shared, what we did is following through with the law as it stands and it's what localities do across the state and it is also what the city has done. And we also know that when we do that, sometimes there are many people for whom it might be their first time in engaging with what the city is delivering on an annual basis. And part of the reason that we wanted to make sure that the letters were being sent out was also to ensure that any New Yorker who would have any questions about this would have the requisite time and the requisite staff that they could connect with to ensure that the final process would reflect that.

q.t: I saw your face on the cover of the New York Post yesterday. Not sure if you saw it yourself.

a.t: I haven’t seen it yet.

q.t: And should property owners be concerned about the rollout of this, about whether the tax will be implemented fairly or accurately? Should property owners be concerned about that?

a.t: No, we are committed to ensuring that this is a tax only levied upon those Whose second homes are worth more than $5 million, and the reason that we wanted to conduct outreach months in advance of when the tax would be levied would be to ensure that that exact premise would be fulfilled.
We are we're happy to get back to you on the exact number, but right now it is a very small percentage.

q.t: Maybe you or the commissioner can answer this question. About how many letters did you actually send out to property owners informing them that they may be potentially subject to the pied-à-terre tax?

a.t: We can get back to you on the specific number. What I do know is that it is a very small fraction of the property rolls that we have put forward thus far.

q.t: And then I had a follow-up question on your announcement, the budget savings yesterday. I know you are approaching this with the survey. I'm wondering: Is the city going to make these cuts based solely on the survey? Is the city gonna be bound to any of those — the findings from the surveys — or is that just one factor the city is taking into consideration?

a.t: The survey is one part of how we are going to assess the different ways in which we can better deliver efficiency and excellence. And one of the reasons that we sent out this survey to city workers is we believe: Who knows the city's functioning better than those who work every single day to make it possible? And so, some of the findings we anticipate will be the kinds of particular things that only a worker could know if they've been working on it for years, if not decades. Other things might also gesture to a need to reframe the way in which we approach any one of the larger topics that the city does work in. When it comes to the savings plan, we are speaking about a 2.5 percent set of savings that we are putting forward as our goal. And what's important about doing so now is that we're also giving agencies and departments the time to reflect on it, as opposed to having this conversation only within the context of the budget process itself.

q.t: It wasn't a Citi Bike, but I'm just wondering if — given this conversation around safety?

a.t: I think that I only want to be clear about it just because of — first, our focus on what happened this morning, [and] second, when it comes to anything that we can do to ensure that New Yorkers are safe, that is always something we will consider. Our concerns as it pertained to facial recognition with age verification for e-bike use from Citi Bike was all of the different kind of data that would be collected by these kinds of companies and the inability for those companies to provide the requisite commitments as to how they would protect all of that data. This is something that is especially pertinent at a time when we've seen data leaks at various levels of government. We wanted to make sure that our kids are not being subject to that for something that we are not yet able to prove a clear connection when it comes to safety, like this morning.

q.t: I wanted to follow up on some of Liz's questions about the bike crash earlier this morning. I know this wouldn't necessarily directly apply, but we reported earlier this year that the admin had stepped in to prevent facial recognition technology for Citi Bikes for minors under 16. I'm wondering, I know what happened this morning, but is that a conversation about age restrictions and access to e-bikes for teens? Is that something you intend to revisit with Citi Bikes/Lyft?

a.t: Just to be clear, what happened this morning was an illegal e-bike, as Liz said?

q.t: But for clarity here, so there was the full list published; under that there was a supplemental list for types one and types two, three [and] four. If you're on that supplemental list and you didn't get mail, you're not necessarily subject to this. Is that what you're saying?

a.t: So, the supplemental roll, which was provided as required, was all residential properties already on the final role. So, you will find even myself on this supplemental roll, because I am a homeowner, right? So, it is all residential properties on this supplemental role. It is the misconception that it is a targeted, specific list of those impacted by the non-primary resident surcharge. is false. It is the entire roll, as we have done for the last number of decades. As part of the final roll, the information is exactly the same, right? So, it is not that specific.

q.t: On the special surcharge list that exists on the website, although they did not necessarily receive mail, for clarity.

a.t:
So, I just want to — for the sake of clarity — establish a few things. The first is, and the reason for establishing this is some of them have been conflated. The first is that just like localities from Nassau to Albany, we publish property tax rolls in accordance with the law, as the city has done twice a year for years, frankly, if not decades and centuries. And the tax property role that was posted last week is a reflection of all properties across New York City, not a reflection of those specifically that the pied-à-terre tax will be levied upon. And that is an important distinction because as you've heard from the commissioner, the pied-à-terre tax is something that will be levied upon non-primary residences that are worth more than $5 million.

When it comes to the recently passed law, there was a requirement to publish this role once again before the implementation of this surcharge.

Now, to the other point. We [also] made the decision to invest in the hiring of dozens of additional civil servants at both [the] Department of Finance and at OATH to ensure that there is work also being done from within City government to establish any of the points of tension that there may be in the assessments of this. What we have heard when we're having this conversation around the pied-à-terre, it's not just the question of properties that are worth more than $5 million of non-primary residents. We also have some New Yorkers who have made the decision to register their property as a trust or as an LLC.

And part of the point of this outreach from the Department of Finance is to ascertain whether or not that reflects a primary residence or not. And one of the reasons that this is being done now is to ensure that New York has [the] requisite time before the implementation of the surcharge. They have until next March to be able to go back and forth with the department to ensure that this has an accurate reflection of that.

q.t: There does appear to be the ball getting dropped here. Your commissioner just mentioned using existing resources; [a] number of neighbors of mine ended up on the list. They've lived there for decades. Their homes are worth well below $5 million. And so, we're talking about pretty straightforward information that was missed. How did it happen, and again, why should New Yorkers be tasked with fixing this?

a.t: So first, I just want to ask you, when you say, “on the list,” are you speaking about the property tax roll or receiving the letter?

q.t: I just want to push a little bit on pied-à-terre because you've talked often about not just delivering policy but delivering good government—

a.t: Yes.

q.t: Why put the onus on the homeowner when I'm sure it's not like a simple computer search? But if they're getting that tax abatement, which is filed through the state, wouldn't you know if that's their primary residence? That's usually how — I mean — that's how the city looks for fraud if you're getting some kind of co-op or condo abatement.

a.t: Yes, and many times those applications are not up-to-date or aren't refiled, right? And so that might be one of the indicators that is happening. And it is entirely possible in that scenario. And this process was designed so that during this period, we at [the] Department of Finance and the city provide all the resources we can to walk individuals through. They can access Department of Finance by calling us. We have constituent services that are ready to help individuals like we already have been for the last week. They can access our website nyc.gov/ptsurcharge or they could even call 311 — 311 is already at the helm, ready to help individuals walk into [the] process like again. We want to ensure that through this new surcharge, we are only impacting those that should be impacted.

q.t:
I have two questions about the second home tax. So, the letters that were sent out —

[Crosstalk.]

So, the PAT tax, as I call it. The Department of Finance sent letters to people who, for example, I spoke to a woman who lives in a co-op. She already gets a condo and co-op tax abatement that the Department of Finance is aware of, yet they still send her this letter. Could the Department of Finance have done more due diligence and [used] a stronger filter before sending out letters, especially if people thought maybe there wasn't enough time to know this has to be someone's primary residence because they already get this co-op condo tax abatement?

And the second part of that is with co-ops and condos. Taxes are paid collectively as a condo, and I was told by someone at the Department of Finance that if there's one second-home neighbor who doesn't, let's say, refuse to pay, that gets fined collectively. Could someone shine some light about that and how this will be applied specifically to co-ops and condos, which, especially co-ops, are kind of unique within New York City, of how that will apply if your next-door neighbor has it as a second home and all the taxes are paid collectively.

a.t: So, I'll answer the first question and then pass it over to our commissioner for additional details. What I would say is that the Department of Finance identified homes that may be subject to the surcharge. As we know, this is a surcharge on non-primary residences that are worth more than $5 million. And as required by the law, the Department of Finance sent informational resources to homeowners to ensure that they understood the tax [and] that they understood the options before them and also, if they did not believe it to apply to them, that they had the time in order to be able to appeal.

a.s: Richard Lee, Commissioner, Department of Finance
a.t:
As the mayor indicated, we did use existing information to identify impacted homeowners for the non-primary resident surcharge. In the specific example that you gave, we can look into exactly what happened, but we used existing information that we have, and it could have been that we don't have updated information on the applications, the filings [and] the exemptions, but we did use all the available information that we had in order to determine the residency status. And this is the period in time in which we are working with New Yorkers that are impacted to ensure that we are only charging the non-primary resident surcharge on those that should be impacted.

On your second question regarding the co-ops, we are aware of this, and we are reaching out to each of the individual co-op developments so they can better this process. It is a new little bit of a new territory for us because of the way the surcharge is designed, but as we start those discussions with those co-op developments, we're happy to give an update.

q.t: Would it be looking at redesigning that bike path?

a.t: I think it is — that is part of it. I also think that when it goes into the question of illegal e-bikes, there is also a conversation to be had both at the city level and at the state level about what kind of legislative avenues we can take to ensure that only the safest methods of transit and the ones that are legally permissible are the ones that are actually being used across New York City.

q.t: I have two transit questions, Mayor Mamdani. So, I think just this morning, there was a teenager riding an illegal e-bike off of the Brooklyn Bridge, right outside City Hall, who was killed in what I believe is a collision with a car. And I wanted you to talk about — this is not the first time in recent weeks or months that we've seen a bad collision involving an e-bike. And I wanted to ask you about what are the ideas that your administration has to promote better regulation and safety around these e-bikes, particularly when it comes to ones that are illegal. How does the city prohibit people from riding the illegal bikes? Or do you think that that is the issue? And then my second question was, it was reported that Andy Byford was at City Hall yesterday to talk about the Penn Station redevelopment — is the city going to chip in any money toward that redevelopment? And also, what do you think about President Trump wanting to rename the station after himself?

a.t:
I am more interested in what the station would be able to deliver to New Yorkers than what we call that station. I think that we speak about our city as a world-class city, and we know that in order to earn that description, we have to be able provide world-class service at every single juncture, and there is still much to be done when it comes to ensuring that's the case when New Yorkers experience Penn Station.

To your first question. My thoughts at this time, first and foremost, are with the family of that teenager. We're talking about a 17-year-old New Yorker who is now dead. And that is something that we should all mourn when we see that a family will have to live with that tragedy hovering over their lives for not just weeks or months, but, frankly, years and decades to come. And when it comes to safety, it has to be the paramount decision-making framework for us whenever it comes to our streetscape.

I've long said, and I continue to believe, that we cannot have a hierarchy of safety on the basis of what mode of transit you use. You should be just as safe whether you're driving a car, walking, riding a bike, getting on a bus or getting on the train. And our focus has by and large been on the question of infrastructure to ensure that that safety is delivered because we know that oftentimes the absence or the presence of infrastructure is the determinative factor when it comes to what happened this morning. That's something that I'm going to follow up on for more details about.

q.t: Sir, I'd like you to elaborate on that, if you would, please. Because I am a little puzzled by this. Given the amount of criticism you've received from some members in the city's Jewish community, doesn't even the appearance that you were deliberately excluding qualified Jewish attorneys from the committee, doesn't even the appearance of that bother you?

a.t: I think the suggestion that there would be any decision-making motivated by religion — it does bother me. This is a city that is beautiful because of the breadth of diversity of those who call it home. And that includes the Jewish community across the five boroughs. And when it comes to the proposal of a lawyer being someone that would be on that committee, when we find out that they served on Ghislaine Maxwell's legal defense team, that was a moment of concern. I think, as I've said in these six months, I've had the opportunity to appoint and reappoint about a dozen judges. In those appointments and reappointments, there have been Jewish judges that have been appointed and reappointed, and that will continue because of a mere fact that that is a reflection of what this city looks like.

q.t: And just to follow up quickly, were you aware when you put out this list — which touted that it was diverse and representative of the city as a whole — were aware that there was no one Jewish on the panel? And did it come up in conversation? Or was it something you were unaware of until the reporting or the letter?

a.t: I did not ask for the religion of each of the person that was put forward. As you know, as the mayor and our administration, we put forward about half of those nominees. The other half were put forward by other entities. And the thing that matters most to me is that in the judges that have been appointed and reappointed, that they do reflect that diversity of New York City, and that diversity includes Jewish New Yorkers and we’ve seen that with the appointments thus far.

q.t: Can you please respond to the concerns that have been raised about the fact that there are no longer any Jewish people on your committee to appoint judges?
