You didn't apparently appoint any of the 18 who were Jewish, and some Jewish legal groups are asking you to address that, to reverse that. Is this a concern? Was it an oversight? And if nothing else, does this present an appearance problem for you at a time when some Jewish New Yorkers are feeling suspicious about your views?

a.t: So, in my six months of being the mayor, I've had the privilege of appointing a dozen qualified judges from a range of backgrounds, including Jewish judges. And I want to be clear that any suggestion that the composition of the advisory committee was motivated by religion is false. And when it comes to, in that same letter, there was a point around Mr. Leventhal and his appointment, as to why it was not considered. I want to be very clear that we decided not to move forward with his appointment because of the fact that he served on Ghislaine Maxwell's legal defense team and collected legal fees as such. And as much as possible we thought it best to avoid any association between the committee that would be appointing judges and the Epstein world, especially given how much of a loss of faith it has created for many New Yorkers and Americans generally in our legal and our political system.

q.t: The report that the DCWP came out with today said that average wages are up after these protections went into place, but that wages are still lower than they were pre-December 2023. Are you planning any other additional steps to get wages back up to what they were before the apps changed their designs? And what are some of those steps that you can take?

a.t: I think first and foremost, I'd say that today is one announcement that is part of a larger vision that we have in our administration, and also at DCWP specifically, of how we can ensure that dignity is accorded to each and every New Yorker. And when we're talking about delivery workers, we're taking about people who are putting themselves through the worst kind of conditions. The moments where we are telling New Yorkers that they should be staying home, oftentimes the ones who are keeping them fed are these delivery workers who don't have that ability to do the same thing. And so yes, we are going to look not only at ensuring that delivery workers are receiving the tips that they used to receive — prior to attempted tricks with design interface redesigns — and also beyond that at every single tool at our disposal. Commissioner, I'm not sure if there's anything you'd want to add.

If I may just briefly, so just to clarify, wages for workers are up very substantially since the minimum pay rate was passed, more than $2 billion; total hourly earnings up from $10.48 to more than $27 an hour. You're right that the tipping amount is lower — it's now up in 2026, thanks to Leader Abreu's legislation. But we have seen that some of the biggest increases in deliverista wages in the United States, thanks to the hard work of the people in this room.

q.t: When you vote for someone and you get a chance to hold them accountable, it's a very powerful part of this system, and I'm grateful to you for allowing yourself — for giving us some time to have this conversation.

a.t: Thank you so much, Lurie. Same to you.

q.t: And as you're charting this new path forward, you've got a number of additional considerations. There's the matter of the significant Haitian population that we have here in New York City and the threat to TPS. There's also that there’s the status of the Democratic Socialist candidates — including ones you've endorsed — who have come under a lot of fire lately. Apparently, for winning their race and beating out establishment incumbents. If you could, I know we have just a minute left, if you can speak a bit to the concern of the Haitian community in New York City and some advice, perhaps, for party leadership as to how they should factor in the reality that their base, that their voters, seem to like what the DSA is offering right now?

a.t:
You know, what I've said is, “What is the Democratic Party if not its voters?” And as you've made it clear, the voters are speaking loud and clear that they want to see a new vision for our Democratic Party. And frankly, it's a vision that has more in common with the new deal than the raw deal that so many of us have been having to explain away to New Yorkers as to why they have to experience that. And what has been so exciting has been to see that that hunger, it is true in different parts of the city, and what it wants to see is something that really brings working people back to the heart of our politics' focus. 

And to Haitian New Yorkers, I know that the judge gave a stay until over the weekend, but Haitian New Yorkers as well as Syrian New Yorker have been having to live in this almost permanent state of insecurity and anxiety because of the refusal of Congress to act, to actually give these families permanent protection. We're speaking about New Yorkers who are part of the life blood of our city. And our administration is not going to allow these communities to be terrorized in these moments of uncertainty. And so, I've directed our Mayor's Office of Immigrant Affairs to connect families to free and confidential legal help, and our city services as a whole will remain open to every New Yorker regardless of their status. 

[Crosstalk.]

q.t:
And then I’m gonna pay it forward to thank all of the protestors who took to the streets during the summer after George Floyd, Ahmaud Arbery, Breonna Taylor — your protesting in those streets is what forced the then mayor to create that commission, which is what allowed us to get those ballot proposals on the ballot, which New York City voters came out and voted for overwhelmingly. Nothing happened in isolation; we all have to support the work of advancement. 

Let's talk briefly about this Racial Equity Plan because it is so significant, and I know that you said it would be out by the end of August. My understanding is that it was supposed to be out at the end of this month. I'd like for you to tell us what you're going to do to address the people's recommendations. I know that commissions like NYC CORE — the Commission on Racial Equity — they set out a report. Talk to us about how you plan to strengthen CORE, and even, if you could, speak to some of the reparations work that they're leading on behalf of the city. I mean, you [can] really talk about what that pursuit of justice will look like.

a.t:
Absolutely. So, I think, as you said, one of the critical components of the Mayor's Office of Equity and Racial Justice, as well as the Commission on Racial Equity, is soliciting public feedback as a part of this. We want New Yorkers to actually be engaging with this vision and to help shape this vision. And so, after we made the release of the preliminary Racial Equity Plan in April, we had a 30-day comment period where we were collecting that kind of engagement, and that's helping to shape the finalized version of this plan, which will be released before the end of August — sometime before then. And what we've also been doing in advance of that is disseminating that input that we received from New Yorkers directly to city agencies for review and consideration as we are putting together that final Racial Equity Plan. 

And I think the last point I'll just make is that it is critically important that, you know — there's often an attempt to rewrite the history of our city as if we were somehow removed from even the legacy of slavery. And what we see is if we are taking an honest and accurate approach to what New York City's role was, you will see that complicity is something that cannot be debated. And you can also see that the striving for dignity is one that we can celebrate in our own city's history when we look at places like Weeksville, and that we have to be able to both acknowledge that and celebrate what it looked like to fight back against that while we chart a new path forward.

q.t:
And so this is why — and y'all know I don't really fawn over politicians, not that I am at this moment — but the one reason I started out this introduction by saying that you were someone I voted for, is because my understanding as to your administration's vision was that you are going to continue the work that the Racial Justice Commission has put forward, equitable access to food and food security being principal among them. 

We talk a lot about food deserts, I prefer food apartheid because deserts are naturally occurring, apartheids regions are not. And so, this vision for the five grocery stores, amounting to real dollars in the pockets of New Yorkers, it feels to me like this is really one of the concrete promises — a fulfillment of a concrete promise that you made during the campaign. How will you build and expand on this? You're literally, you know, under two years in your administration, what's your plan to expand on this project so that we are seeing a spirit of affordability, if you will, spread throughout the city?

a.t:
Well, you know, I think it's exactly as you said: you have to earn the trust and deliver on the hope that people have had. And what we're talking about with this is — it's not just an idea or an initiative. We are going to deliver these five city-run stores by the end of 2029. The first one is going to be delivered by the next year at La Peninsula in Hunts Point in the Bronx. And just to your point about how this fits in with a longer view of racial equity and also the long shadow of, frankly, policies that have disproportionately impacted Black and brown New Yorkers across the five boroughs — La Peninsula is also where we had Spofford Juvenile Detention Facility. And so, a site that used to be a place which was, you know, found time and time again, to be, you know, taking advantage of so many young people and violating the law in its doing so, is now going to be a place where people come to for affordability and for being that little bit closer to dignity. And then the next site that we've announced is La Marqueta, which is going to be in El Barrio in East Harlem. And that is also carrying the flame forward from Fiorello LaGuardia's opening of that site as a city-run market providing lower-cost produce to those who were being priced out of what was being sold at the time. 

So, it has to also be a recognition of what has come before and looking to build on that work. And frankly, Lurie, that's why it's a real pleasure to be on the show because when I think about us releasing the Racial Equity Plan before the end of August, and I think about our implementation of that as a new framework across every single city agency and department — it's only possible because you and others were doing the work prior to the administration, so that we could have something to pick up on as opposed to have to build it from scratch.

q.t: I'm so glad to hear you say that because that Racial Equity Plan, that was one of my babies, that was one of the things I was very happy and very proud to be a part of. And frankly, I'm still glad to see that there is also a vision within your administration that does the equitable access to resources like groceries and equitable access to data, like the data that would inform what it takes to have a true cost of living measurement in this city. Extraordinarily important, all of which went into, my understanding is — and all of that went into the way that you seek out this NYC grocery recipe for affordability. Talk to us a bit about that and then I do want to turn back to the Racial Equity Plan, because both of them are so intimately intertwined.

a.t:
Absolutely. So, when it comes to our New York City-run grocery stores, we're talking about five grocery stores one in each borough. And what we just announced was that each of these grocery stores is going to have a 30 percent discount on core — on a core basket of goods. And this is 30 percent relative to the typical retail price in New York City. And it's going to apply to all fresh produce; meat, seafood; along with around 20 other items like cheese, milk and bread; as well as pasta soup, beans, nuts, rice and flour. And we're expecting that New Yorkers will save $90 a month as a result of this [and] about $1,000 per year. 

And the reason for the 30 percent is one, it is something that will make a tangible impact in the amount of money New Yorker's will have left in their pocket. And two, it's also a reflection of the amount that costs have actually gone up since just before the pandemic at the grocery store. And this is one way that we can make it a little bit easier for New Yorkers to buy the things that they need to keep their family healthy and to keep their family fed.

q.t: You are listening to the Lurie Daniels Favors Show on Sirius XM's Urban Views, where talk empowers and becomes action. And it's not often that I get a chance to talk with people that I actually had an opportunity to vote for. And voted for with some real intentionality behind what it is I want to see happen in my city. And I'm joined right now by someone that I did vote for, his name is Mayor Zohran Mamdani, the 112th mayor in New York City. He was sworn in as mayor on January 1, 2026. Prior to that, he represented the 36th New York State Assembly District and its neighborhoods of Astoria, Ditmars-Steinway and Astoria Heights. And he is here today to talk more about this massive unveiling that took place yesterday in New York City. There is going to be a significant change in the way we buy our groceries. Mayor Zohran Mamdani, welcome to the Lurie Daniels Favors Show, it's a pleasure to have you.

a.t: It is such a pleasure to be on the show. Thank you so much for having me. And I will just say before we even jump into the topic about grocery stores and our city-run plan; I do really just want to acknowledge and appreciate your work. Frankly, as one of the original commissioners to the New York City Racial Justice Commission, because it has been — it has been the foundation for a lot of what our work has looked like, in releasing our first-ever Racial Equity Plan and even when we're talking about groceries, we know that we can't disentangle that from the ways in which so many neighborhoods across the city have not been provided with the food access that they deserve.

q.t: At the end of your tenure, what does New York City have to look like for you to consider your term to have been a success?

a.t: A more affordable city.
Thank you so much.
Such a pleasure.

q.t: You and the president have had a contentious relationship, but you've visited the White House at least twice, and both times it seemed to be cordial. And last time you published a photo of you two smiling, saying you had agreed to work on housing in the city. But last week the president shared a video calling you and democratic socialists “hardcore communist bastards who must be stopped, criminalized and deported.” Now, you told the New York Times that this is something that, you know, you don't even blink your eye at anymore, but could you describe your evolving relationship with the president?

a.t: It is a relationship that clearly has many a disagreement. And neither of us are shy about their disagreements. I've been clear with the president directly when we've had conversations around ICE that I believe it's a cruel agency, I believe it's inhumane, I believe it does nothing to serve in the interests of public safety and that I believe it should be abolished. And I've also said that I look to those conversations with the president for ways that we can work together to be productive for the benefit of the city. And so, wherever there are places of agreement, whether it's on zoning or it's on the possibility of significant federal investment in housing, I will embrace those opportunities. But I will always be honest through it all and make clear where I stand on federal policy, much of which has really looked to upend the lives of not just working New Yorkers but working Americans.

q.t: When you were running for mayor, you submitted a written statement to a reparations convening that read in part, “New York City participated actively in the slave trade and furthered its legacy through racist institutions, policies, and laws. The city should reconcile and repair this legacy of slavery, stolen wealth and discrimination.” You added that you were proud to support the new reparations commission examining Wall Street’s complicity in the slave trade. One of these commissions is set to release its final report next summer. If a commission studying reparations in this city recommended cash reparations for people impacted in New York City, would you support that recommendation?

a.t: First, I want to say that I stand by what I submitted. It's the truth. It's not a personal assessment. And we often think about slavery and the complicity in slavery as being exclusively to certain geographic areas of the country. Here in New York City, we were very complicit. And so, I look forward to whatever those findings are. I can't give you an answer in advance of them, but I can tell you that this is critically important because this is also what it looks like to acknowledge what history truly was.

q.t: So, your affordability agenda, as you just pointed out — and a lot of your supporters point this out — Black New Yorkers will inherently benefit from this. Do you believe, however, that you have to have policies that are specific or even exclusive to Black New Yorkers? What people call the “Black agenda.”

a.t: I think it's important that you have aspects of both of these things. Deed theft, for example, disproportionately impacts Black voters. We have to have an answer for that alongside issues that impact millions of tenants across New York City. If we see something that is a scourge, which is what deed theft is, that is predominantly targeting older Black New Yorkers under the guise of “Do you want help to transfer this property to the next generation? Do you want to refinance?” That has to be addressed. So, I think it is less of an either-or and more of an all-of-the-above.

q.t: Let's say that affordability is part of it, as you just said. What about the cultural part of it? I mean, so you've had thirty years of very aggressive policing, including stop and frisk, which disproportionately impacted Black and brown young men, vast majority of whom were not guilty. You have said that New York City has the most segregated public school system in America, your most prestigious high school in the city. Last year I think they admitted eight Black students out of over 700; this year, they admitted three. Then you have what you just said about gentrifying Black neighborhoods. How do you deal with this other part of it, the kind of more cultural part of it?

a.t:
Well, I think first you have to recognize the scale of what we are looking at — and as you've said, the scale of something that is built up for years. And then you have to ask yourself how to deal with it in the short term, medium term and long term. And I think we talk about our schools — our public school system in New York City, our public school system in the United States of America — is one that there are many who would love if it [were] to be deconstructed and stripped for parts. We need to make this a shining example of public education. And so, I'm proud of our chancellor, Kamar Samuels, whose focus is on delivering a level of rigor in the classroom and an integrated school system. 

And sometimes these kinds of things have been spoken about as if they're intention, when in fact they are reflections of what a successful school system looks like. And when it comes to policing, I firmly believe that New Yorkers should never have to choose between safety and justice. And so, to me, yes, I'm proud of the fact that we have the fewest murders and shootings and shooting victims in recorded New York City history over the course of these first six months and that we are investing in the work to not just respond to crime but prevent crime as well. And that also looks like ensuring that we are providing enough summer jobs for kids across the city, that we are creating the first Office of Community Safety. And again, that we understand that stability and cost of living isn't just specific to one kind of New Yorker. And what I mean by that is sometimes when I'll say cost of living, someone will think, “oh, this is only for tenants.” It's for homeowners too. 

There are a lot of Black homeowners who have built stability only to have it snatched away from them because of deed theft. So, we've created the first Office of Deed Theft Prevention, and I want to acknowledge Councilmember Chi Ossé, whose leadership really paved the way for that. And similarly, we also found a property tax lien sale system set up by Rudy Giuliani that was six times more likely to sell a lien in a Black neighborhood than in a white neighborhood. And as soon as you sold the lien — fast track to foreclosure. And I used to work as a foreclosure prevention housing counselor. And so, we suspended that for six months and said: “Do a study to figure out how we can ensure that people are paying what they owe the city and that we're not using that as a pretext to kick them out of the city.”

q.t: Are you saying that your economic agenda is — you’re hoping that it will address the Black flight, what — that some people have called a “Black exodus” from this city. Is that what you’re saying?

a.t: I think that it’s a critical part of it. And the reason it’s a critical part of it is that the absence of that agenda has driven so many out of this city. And we are effectively seeing the reversal of the Great Migration. And it's not for a lack of love for this city. You'll find New Yorkers everywhere across the country — they're still New Yorkers. They'll tell you they're New Yorkers. But they haven't been able to afford New York. And even the people you meet in New York City, sometimes when you ask them, “Where do you live?” Pennsylvania, Connecticut, Jersey City. They just can't afford life here.

q.t: Was that a good thing or a bad thing?

a.t:
I mean, it was a good thing in that I could introduce myself; it was a bad thing in that the first question was typically, “who?” And I remember I went to a church where the pastor very kindly ended his sermon by taking everyone through how to pronounce my name. He would say “Zohran,” they would say “Zohran,” he would say “Kwame,” they would say “Kwame,” and same with “Mamdani.” And I think in that time I was running not only against other candidates, but also against one particular candidate whose father had a deep and long and storied relationship with New Yorkers at large and also with Black New Yorkers. And so, I did not begrudge anyone not taking a chance on someone they hadn't heard of. What I was so thankful for was that support in the general election — which was at a point at which I had been able to introduce myself more. 

And I think also when we talk about the affordability agenda and we talk about the cost-of-living crisis, every New Yorker experiences it — but it is not evenly experienced. And Black New Yorkers have borne the brunt of this crisis. For all of the conversation around fear of capital flight, there's a real flight that has happened: we've lost 200,000 Black New Yorkers from New York City over the last few decades alone. The population of Black children and teenagers down by 19 percent from 2010 to 2019. And that is a hollowing out of this city. So many of the most iconic Black neighborhoods now seem more iconic for the history than what the future could hold because of that fear of displacement. And to me, when you deliver on that agenda, you also deliver on the promise of Black history being something that can continue to be written in the city, not something just that we read about.

q.t: I want to give you three data points for you to respond to. So, first in 2020 Democratic primaries on Super Tuesday, Bernie Sanders, who's also a Democratic Socialist, loses the Black vote in every primary for which we have election — election data. Then you run for office, you lose the Black vote in the primaries, win it in the general, and now have high approval ratings among Black New Yorkers. But last month in D. C., Janeese Lewis George, a Democratic Socialist-backed candidate who happens to also be Black, actually won the Black vote in her primary for mayor. Should we look at these as all isolated candidate specific examples or is something happening in the relationship between the Black electorate and the DSA?

a.t: I'll leave some of the assessment and the punditry to those for whom that's their job. What I will say though is the obstacle I found most in my primary was less of how I described myself and more of who I was. Because — and what I mean by who I was is that most people had never heard of me. And so, when I went to speak—

q.t: Who was the first?

a.t: David Dinkins, the first Black mayor of New York City, was also the first Democratic Socialist Mayor. And you know, he gave us this description of the city as a “gorgeous mosaic.” And his vision is one that has stayed with many. It stayed with me as well.

q.t: Oh really?

a.t: I am the second.

q.t: So, you are the first Democratic Socialist mayor of America's largest city.

a.t: I have to push back on that.

q.t: And you still speak?

a.t: I speak enough to, as we would say, you know, just enough to hustle.

q.t: So, do you have any friends from that time that you keep in contact with?

a.t: Yes, yes. I have a number of friends, because you know I was in Uganda for the first, let's say, five years of my life. I would go back, would try and go back once a year, and so, there are a number of friends that I grew up with. And it's lovely because there have been times in New York City, I'm walking down the street, someone will come up to me and start speaking Luganda. And it just feels like this beautiful moment.

q.t: Cape Town, South Africa. Your middle name is Kwame. I think you're the first Kwame I've ever met who wasn't Black. How has your African origins impacted your life and your worldview?

a.t: Oh, that's a lovely question. I'm so proud to be a son of Africa. And as you've noted, I was born in Kampala, Uganda. I have the middle name Kwame because my father named me after Kwame Nkrumah who was a pan-African leader and obviously the first leader of Ghana in post-independence. And so, I always grew up with a notion of what it meant to be not only Ugandan but also African. And it has been a joy for my whole life to know that home comes from so many different places, and I can think of no better place to be at home than New York City because it is a constellation of so many from across the world who have those similar roots. And you know I met a Ghanaian uncle in Harlem at an event a few weeks ago he gave me a soccer ball with Kwame Nkrumah's face on it and all of his favorite quotes and now that sits in my office.

q.t: You're born in Uganda, you stay there until you're five and you guys moved to—

a.t: Cape Town.

q.t: You have described yourself as not as an African American, but as an “American who was born in Africa.”

a.t: Yes.

q.t: What's the hurdle there?

a.t: I think, you know, the hurdle with anything that has a cost is both to find the replacement of that revenue that will be in the hundreds of millions of dollars and also a shift in how we think about aspects of public transportation.

q.t: And is there a reason that you told the New York Times that you were still in active conversation with the Legal Department in regards to possibly following up on that arrest warrant when you were previously told that that necessarily couldn't happen.

a.t: I've said that all I have to say on that topic. Thanks everyone.

q.t: Going back to the topic earlier when it comes to prime minister of Israel, I understand that you're making it clear that you are criticizing a particular politician, not the ethnic group, but there have been growing concerns amongst elected officials, some of your allies, such as the Attorney General Letitia James, about the fact that comments and rhetoric may be rising temperatures. Do you take those concerns to heart and what is your plan to bring down those temperatures?

a.t: So, I think, to your point, when I make criticisms of Prime Minister Netanyahu, they are criticisms of Prime Minister Netanyahu. And what I shared were not even frankly personal assessments, they were objective facts. And my responsibility as a New Yorker and as a mayor of this city is a responsibility to take care of each and every person who calls the city their home. And that is not based upon whether or not they agree with me, how they feel about me. My job is to make sure that they are safe, that they're thriving and [that] they continue to call this city home. That's always going to be my North Star on how we can do that because this is an incredible city and it's a city where everyone needs to know that they're belonging to it is not conditional on how they feel about the mayor.

q.t: Two questions on the sheriff. One, why did it take so long for your administration to fire Miranda? And then two, are there any city employees who were served subpoenas or had their homes visited by feds last week on the same day when the feds visited Miranda?

a.t: So, I will get back to you on your second question. What I will say to the first question is, one of the things that we understand within our administration is the critical importance of the position of the sheriff and finding someone who embodies the integrity that that position has to hold. And earlier I was being asked about Haitian New Yorkers. I'm incredibly excited that after this, I will be going to the inauguration of our new sheriff, who will also be the first Haitian American to serve in a position of leadership in law enforcement here in New York City.

q.t: So, I wanted to ask you, going back to the 12-year-old that was shot in the Bronx, our reporter was able to speak to the family of Jacob earlier today and they said that you were at the Dominican Day parade yesterday, but you didn't spend any time at the scene or visiting the family. I wanted to get your response to that criticism. And also, have you spoken to Trump directly about TPS for Haitians and Syrians?

a.t: So, I will just echo what I shared earlier: I'll keep the conversations between the president and myself, between the president and myself. However, on the first question, our administration has been in touch with the family. I've also reached out to the family, and the family is going through something that no New Yorker should have to go through, and that is the kind of heartbreak of having to bury their son. And we are looking for every which way that we can be there for them in this time and also looking to ensure that there are no additional New Yorkers who ever have to experience a heartbreak like this. Again, we're speaking about a 12-year-old boy who was on his bicycle outside of a bodega and lost his life as a result of that, through no fault of his own. And I've also seen some commentary trying to blame Jacob for his presence outside of that bodega, and I think that is frankly unacceptable and it's distracting from the fact that gun violence is to blame for this, not a 12-year-old boy.

q.t: [Inaudible] followed up on your call to accept the ICC and make the arrest?

a.t: I've made my thoughts clear. I'll keep the conversation to the president between him and myself

q.t: I was just wondering if you could also respond to Prime Minister Netanyahu's comments on Fox. I don't know if you saw them 24 hours ago or so, saying that you, in fact, were fomenting hate. It was brought up in the context of the Upper West Side attack that is suspected to be a hate crime. I'm wondering what you make of his comments. And if you have spoken to any federal officials, including President Trump, about your call to accept the ICC and arrest him.

a.t: So, I'm not interested in getting into a back and forth with Prime Minister Netanyahu. What I will say is that here in New York City, one of my top priorities is keeping Jewish New Yorkers safe — keeping every single New Yorker safe. And we know that while Jewish New Yorkers comprise a minority of all New Yorks, they comprise the majority of the victims of all hate crimes, and it is unacceptable. And I am thankful, as we have seen over the past few days, that the Asian New York and the Jewish New Yorker who were stabbed are in stable condition I continue to wish them a full and a speedy recovery and I'm also thankful to the NYPD for having acted quickly and swiftly to apprehend Raul Morales, who has now been charged as you said with not only attempted murder but also a hate crime, and I look forward to him being prosecuted to the full extent of the law, because as we know here in this city, we have no tolerance for hatred. We have not tolerance for bigotry. And I also want to make one thing clear, which is that we have to not only do the work in response to these kinds of crimes, but also to prevent these kinds of crimes. And that's why our administration made a decision to increase funding for the Office of Hate Crime Prevention by more than 800 percent earlier this year so we can start to do the work of rooting out antisemitism and bigotry of any kind from across the five boroughs.

q.t: A number of people who are survivors of 9/11 are calling on you not to go to 9/11 memorial services. I wonder how you feel about the fact that they're trying to keep you away.

a.t: I will proudly honor the families, the survivors, the first responders forever impacted by that horrific terror attack by standing alongside them at this year's 9/11 commemoration, reaffirming that we will never forget the solemn day felt by all of us who call this city home and, frankly, by all of us who call this country home.

q.t: Today is the deadline for the expiration of TPS for Haitians and Syrians. I wonder what the city is doing to help those populations here. And are you on alert for ICE-related enforcement actions?

a.t: We know that Haitian New Yorkers, Syrian New Yorkers, they are a part of the fabric of this city. And we also know that while a judge stayed that decision until today, that it still has left so many living in a state of permanent insecurity and anxiety. And we are speaking about New Yorks who have been a part the lifeblood of the city, have helped to make this city what it is. And our administration is not going to allow these communities to be terrorized on their own. We are going to be standing up for these communities, and we have instructed our Mayor's Office of Immigrant Affairs to continue to connect families to free and confidential legal help. That is something that is going to continue, as is the fact that our City services are going be accessible no matter what the person calling status is. And at the federal level, we also know that Congress does have the power to give these families permanent protection, whether they be Syrian New Yorkers or Haitian New Yorkers. And it should use it now before more parents are separated from their children. And it is something that I am very much adding my voice to the call for Congress to take this action to do.

q.t: I'd like to get your reaction to the shooting that killed the 12-year-old in the Bronx. And for example, you know earlier this year the commissioner separated the Bronx into two police precincts precisely to curtail this kind of violence. So please, your reaction: Does more need to be done?

a.t: There's always more to be done. We can never accept that a 12-year-old boy sitting on his bicycle outside of a bodega could be killed in our city. And my heart breaks for the family of Jacob Freytes. We are speaking of a young man who should have been able to do what every New Yorker should be able to, which is just live their life in the summer in the city. And I was only a few blocks away from where he was killed just yesterday at the Bronx Dominican Day Parade. And even at a day that so many look forward to for so much of the year, it hung over that parade because it is an ache in our souls. And I am so appreciative of the work of our NYPD of having gotten more than 2,000 guns off of the streets in these first seven months and in the fact that they have already apprehended William Ferrer for the murder of Jacob and for the shooting of two others. And yet we also know that we can never say that enough has been done when we are seeing our children being killed on our streets.

q.t: And one more question for you. I know that you mentioned at a board meeting that La Marqueta was supposed to be potentially a draw for people from other neighborhoods to come and visit that market, that the City-run grocery stores would be a novelty or at least something that people were excited to go to from other neighborhoods. Do you see that being the model for all five markets across the city? I mean, we came here today to East New York and there wasn't an announcement of a new location here. Could you see the type of thing happening?

a.t: Yeah, I think to enhance what the mayor had just said, we are looking for these NYC grocery stores to enhance neighborhoods so that businesses there like the local bodegas and independent grocery stores and other small businesses in that neighborhood are strengthened through this NYC grocery initiative. So yes, we're envisioning that as part of the NYC Grocery Initiative to strengthen neighborhoods.

q.t: Question about the essential basket of goods — You said they're going to be 30 percent cheaper than they would be at the grocery store down the street, or even if there's one not down the streets, if it's a food desert. How are you going to keep people from taking advantage of that deal, basically, and is there going be a limit on the number of items that someone can take that are discounted at that level from that essential basket?

a.t: So, our RFP makes very clear that this is a program for New Yorkers to be able to put food on the table, not a program for people to be able to make a quick buck through reselling. I'm going pass it over to our EDC head, Jeanny Pak, to add some additional details.

Yes, if you look at our RFP for the operator, we are looking to make sure that we target New Yorkers, whether it be [through] a sort of a library card-esque [system], and also, we manage who's buying and that it’s focused on everyday New Yorkers. So, we are mindful of that, and we're going to make sure that we have all the things in place to ensure that that does not happen.

q.t: Mr. Mayor, I know that you talked about the fact that the grocery stores are not gonna sell lottery tickets and cigarettes. Do you think that the income from those things in bodegas will offset the possibility of a loss of business? Because the bodega owners are really worried that they're going to be hurt. And so, is your argument that the other things that they are able to sell will offset that loss?

a.t:
My argument is multifaceted. The first thing I would say is that this is a model that builds off of what we already see in existence with Essex Street Market. And with that approach, there is a discounted approach that has not yielded any kind of a negative impact on bodegas or grocery stores around it. And we know that because if it had been, it would be something that we'd be talking about. And yet, what it has been is instead accepted as a fabric of life in that neighborhood. The second is that we are not looking to compete with bodegas or grocery stores when it comes to their ability to survive. What we're looking to do is to provide affordability that is guaranteed to New Yorkers. And we know that a lot of what drives revenue for these bodegas [and] grocery stores, those are things that make it possible for them to continue to operate. Those are not things we have any interest in competing for. 

The last point that I would say is the absence of affordability in this city has pushed so many working-class New Yorkers out of the city. And those are working-class New Yorkers that could be customers for these bodegas, that could be customers for grocery stores across the five boroughs. And instead, we've seen an exodus. And we also know that, where we are in New York City, it's important to acknowledge that the affordability crisis has affected every New Yorker. However, that effect has not been evenly borne. Two-hundred thousand Black New Yorkers have been pushed out of this city in the last few decades. And that's effectively a reverse great migration. And that’s something that we have to bring to an end with every single tool at our disposal.

q.t: I have an off topic, but I'll hold that until the appropriate time. It sounds like what you're essentially offering these purveyors of grocery services is you cover the property tax, you build out the building, you cover any sort of recurring rent, but they have to bring in the food, discounted a certain amount, high quality of wages. I mean these are millions of dollars effectively shuffling back and forth. So, I'm wondering why not just spend these millions of dollars and give to agencies like the Campaign Against Hunger or City Harvest or, you know, just direct established food programs.

a.t: We see in this city an opportunity to take an all-of-the-above-approach. We are going to continue to work with incredible partners like the ones that we're here with today, as well as ensure that food pantries across the five boroughs can flourish. And what we have seen is that far too often when it comes to City government's approach to delivering on affordability for groceries, there have been — there's always been the question of intermediaries, whatever it may be. And we are excited to deliver directly to New Yorkers that lower cost of essential goods. We're talking about a 30 percent discount across essential goods that will be the same at every single one of those five city-run grocery stores. And what we are also talking about is city-run grocery stores, which will not be selling cigarettes, or alcohol, or lottery tickets or hot foods — those are a lot of the [items] that drive revenue for a lot of existing grocers, existing bodegas. This is an approach that looks to address the question of affordability and food access without also harming the ability for other entities to continue to exist.

q.t: What would you say to local grocery store owners who say a municipal grocery store will siphon business from them, potentially lead them to raise prices for customers or shut down? And is your administration considering other alternatives such as maybe helping grocery store owner subsidize rents or increase their purchasing power in some way that they can then pass on to the customer?

a.t:
So, we've talked about five city-run grocery stores, one in each borough, and thus far we've announced La Marqueta in Manhattan and La Peninsula in the Bronx. And these two sites showcase the example of when you are speaking about a dense neighborhood, there is more than enough market for both existing grocers as well as one city-run grocery store. When we're talking about La Marqueta, we're talking about more than 65,000 New Yorkers who live within 10 minutes of that grocery store site. When we're talking about La Peninsula, we're talking about more than 150,000 New Yorkers who live in the Hunts Point area alone. And what we've seen is that the city already operates subsidized markets, for example, at Essex Street Market. And those are operating near multiple grocers, multiple bodegas and we have not seen harm to local stores or operators. 

What we've also seen is that this is not the only approach that we have to dealing with the question of food, food insecurity and also food operators. Just last week, we were proud to announce OPEN, which is not only a more than 50 legislative reforms and regulatory reforms that will lower the cost of keeping a business open and the time that it takes to liaise with City government; but is also a permanent approach for us at City government to cut red tape to ensure bodegas, grocery store owners, a wide variety of small businesses across New York City can continue to flourish. Because we see this as a city that is big enough for more than the thousand existing grocery stores that we currently have and five city-run grocery stores, one in each borough.

q.t: It's great for you. Again, I appreciate you, Mr. Mayor. Thank you again. Please, please come on back anytime.

a.t: Absolutely. It was a real pleasure. Thank you, guys.

q.t: I know, right? We're gonna be praying for a long time. It's cool. I'll live through you. I’ll live through New York.

a.t: Live through me. Next year, we'll be back.
Absolutely.
I mean, you see the Celtics are posting Knick's highlights right now. That's how good things are.

q.t: Thriller, alright. Mr. Mayor, it's been an absolute pleasure. I know the roomies are enjoying this interview, and we hope to have you back on again soon. I hope not for another finals victory because I want Chicago to get something.

a.t: Brother, you're gonna be praying for a long time.

q.t: It's factual. It's The Shade Room, Mr. Mayor. It is The Shade Room. That's all. Working Families Party.

a.t: Partners.
Okay, Barack Obama.
Hope.
Michael Jackson.
Thriller.

q.t: Oh, this one. How about this one? Trump.

a.t: President. It's factual.

q.t: Alright, let's do some rounds of “first thought” so the room of shade gets to know you better. Now we're gonna throw some names out, and you give us the very first sentence that pops in your head, cool?

a.t: Okay.
Alright, Kamala Harris.
Madam Vice President.
Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, AOC.
Fighter for working people and a friend.
Ah, shout out to her.
Shout out to her.
DNC.
Work in progress.

q.t: Yeah, yeah, that's one of the top ones. Shout out French. Okay, all-time favorite movie?

a.t: Okay, I have to give it to Mississippi Masala, which is a movie that my mother directed. And not only do I love that film, but I also wouldn't be alive if it wasn't for that film because that's how she met my father.
That is a great story.
I would say the Odyssey, but I'm alive already, and that didn't make me alive.
Yeah, there we go.
Brought me back to life.

q.t: Okay, how about this — favorite song right now for you?

a.t: I know it is not a recent song but “Stay Schemin.”
Oh, wow, that's a good record.
I think that's French Montana's best verse.

q.t: Shouldn't have done it. All right, let's have some fun, man. Let's have some fun. How about this? Although we know your story is still being written, when they make the Mamdani movie, who's playing you and who's playing your wife?

a.t: Okay, playing me would be Ashton Kutcher from the popchips commercial. If you don't know what I'm talking about, check it out. And playing my wife, nobody can play my wife.
Well said, Mr. Mayor.
Yeah, I guess it's just going to be Ashton Kutcher as me.

q.t: Yeah, got you on The Shade Room. We good. Now, how about this? Now, this one, don't get mad at me, man. [What’s the] biggest fumble you feel? Like, you're like, “Ugh.” Like, was there one of those moments?

a.t: Biggest fumble — you know, someone was talking to me about this today. It wasn't even when I was the mayor, but it still lives with me: which is eating a burrito on the train and taking a photo of it. Shouldn't have done it.

q.t: Yeah, we're glad we got you out of there.

a.t: I was like, I gotta be in The Shade Room.

q.t: Whoa, you're better to than me. I still need —

a.t: I had that claustrophobia. It was hitting me.

q.t: Oh, wow, I know they're gonna be happy. I sure get to paying fines a lot in Chicago. How about your biggest accomplishment today?

a.t: Today, honestly, it's a tie between being here with you guys and having survived being in a stuck elevator earlier this afternoon.

q.t: Absolutely. Absolutely. That's a great accomplishment. How about this week? How about this week? Anything big happening?

a.t: This week, you know, at the top of the week, we introduced a program called OPEN, which is more than 50 reforms that we are going to do to change the regulations for small businesses to make it cheaper for them to keep their doors open, to make it easier for them to deal with City government and to cut a lot of the fines and fees that they have to deal with on a daily basis.

q.t: Love that, love that. Biggest accomplishment thus far, you feel?

a.t: I got to say, putting us on a path to universal childcare. The team did incredible work so that Governor Hochul and I could be standing together on that eighth day. Sometimes politics feels like it's irrelevant from a working person's struggle, from a working person’s life. When we stood together on that day and announced that there's going to be free childcare for two-year-olds — for thousands of two-year-olds this fall, for even more next fall — it was something that you didn't have to explain to someone because when they're spending $20,000 a year, that explains itself.

q.t: Yeah, man. Yeah. Now let's get to this. What [are] two things that surprise you about being mayor?

a.t: You know, there's the phrase, “don't sweat the small stuff.” And one of the things that surprised me about being the mayor is that actually the small stuff is not only critically important, because I think we all understand that what City government should do, but it's also important to New Yorkers. Like, I'll give you an example. We fixed a bump on the Williamsburg Bridge, and we thought it was good to do; it was right to do and important to do. But we thought maybe in about a few days, people would have forgotten that. That is still something that people bring up to me, because it shows that if people can't trust government to deliver on the smallest of issues, then why would they ever believe that government could deliver on the biggest of problems? And when you can win that trust by earning that trust, it's something that leaves people far more willing to believe that tomorrow could actually be better than today.

q.t: Exactly, exactly. And congratulations too on the Knicks watch parties. I thought that was really cool too. New Yorkers getting a chance to be out right outside and feel some of that energy. That was very cool—

a.t: You gotta be outside; it's New York City.

q.t: Amazing, amazing, mayor. Now, let's turn to the World Cup. [The] 2026 FIFA World Cup generated around, oh, they say like $15 billion in total revenue, which was record-breaking. Now this massive windfall shattered FIFA's initial projection of $11 billion, making it the most financially successful tournament in football history. And that was a win for FIFA, but live sports, as we know, have gotten completely out of reach for young people and the middle class. But your administration secured $50 tickets, free shuttles and massive borough watch parties. For people that consistently feel priced out of big cultural moments, why was making the World Cup accessible to everyday New Yorkers such a line in the sand for you?

a.t:
Well, I think, you know, you said it yourself in the question, which is the fact that for too many New Yorkers, and frankly, for too many Americans, sports has become a luxury commodity. It's something that they could only afford if they're willing to give up a rent payment. And we didn't want the World Cup, which is the most watched sporting event across the globe, to be one that New Yorkers just knew they were physically close to but would never even have a chance to go see. 

And so, we were proud to secure a thousand tickets that would be $50 a piece — the only host city that was able to do that — and also proud to take Fan Fests, which, when I became the mayor were set to be things that New Yorkers would be charged to attend and instead made them free. And we wanted that because we want everyone to feel the magic of the game. 

And we also know that as we see these profits climb that too often the lesson of that is that you can keep charging more and more and more. But what makes these sports moments so special is that they are actually built on the passion of everyday people. And if those people can't afford these games any longer, then sport is becoming something that, frankly, it shouldn't.

q.t: Amazing, amazing, well said. Now, The Grio recently highlighted a poll that shows like 80 percent of Black New Yorkers feel you are genuinely, just genuinely unifying New York, especially on deep-rooted issues like wealth and housing and even education. Beyond the headlines, you know, specific moves that — what are the ones that you are trying to implement for long-term wealth and stability for Black working class and communities?

a.t:
You know, we often talk about Black history, and one of the things that I want to make sure is that in this city we can keep writing Black history and not just remember what's already been written. And one of the ways we do that is actually making sure that this city is affordable, whereas right now it's the most expensive city in the United States of America. And we've seen over the last few decades, 200,000 Black New Yorkers have been pushed out of this city. From 2010 to 2019 alone, we saw the population of Black children and teenagers declined by 19 percent. And when we look at what these costs are that are driving this kind of a reversal of the Great Migration, housing is one of the primary costs; childcare is another one of those costs for working families in this city. 

And so, one of the focuses of our administration has been delivering universal childcare to New Yorkers. And so, just on day eight of our administration, we secured an agreement with Governor Kathy Hochul for $1.2 billion so that we could deliver free childcare for two-year-olds for the first time in New York City. And this fall, we're going to have 2,000 seats of free childcare for two-year-olds; next fall, 12,000 seats; and then by the end of year four, a seat for every single two-year-old. And that is what will take what would otherwise be a more-than-$20,000-a-year expense and make it free for families no matter where they live in the city.

q.t: Not mad at it at all. But we got to address the elephant in the room, Mr. Mayor. Your address at Netanyahu was powerful, and it didn't just go viral; it felt like a national address, you know what I mean? Like our audience of Gen Z and millennials, they were locked in completely on accountability and global leadership right now. And you spoke directly to a generation that feels like politicians usually skirt around these issues. Was that address a message to New York, or were you intentionally setting a standard for national leaders to follow?

a.t: I was speaking to New Yorkers, and I also know that there are more than just New Yorkers who have been aghast at this genocide over the last few years, and not only the continued denial of that genocide but also the fact that it continues itself. And I hear that anguish; I hear that despair no matter where I am in New York City, and I also know that it's something that is true across this country and, frankly, across the world. And I think it's important to be honest with the people of this city about both the truth as well as what we believe accountability looks like.

q.t: Yeah, absolutely. I mean, New York's been on fire right now. I mean, you got that happening; you got the finals. You didn't just come in off of a — what is it? Three nights sold out [at] Yankee Stadium with Jay-Z — that's amazing. Taylor Swift gets married in Madison Square Garden. This has been a really, really legendary year for New York.

a.t: There's only one place to be, and it's New York City.

q.t: Now, it's a real pleasure to have you in the Shade Room. First of all, let me go ahead and tell you, congratulations on the New York Knicks. Fifty-three years and you get a finals victory. How are you feeling?

a.t: I'm still on a high. I mean, it's still orange and blue skies out here in New York City. And I gotta tell you, it’s 53 years of wait. And I mean, we hadn't even been in the finals since 1999. And for us to be able to see this team go all the way, it's still giving New Yorkers a spring in their step no matter where they are.

q.t: Alright, our first guest is making history, shattering expectations from tackling a massive $12 billion deficit to balance the New York City's budget, without cutting core services, to freezing rent for over a million residents and launching major housing initiatives. Now, he is rewriting the policy rule book. He is joining us tonight. That's right, the big guy himself, the man of New York City, Zohran Mamdani. What's happening? What's going on?

a.t: What's going on? Thank you for having me. It's a real pleasure.

q.t: All right, Mayor Mamdani, I truly appreciate it. Look forward to seeing you when you come through Washington, D.C.

a.t: I look forward to it. Thank you so much.
All right, thanks a lot.

q.t: It's three months left, three months before the election. And I believe one of the greatest mistakes that politicians keep making, or even groups, they say: “We need you to vote.” Well, I can't get somebody to vote unless they're registered. I can get them registered unless I'm really explaining to them why public policy matters and why they actually have to vote. What are you telling these candidates how they have to communicate and how do they appeal to low propensity voters or voters who have checked out of this process, because 90 million people did not vote in the 2024 election. Move a 5 percent, Kamala Harris is sitting in the Oval Office. And I just fundamentally believe, especially for African Americans, Democrats are not spending enough money, enough time, that they're using an old playbook. Your campaign, I believe, showed people how you should be running in 2025, 2026. What are you telling other Democrats nationally in terms of what they should be doing?

a.t: First, I just want to say thank you for the kind words, and I think to your point, we have to stop lecturing voters as to why this election is important, and we have to start earning their interest and their support, and the quickest way to do that is by speaking to them about a political agenda that they understand as relevant to their struggles. Too often it sounds like we're putting forward a policy where a voter is spending more time trying to decide if they're eligible for that policy than whether it's going motivate them to actually vote for that policy. And to me, I think about the early days of the Democratic Party, some of the slogans and phrases that came out of it — “a chicken in every pot.” These are the kinds of things where you didn't have to think and wonder what that meant and who it was for. It was a universal message as to what that politics would deliver for you. We need to be able to deliver on that kind of universalism and have it direct to the working-class voters across this country who have for a long time not seen themselves in our politics.

q.t: We talked about education; we talked about charter schools. Listen, you spend a ton of money in New York City on schools. There are parents who are not happy with the education their kids are getting. And so, how do you make that quick turnaround? If a parent's got a kid in ninth grade, they can't wait for a four- or five-year plan to finish. Their kid is gone.

a.t:
I think first and foremost, you have to actually listen to parents and understand what kind of obstacles they're facing in their child receiving the world-class public education that they deserve. Too often, what we do is explain away the problem, then actually recognize it and start to plan how do we respond to it. One of the first things that I did was bring in Chancellor Kamar Samuels, who has been doing a very good job in the work of leading what is the nation's largest public school system. And one thing that truly appealed to me when I was considering him and continues to [appeal to] me as he has led this public school system, has been his insistence on the importance of both rigor and an integrated school system. Too often what you will find is that these two words are posed as if they are somehow at odds, when in reality they are both reflections of a functioning and successful school system. And so, what our focus has been is — how do we put the investments into our school system that are necessary?

A lot of them — you know, you were bringing up a student in ninth grade who can't afford to wait four years — a lot of it has to do with how do we bring in the investment before they're in ninth grade, so that we're not trying to catch up after the fact. So, a lot of our work has been that $1.2 billion agreement with the governor to deliver universal childcare for two-year-olds for the first time, to fix the system for three-year olds because too many parents were saying, “Okay, I've got a seat, but I have to walk two, three, four miles in order to drop my child off there. How do we bring that closer to home?” And then how do we also pour in the investments to ensure that children who require a specialized program, that those children and those parents are actually receiving the support that they need so their children can flourish in these educational settings. Because for a long time what we've seen is the city's inability to provide that kind of support to children of special needs, it then pushes those families out of the public school system and it fails in the spirit of what this system should be.

[Crosstalk.]

q.t: So, on that particular point there, so what do you say to Senator Chuck Schumer, Representative Hakeem Jeffries, DNC leader Ken Martin and others in terms of messaging? Because again, when I sort of see this landscape, when I see this conversation taking place, there's a different conversation that's taking place on CNBC, on Fox News — they almost are the same — than what's happening in living room. And so, are you telling Democratic leadership, lead with policies and not labels, because if you lead with a label, people automatically start thinking something totally different?

a.t: But what I would say is not to listen to me, but to listen the voters themselves, because when those voters have spoken, us listening to them is what has been the premise of us being able to deliver for them. And I think you're onto something in the focus of the agenda not being how you describe it, but in fact what it's delivering for people. You know, I'll tell you, as a democratic socialist, oftentimes I'm asked what has it meant in my conversations with New Yorkers, and most often when I've knocked on a door when I was running to be mayor, people didn't ask me how I describe my politics, they just asked if there was room in my politics for them. And there was a time when we were very clear as to what this politics meant. You know, you think about freedom from fear, freedom from want, freedom of worship — these are the kinds of things, the ways that we would describe what this could mean. Today, for a lot of Americans, it feels like politics is irrelevant to their struggles. It feels like it's something that the less time they spend on it, the better that they feel, and we want politics to be something that not only a few people can afford to think about but rather something that can deliver the many the dignity that they have long been denied.

q.t: So, how do you, so right now you have this raging debate. First of all, I don't necessarily believe that it is, I believe it is a raging debate in New York media circles as opposed to what's happening all across the country in terms of DSA candidates winning in New York, mayor of D.C. and a couple of other places. And one of the things that I've said is that the reality is Democratic Socialism America policies play well in very blue districts. Reality is that for Democrats nationally, especially in Congress, in order for them to, in order them to let's say win the House, you're gonna have to win in places that are purple, places that might lean red. And so, how do you respond to folks who say that, “oh my God, these DSA folks are taking over the party, that they're going to destroy the party, and we're not going to be able to win because we're going to get branded as, as socialists and communists.”

a.t:
Well, you know Democrats have been branded as “socialists” for longer than I can remember. I remember President Obama being called a socialist almost every single day by Republicans across this country. And it didn't stop him from delivering not just on a first term, but a second term and things that we still talk about to this day. And I do have to push a little bit on the premise around blue and red and purple, because I believe what's at the heart of this agenda is the struggle of the working person. And as much as we believe ourselves in New York to be exceptional, we also know that working people aren't just struggling in New York City, they're struggling everywhere across the country. And this message is about, “How can we ensure that when you work every single day, that you come home at the end of the day, and you can actually afford to pay those bills for your housing, for your childcare, for your groceries? How do we reduce the distance between those two things?”

And here in New York City, we've talked about building more affordable housing, universal childcare, city run grocery stores, real tangible things. I think that these have the potential to connect with any working person that's struggling anywhere. And I think for those who are concerned about “what is this party?” my answer would be that, you know, what is the Democratic Party if not its voters? And what we've seen from its voters is that people are hungry for a vision of the Democratic Party that has more to do with the New Deal than with the “raw deal” that so many Americans have been forced to accept over these last few years.

q.t: Speaking on that, so you call David Dinkins a democratic socialist mayor?

a.t: Yes, yes, he identified himself as a democratic socialist. He was also our first Black mayor. And in many ways, he was an inspiration, not just for me, but for so many New Yorkers with his vision of what the city could be. And even just recently, I was celebrating Mandela Day, and I was looking back at images of how David Dinkins welcomed Mandela to this city and what it looked like to actually be a mayor with humanity at the core of the agenda.

q.t: One of the things that you had to deal with early on was a lack of a senior African American leadership. How have you fixed that problem?

a.t: So, I'm proud to say that we have a deputy mayor for community safety, the first ever deputy mayor in that position with Renita Francois, who is leading the work of ensuring that we all have an all-of-government approach to public safety and understand that we don't just respond to crime, we also do the work to prevent crime. And what she's been able to do has already had tangible results, especially for young people across the city, and it's a lot of work that needs to be built on. And I think this gets back to the point that I've been sharing over the course of the campaign, which is that not only do we want a City government that is delivering for New Yorkers, we also want one that looks like New Yorkers. And so, we can see that, whether it's in a deputy mayor or a chancellor or commissioners all across this administration, it's a reflection of what the first democratic socialist Mayor David Dinkins once described the city as, which is a “gorgeous mosaic.”

q.t: On the point, you talked about paying for a lot of this by increasing taxes. What is going to be the burden on homeowners, because again, you talk about those older homeowners, many of them fixed income. If you all of a sudden have an increase in property taxes, that's going to make it very difficult for those single-family homeowners on fixed income.

a.t:
We're not talking about any burden on a fixed income homeowner. What we're talking about is a burden on non-resident New Yorker who owns a secondary home that's worth more than $5 million. And that is very few and far between in this city. And yet what we've seen is that a city where, as you said, a homeowner on fixed income is struggling to make ends meet, it's also the wealthiest city in the wealthiest country in the history of the world. And our job is to ensure that that wealth, it reaches the struggles also that New Yorkers they're facing in affording life in this city. That's why we've been focused on increasing taxes only for the wealthiest New Yorkers, the most profitable corporations. And when it comes to those who are struggling in this City, it's: “How do we deliver for them each and every day?”

I'll give you one example. When it comes homeowners, we saw that Rudy Giuliani policy called the “Tax Lien Sale.” The city was selling tax liens in Black neighborhoods at six times the rate it was selling them in white neighborhoods. And I used to be a foreclosure prevention housing counselor before I was an elected official, I would see up close what it meant when that lien was sold; it meant you were on a fast track to foreclosure. So, what we did, one of the first things we did was coming in, we said: “Look, it's not worth the amount of money this is bringing into the city if it means it's at the expense of homeownership.” And so, we put a pause on that lien sale for the first six months with a study instead to look at, yes, how can we make sure that everyone is paying what they owe the city, but also, how could we make it's not happening at the expense of their ability to stay in this city?

q.t: You talked about childcare. Obviously, that appeals to a lot of parents. And the reality is that you have seen significant erosion of your Black population. New York City used to have the largest Black population in the country and Chicago was second. Atlanta was third. You've been losing. What are you going to do to stem that tide? What I keep hearing from my listeners and viewers is that they simply cannot afford to stay in New York City.

a.t:
And that's what we've heard — the same thing — and we've heard it for years. And as you know, any time we talk about increasing taxes on the wealthiest or the most profitable corporations, there'll be talk of a fear of a capital flight. But there's a real flight that's already been happening for years, and that is the flight of Black New Yorkers out of this city because they can't afford the ever-increasing cost of the city. And just to put a number on it, we're talking about more than 200,000 Black New Yorkers having left this city in the last few decades alone. And from 2010 to 2019, our city saw a decline in the population of Black children and teenagers by 19 percent. So, our focus here is how do we make it easier to stay in New York, because we don't want to be an administration that presides over what has effectively become a reverse Great Migration. We want to be the administration that brings that to an end and instead says that this is a city that doesn't just celebrate Black history, but it's a city that allows Black history to keep being written.

And so, what we have seen is the number one cost is housing. So, we have committed to building 200,000 new affordable homes as well as preserving 200,000 existing affordable homes over the next 10 years. We're doing this while also focusing on homeowners because we know that for many Black New Yorkers, homeownership has been that path to stability. And what that has meant is creating the city's first-ever Office of Deed Theft Prevention so we can bring an end to the scourge of especially older Black New Yorkers being taken advantage of under the guise of refinancing or planning out the shift of possession of the property to the next generation and instead protect their rights as homeowners. And we do this as well as delivering on childcare because when it comes to the cost of living, childcare is the second-most-expensive thing and it's considered a good deal in our city today if you can get childcare for $20,000 a year. And that's just something that we can't accept.

q.t: Fantastic, enjoy Staten Island. Have a great day.

a.t: Thank you, my friend.

q.t: Very, very good. Mr. Mayor. Thanks so much for joining us. And keep going and we'll check back in every six to seven – every Knicks championship, you'll come on this show.

a.t: See you next year.

q.t: And are there any other leaders that you would also like to arrest? Because I have a list.

a.t: Brother, anybody who the ICC has called for, I think we should be honoring.

q.t: So, that was brought up to you? That was brought up to you.

a.t: Yes, yes. And yet I know for many New Yorkers, when they see a clip, it doesn't begin with the question it begins with the answer.
Right.

I think the focus always has to be on the work that you're doing and how you find a balance between, you know, not giving your kind of a classic, you know, a political deflection where you don't want to answer any of those questions and focusing on the work and still finding that together.

q.t: We do have some leaders in this country who appreciate, who appreciate that work, and I'm cognizant of your time and I really appreciate you being here. And the final question, which I have to ask you because it's dominating the news today, you know, is the Netanyahu thing and arresting Netanyahu. Understanding where you're coming from there, is there a sense you have it, maybe? Is that a distraction from all these other things that you want to do? Is that taking a little bit more of the media space than you realized?

a.t: Well, I think I have a responsibility to be honest with New Yorkers, and when I'm asked a question to answer it honestly, and I also know that for many New Yorkers–

q.t: Have a caprese salad for me, my friend. It's a beautiful thing.

a.t: I got you brother. But yes, you grow up in this city, you have caricatures of so many people and you have to leave those at the door. And you also have to be willing to move beyond them and for some of those conversations to be actually good faith ones to offer people the ability to critique you to you. And I think, you know, sometimes when you're the mayor, you're in a position of power, you want people to just tell you: "Oh, you're incredible. Here's what I love most about your agenda." It's like you're not actually going to get anything done if that's how you want to be treated.

q.t: A slightly low bar for a conversation. Now what about, did you have caricatures of them? Are there, you know, look, I saw when you tried to go to Staten Island, that was a rough ride, but are there caricatures that you've had of those folks that have been shattered when you've spent time with them?

a.t: I think when we talk about Staten Island, what comes to mind for me is when I went there, I was being protested outside by a number of Staten Islanders who were very supportive of the president, deeply opposed to me. And then when I when inside the restaurant, there were other Staten Islands who were excited about me coming there. And to me, it also shows me that you can just paint a broad brush and say, you know what, I'm not going. It's actually funny that you mentioned it because right after this, I'm going to Staten Island. Yeah, I didn't plan that.

q.t: We got it all. What's your outreach like to those communities? What have you learned from those communities. What have you learned from those people? How do you interact with them? And how do you take in their criticisms of you or their fears?

a.t: I think that the first thing you have to do is walk into those conversations without having already made a judgment. And when you walk into it with an open mind, then it means that you can actually have a conversation and make a decision as to how you feel after you have that conversation. And I think in a lot of our politics, we label people and then disregard them entirely. We treat them as if they're not even people worth engaging with. And look, I'll have conversations with more billionaires that oppose my fiscal policies than those that don't, but there's still more things to actually be discussed about with them. And similarly, what I've also found is, to our benefit, the caricature of me and what our administration would mean was so immense that when I walk into a room and I don't immediately strangle three people that are in front of me, people are taken aback that that might not actually be as bad.

q.t: Right, so that it's, there's a wide variety of interdictions that you can do in those various situations, not just after the fact, make those arrests. So, there's whole cadre of groups that, you know, look, they stood in opposition to you. There was a great amount of fear, and we can run through them from the Police Department. I think there was a lot of fear there. And I know, listen, the cops in this city – they do incredible, incredible work. And they don't necessarily get the recognition and the care. I think there was a lot of hostility to them for a lot of years. And I think that's unfortunate. I think they're, like you say, that's something that you have to battle with. There's Trump supporters. New York City has everything. There's the billionaire class.

a.t: We got it all.

q.t: To that point, the Department of Community Safety, which was one of those things that you had ran on, which I think was sort of reprioritizing some of those assets so that not necessarily it was always police were the first responders to everything, there was also – how has that come? I know it, the money for it didn't exist, you had to do an executive order, I believe. What's the status of that? How has that grown?

a.t:
So, we've created that Office of Community Safety. We have for the first time in New York City now, a deputy mayor for community safety, Renita Francois, who's doing great work in putting together what is right now a quarter-of-a-billion-dollar budge, in a lot of the very kinds of things that you're talking about. And I think one of the clearest examples to me is we have asked police officers to do almost everything we can think of when it comes to dealing with the failures of not just the social safety net but also violent crime and also and also, and also across the five boroughs. And what we found time and again is that these same officers who signed up to join the Department, to respond to violent crime, to prevent violent crime, are also being tasked with responding to a mental health call. And this is the kind of work that undermines both our ability to deliver on public safety as a whole and it shows that we need to develop a new model here.

And so, one of the focuses coming out of the Office of Community Safety is, how do we provide the investment and the support so that when a New Yorker calls for help with a mental health crisis, that they can also receive that help from mental health professionals as well? And that's something that continues alongside the incredible work that the office is doing with gun violence prevention, which is work that we always need to do more and more of, because we know it's an epidemic in this city and across this country. And a lot of that prevention work also comes with investing in gun violence interrupters, in the Crisis Management System.
