And I've had the privilege of meeting a number of young people who themselves have been victims of gun violence and they've told me how organizations like the ones that New York City invests in are the ones who will respond to them in the moment and make sure that retaliation isn't something they're thinking about, but rather recuperation is what they're focused on.

q.t: That's what I'm talking about. But you're comfortable with those kinds of discussions?

a.t: I'm comfortable with disagreement. And I'm uncomfortable with disagreement that doesn't end the conversation entirely. Because I think what motivates a lot of people is, "How do you deliver public safety?" And the thing that I've said time and again is, we cannot have New Yorkers choose between safety and justice. And yes, I am doing the work with our police department, and we have been able to deliver the lowest number of murders and shootings in recorded history. And at the same time, I'm doing the work to close down Rikers Island and ensure that we are actually building the four smaller borough-based jails that brings an end to a horrible chapter in New York City history. And I think to your point, when we're thinking about safety, there cannot be a hierarchy of safety where you experience it more or less depending on where you live in our city or how much money's in your pocket. And there also can't be a definition of safety that is purely after the fact, meaning that how you respond to violence. We also have to do the work of investing so that we prevent violence and to that

q.t: It's sort of like how soccer used to be. In the NASL in the '80s, there had to be two Americans on every team. So there's gotta be two socialists in a room.

a.t: Look, man, now we have quarters, and I didn't think that day was going to come with the World Cup.

q.t: Are you allowed to have more than one socialist in the room?

a.t: We're actually just trying to change that law.

q.t: If someone says, "We're going to abolish all prisons and borders," I do go, "I don't think that's a good idea." It feels like order and security is also a progressive value. Why shouldn't people in neighborhoods with less resources have the same safety and security that neighborhoods with lots of resources [have]? Are there tenets of those that are following in the wake of Zohran Mamdani's success that you're not comfortable with or that give you pause?

a.t: If you have more than one socialist in a room and there isn't disagreement, then you don't have more than one socialist in a room.

q.t: Getting back to the original idea of redefining what democratic socialism can do for a city this complex and this size and the realism that has to go along with it and the budgetary restrictions and things that you have to get there, do you in any way have that conversation with – so now democratic socialism is considered the hottest trend in the Democratic Party. And there's energy, grassroots energy and all, and these democratic socialist candidates are popping up, and you're having to answer for every one of their policy positions. And there are some – Look, maybe I'm an old man or a shit lib or whatever they want to call me, but-

a.t: Who's calling you this?

q.t: And sometimes it's a small – I tell you, this seems like a ridiculous thing: One of the most important things you did was getting people to take some of that scaffolding down. Like it's things that you do. The scaffolding is so a part of the landscape that I almost thought of it as like, "Oh, that's how buildings are," like they're built and people just hang scaffolding like Christmas lights [and] just never take them down. Like that's just a crazy, weird thing. And when you start taking them down, you're like, "Oh wow, New York's beautiful.

a.t: We treated it as if it was part of the physical landscape of the city. And I think that so much of what the approach has been is: "It is what it is. This is how it's always been." And that's just not acceptable. And I, to your point – when you are able to change these kinds of ways that New Yorkers measure their quality of life, it gives them – it's an invitation to them to hope and believe. But if you don't change those things, then why should they take that step?

q.t: And it's difficult because here's your dilemma. You make this place too nice. Then rents are really gonna – you're in a vicious cycle. In some respects, look, we joke about it, but there are a lot of people in Brooklyn that are resentful. As Brooklyn started to change and develop, it gentrified. And suddenly the people that lived in Brooklyn, as my family did when they came here, couldn't afford to live there anymore. It's as though when they finally came in and made the neighborhoods more livable, that drove out the people that had been living there. And I imagine that's a difficult problem to solve as well. It's this strange trap.

a.t: And I think anyone growing up in this city has gone through the experience of looking at a construction site in their neighborhood and asking themselves: "Is this for me, or is this going to push me out?" And one of the key things here is that we have to both build more housing than we've ever seen in our city in a long time and do it while strengthening the tenant protections that we have in this city so that we're not forced to choose between the tenants of today and the tenants of tomorrow. And I think to what you said, there are a lot of New Yorkers who rightfully associate even just investments in their own neighborhood as if it is the appetizer to displacement.
Right.

And we have to show that these things are not, in fact, tied together, that you do not need new residents to invest in that old park. You can do that. And I think, you know, when we go back to this conversation around the fiscal deficit of $12 billion, there is – in that moment, it is all too easy to say, "My only focus right now is to get out of this fiscal crisis, and then everything else we'll figure it out next year." We wanted to also use it as an opportunity to show that we mean what we say – that you do want to still fund your parks, your libraries, your cultural institutions, and do it in a way that annualizes that funding as opposed to making it subject to every single year's budget dance with the City Council. That's also to me what is a critical part of earning those New Yorkers' trust back is that they see those investments in their neighborhood and they'd see it before anyone's ever going to [tell] them that "you may have to leave." We want them to stay.

q.t: What were those – are those zoning decisions? Was that Robert [Moses]?

a.t: A lot of those are zoning decisions. They're decisions around capacity and also around size of building, scale of building. And you'll walk around the city, you'll see buildings that are incredible, that we associate with our city, yet you could not build them today because they were built prior to those zoning changes having happened. And one of the critical things here is we have to treat the cost-of-living crisis as both a short-term crisis and a long-term crisis. We have to take immediate action. And then we have to do the long-term work of being able to build 200,000 new affordable homes over 10 years, because if you do not have a city that is growing, a city that is building, then what you have is a city that is dying.

q.t: Get on that wall. You're shaking too many hands! I see it every day! The big talking point is, "My God, this communist lunatic is going to drive out our billionaires," as though that is the reason that people are drawn to New York, that tourists come here and go, "Let's go down to Little Billionaire." And it's the area of New York where the billionaires live, and we can enjoy a small slice of how they live. But the real danger to New York is not the couple of billionaires who feel as though taxing their second home is too burdensome for that, but the exodus of essential workers who can no longer afford to be anywhere near this area. Wouldn't that be much more devastating?

a.t: And I think what you're saying speaks to the fact that for all of the conversation about an imagined capital flight, there already is a flight. It's just of working-class people. And we know that the racial dynamics of this are also immense. We've seen over the past few decades, our city has lost 200,000 Black New Yorkers. From 2010 to 2019, the population of black children and teenagers declined by 19 percent. And you can feel that in this city, in neighborhoods that are shells of what they once were, and small businesses that don't have those same customers coming through that came in for years, and classrooms that are a little less full. If we want to be honest about what it's going to take, it's not just going to be one day to the next, it's also going to have to be a complete shift. I'll give you an example of this. When we talk about housing, since the early 1960s, New York City started to make decisions that would render it unable to build the level of housing it needed to keep up with demand. To change that–

q.t: See, that, I think, it brings up such an interesting point. And don't get sick. I don't know what they're doing. You protect – get this man some Purell, and you do not get sick, brother!

a.t: I'm on that Emergen-C. Every day, I take that vitamin C.

q.t: Could this still be a middle-class city?

a.t: That is what it has to be. And I think if we allow it to continue on the path it's been on for many years, it will become a museum of where working-class people once lived. And we don't want this to be something that people can visit to pay tribute to what it once was. We want it to be a living, breathing testament to that energy. And I think what is one of the most concerning things that I hear is when I turn to someone who is working as hard as they can for the city and I asked them how long their commute home is, and they tell me it's hours because they're going to another state or another city. That's a reflection of a failure to ensure that those who build the city can live in the city, and the reason I think that affordability will be our greatest challenge and also our greatest opportunity is this is what is pushing people out of this city. You cannot disentangle the cost of housing, of childcare, of groceries from the exodus of working-class people from out of the city. Some of these things are New York City specific. Some of them are true across the entire country. And we have to finally change direction so that people can actually afford to live here.

q.t: And maybe, I think, it was one of the things that I think drew people to you. It didn't just feel like platitudes. There was a specificity to the affordability argument. I see a lot of politicians that perform the rhetoric of that argument. "We need to get back to kitchen table issues," and all that, rather than going out to a halal food truck and go, "Why is this $14? There's like three pieces of chicken in here." Like, why does that cost that much? Is affordability the toughest challenge that you think you'll face?

a.t: I think so.

q.t: You know what? Nobody puts Rudy in a corner.

a.t: Let's not go there!
Let's not go there.

It is easy, when there is this much noise, to tell yourself that all of it is exactly that. Tune it all out. But that's also what – It will leave you in an echo chamber. You cannot have it that you are only surrounded by people who agree with you. You might as well just stay home at that point. And I think that the job that I have, that my team has, that our administration has, is, how do you listen to all of it and then separate out what is actually worth engaging with and what is just driven by the algorithm and written in response to what the algorithm responds to and rewards. And I think that the other part of this is, no matter how good we may feel about whatever achievement we have or how this six months has gone, you always have to push yourself because every day is an opportunity to do better for New Yorkers. And I, and I think that's something that I love about this city is, you especially see it in, in kind of sports culture, but I would say even in, in the cultural aspect of the city, there is this sense of having to be the best, of driving yourself each and every day. And yet in our politics, that often feels as if it's missing. There is somehow in a city that is the best in the world at so many things, mediocrity has come to be accepted as the standard in our politics. And I think that it's something that we shouldn't accept any longer.

q.t: That was the first draft of that song. But the caricature – so, Trump will tweet out, "Communist lunatic," and – are there criticisms that bother you? Are there ones you laughed [at]? You know, the city tweeted out during the heat wave, "Put your thermostats to 78." And immediately Ted Cruz from Texas is like, "The warmth of collectivism." Meanwhile, Texas tweets out the same thing and so does the Energy Department of the United States of America, which they pull off of their website out of fear that now they will be associated with this. Do any of those criticisms permeate? Do any of them land? Have you heard any of the criticisms where you thought to yourself, "Actually, that's constructive and I will think about how to make adjustments to that."

a.t: Look, I took offense when they came for socialist icon Rudy Giuliani's energy policy. I said, "Say what you want about me."

q.t: And this gets us back to – so the contrast between the caricature of you – if you spend any time speaking to you, there's a grounded seriousness and reality to the way that you're approaching these problems. Look, there's gonna be mistakes, there's going to be – first snowstorm is not gonna be the same as the second snowstorm, as Fat Joe has in his song. Today's snowstorm is not, but–

a.t: That was the first draft of that song.

q.t: Right. That's all they do is they just run it through that.

a.t: And you look at that, and it's not just the amount of money, it's also the number of vendors that we went through to get to that point. It just speaks to an approach to contracting that does not actually save you money, and it doesn't build any kind of long-term fluency. What it does is just lock you into commitments that will cost you money and oftentimes won't even perform those services.

q.t: Was it just like the Microsoft paper clip that just pops up?

a.t: It's like – I thought you lost your job. It's just "Ask Jeeves," he's just back.

q.t: You don't comb it through like that.

a.t: No, but we do comb through. And there were a number of things where you can't provide a justification for it. And if you can't provide one, then why should the city be spending that money? And a lot of times, it comes from a vision of government where you want to hollow out its capacity and privatize as much of its responsibility. And oftentimes, it's done in the name of fiscal prudence. And yet what you find is you end up overpaying for that external capacity than what it would look like if you invested internally. I mean, you know, we've talked about in the past this – you know, the previous administration had an AI chatbot that cost hundreds of thousands of dollars that was not even usable.

q.t: Were there stuff in the budget as you went through, you're like, "$100 million on mittens, what is this?" Did you find things that you couldn't believe? You were just like, "Where's these love seats? What's going on?"

a.t: I haven't seen that specific example.

q.t: Hey, you know the CSOs coming in here. Yeah, I've got like five CSOs over here.

a.t: Me and my CSOs were hanging out, catching up.
Beautiful.

And the CSOs, they found about $1.7 billion in savings across City government, and they're actually going to continue that work. Because when you look at the size of our budget, and you also look at what the approach has been to the finances of our city, we know that there are more savings to be had. And sometimes these are the efficiencies that come from when you're actually pressure testing how we've been doing things. There's savings to had when you actually say that you know, could that contract that you're giving to a consultant actually be done in house? And it can be a lot of times.

q.t: And so, that's, and then do you have to look at it? Cause I guess there's sort of different areas like we'll spend less here, but we need to raise more revenue here. Is there a kind of interplay between the kinds of taxes? Cause Albany, I imagine is not going to go along with really raising taxes in the same way that you might want.

a.t: I think what you'll find, actually, is there are a lot of people in Albany who do agree with the vision of raising taxes a little bit more on the wealthiest so that everyone can afford life in New York City. But what it is, as you said, is it can't just be one thing. It has to both be a conversation about revenue and a conversation or about savings. So, we actually created something called Chief Savings Officers for the first time, where we had in every single agency and department–
Oh sure, CSOs.
CSOs, come on.
It's sitting right there.
You're at the water cooler. You know, you're talking to your friend, you're like, "Hey, have you heard about the CSOs? What do you think about the CSOs?"

q.t: I know, seeing him stand – I think that was his truck in the parade, by the way. I don't even think that – I think actually he just drove. He drove there that day and just got in the back of it. I think that's how it worked.

a.t:
God bless. But to your actual question, I think one of the key things is you have to ask yourself, is this arbitrary or does this have a rationale? And what I mean by that is, for example, with the pension system, we had a deferred payment that was spread out over about 22 years or so. And every year, the cost to the city was increasing, and then it was going to just fall off a cliff in terms of the city – it was gonna go up about maybe $6 billion a year, and then the next year it's gonna be $0. And some of the challenges that we're facing are challenges of this moment specifically because of just how much under-budgeting there was, how much money the city was spending, but not showing on its books for a lot of its different social programs and services.

And so, when we looked at that and we said, if you just spread what had already been 22 years, if you'd just extend it by a few years, you would then be able to take savings that you will get the year after as you're scheduled to but instead spread them over. Then you can actually make sure that you're able to steward this in a way that's more healthy, in a medium-term level. Now, I know that there are others who've seen municipalities move around their pension obligations and there's a worry of what does this mean for, you know, are you going to honor that, this, that and the other. The thing that's different in New York City is that we are not only funding our pension systems at a much higher level than many of the other municipalities that are being cited, but also that it's not a question of if we're going to get to 100 percent funded. It's just a question of when in the 2030s we would do so.

q.t: Can I tell you something? There is a monster truck-sized hole in my heart.

a.t: Yes, it's one of the best TikTok pages to go to.
He's the best, so, so funny.
I never appreciated those cars until I saw those videos.

q.t: No – oh, when he went after the Celtics fans, when he said, "I own you"?

a.t: God bless.

q.t: It's very, it's very hurtful. It's very hurtful.

a.t: We'll continue on. Did you see his comment on the Boston Celtics Instagram page?

q.t: Right, right. Although that's – what do you do with – there are certain things that, they sort of call them gimmicks as you start to balance the budget and a lot of the mayors have done that. They're sort of these things that they pass along to other – I think Bloomberg was one of the ones who did it. How does straightening out that without pulling from different pension funds that are going to, you know, mature in 2032? How do you begin to straighten those finances out without having to use kinds of, you know, it's in some ways it's like you're the GM of a football team that's got a salary cut, you don't want to go into that second apron for New York City, man. And so, how do you begin to do that in a manner that is more objectively grounded and not really budgetary magic.

a.t: Well, first, you brought it up, so I just got to say I'm already missing Mitch.

q.t: Julie Menin. Upper East Side – wealthy Upper East side lady, we all know the caricature, you know, they don't pick up after their dogs, you know what I'm talking about. You're the fiscal conservative in that relationship. Did that surprise you?

a.t:
You know – it is – when I've talked about wanting City government to be remade in the image of a struggling New Yorker, one aspect of it is that we be as careful with our money as working New Yorkers are with theirs. And one of the many reasons for that is that this is their money. And when we're looking at – when we looked at that fiscal deficit, what was hard – one of many things that was challenging about it, is that you couldn't blame it on an external reality. You couldn't say, "Oh, it's the fiscal crisis of 2008. Everyone can see what's going on across the country and the world."

This was, in many ways, purely of City Halls doing. It was mismanagement and under budgeting, and it had been building for years. And I think that one of my goals is how do we right the ship, not just in a 12-month interval, but frankly on a medium- and long-term. Because if you're just trying to survive on a calendar year basis, you're in many ways going to have to rob Peter to pay Paul. And eventually that bill is gonna come due. And the thing that I'm looking forward to next year is that we're not gonna have to inherit a $12 billion fiscal deficit, no matter how tough it is.

q.t: You're the fiscal conservative, like even with the City Council you've got uh, uh, what is her name? Menin? Sue Menin?

a.t: Julie Menin, Speaker Julie Menin.

q.t: What about in terms of housing? What have you been able to deliver? What's frustrated you? What's the next step?

a.t: Well, I think I'll just take a step back to tell you, Jon, that the most challenging thing overall was when I came into this position, I expected that it would be difficult in terms of the finances of the city, especially given my predecessor's approach to those finances. What I did not expect was $12 billion worth of difficulty.

q.t: Right. And again, not when they – when people immediately cried communism, it's not unprecedented. The two years is unprecedented, but this has been done for one year by others.

a.t: Yeah, they have done it in the past, yeah.

q.t: Exactly. "Zohran Mamdani, the aphrodisiac." So, what about what you're trying to deliver [that] has been slightly more complicated than what you thought it would be? We can walk through it. Housing. So, you were able to get through a rent freeze, a two-year rent freeze. Yes?

a.t: Yeah, the independent Rent Guidelines Board established a two-year rent freeze for over 2 million New Yorkers who live in rent-stabilized housing.

q.t: So, in some respects, Zohran Mamdani's mayoralty has been an aphrodisiac for New Yorkers to begin to repopulate this grand experiment.

a.t: I can see the attack ads now.

q.t: Is that all over the city, or is that – does that vary in boroughs or that's the average for all five boroughs?

a.t: That's the measure across the five boroughs that that's how much your family would have to earn to be able to absorb that kind of a hit. And people earn less than that and they find ways to make it work, but not without it being to the detriment of themselves in their financial situation. And I think that, you know, I never thought that I'd be the guy making it easier for aunties at the family function to pressure you into having a kid, but here we are.

q.t: I think it's a question of also how you're gonna get there because I think, you know, if I may and you tell me if you think this is wrong, as I watch you pursuing your agenda it doesn't seem radical it, it seems workman-like. You know, when you talked about universal childcare, you didn't seize the means of childcare and create a "Soviet-style system" where they all get the same little uniform and they all come in at four years old and they you know pray to the gods of socialism. You didn't even really raise – you went to the governor, and she was able to help, you know, fill in a little bit of the financial gap. You created a pied-à-terre tax for, you know, second homes of the over $5 million in value, is that correct? Like these are not particularly radical reinventions. It feels like smart prioritizing, if I may.

a.t: Well, I think that a lot of it comes back to how do you judge the success of your work? And I think you have to judge it by what you deliver. And one of the cornerstones of our campaign was universal childcare, given the fact that in a cost-of-living crisis, childcare is the second highest expense for families in New York City. But we're talking about $20,000 a year for a single child. And in this city, you have to make $334,000 to be able to afford that kind of expense. And to me, it is, how do we move as quickly as possible?

q.t: And it is, you know, it's such an interesting thing because when you talk about the demonization, you know, I always think people always say, "Oh, that's anti-capitalist." And in some respects, I think it's the opposite, you know, capitalism, I think would have faced a much stiffer opposition from communism and socialism in the 1930s, if the New Deal hadn't been instituted. If we hadn't had created a more robust social safety net, revolution would have been much more on the table without Social Security, without better housing for people. And I wonder if that's similar today, that in some respects, what you're doing is actually a reform movement for capitalism to some extent.

a.t: I mean, some of the things that you've said, Social Security, if you go back and see how that was treated when it was first introduced, right, it was described as the "Sovietization of America." And now it is thought of as one of the most American things that we could ever be talking about. And I think about, you know, when you go around New York City and you see these monuments to FDR, to the New Deal, you know you go to Four Freedoms Park on Roosevelt Island – it is a sad reflection of the state of the Democratic Party that a lot of what is said in those programs and those visions today would sound as if it [were] a bridge too ambitious for the party that we belong to.
Right.

And I think that's part of my hope as a Democrat is how do we ensure that New Yorkers and Americans don't have to look to the history books to be able to find a party platform that speaks about. A freedom from want and a freedom from fear.

q.t: You just thought like, what if I label myself something that scares people the most, "I'm a Muslim democratic socialist, and I'd like to run your public transportation system." So, is there in some regard, is this a is the idea being if I can show myself to be a competent steward of the day-to-day functioning? Of maybe certainly one of the most complex city systems in the world. I can demystify. I can maybe take some of the fear out of what it means to be a – I can take these labels that are so loaded with fear, and I can maybe take a little bit of that caricature out of them.

a.t:
I mean, my true goal is to deliver for the people of the city, and if in the process of doing so, we can demystify so much of the fear that has become the norm in our politics, I welcome it. And I also think that for a long time, we've discussed democratic socialism as an intellectual debate. We haven't been able to point to what examples look like of it delivering for people. And now we have that just over six months and I think that – it's an incredibly exciting opportunity because there's a reason so many New Yorkers lost faith in City government and the political impulse of lecturing someone as to why they should believe and why they should vote, as opposed to asking yourself, why is it that they lost that faith?

When you're governing, you have the opportunity to not just listen, but also then respond in action, not in words. And I think that what's been so exciting is to see that New Yorkers understand that some things will take time and some things that can be done immediately. And if you're able to show that you're doing both, then it is exactly the kind of extension of an arm to say, would you like to join this movement? And I've just heard from so many that they would.

q.t: That's for sure. So, to that end, was there ever a consideration for you because of the priorities that you have, what I take on the label of democratic socialist, knowing that it comes with a lot of other baggage that may not be helpful to you in your pursuit of what are – what was it about what they were saying that drew you – as opposed to running as the things that you're suggesting to me, if you ran on these as a Democrat – it's not I wouldn't say like, "What? What the heck?" You know, it sounds very much in line with that. It sounds like what you're doing differently is you're being competent or ruthlessly pursuing those goals and chipping away at them. So, why take that on?

a.t: You know, I want to be honest with people about what it is that I actually believe in. And I also think what we've seen over many decades is a fearmongering in our politics where anything that we disagree with or anything that portends significant change is described as if it is socialist, you know, at times as if, as if is communist. And the intent of that is to end the conversation there and then. And it especially happens when you're talking about something that would disproportionately benefit working people. And I think it's important because we keep speaking about some of the inequities and inequalities that we see in our city as if they are bugs in a system as opposed to features in them. And if we truly want to reckon with one in four New Yorkers being in poverty, we have to also ask ourselves about if it's important to change the framework with which what we determine success to be. And also, you know, being a Muslim democratic socialist, I thought it would be pretty straightforward.

q.t: There we go. This is where I'm getting to is, is it really about the label?

a.t:
I think if you go back to some of the Democrats that we most admire – FDR, La Guardia – you will see a lot of democratic socialist principles in their vision. And if you think about a lot what we've come to accept as just the facts of life across our country, a lot it is also still driven by democratic socialist principle. Now, if today, you and I were to introduce the idea of a building that lends out books for free. We would be slandered in the same way that so many new ideas are slandering today, and yet that's the library. And the same thing with the Fire Department [and] the same with Public Schools.

And it's to say that a lot of politics has been a debate about who deserves what, and I would prefer a politics that debates how we can deliver that to everyone. And to deliver it at a standard that is so good that no matter how much money in your pocket, you opt for that. And I think, at its best, the New York City subway is an illustration where no matter how much money you have in your pocket, you understand that if you want to get from point A to point B, [the] best way is to get on that train.

q.t: Right, so in some respects, is it about the priorities that you have are about quality of life for those even if they don't make? Because universal Pre-K or universal childcare – those kinds of things, you know, de Blasio might have brought that up or, you know, it's not something that – I think that the caricature of democratic socialism is that you're a different – it's a completely different ideology than those that we have seen, or is it perhaps just a different nomenclature.

a.t: I think part of it is that words have lost their meaning over time.

q.t: Wait, you're moving me?

a.t: I'm moving you.
[Inaudible] Stalin.

I think that to your point, there are a lot of politicians of a variety of ideologies who will speak about housing as a human right, for example, or health care as a human right or they'll talk about dignity. I think where the rubber meets the road is, are you actually willing to ensure that which no one should be priced out of, no one is in fact priced out of it? So, I'll give you an example: childcare. It's hard to find a politician who'll say childcare should be more expensive. They'll generally say it should be more affordable, right?
Right.

But are you willing to take the step to provide childcare as something that is guaranteed to New Yorkers regardless of how much money they have in their pocket? So, one of our focuses has been universal childcare. Take the successes of free childcare for three-year-olds of Pre-K and extend it to two-year-olds. Now, it's not just as simple as saying, "Oh, yes, I want to do that." You have to also be willing to fight for the revenue you need to do that. And so, [on] day eight of our administration, we secure an agreement with the governor for $1.2 billion that unlocks free childcare for two-year-olds for the first time in New York City. And our dream is that this will extend not only to the 2,000 two-year-olds this year or the 12,000 next year, but every single two-year-old by the end of four years. And it's not just a dream, it's a promise and it's commitment.

q.t: Wait, I'm doing this in Jersey. I'm out of your jurisdiction, man. I'm not even around there.

a.t: You were doing this in Jersey.

q.t: But here's the thing. Here's what I love about that. You walk the walk. That's the important thing. Somebody had to seize the means of this production.

a.t: It was this specific production that I was talking about.

q.t: Wait, what?

a.t: I'm sorry, brother.

q.t: See that, to me though – that statement, if a Democrat was running, or even a Republican to some extent, that feels like something that everybody would say, "We want everybody to be able to thrive in this city." Is there something about democratic socialism as a theory that brings those to bear? In other words, is it about the safety net? Is it about, you know – the caricature is "You're a communist who's going to nationalize the industries. You're going to take over Goldman Sachs."

a.t: I'm actually coming on this podcast to let you know that it's now my podcast.

q.t: But you – so that's the interesting thing. There's a caricature of democratic socialism and there's a reality of democratic socialism and then there is just governing that has very little to do with democratic socialism. So, can we tease those apart a little bit? What would – in your mind, what is governing by the principles of democratic socialist? What does that entail?

a.t:
It means making the choice every day to fight for working people. It means that you believe that everyone in your city deserves to live a dignified life, no matter how much money is in their pocket. And what we've found is that this city is many things all at once. It's both the wealthiest city in the wealthiest country in the history of the world. And it's also a city where one in four people are living in poverty. And so, that you'll often hear the phrase, "Don't sweat the small stuff." To me, being a democratic socialist is also sweating the small.

Because for a lot of New Yorkers, it's those things that are the measure of how difficult or easy their life is, whether they're able not only to pay for their rent or their childcare, but whether they are able to also rely on City government to get around their city, to breathe in their city, to experience life in their city. And I think that we've forgotten that at the heart of what we want to deliver is not just the existence of a public sector, it's also the excellence and efficiency of a public sector. I want New Yorkers to be choosing this City government every single day as opposed to feeling as if they're subjected to it.

q.t: Sir, we're being recorded right now. What are you doing throwing in the D – you're throwing in the S word? Don't throw in the S word.

a.t: Apologies, I didn't mean to use a slur live on this podcast.
Son of a [].
I just wanted to make sure that we're going to be together in the cell when we're all rounded up.
Alright, fair enough.
You and me.

q.t: I appreciate it. How are you feeling now? So, you have been the mayor for – you started January 1, it is now July – seven months. What's the reality of being the mayor? Is – how does it feel after – what is the difference between the rhetoric of running for mayor and the reality of governing as mayor?

a.t: Yeah, I think there's often a lot made of a campaign as if it is easier and a governing as if is a harder experience. I think both are challenging. I think what is lost though is that governing comes with the opportunity to deliver. When you're campaigning, you're asking people to believe; you're asking them to put their trust into a politics that's often disappointed them. And when you're governing, you can earn their trust by what you deliver. And so, it is much easier to have a conversation about this vision today when we've been able to pave 175,000 potholes; put the city on a path to universal childcare; win more than $60 million for tenants whose landlords made negligence into a business model. When we have that conversation now, you can point to what these last six months have looked like under democratic socialist principles. When you have it during the campaign–

q.t: I don't know if there's a shed behind City Hall where they keep them, but they're still there.

a.t: I will get back to you, brother.

q.t: It's the most beautiful – one question, sir, at City Hall, at the end of the Canyon of Heroes, in the parade, there was a great deal of Knicks memorabilia that was hung up around in decorative fashion. Giant Knicks caricatures, Knicks jerseys. I guess my question to you is, may I have those?

a.t: You know what? I'll ask the team where they are.

q.t: Are you still feeling the afterglow, the joy of the halo effect of the New York Knickerbockers' incredible run to the championship this year? Do you still feel it?

a.t: One hundred percent. It is – "Knicks in five" has become a greeting in New York City.

q.t: So, ladies and gentlemen, we have the distinct honor and pleasure today to be welcoming the mayor of the great, great city. That is the one that never sleeps, the biggest apple of them all: New York City. Mayor Zohran Mamdani is joining us. Mayor, Mr. Mayor, your honor. His honor, your honor. How are you?

a.t: I'm doing well, man. Thank you for having me. It's a pleasure to be back.

q.t: To Dr. Martin, a point of clarity on Legionella: Initially, I think you and the team believed that there was a single source of the Legionella infections, right? It sounds now as if you believe there may have been or are multiple sources of Legionella. Can you clarify that for us?

a.t:
So, we started with 183 cooling towers, 76 of which were PCR positive. Let me explain what that means, right? So, the PCR-positive towers mean that we find evidence of DNA of Legionella in that tower. Now the DNA could be live, or it could be dead, right? The only version that can hurt you is the live Legionella bacteria, so we now have a preliminary list of 34 cooling towers that have that live Legionella bacteria. Now, the next step is, quite frankly, my favorite. This is the nerdiest step, and this is the whole genome sequence step. We take the bacteria that we found in those 34 towers, and we identify the samples from our patients, and we try and make a match. And what we typically find in these clusters is that there is one tower. Last time in Harlem, there were two.

My expectation is that we're going to have a similar pattern here, where there will likely be one tower, or perhaps two, that actually do have the same DNA pattern as the one that caused this cluster. Why are there so many? I think there's a question underneath that question, which is, why are there so many bacterial culture positives? As you heard us say earlier, this is a bacteria which is ubiquitous. It's everywhere. And the vast majority of these towers have infinitesimal, small, trace amounts of Legionella bacteria. Some have enough to cause a cluster. Our job now, now that we've eliminated the source, is to identify specifically which tower caused this cluster. So, that's the work ahead of us.

q.t: Really quick, back to Legionnaires, on the NYC Gov website, it says there's a six-month delay in posting inspection results to the public. Is there any way that that six-month lag could be updated so people can see when their buildings are being inspected on a faster timeline? And secondly, during the speaker's press conference yesterday, she called for there to be a dedicated hotline during peak Legionella season just to notify the public and inform them of — can they walk past this building outside? Is it safe to do so? Or do they need to be wearing a mask, et cetera. Is that something that the Health Department would consider doing, especially in the summer months when we're seeing it more rampant?

a.t: I think we will consider any proposal that we believe to be helpful to both public health and awareness of public health. What I will say is that we've also had a Health Department that has had a number of town halls, press availabilities [and a] presence physically on the streets as well. I recall, in fact, speaking to the health commissioner over the holiday weekend, which is when this began, and asking that we do everything that we can. And this was his vision to ensure that we were physically present at that time — to be there. And also, as you said, to the website as well as in any of these press availabilities, but we will always consider anything that we can do that can further that guidance, and I'll just pass it over to the commissioner on the first question.

So, transparency has been a key focus throughout this whole investigation. And you've seen our administration be more transparent than any other administration with regard to handling this cluster. Let me explain that. So, in the past, we would only release the names of the cooling towers that were bacterial-culture positive. What we decided to do this time was to expedite the whole process, because the culture-positive step takes two weeks. New Yorkers don't have time to wait for two weeks.

And so, we decided to make the decision of releasing the names of the towers and the addresses at the PCR-positive step, which is a much quicker test to get back. We're committed to identifying every single way that we can be more transparent. And so, I'll speak to the mayor's point and then come back to what you mentioned about the speaker. We are eager to identify ways to push nation-leading Legionella laws even further to keep New Yorkers safe.

q.t: I just wanted to follow up on Melissa's question about why Netanyahu specifically is often targeted in some of your comments. For example, Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro, was arrested for a warrant that was here in the U.S. And you were very against that. So, I guess how do you — do you place more emphasis on the warrants that were issued by the International Criminal Court than here in U.S.? How do you reconcile those two?

a.t:
I would say that the International Criminal Court is a body that seeks to hold those across the world accountable for crimes against humanity, for war crimes [and] for things of that nature. And I think that the United States should not only be a party to that court but should also execute the warrants that that court issues. And what I have spoken up about, Nicolás Maduro, who I've also described appropriately as a dictator, is that the violation of international law is one that has to also be taken very seriously.

It stems from the same belief in the International Criminal Court, and now he is here in New York City. On that day when the United States did violate international law, I made clear that I was in opposition to that, and it all stems from the same belief in how can there be a sanctity and something beyond an understanding of the world where might is right and justice is simply decided by those who are the strongest.

q.t: A two-fold question: How do you respond to the critics that say that you're trying to create a one-sided narrative of the conflict that many Jewish New Yorkers reject about October 7, the Gaza War and using the Mayor's Office to do that? And second, do you also consider October 7 [inaudible] genocide?

a.t:
I consider October 7 to be a horrific war crime. I've considered it to be something that should be deeply opposed with every single fiber of our being. And what I would also say is what brings me to my conclusions about Israel and Palestine, about the world beyond, is a belief in the universality of humanity. And what universality means is that we cannot pick and choose which crimes against humanity we oppose. We must be in opposition to all of them. And I think that, you know, to the earlier question of which ICC warrant would you honor, it has to be all of them. And I think that the other point to be made clear here is that I'm the mayor of every New Yorker, and that means that I am the mayor of those who agree with me and those who disagree with me and those who frankly don't even know what I think on any issue.

And my responsibility is to deliver for all of those. And frankly, I know that there are Jewish New Yorkers who agree with my analysis, there are those who disagree with my analysis and my responsibility to them is to ensure that they are cherished, they are celebrated and they are safe in their city. And that never are they made to feel as if their opinions on any one issue is the precondition for that safety.

q.t: My first question?

a.t: [To] your first question, to that, I always want to make sure that as the mayor, regardless of what others opine, we do a thorough review internally before coming to a decision.[Crosstalk.]

q.t: Again, I wanted to stay on the same topic about Netanyahu. The United States doesn't recognize ICC warrants, so I'm wondering how much of this due diligence was always meant to be failed? Do you feel like this review was, for some people would say, political theater? And then I want to go back to the idea of Legionella and what the speaker said in her op-ed in the New York Post. Do you think some of the points she made were valid, or do you feel like she's taking aim and using this particular issue for political advantage?

a.t: I'll leave it to New Yorkers to make that determination. What I'll say is that my focus is on the public health of it all. And every conversation that I've had with our commissioner [and] with our deputy mayor has always been: How can we deliver for New Yorkers right now, those who are living in the Upper East Side, those [who] are fearful of contracting Legionnaires’, as well as those who have contracted Legionnaires. And what we've done time and time again is follow public health experts and their advice. And that is something that we will continue to do. Because we've seen what it looks like when public health is politicized across the country. We want this to be a city where it's clear that the guidance, the actions [and] the information that we share with New Yorkers, [are] done without any political incentive in mind, but rather with a public health incentive in mind.

q.t: I just want to follow up. Can you tap into the disappointment that people in the Palestinian community feel that you're not going to be able to arrest them, and are you urging them to protest?

a.t: I'm simply saying that this is a city where — if anyone feels a level of frustration or opposition, protest is something that we will always respect. I leave it to New Yorkers themselves to make that decision. And when it comes to Palestinian New Yorkers who are disappointed, I understand it. Because we are talking about someone who has been charged with crimes against humanity. Someone who has visited this city on many an occasion and who has been welcomed by previous mayors. And I want to make it very clear that that welcome ends with me. I will not be welcoming Benjamin Netanyahu or any other war criminals when they come to this city, and I do believe that our federal government should join the International Criminal Court and ensure that there is accountability when it comes to crimes against humanity.

q.t: Mr. Mayor, I'd like to approach the Netanyahu issue from a different direction. I wonder what you would say to your Palestinian supporters and others who voted for you because of your vow to arrest Benjamin Netanyah. And are disappointed with the fact that you can't do it. Some of whom have taken to social media, saying, “Arrest him anyway, because ICE doesn't ask for permission that you should just do it.” And also, the second part of the question is, what do you think that these people who were frustrated with Netanyahu should do when he arrives in New York City for the United Nations meeting?

a.t:
I think one of the bedrocks of our city is protest. It is something that has been a part of what makes our city so special: that New Yorkers can express themselves, whether they are in support or in opposition, no matter [the] topic. And I've always said that when we respect our Constitution, we also respect our First Amendment. And here in New York City, it'll always be a place where you can exercise that. And when it comes to the first question, you know, I have made clear both that I believe that this is an arrest warrant that should be executed.

And also, that I would follow the laws that we had and I would be respectful of those laws, and that is why I asked my administration to review of all applicable law, and I believe, however, in that same finding that the United States government does have the ability to both joining the International Criminal Court and execute that warrant, and that is something that I want to see happen.

q.t: I see, you know, appointing someone from McKinsey and someone like Lina Khan with her background seems like a bit of an odd couple. I'm wondering where you see their views on economic justice actually lining up, and I'm wondering if you're concerned that the agency could be in for a bit of a bumpy ride if these two can't sort of meld their worldviews.

a.t:
Well, I think what you'll actually find is that both Lina’s and Tony’s worldviews are aligned in looking to uplift working New Yorkers across the city and in understanding that we must also measure the economic strength of the city by whether it is able to lift up those who are currently being priced out of the city. And what I've seen even now in the incredible work of the civil servants we have at EDC is that there are so many who are currently there who are dedicated to this new vision. And I'm confident that in both of their appointments, what we're going to see is not only shared alignment, but also the execution of a vision that will have real tangible results for New Yorkers.

[Crosstalk.]

q.t: Did they specifically tell you this was not possible?

a.t: That's a review that I asked them to do. They made it clear that this is not possible through applicable law, and that is something that I now believe is clear: that the federal government has the authority to do and that they can execute.

q.t:
In terms of the Netanyahu decision last night, why did you decide to address the public in that way? Because that's usually reserved for much more serious situations. And in relation to Netanyahu as well, when exactly did your administration tell you that this was not possible? Because when you floated this idea last year, legal experts all came out and said, “This is not a possible thing that the city can do.”

[Crosstalk.]

a.t:
Jeff, you said that usually that kind of address is reserved for a more serious topic. Yesterday, I was on Staten Island for a meeting with faith leaders, and a young man from Gaza attended that meeting as part of an organization that houses refugees on Staten Island. He did not have one of his arms. He was one of the many children that have been maimed by this genocide. I think that is quite serious. I think there are tens of thousands. I do not think; I know. There are tens of thousands of children who have been maimed, who have been forced to undergo operations without anesthesia. And when we speak about the more than 70,000 Palestinians that have been killed. We know that likely that number is even higher, and yet we do not even know what it reaches. And also, we know that it is not a faraway issue.

I have met Palestinian New Yorkers who have told me how they've spent decades in this city building their lives, saving money to send it back home to build a home in the village they grew up in only to see it obliterated in an instant with an Israeli airstrike. And then that same older New Yorker tells me of how his son called him and begged him to send him money for food, that his grandchild was starving, and that he couldn't do anything about it. And so, I say that this is something that has not only offended the conscience, the morals [and] the mere humanity of so many New Yorkers, but it has also ripped apart the lives of many who've been personally affected by it as well. And I view that as a very serious issue. And I think that it is incredibly important that we ensure that we have done all of our due diligence when conducting a review. And so, I wanted to ensure that no matter what we heard from anyone on the topic, that I actually asked my team to do that. I'm appreciative of their work.

q.t: [Inaudible]. You've been in office for six months, and you talk about promising to arrest the prime minister on the campaign. [Inaudible], I remember hearing you say it. Why did you not want to provide an answer to this question earlier than you did? Did you forget to look into the legality of it until it came up in this New York Times interview over the weekend? Why did you not make a [inaudible] determination on it?

a.t: I've been very clear about the fact that I believe that the warrant that the International Criminal Court has placed upon Benjamin Netanyahu is one that should be honored. And I've also been clear about that fact that I would follow and respect our local laws. And so, I asked my team to do a review of all applicable law, and it's clear that the city does not have the authority to execute this warrant. However, what is also clear is that the federal government does have the opportunity to execute this warrant. And I call on the federal government to join the International Criminal Court and to execute both this warrant as well as any warrant that the International Criminal Court holds.

q.t: [Inaudible] fines for building owners. Have there been [any] Legionella-related fines since the Council laws [inaudible] or were you talking about fines prior to this?

a.t: So, the 2025 cooling tower fines and violations totaled over $600,000 in terms of all of the cooling tower operators that were not compliant with the law, so that was a 2025 number. And so, we have just begun the implementation and the promulgation of this new law in May, and what we see from the data is actually the vast majority of cooling tower operators have been compliant, giving us the information that we need, which is good and we expect that, by the way. Now, for the groups that have not been, it's a couple reasons; some of them have not gotten a cooling tower operational yet. So, their cooling tower has not been operational, and for the ones that have a cooling tower that is operational and have not given us the required information. Of course, there are consequences and there are fines.

q.t: It seems to me that if 34 of the towers came back as having had live Legionella, that seemed to me, and according to some people I've spoken to, to be higher than what we anticipated. We thought maybe a small number would have come back positive. So, separately, what does that tell you about whether or not the procedures in place already, to try to prevent live Legionella bacteria in these cooling towers are working? Where’s the breakdown that so many of these towers on the Upper East Side were problematic?

a.t:
So, first of all, this bacteria is ubiquitous. It is everywhere. It is found in nature commonly. And to give you a sense of how common it is, when we looked at the data for last year's Harlem cluster, we had 12 of the 47 towers in that case that had live Legionella bacteria. So that's the first piece. These numbers are not out of what we've seen in the past. And in fact, the overall rate of Legionella bacteria in these cooling towers has decreased over time because the enforcement is working.

Now, in terms of enforcement, let's talk about that. So, over the course of the last year, we've issued countless violations. Just in the last years, [there have been] 1,300 violations to cooling tower operators and owners. And this amounts to hundreds of thousands of dollars and finds. And the reality is that, you know, our job is to enforce this law and to make sure that we hold cooling tower operators who are not following the law accountable to the full extent of the law. And that's what we're going to do here once we identify which tower or towers are responsible.

I'll just add one thing to what the commissioner said, and I also want to acknowledge the deputy mayor who's here, who's been overseeing a lot of this work. We will not rest until each and every New Yorker is living [with] the public health that they deserve. And that means not only continuing to address this cluster but doing the work after this point to ensure that what has become an annual event in New York City is one that we are developing far enhanced processes for. Because what we've found over the course of this process itself is that there are so many more procedures that the city had been taking years prior that, in fact, could be expedited.

And I want to credit our Health Department and the leaders that are here on this stage for having taken that decision time and again, and we also know that while we are able to stand here and tell New Yorkers of the fact that no new symptoms have been developed for anyone in the last 10 days, [and] that we are confident we have found the source. We know that there are still New Yorkers who are in [the] hospital as a result of this cluster, and so we will continue to do this work and also continue to monitor this.

q.t: And what is your response to the criticisms that were raised by Council Speaker Julie Menin on the Legionnaires' situation. And specifically given the fact that so many cooling towers turned out to have had live Legionella bacteria and then maybe more than we expected came back positive for live Legionella. With the benefit now of hindsight does that suggest in any way that blanket disinfecting might have made sense in retrospect?

a.t:
So, I'm frankly less interested in the politics of it all, more in the public health of it. And what I will say is that previous administration procedure had been that we would wait for the results of culture. And that would mean two weeks. We made the decision to do both culture tests and PCR tests. So that meant that we could actually test immediately, disinfect any of the cooling towers that came back, and then additionally, wait for the culture results. As you've mentioned, there are four additional culture results that came back positive beyond the PCRs. And the other point here is that we know that Legionnaires' is something that has affected our city over many, many years.

And we are both trying to stop this cluster in the moment and ensure that we are not weakening our ability to stop it in the future. And when I sat with public health experts, what I was told time and again is that if we were to do a blanket disinfectant of every single cooling tower across the Upper East Side, that would weaken those cooling towers' ability to protect against Legionnaires in the years to come. And so, we want to make sure that everything we're doing gives people both the safety and the public health they deserve and the confidence that this isn't going to be something that returns. I'm going to pass it over to our commissioner to add some details.

Thanks, Mr. Mayor. So, we'll talk about Speaker Menin and the investigation. But first, let's talk about the people. Five New Yorkers have lost their lives because of this disease, and our hearts are with their families and their loved ones. Every single one of those deaths for us underscores the importance of identifying the source and eliminating the source that caused this investigation in the first place. So now turning to the investigation, the good news is we are in a very reassuring position. We feel confident that we've eliminated that source. You know, when we look at the data, the data demonstrates that the last new diagnosis of Legionnaires’ disease was on July 15th, so about a week ago, as you heard the mayor say.

And then in terms of the last person to develop symptoms, they did so over a week ago, over 10 days ago. And so, we feel fairly confident. When you also add in the emergency room data, you're not seeing any concerning spikes or signals. Our focus has been and continues to be on accountability, accountability — identifying the cooling tower owner or owners that [are] at the source of this and holding them accountable to the full extent of [the] law. Now turning to Speaker Menin's point, here's what would happen if we blanket disinfected.

Number one, as you've heard from the mayor, every time we do this biocide treatment, it actually does degrade the cooling towers and thus, in the future, allows them to potentially harbor more Legionella bacteria. Now, it's always about finding the right sort of happy medium, but that's the first. The second is, had we blanket disinfected from the beginning, we wouldn't be able to actually get the samples. And we need the samples to know what caused this, and then that will give us an opportunity to learn.

q.t: I mean, I know he's dead.

a.t:
Yes, but my point is that they did. And in the video, I made very clear, as I have before, that my interest in executing that warrant is not specific to Benjamin Netanyahu, but to anyone who they put a warrant towards for war crimes and crimes against humanity. And part of that is a reflection of a universal politics, and it is from a universal politics that I can look [at] October 7 and describe it for what it is, which is a horrific war crime. And I can also look at Benjamin Netanyahu and see the way that he has orchestrated this genocide and also deem him to similarly be a war criminal.

And I think especially at a time when there are those in Washington who are discussing measures to take apart the International Criminal Court, what so many are looking for is a sense that there is, in fact, a rule of law across the world where there are crimes that are so grave that they offend all of humanity. And I believe that we should hold those who perpetrate them accountable, no matter who they are or where they're from. And when it comes to the ICC, they've put forward warrants, whether it's Yahya Sinwar, Benjamin Netanyahu, I think a few other members of the Israeli government. I believe all of them should be honored.

q.t:
Some Jewish groups have noted that in your video you didn't include a reference to October 7 or Hamas leaders who carried out that attack. And it's not easy always to pin you down on this subject, forgive me, because there aren't many perfect analogies to draw. For instance, not all world leaders or alleged war criminals have ICC warrants, or they're not planning to come to the UN General Assembly, or perhaps they're dead.

So, my question is would you, if circumstances were different, would you have vowed to arrest the leaders of Hamas, who perpetrated the October 7 attack, if they were visiting New York? And if so, why not include something about that to show New Yorkers that you're presenting a more balanced approach? Why not include that in your video?

a.t: Didn't the ICC put forward a warrant for Yahya Sinwar?

q.t: The question that we have for you or for the new president is about the affordable housing insurance program, something that the EDC is going to oversee in conjunction with HPD and HDC. The RFP or RFEI is already out there. What are you looking for in that program, and what kind of goals are you going to achieve in terms of providing affordable housing to providers? [Inaudible.]

a.t: You know, we are incredibly excited by this program. It's a program where we are putting $100 million over a few years to address what has been described to us by affordable housing stewards as one of the most difficult rising costs that they have to deal with at this time, which is that of insurance. I've heard from a number of landlords of affordable housing that this is something that is rising by more than 100 percent in their own estimates. And what we've seen, I think in the example, though Leila might correct me, I think it's Milford Street Captive, is an example of what it can look like when you are pooling risk and actually able to provide insurance at a cost that not only reflects what that risk is but also is one that allows these landlords to continue to do business. So, I would say the prevailing directive with this entire process is how to deliver lower cost insurance for landlords who are currently being priced out of the market because of the manner in which the cost-of-living crisis is hitting them.

q.t: I'm going to turn it back to Max's question. The mayor agreed with the premise of Max's question that the EDC has operated as concierge service for wealthy [inaudible].

a.t: So, let me just first state this very clearly: What I agreed with was the citation of what the EDC has in the past helped to develop across our city. And the fact that what we are looking to develop goes beyond those examples and in fact typifies a new kind of approach. But I'll pass it over to Tony.

Look, this agency has a long history. Thirty five years since Carl Weisbrod started it a long time ago. There are projects in that history that I think today we wouldn't do or would do differently. And every mayor chooses a different way to implement their agenda. That's what the Swiss Army knife is for. Policies made in this building. I felt that when I used to work in this building and I'll feel that now. So, the direction, the vision, is going to be a mayor's vision, and my guess is that may change some of the direction of EDC. I’m certain that's true — exactly how and with which projects, TBD.

But I don't think there's any question there's also been some wonderful things that EDC has done that I think there should be a lot of pride. And there's a lot of people working in New York because of things EDC have done. So, it's a mixed portfolio and frankly, every administration comes to build on the work of the administrations before, and this one will too. So, I'm pretty confident we'll have our own direction following a vision laid out and supported by many, many New Yorkers.

q.t: Is this something you’re going to lobby for in Albany, though, with state lawmakers?

a.t: It's not really EDC's job to do that. We're not lobbyists for individual wage attacks or wage actions. It's really not our focus. Will we work with the business community and help them work their way through and understand our positions and be supportive of it, hopefully? Sure. That's part of my goal. But we're not really the Albany office. City Hall has very strong capacity to deal with that. They don't need my voice. But if they call on it, I’ll be there.

q.t: Tony, I was just wondering if you support raising taxes on businesses and if that's something you're going to go in Albany forward to state lawmakers, if that something you are going to push. And then separately, I also was wondering if support raising the minimum wage and what your thoughts are on that as well.

a.t: I have long been a strong supporter of raising the minimum wage. We fought pretty hard for it the last time I was in this building, and that's part of the reason we achieved a $15 minimum wage, which at the time was a great step forward and was part of the reason that we moved 800,000 people out of poverty and near poverty. It was one of the biggest reasons, along with pre-K, along with the rent freeze. I think there's opportunity to do more of that. Policy on those issues is made in this building, not in that building. So obviously [I’ll] be deferring to the crowd behind me on that. But as a personal matter, I do strongly believe that raising the minimum wage can be a very important tool. It was one of the elements of the mayor's platform. So how, when, under what circumstances, at what pace — all TBD. And obviously it's not the city's choice; it's the state's choice. So, obviously I'm going to leave that to others. But if you ask me in general, do I believe the minimum in America is too low? And then New York is too low? Yes.

q.t: [Inaudible] to find somebody that would approach the job in the way you were looking at them.

a.t: I think that we actually had far more people than we had the time to interview in terms of a willingness to approach this job in the manner that we'd hoped for. However, we always wanted to ensure that we were fully confident in who we were picking and that's where we found ourselves with Tony.

q.t: I wanted to ask you about the length of time it took you to find somebody to fill the president CEO role. How much of the change in the approach to this job factored into finding someone? Do you find candidates were resistant to the idea of equal focus on economic development and economic justice? And also, I heard you were down to two candidates right to the end. Is that the case? And who was it?

a.t: What I will say is that we have long considered this to be a critical position in our administration. And we wanted to make sure that the way that we treated this process was also with the seriousness and the depth that this position requires, both in the fluency that it demands of someone and the imagination required to go beyond what historical precedent has seen when it comes to what this agency does. And we're talking about interviews that we've had over many months with incredible candidates, and what I can say is that Tony has long stood out to me as someone who both characterizes what is possible in City government and also the fluency required to get things done by having worked in a wide variety of positions both inside and outside of city government.

q.t: This administration, as you mentioned, is elected with a mandate to steer city initiatives towards working people. But the EDC in the past has been at times used as a somewhat unaccountable sinecure for the real estate class and developers. They built Casa Cipriani, which many of us have not had the pleasure to go to. They built the infrastructure for a stadium owned by literal monarchs. Can you give examples, maybe beyond the groceries or pilot, of how you're going to direct this agency or development corporation towards working people in New York City to make it more affordable, especially if it's currently geared in kind of a different direction right now?

a.t: You know, I think there was a moment during the course of the campaign where the EDC was described to me as the Swiss Army knife of City government. It is one of the most nimble and agile departments that the city has, and much of its agenda is a reflection of the administration's agenda at large. Yes, the EDC has been those things, and the EDC is also where we have the New York City ferry system. And it speaks to — even before I go further into this question, I do also just want to acknowledge that those that we have at the EDC today — Jeanny Pak as well — I really want to acknowledge their incredible work over these past six months. It is thanks to them that Tony is stepping into a role, not having to build all of this from the ground up. In fact, what he is inheriting is an intensive amount of preparation toward city-run grocery stores that showcases what is possible when the capacity of a corporation like EDC is matched with a vision that is measuring its success by whether it is reaching to address the problems of working New Yorkers. So, I think that there are a wide variety of examples, and what I see in Tony and what I see in Lina are two excellent public servants who understand both the ambition that has often characterized EDC and what a new era for EDC could look like.

q.t: The first, I guess, is for you and for Tony. So earlier in the year, you boasted about canceling a contract DSS had with McKinsey as an example of you rooting out government waste. I don't know if — Tony, if you were working on this specific contract, and if you want to speak about how McKinsey’s role, how McKinsey plays a role, and I know this economic justice, I know a lot of the stuff they do, Tony hasn't been a part of, but there's a litany of things that don't seem aligned with you. And my second question, it is on topic, because yeah, he mentioned it. Department of Health does not have enough water inspectors to inspect for Legionnaires' disease. They can’t inspect Legionella; that's due to a number of factors. What have you done as mayor to speed up the hiring? It could take months to hire people when the lines have been approved. I know hiring people to the city was a big part of your transition, but what have you actually done to speed that up, not just to the Department of Health, but to make it an easier process so there could be more water inspectors to actually inspect for this?

a.t:
So, I'll go with the first question, then I'll go to the second question. I think on the first, as you know, we have been focused on cost-saving measures across City government, and I think that it does save money when you take the top talent from McKinsey instead of having to employ them for a contract. But in all seriousness, what I see in Tony is a breadth of experience that, as you've heard from Deputy Mayor Su, is experience that also looks at what the benefits are of insourcing and building public capacity at a time when outsourcing was all the vogue of how we could actually improve efficiency, and also a breadth of ambition. And sometimes the way it is caricatured is the more experience you have in City government, the less ambition you have for what city government can do. And one of the things that really stuck with me on that morning when we had breakfast at that diner was not only his willingness to speak to a candidate who at that point was still, were still a ways to go in that primary, but also the real sense of possibility of what City government could still offer and what we could bring together as a new administration to connect with the ideals that make the city what it is. And to your second question, I'm also going to invite our commissioner to just come up and join me.

[Crosstalk.]
Yes, I did spend some time on that contract early on. Most of my work in McKinsey is for government, nonprofit and pro bono work. That was part of the government work that McKinsey did.

And to the question about hiring as a whole, one of the first things that we did when we came into City Hall was looking at what the obstacles were in hiring. And one of them was a directive given to OMB of two for one of in making it impossible for agencies to actually hire unless they had a specific number of vacancies that were being created at the same agency. And while we were still pursuing and continue to pursue savings, we also wanted to take away the unnecessary roadblocks in how those hires could actually happen. That work both continues, though we have already implemented that, but looking to speed this up. And when it comes specifically to the ecologist that you were speaking of, we have also seen a number of those hires over the course of these last few months. I'll pass it over to our health commissioner.

a.s: Alister Martin, Commissioner, Department of Health and Hygiene
a.t:
So, first of all, let me just say a few words about our team. I'm proud of our team. They've run an incredible investigation and have been nonstop from the first moment we found out about this. With regard to the new hires that came in, the majority of those folks are either onboarded or matriculating in. In fact, on the first weekend that this happened, where we identified these first two cases, I myself was out there in the Upper East Side with some of those new hires. And so, for the remaining positions, we're eager to hire and onboard those folks and have them hit the streets with the rest of our really incredible staff. So, thank you.

[Crosstalk.]

q.t: [Inaudible] what the mayor has said?

a.t: Yes, I mean, we're still working — we only have two, I think, so far. And I think we're working on the other three now. On the broader issue of partnership, as the mayor mentioned, I don't believe there are permanent adversaries and permanent allies. I've been around too long for that. I do think there are those in the business community who support a lot of what this mayor is trying to do. And I don't mean just business leaders, I mean people working across the city who support — and a lot them voted for this mayor. So, I think the breadth of support for the particular agenda is there, but I do think the support for the city’s success is even broader, if not universal. So, I think finding ways for us to sit down, laying out the agenda that we have, making very clear the values that this mayor and the people who supported him and all of us in this administration believe; and how those values intersect with the objectives that businesses have, which is to grow and employ people and be successful. Those are not — as Julie said, multiple times — those are not in conflict, they can be in confluence. But it takes work and it takes understanding on both sides. And I think the foundation of that is mutual respect. And I certainly will respect some of the views that some of these leaders may have even when they differ, and I expect that they will respect the views of a mayor who represents so many New Yorkers.

I'll just say the business community in New York City is vast. It spans the independent pharmacist, to the Fortune 500 company, to the scrappy startup seeking investment, to the bodega. And one thing I was so proud of my time in the FTC is making sure that all market participants in all businesses were really having an opportunity to engage with their government, and I'm excited for the same to be true at EDC.

q.t: My question is, I guess, to start, for both Tony and Lina, how do you see the EDC's relationship with business now that you've been appointed? Are you looking to grow those relationships and obviously bring business back to the city? I also wanted to ask about city-run grocery stores. Is that going to be a top priority? I know that’s something that the mayor has already tasked the agency with.

a.t: So, on the second one, yes, for sure it is a top priority. The mayor made that clear actually during the campaign.
