q.t: So as a man born outside of America, when you came here, did sport give you a belonging immediately?

a.t: Absolutely. I mean, initially my sport was chess.

q.t: Depends on [who] your perspectives are, I'll be honest with you. But anyhow, I'll bring these two with their Arsenal connections in a moment and has what the Knicks did and maybe even what you saw with Arsenal and how it affected London. Has that changed your perspective of where you put sport in your list of priorities as a politician?

a.t:
I think it's shown us the intangible value of this game, one that sometimes is derided as if it's a distraction. It is a cornerstone of how people understand themselves in the world around. And, you know, you're asking me questions about New York City. Eight and a half million people live in New York City. And in the largest city in the United States of America, it can also feel quite lonely sometimes for people. It can feel as if they're alienated from those around them.

And these are moments that bring people together. And I'll tell you that for me, just individually, before I was the mayor, sports have just always been such a way that I've understood who I am, what I believe in [and] how I build my day. And I think that part of fighting back against the commodification of sport, the insistence that it becomes yet another luxury product, is also a recognition of what it provides so many people, not just in those 90 minutes or, you know, additional time. But frankly, even what it represents to so many more.

q.t: You are a genuine New York Knicks fan. You're a genuine Arsenal fan as well, which I will come on to in a moment.

a.t: It's been a good year.

q.t:
Look to the UK audience. They may not know a great deal about basketball,

and we've talked about it a fair bit since we've been here. Okay, because it is such a massive story. And it doesn't matter if you know basketball or not. Anybody who supports a team to end a 53-year drought for something, everybody knows what that means. What have you noticed [that] has changed about this city because of a sports team winning as the mayor?

a.t:
It feels like the Knicks transformed the biggest city in the country into the smallest town in the world. It feels like they created a fabric that connects all of us. And it didn't matter whether you've been watching this team for decades or you just started watching it in the final games. But everybody was living and breathing this team. And it felt as if time stopped when the games began. And the beautiful thing was some of it was organized [and] some of it was beautifully unorganized.

You know, we would watch – you'd go out and you'd watch the game at a bar, or you'd be in a backyard or at a friend's place. There'd be people who'd just be broadcasting the game on the wall across the street. And I think it just spoke to this energy that this team gave this entire city and the fact that the city could look at the team and see themselves, not just in the players. You know, Jose Alvarado grew up in New York City in public housing and is a son of Brooklyn and Queens, but also in the way that the team played. They really embodied the spirit of the city.

q.t: So, what are they? Sorry, when you say "kiosks," what are they?

a.t: When you're walking around New York City, you'll see these-kind-of-larger kiosks on a number of sidewalks, and you'll see [they'll] give you the weather; there'll be different updates [and] sometimes there are advertisements. And what we started doing with the Knicks is broadcasting the game on those kiosks. So, you could just be walking around the city, and you can catch the game and we're going to be doing that tonight as well for USA.

q.t: Do you notice a difference in this city because of how they have started? Or is it not irrelevant how they have started, but very much below still what the Knicks did?

a.t: It's hard to compare anything to the Knicks. You know, we waited 53 years to win that championship. I will say that it does feel like New Yorkers have an extra spring in our step. And, you know, tonight we're very excited because we're going to be broadcasting the USA [vs.] Türkiye game on a number of kiosks that we have around New York City – LinkNYC kiosks.

q.t: The mayor of New York City, Zohran Mandani, is with us. We were just talking about the positive effect of the USA – first of all – and their start to this World Cup. What have you made of that?

a.t: It's been incredible. First of all, it's great to be here.
Thank you for joining us.

Thank you for having me. Thank you for being in our beautiful city. And the start that the US Men's National Team has had, it's given everyone just a sense of real excitement. We always hope and pray for the host nation's bump. But what we've seen from these first two games [is] that tonight is not a decider, but rather an option to see more players. That's more than we could ever ask for.

q.t: I'm wondering if you can build off of all of these primary questions. You obviously said there needs to be change within the Democratic Party. You saw this play out for the candidates that you endorsed last night. Do you see yourself looking into more national races, speaking out to maybe mayors or governors in other states where you see that change could be influenced? And do you see yourself getting involved in national politics that way?

a.t:
I'll say that I've had conversations with other mayors, with other leaders across the country over the course of the time that I've had the privilege of being the mayor of our city. My focus has been on ensuring that our city is one where we see partners at every level of government in enacting this affordability agenda. And I've also said before that the struggle for a working person — it's not unique to our city. Working people are struggling across the country. 

And part of my hope in working to elect these congresspeople, these state legislators, is also to help write a new chapter in our party's history, where working people are back at the heart of that struggle. And I believe that that will be key in not just the midterms coming up in November, but also in the years to come where Americans will be asking themselves: “Is this a party that is willing to go beyond just standing up to the cruelty of the federal administration, but also a party that's willing to stand up for a vision that looks at the struggles that working people are living through and actually addresses it with ways that it can make their lives easier”? Thank you so much.

q.t: I'm just curious, going back to the primaries, are you worried at all that Darializa’s election might complicate campaigns for Democrats as a whole, not including, as we talked about earlier, with Republicans attacking, but just campaigns in more moderate districts?

a.t:
No. I believe that Darializa’s campaign — which was built on a politics of life, on a vision of babies, not bombs, on a call to abolish ICE — is one that is in line with what many working people want across this country. And I think that you will be hard-pressed to find someone who believes that the status quo is serving them today. 

And what Darializa offers — alongside Claire, alongside Brad, alongside every one of the five state legislative candidates that also prevailed yesterday evening — is a vision for a new kind of politics, one that asks: “What can we stand for beyond just standing up to the cruelty of the federal government”?

q.t: Just a really quick second question. Moving off of the primaries, I know news broke this morning that the NYPD and the FBI had served a series of warrants looking into the ongoing corruption investigation of the Police Department. I just wanted to ask you your reaction to that.

a.t: Our government should serve the public with integrity. Any corruption would amount to a serious violation of the responsibility within the NYPD and a breach in public trust. As Commissioner Tisch said earlier today, this is an investigation that the NYPD is conducting with the FBI and the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of New York. Commissioner Tisch has already shown a real commitment to cracking down on corruption and ensuring that the public servants in the NYPD are held to the highest standards. I'm confident that she will lead us through this process.

q.t: I just wanted to ask, after the success both you and the candidates you supported saw yesterday, do you plan to throw your weight behind other races in the future?

a.t: I can tell you that for right now, I am just reflecting on an incredible evening and incredible campaigns that have been run over the course of many, many months. However, I made a promise a year ago to New Yorkers that I would use every tool at my disposal to fulfill our affordability agenda, and electing more partners to do so is exactly one of those tools. And I will always look to ensure that we are exhausting every avenue we have to transform the nation's most expensive city into one that's affordable.

q.t: For the DSA members, they had to apologize for past social media commentary, the way they phrased things, talking about policies that didn't have anything to do with making it in the city and I wanted to get your opinion on it. Are you going to take them to [the] “Mamdani School of Politics” and avoid having their worst moments be the face of the Democratic Party in a contested midterm election around the country?

a.t: I think we can see from each of these candidates that they have exactly what it takes to succeed and we've heard from Republicans time and again, that they're going to try and make these candidates the face of the Democratic Party. To them, I say that we are ready for that, because for far too long we have been told that it is not possible to fight for working people and win. These candidates have shown that they can. Let the Republicans talk about that more.

q.t: I'm looking at the results from the New York Times and Avila Chevalier, just for instance, overwhelmingly won precincts with younger voters, college-educated precincts, higher-income areas and she lost, though more narrowly, low-income areas, majority Black precincts [and] majority Hispanic precincts. Why is that? And why does the message of your democratic socialists seem to not prevail when actual public housing residents, actual low-income New Yorkers get a chance to vote?

a.t: I haven't dug into the granular details of yesterday evening's results as yet. What I will say, though, is what we've found time and again is that a message of fighting for working people is one that resonates. I stand here as a mayor who received more than a million votes when I ran to hold this position, and I know that whether we're speaking of Darializa, we're speaking of Claire, we're speaking of Brad or we're speaking of any one of the five candidates who ran for state legislature that I endorsed, there was a connection with not just enough voters to eke out a victory but in many of those cases, enough voters to create a mandate.

q.t: [Inaudible.] Are you now moving full forward with tax the rich?

a.t: I've been clear about the policies that I hold. I've also been honest with New Yorkers about what I believe is necessary to deliver on that affordability. And I'm proud to be standing here speaking about 2-K, which is only possible because of the partnership we have with Governor Hochul, [and] I look forward to that partnership continuing.

q.t: My second question is I'm wondering, you know, you had some congressional victories but also some state victories last night. I'm wondering how you think those victories will help realize your agenda in Albany and have you had a conversation with those winners about your new agenda in Albany? And I'm wondering, do you think this also shifts the sort of balance of power between yourself and the governor to have an additional number of socialists now in office?

a.t:
I'm incredibly excited to have endorsed eight candidates, five at the state level, three at the federal level, and to have seen every single one of those candidates win last night. And what their successes represent is a shift in the balance of power between working people and special interests. And finally, working people are going to have more of a voice in the halls of power wherever that hall may be, be it Albany or be it in D.C. 

And I'm excited because a year ago today I was elected as the Democratic nominee with a message of focusing on making life in this city more affordable. And in each of these candidates I see partners in that work. Whether we're speaking about Eli Northrup, who will now be the state Assembly member for the district that I grew up in, or we're speaking about Claire Valdez, who will be the congresswoman of the neighborhood I used to live in before I became the mayor, we're going to see people who understand working people as their compass and who understand the results that those working people want to see.

q.t: Two questions for you about the races last night. I'm wondering if the victories show that communities are open to DSA's messaging, but I'm wondering; we've already seen from some Republican candidates how they plan to message the victories last night, sort of going out and saying that Democrats are interested in these severe sorts of stances, such as incarceration and no deportation. So, I'm wondering if you're concerned about whether that victory — how that will play in November as Democrats try to win back the House. And I have a second question.

a.t:
You know, every time the fight for working people takes a step forward, you will hear Republicans say that this is actually going to jeopardize the existence of that very fight. A year ago, when I won the Democratic nomination to be the mayor of our city, we heard ad nauseum from Republicans not just across our city but across the country of how this was going to make it more difficult for working people to live a life that they could afford. And what we found time and time again is no matter what attempts there are at mischaracterizing any one position or policy, what is shining through for New Yorkers and for Americans is a focus on the working person. And when I walked the streets with Claire, with Brad [and] with Darializa, what we spoke to New Yorkers about was how we could make it easier for them to afford childcare, for them to afford their rent check, for them to afford to live in the district that they grew up in. 

The other night I was walking with Darializa in Harlem, a man came out of a bodega and in his hands, he had Huggies. He had two packages of Huggies and he was heading home. And she often speaks about a politics of life. She speaks about babies, not bombs. What could be a better example of what the people of the district want to see versus what the people of the district have been forced to experience, which is tens of billions of dollars being spent at a national level to bomb children overseas while children in our own districts are struggling.

q.t: Responding to last night's election results, President Trump said that “America the beautiful will never become a communist country.” We know you have said you're not a communist. However, do you hope that America — is it your goal to make America a socialist country?

a.t: My goal is to make America a place that every American can afford. And frankly what we see is while that is an especially challenging goal here in New York City, the nation's most expensive city, I know it's an issue that every working person across the country is facing. And what we need is a politics that puts working people back at the heart of what we focus on and what we fight for as opposed to making them a footnote.

q.t: Gloria touched on a little bit of what I was going to ask, but your chosen candidates will now likely cause the number of socialists in the House to rise from — to double from two to four at least, I believe the number is. But what are two specific examples of federal policies that they could change with their votes, given that we're talking about four socialists?

a.t:
I think what we can see in their candidacies and what we will see in their leadership is a commitment to humanity. And when it comes to domestic policy, I know that for many of them, one clear area of concern is the cruelty of ICE. You've heard from a number of — not just the candidates who became congresspeople last night, but rather candidates across the country — the need to abolish ICE. It's something that I've echoed myself. And when I think about Darializa 's campaign — one part of her track record that stuck out for so many in that district and stuck out for me was a track record of speaking up for New Yorkers who had been unjustly detained by ICE and starting to create an immigration policy in this country that has humanity at the heart of it instead of the cruelty. 

And then when she speaks about babies, not bombs — when Claire Valdez speaks about a foreign policy that understands human rights for all — when Brad Lander commits to co-sponsoring Block the Bombs, all of that is reflective also of a commitment to a new approach to ensuring that we're fighting for working people and that we're ensuring that every dollar that we're paying into our taxes is a dollar that also reflects our values in the way it's being spent.

q.t: We now have three potential DSA-aligned members of Congress. What do you think we should expect from those members? Is it single-payer funded health care? Is it abolishing borders? Or do you think they should be singularly focused on cutting off aid — military aid to Israel?

a.t:
What we're going to see from the three congressional candidates that I was so proud to endorse and who all won yesterday in Darializa Avila Chevalier, Claire Valdez, Brad Lander [and] as well as what we're going to see from the five state legislative candidates that I endorsed that won yesterday evening, Illapa Sairitupac, Eli Northrup, Samantha Kattan, Aber Kawas and Brian Romero, is a singular focus on the fight of the working person. 

The working person is struggling in our city to afford basic needs. And what you will see, whether it's a vision on making health care more affordable, on making housing more affordable, or on a vision — as Darializa often talks about of — investing in babies, not bombs, is the kind of conscience, the kind of clarity, the kind of conviction that has been missing in our politics for far too long. And I cannot wait to work with them on accomplishing that.

q.t: I want to ask you about the results from last night. But firstly, have you spoken to Congressman Hakeem Jeffries since last night? What would be your message to him having beaten two incumbents? And is this a personal victory for you, or do you actually see this as some sort of realignment for the Democratic Party across the country? And I do have another question, if I may.

a.t:
I'll be speaking with Congressman Jeffries later today. And I'm looking forward to working with Congressman Jeffries on delivering for the people of our city. And what I see these results as a reflection of are the fact that New Yorkers are hungry for a new kind of politics. They are hungry for a politics that understands working people should be at the heart of it. And they're hungry for a politics that looks at the wealthiest city in the wealthiest country in the history of the world and understands that it's unacceptable that one in four are living in poverty. 

It's unacceptable that too many New Yorkers are spending all of their day trying to figure out how they're going to make their rent check or pay for their groceries or pay their Con Ed bill. And what we saw last night was a hunger for leaders who will be there on the front lines looking to make it easier for working people to afford life in the greatest city in the world.

q.t: For the spirit of the day, I had this program [and] I said, one of the biggest gifts I can give to my fellow entrepreneurs, especially on the food space, is the learning that I had so I could share those. So, I started [the] Chobani Incubate program. It became one of the best programs in the country is to pick food startups, and especially in New York and across the country, [so] I thought [it is] a good idea and started with the founders that, you know — like minded — that I could bring them into the Chobani environment to show everything that I have gone through so it could help their business. And during the pandemic, it got disrupted and ended. And today I'm announcing in this event that I'm bringing Chobani Incubator back to New York City.

a.t: That's incredible. And I am proud to somehow take credit for that. Thank you all so much. It's been such a pleasure.

q.t: May I add one thing?

a.t: Please. Please. Please.

q.t:
Can I knock [on the] door and say, “Hey, I need to get this permit or this initiative?” I'm not asking you not to look at it, but can we make it faster? Can we remove the bureaucracy? Can we have one place we can get all the answers? I don't know if you have any questions?

Any thoughts on these things? But I think — how do we remove bureaucracy? How do we make this easier for businesses?

a.t:
And I think, you know, soon after the general election, I was sitting — I met a few community leaders in the Bronx, and one of them looked at me, and he had been supportive. And he looked at me and he said, “Well, now I know my permit will get approved.” I looked at him. I said, “No, no, no, brother, that's not how this works.” That's not me.

But I think the point is that for too long in politics, you have to bet on the right politician to be able to get the response that you need. What we want to do to your point, though, is be that partner so that whether or not you've ever met me [or] whether or not you ever met Jeanny, you know the city is investing in your success.

And I think that what your story also indicates is somebody who made a decision despite the headwinds; we want to make it easier for people to make that decision. And what that means is setting up a business climate that people understand. The regulations are not changing every single year. I had a conversation with a business leader who said, “Look, I can come to terms with the fact that we'll have disagreements on policy, but I just want to know what the policy is so I can build a company that can relate to that.”

And I think that that kind of stability and also a different orientation, because for a long time I've heard from small businesses especially that it feels like City government is more interested in punitive action than in ensuring compliance. You find a violation. What's the point? Is the point to bring you back into compliance or to fine you for the violation?

And so, one of the first executive orders I did was we need to catalog all of our fines and fees and figure out how we can actually reduce the cost of this and get people into compliance. And I think that that's the point is: How do we make this a quicker City government? How do we make it a more responsive City government?

How do we make it such that everyone can look at this city and say, “This is where I want to start, and this is where I want to stay”? Because what I love about your story is it doesn't just begin in New York City, it's still in New York City. Thirty years ago, you were on the train, and 30 years later, you're here.

And that's what we want. We want this to be a city where you can start, and you can continue. And I just have to say thank you so much, Hamdi.

q.t:
You have to be the best. You know, one of the best chefs comes from France, nose up in the air, and they come and they open restaurants here. And then six months later they close. It's like, well, I guess the name doesn't mean anything. No, the name could mean something. But you have to work super hard in here. And that is [one of] the things that is unbelievable.

This energy is nothing like this anywhere else. But then what are the, you know, the headwinds? How can we remove the headwinds? And I think as an entrepreneur and [a] businessperson, one of the biggest recommendations I can make [to] this room is when you say New York City open for business. I know that people look for incentives and breaks and all that kind of stuff.

What people look for is [a] true partner.

a.t: Yeah.

q.t:
[Inaudible] But the point is, I said, we're not just going to sponsor it; we're going to put our hearts and souls into Team USA. Every single package — and I personally spent six months changing every single packaging that has Team USA's logos on them [and] the players on them, and we also support the Women’s World Cup next year.

So basically, if you go to Official Chobani, you'll [see] Team USA. And I said Team USA is going to go far. And now the people are starting, and I actually put an ad out there that we're going to get this this year. The point I'm making is New York City gives you ideas [in] unexpected places. The only reason I'm wearing this hat and sponsoring Team USA and talking about soccer is because I watch my son playing in downtown. And I said, “We can do something about this.”

I am an entrepreneur who was an immigrant, like millions before me that lived in a one-bedroom apartment with so many others try to learn languages [and] ride on the subway. Before I [became] this — we are doing an investment [of] $2 billion this year on infrastructures, plants, manufacturing sites around the country.

But still, I'm riding that subway [from] 30 years ago. And today — when Jeanny said, “There's so many students that are coming here; so many people are coming here to starting their business.” — those people who are invest in the future, $2 billion, or sponsoring new soccer fans are in the subways today. They're trying to figure out what they're going to do with their life.

But the point I'm making is when you get the juice, the energy, the ideas, the grit, the fighting. You know that unstoppable spirit everywhere is beautiful, but you're never going to get anywhere else than this. But like you said, if you make it here, you make it anywhere. Because the competition here is unlike anything else.

a.t: Yes.

q.t: So, I go to every practice and every game, and I saw there's a mattress brand on it. Nothing wrong with mattresses. I said the kids should not play with the mattress brand on their jersey on. So, I decided to reach out to the leadership says, “Wow, we really need a sponsorship, not only for the jersey, but [also for] the coaches and all the other stuff.” I said, “Well, let's do it.” So, this was my first sponsorship, [which] was with DUSC. And if you go to the DUSC website, it has Chobani [on] them. Then I said, “What about Team USA?” So, we reached out to Team USA, and this is why I came in with this hat. Chobani is [the] Official Nutrition Partners of Team USA. We are one of the biggest sponsors of Team USA.

a.t: Incredible.
And the reason I did that—
From Downtown United Soccer Club — from DUSC to [Team] USA.

q.t: Thank you. Do you know how my soccer journey started here?

a.t: Please.
So, my son played at DUSC.
I played at Manhattan Soccer Club.

q.t:
It had been closed, [the] same community and basically the same products. It was making yogurt before me. It was bad, but it was yogurt. So, when I saw the same people, it's like I was one of them. We built this together. So, one of the proudest moments for me was — when I knew that I survived in 2016 — to make every single person [a] partner in the company. Because our future depends on everyone to succeed, not just, you know, shareholders, but every stakeholder.

But in reality, if every stakeholder — the workers, environment, families, communities, consumers, everyone — if everyone succeeds, the company becomes even more successful. The shareholder gets even more successful. To me, this is the timeless model that is going to be relevant in the future. The companies [that] are really paying attention to these things are going to be the [ones] who [are] going to be relevant.

The world is changing dramatically. So, New York City is creating this platform for the companies to succeed. And what Jeanny is saying, what you're basically saying is, “Hey, I want to help you to bear those costs. And we [will] do this together.” And this way the business becomes the engine with the NGO, with the city governments, with, you know, all the stakeholders together that make this work for everyone, which is because post-pandemic, the world has to change and the city needs to reinvent itself [with] a new economic model that works. Basically, we're saying if we are — and I think that's a question back to you, sir — is New York City open for business?

a.t:
Yes. And I think I think to your point, not only are we open for business, but we are looking to be the best possible partner to business. And that's not to say that — you know, you will hear that from many a city, that they will want business to come to them. I think what separates us is both the intangibles of this city, but also the ways in which we want to invest. And what that really speaks to is — you look at the EDC, and you look at the Brooklyn Army Terminal. This is an example where we've put in about $100 million, and that $100 million will create more than $2.6 billion in economic activity. Because what we're seeing is that when we can invest to make it easier for businesses to start up, we can give them that first access to capital. And what I've heard a lot from small business owners is [that] their issue is not access to consumers, it's access to capital. How can we unlock that for them? So, whether it's on the side of New York City putting in $20 million into Ponce Bank, this storied Puerto Rican institution uptown and in the Bronx that is helping small businesses start up their hopes and dreams, or it's an EDC putting in $100 million, we're seeing the different ways. And I know that when Chobani was looking and made the decision to have your global headquarters here, some of the things that EDC put forward [were] ways that it could work together, whether it's assistance in site selection or workforce development. And I know one place that they worked closely with Chobani on was how we can also get connected with New York City Service Corps and really bringing together police officers, firefighters, other members of our city workforce to help in what Chobani does on an annual basis of distributing food across the city.

And I think to that point, we are both so excited at what we can achieve in this city, and we also want to welcome everyone from across the world to be a part of it. Because when we think about the accomplishments that public-private partnerships have created, it's not just, you know, the examples I've shared between EDC and Chobani. I even think about public housing in New York City. It's one of the last places that a working-class person can afford housing. And it's also the reason that we have the mini fridge in the United States of America, because a few decades ago, NYCHA, the New York City Housing Authority, put out an RFP for a specific-sized refrigerator for a public housing unit. And that's how that size refrigerator was developed. And now it's a mainstay of college dorms across the country. For different reasons. And to me, now, that public private partnership when it comes to public housing is about clean energy and about how we can bring heat pumps into public housing and deliver on not just quality of life but also tackling the climate crisis.

But I think in this room — in Chobani — in so many other perspective businesses, we have the possibility to ensure that New York City keeps being the place that everyone looks to as where they want to be. And I think that's the — what we want in City government is to finally embody what we see in business, what we see in sports [and] what we see in arts in the city, which is a relentless drive for greatness.

And I think for too long in our politics, we've brought the bar much lower and we've just said, “This is how it is. We'll always be fine; we'll always be great.” And it's not the truth. The reason that every other industry is succeeding in this city is because they push themselves, and I think we have to do the same.

And, you know, I just want to go back [to] one of the things that you shared earlier; one of the best days that I've had as the mayor of the city is when we celebrated Soccer Streets. For those who don't know, just to expand a little bit more on what Hamdi was saying, Chobani made the decision to invest in an initiative that we put together for the World Cup to transform 50 New York City Public Schools and the streets outside them to make them car-free and to make them places where kids can play soccer, can learn about soccer [and] can draw murals about it.

And I just want to say thank you to you, because so many of us are watching the World Cup in this moment. And, you know, I went to sleep last night to Algeria [vs.] Jordan playing as I closed my eyes. And what you are doing, and what so many other businesses are doing, is investing in it to make sure it's a moment that children can also remember as when their potential was being unlocked.

And that's what we want: is that in 20 years, when the U.S. Men's National Team is right there at the World Cup final, and they're looking back and we're asking ourselves, “Where did that striker's journey begin? Where did that goalkeeper start playing”? And we look at the things that businesses worked with City government on to create these kinds of initiatives. It's really what I think also unlocks the potential of the city. So, thank you very much.

q.t: The intangibles. And same thing that goes into the workforce and the safety and all those things — how much those are [more] important than how much tax you avoid. And it's not even a comparison. I truly believe in it. I grew up and said, in the factory, when things are good, the people who live in high towers get the path, get the rewards. But if things are bad, the factory workers pay the price, like the factory [being] closed. And that's [how] I started my business. The factory closed because somebody in Chicago decided that it wasn't profitable enough after 75 years. When the same people built Chobani with me, the same people, same factory—

a.t: Who had been closed down—

q.t: I came from a similar background. The business that I saw didn't work, the communities [where] I grew up in in Turkey. And I immediately blamed the business. When I arrived in America and southern upstate New York — [in the] early days, I was here in New York City, and I was going to tell you, [the] memory of New York City for me is riding from Brooklyn to Manhattan on a train, on a subway train, having my bagel and watching everyone. And basically, the spirit that stays with you, that you can never put value to — all those interactions that you [have] from the day that you come here until you start your business and how much those interactions impact the business that you start with — nowhere else can you see this. And Jason shared some numbers [about] diversity and all the other things. The stuff that is the most valuable is the one that you cannot put price on when you—

a.t: The intangibles.

q.t: And that's what you believe?

a.t:
Absolutely. And I think to your point, what we want to do in this city is to make it a place where everyone can flourish. Because I think, as you've said, we know our city has a history of incredible generation of wealth. It's the wealthiest city in the wealthiest country in the history of the world. We also know that that is true while one in four are living in poverty. And that's not a sustainable set of facts. And what we've also seen is that a lot of the inability of City government to provide for the needs of working people has then outsourced a pressure onto companies. I speak to business leaders who themselves are having to give supplements for childcare payments to their workers, who are having to find ways to deal with a skyrocketing housing market in their own kind of incentives and bonuses.

And so, one of the focuses that we also have is: How do we drive down the cost of doing business by creating more service for that which companies are having to pick up the dollar for? And with housing, it looks at how can we make it as easy and quick as possible to build housing in this city. We're looking to drive down the time it takes to build housing, whether on the private market or the public market. And on childcare, which is the second largest cost for working families in the city, [we are] delivering universal childcare, of which [the] 26 is the deadline to apply if anyone here has a two-year-old. It is a way that we can save families money because, look, a lot of the business leaders here and those who are watching may have businesses where their employees are making six figures. And yet we also know that when you're having to pay $20,000 a year, you will blink at that, even if you're making $100,000; $200,000; $300,000; even $400,000; or $500,000.

And so, how can we make it easier for that family to put its roots down here? And I think, to the last point, [we] also want to make this a city where it has the best quality of life, the best quality of service and the best quality of safety. And when it comes to quality of life, that means investing in city services so that you can go out, as Jeanny said, and celebrate the Knicks winning their first championship in 53 years, and the next morning you can go to the same street and see that New York City Sanitation has cleaned it all, and it's as if it as if it never happened. And I love that it feels like there's a real civic pride, because in the Knicks parade, the loudest cheers were for the players and then it was for Sanitation, you know, when they came through the streets.

And then on quality of service, it's also that we want people to demand — You know, when I go to the grocery store and I pick out my zero percent Chobani Greek Yogurt, I'm picking it out before I knew Hamdi. I'm picking it out because of what it represents to me, the memories I have of the yogurt, the quality, the taste of the yogurt. But I'm picking it because it earned that trust. I want people to feel the same way about government. We can't make the same level of Greek yogurt, but we should earn that trust. And that comes from also demanding excellence from ourselves.

And then the last point is about safety. You know, we want this to be, as it has continued to be, one of the safest big cities in the world. That means that any indication of crime is an opportunity to deliver more, to keep driving that down. We're proud that in these first six months, we have the lowest recorded levels of murders in our city, of shootings in our city. And we're also not going to pat ourselves on the back and say, job done. It means there's more to be done.

And I think just a question to you, Hamdi — you were saying this a little bit earlier, but you know what your company embodies, it is also an indication of what we were talking about, about investing in workers. Now, when I think about Chobani, beyond what it is that you sell, it's also the higher wages, the parental leave [and] the childcare. Can you share a little bit about why you made the decision to have that as part of your company culture?

q.t:
And that was, “Hey, the city needs to work for everybody.” You know, the wages, housing, early childhood education. And then there is certain blame that goes along with the businesses. And now we are here gathering around the business, opening — New York City open for business, and understanding the value of the business and entrepreneurship innovation. My question to you is when you are walking that fine line, which I truly believe, that if the economy is not working for everybody, that economy is not going to be sustainable for the future. The cracks [need] to be closed. And those issues, especially most important one, where is the wages are not good enough, where every child has a safe neighborhood to go to school — to which you champion — where hunger shamefully needs to be wiped out. You know, everybody should have access to good food. But in that environment, I believe is not against the business.

If those environments accomplished and businesses and the government come together to create that environment, healthy way, the business flourish even further and better.

a.t: Absolutely.

q.t: And that brings the question that it would be in every businessperson's mind, that you have very strong opinions coming into election, coming to leadership in New York City, and if I may—

a.t: Please.

q.t:
Mayor, you’re so kind. I still — I want to go back to that event that we did on the street the other day before the World Cup. I had no idea what to expect — just idea came from one from another one — and I found myself with the mayor on the street, kicking the balls after 30 years — [something] I've never done before. And when those pictures spread around, especially in Turkey, and I had my Fenerbahçe jersey on, and you had your Arsenal, and a month of response I had from that picture was enormous. So, you're a rock star not only here in New York, but [around] the world, especially the country that I call home in Turkey. But I think the best part of that was we can come together and make life better for neighborhoods, for children and have fun at the same time. So, I come back to this notion — that was my second gathering with you, and this is the third — there's something in the air. Seriously, that like, I don't know, sometimes you can't even identify what it is, but maybe it's you, maybe it's your leadership, [there is] something going on. Knicks is winning; World Cup is going well.

There is something in the air. I feel it. And I think my first message on this gathering, when it's about the economic future of New York City: investment, innovations and entrepreneurship. I would say it's never been this exciting to be in New York; it's never been this exciting to invest in New York and start your business in New York. Despite the fact that there was enormous amount of conversation, noise that during the pandemic, after the pandemic, after the election, after all the conversation that we were having — that how we could make the life better for neighborhoods and workers and children and schools, that people would flee their businesses from New York — but it happens to be completely [the] opposite. And more people are coming.

So, that comes to my presence in New York. I had a space in Lafayette Street right after the pandemic. This happened once before, mayor, every time that I saw the New York kind of get to the bottom, like there was some desperation — maybe there was some question marks if New York ever going to come back — I doubled down. Because you never question — you never doubt New York City, ever. Because if you know something that New York always comes back and comes back stronger and comes back in a different color, different way, different — better than ever before, because I saw it happen in my business. So, immediately after I said to my team, let's look at one of the best neighborhoods so I can invest.

So, we came to where Bowery Street is and we saw this building — it was on the screen — and immediately went in and I brought my two boys and said, “What do you guys think about this?” And they said, “Yeah, we love it.” They were seven and ten. So, they had — and I didn't even question it. Today it already doubled its value, already doubled its value. But my point is, where else in the world you're going to tap into 100 — 360 degrees everything. No where else.

a.t:
Well, and I think what I have to say also is thank you to you and to every business leader here, because I agree with you that you should never bet against New York and never bet against a New Yorker. And yet I also, I have to say that as the mayor of our city, part of the reason we say “don't bet against the city” is because of the bets that people are taking in this city, on this city. We don't just get here by ourselves. We get here because someone like you and other business leaders, at the height of the pandemic — when all of the incentives would say, “make a different decision, go elsewhere” — you decide to believe in this city, as so many have believed in it before. And I think what's so exciting is, as you said right now, it truly feels like while that decision may have been difficult, now it's a much easier decision. And yet it speaks to the fact that what makes this city so special is that so many have kept believing in it to this point.

And I think, you know, you look at where we are now. Since 2021, more than 500,000 college graduates have made this city their home. More than a million young people call this city their home. We're seeing the leasing of office space is 43 percent above a five-year average. You know, we're looking at the venture capital of Q1, $11 billion. The indicators are all there. And yet we want to make this a city that every day we're doing what we can to make it as easy as possible for someone to make the same decision as you did. And if you're a business leader and you're thinking about this, I would have to ask you, Hamdi, if we can also bring your kids to them, you know, for any of their site visits.

q.t: Thank you. Such a pleasure. You're welcome to come back. You are now officially a friend of the show.

a.t: Thank you. I really appreciate that. I'll talk to you soon.
All right. You be well.
Bye-bye.

q.t: There you go. That's a nice, humble answer. Well, thank you, mayor, for taking the time out.

a.t: Such a pleasure, Reecie.

q.t: There we go. So, I got to put you on the spot. What do you think if people had a superstition for the next go-round? What do you think people need to tap into more? The fact that you're the mayor as the good luck charm or Jordyn Woods — who is Karl-Anthony Towns’ fiancée — her lucky bag. Which one do you think deserves the most credit?

a.t: It's got to be Jordyn Woods and the lucky bag.
Okay.

Come on. I mean, I had the privilege of meeting Karl-Anthony Towns and Jordyn Woods and their families. And, you know, even when I saw that bag, I just said, “Thank you,” because we needed everything to get us over the line. And, you know, I'm happy to be the mayor, but it's not my credit to take.

q.t: I got on blue. I don’t know if you can see me —

a.t: I see you. You got on blue. I have a little orange around where I am. So, together we make it work.

q.t: All right. Before you go — I know you got to run — I got to say, go Knicks.

a.t: Come on. Come on.

q.t: Absolutely. And let me just add that the data that you can collect and say, “Well, we had 2,000 slots, but 200,000 people signed up” — I’m just making up a number — then that makes a stronger case to expand those services quicker. So, people got to apply so that people know the demand.

a.t: Yes, ma'am.

q.t: That's a very, very important point. I do want to ask, though, what do you say to people who hear 2,000 seats or 12,000 seats and think, [inaudible]. Like, “Why should I even bother to reply? It's too many people. I'm not going to get it.” What do you say to those folks who maybe do need the service, but they haven't applied yet because they're skeptical that they will be eligible or skeptical that there is even room for them in the program?

a.t:
What I would say is this is a program for each and every New Yorker, no matter what their story is, no matter how much money they have in their bank account, no matter their immigration status. And it is an opportunity for them to save tens of thousands of dollars. And to someone who may apply and not get it in the first year, all you will lose is what you are already in today, which is an opportunity that you could save all that money. 

And if not, then the next year there will be 12,000 seats. And I think that I understand people's — their skepticism, because it's a skepticism that reflects their experience with government thus far. And we know we have to earn their trust. We have to earn their faith. But the beautiful thing is that every time we successfully do so, it gives them a reason to keep believing. And that's what we see in this program.

q.t:
Right. And we have to talk about the contributions to [the] Black community in your cabinet, in your leadership. You recently appointed a deputy mayor that I was very, very happy about. Shout out to Deputy Mayor Renita Francois. And you've got really, really good people throughout your team. But one of the things — it's not just what I call a “neon Black” kind of policy — [is] universal 2-K, a promise kept from your campaign.

And there's a critical deadline coming up about that, right? And I want you to tell people about that because my husband is a mayor, too, and I see often how people, you know, they want programs, but then they don't necessarily tap into the programs when those programs become a thing.

a.t:
You know, it is such a good point that the worth of a service you provide is only as much as people know about it. And we know that here in the most expensive city in the United States of America, after housing, childcare is the number one cost for a working family. And so, as you said, we ran a campaign about universal childcare. We are now delivering universal childcare for two-year-olds for the first time in New York City history. And we are maybe two-thirds through the application process; we have until June 26th. So, if anyone is listening to this show and has a child that is turning two years old or is already two years old, then this is the time to go to myschools.nyc., apply for what is high-quality, free childcare that will save you at least $20,000 a year.

And, you know, it's actually not a separate conversation from the one that we're having about Juneteenth, because we know that at the end of four years, we're going to deliver free childcare to every two-year-old. But we have to build that up and phase it in. So, our first year, we're doing it to 2,000 seats. The next year, 12,000 seats. And in this first year, we had a choice of where do we want to begin. And we made the choice that we wanted to start with the places that are often last, the places that are often facing a choice of [being] last in line or not at all.

And a lot of these neighborhoods — neighborhoods like Brownsville, East New York, Canarsie, the Rockaways, Fordham [and] Washington Heights — these are neighborhoods that have been disproportionately hit by the cost-of-living crisis and also neighborhoods that Black New Yorkers have helped to build over generations. And it's time that they see a City Hall that is looking to them first, as opposed to even questioning whether it's looking to them at all.

q.t: Right, right. And I think it's so important to, like you said, to recognize, especially when we're looking at what the Trump administration is doing — still in court trying to sue to remove exhibits about slavery in different cities across this country. And you, you posted on your Instagram and on your social media; you commissioned a special project for Juneteenth. Can you tell folks real quick about that?

a.t:
You know, Juneteenth is a day that has a national resonance. It's also a day that has a local resonance here in our city. And we want to shine a light on that. You know, I'll give you just one example. There's the project as a whole. There's also one story that has really stayed with me today about Weeksville. And Weeksville is this incredible testament. It was one of the largest neighborhoods of freed Black New Yorkers before the Civil War.

And what it did was invest in freedom through the creation of its own newspaper, the creation of its own schools [and] its own homes. And part of what we are trying to really share with New Yorkers is the fact that Black history is New York City history. The two cannot be disentangled. As we celebrate Juneteenth, we are also celebrating this city. And it's an opportunity to recognize and appreciate all those contributions.

q.t: Okay, okay, okay. This time last year, mayor, you were running to be the mayor. Now, you have been in the seat, you have done big things. What message do you take to the Black community? Because I know you were everywhere this Juneteenth. What message do you take back to the community that helped put you across the finish line? Because we know that you won a majority of Black voters in the election. What did you have to say this Juneteenth?

a.t:
I think the first thing is today is a day of celebration. Today is also a day of recognition of the enormity of the contributions of Black New Yorkers and Black Americans to the story of this city and this country. And also, a recognition of all that is still to be done. Because we know that as we celebrate, that should not also be an excuse to absolve ourselves of the responsibility, especially in government, for all that is still to be done to make that freedom truly felt by each and every person in the city.

And for me, it also has a special resonance, because I'm speaking to you right now, just after having spoken to the congregation at Greater Allen A.M.E. Church out here in Queens. And this is the church that — like many churches over the course, as you said, Reecie, of my primary campaign [and] my general campaign — that gave me a chance. When I said my name, people would typically say, “Who?” Because they had never heard of me. Understandably so — I began the race polling at one percent.

And still without having to give me that opportunity, they still gave me a platform time and time again to introduce myself. And it is such a — it is a real decision when you choose to give someone your time. And it is a beautiful thing that I get to come back and say, “Thank you for having done so.” And now to deliver on that belief that I shared more than a year ago.

q.t: Mine is good. Is yours “Blackity Black?” I can say that. [Inaudible].

a.t: I can confirm it.

q.t: Thank you for being here. Happy Juneteenth.

a.t: Happy Juneteenth. How's yours going?

q.t: All right, y'all, I gotta bring in my very special guest for the Reecie Colbert Show. It is a big week for the City of New York, and so who else better to come to the day party other than the one and only mayor of New York, Mayor Zohran Mamdani. Welcome to the Reecie Colbert Show.

a.t: Thank you so much, Reecie. It's such a pleasure to be on. Thank you for having me.

q.t: Well, thank you for being with us. We're glad to have you today.

a.t: Truly thankful for the opportunity to share this with your listeners.

q.t: So, this would be free childcare?

a.t: Yes, free, high-quality childcare. 2,000 seats this year, 12,000 seats next year, and then a seat for every two-year-old by the end of four years. And right now, the applications are open. We're almost in the final third of the application period. It closes on June 26th, and if anyone listening is interested and lives in these neighborhoods, please go to myschools.nyc.

q.t: Switching gears a little bit here, I've been hearing about a new childcare program that you have going on, a collaboration between New York City and the State of New York, and it's something that many African Americans or Black people will potentially benefit from. Tell us about that.

a.t:
You know, it's exactly as you say; we were so excited on just the eighth day of our administration to secure a $1.2 billion source of funding from Governor Hochul at the state level to deliver free childcare for two-year-olds for the first time in New York City history. And we've seen that for far too long in moments of significant investment, Black New Yorkers are faced with the choice of either being last in line or not at all. And we are seeking to rectify that with this program.

And so, in this first year where we deliver 2,000 seats, we made the decision that we would deliver those seats in neighborhoods that are often left behind. Like Brownsville, Canarsie [and] East New York in Brooklyn or the Rockaways in Queens or Fordham in the Bronx or Washington Heights in Uptown Manhattan. We are looking to finally relieve that stress of paying at least $20,000 a year for childcare that so many working families are facing in this city.

q.t: There was pushback of even getting Juneteenth to become a national holiday, and perhaps there are some in New York City of various ethnic groups who don't really see its importance. What is your broader message to all of New York, to everybody of different backgrounds?

a.t: That we cannot tell the story of this city without also telling the story of Black New Yorkers. That so much of what we love and pride ourselves on are in fact the results of not just years or decades but frankly centuries of Black New Yorkers writing not just Black history but New York history and American history. And we know that to be the case across this country.

q.t: What is your Juneteenth message to the city?

a.t:
First and foremost, it's a day of celebrating freedom and also the dedication to freedom that we've seen so many Black Americans and Black New Yorkers be at the forefront of. And it is a special day in that it marks 161 years specifically since Union General Gordon Granger arrived in Galveston and enforced the Emancipation Proclamation.

But we also know that Juneteenth is not just a celebration of laws being enforced; it's also a celebration of joy, of determination, of resilience of Black Americans over centuries of delayed freedom, of withheld rights [and] of restricted opportunities. And I'm so excited to be celebrating this incredible day with New Yorkers across the five boroughs.

q.t: Well, joining us now is New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani. Thank you for being with us once again on the BIN.

a.t: It is such a pleasure to be back. Thank you for having me.

q.t: Had the suspect had a prior interaction with the police? And then, apart from that, did he [inaudible]?

a.t: There is no documented EDP history with the NYPD.

q.t: Commissioner, were of the two of these guns fired, were you aware? Also, was there, in the process of negotiating with the suspect, were there demands that he was making, or did he say anything about the nature of the dispute?

a.t:
So, we do not know which of the weapons was fired. We do know that there was a weapon that was fired, but we don't know if it is the two that we are showing there. We assume that it was, and I believe that the hostage negotiation team was unable to make contact with the subject having called him several times.

[Crosstalk.]

q.t: Well, you were prepared. Thank you for stopping by.

a.t: It's such a pleasure.
Enjoy.
Thank you so much for having me.
Anytime. Anytime.

q.t: And you put in the order months ago. That was very brave of you.

a.t: You gotta plan. You gotta be ready. As a fan, you'd never want to talk about it, but as the mayor, you gotta be ready.

q.t: Yeah, those tears are real, man. The tears of joy are real. Tell us about the key to the city. You're going to [give to the] players. You have one with you.

a.t: I do. I have one here with me. This is the key to the city that we will be presenting to each of the players, and it is the first key that our administration is giving out since, you know, it's been only six months, and it is designed by Azra Khalfan. It is manufactured by him [and] designed by Aneesh Bhoopathy, and the typography of the key is actually designed by Tobias Frere-Jones, who designed the typography of the 9/11 Museum, NYU — a lot of the kind of iconic typefaces in our city. We're so honored that he did this.

q.t: I know it's been great to watch you make this about the fans and people in the city, but I know your phone's been blowing up with VIPs. So, who are some of the people that are gonna be spotted? The notable people who are gonna be spotted today?

a.t:
Well, you know, I think a lot of those notable people will be invited by the Knicks organization. Today, we have the parade, but then we also have the ceremony at City Hall. What I can tell you is that my focus is really about the players and about the fans. You know, we have a few thousand people that can fit into City Hall for that ceremony. 

Oftentimes, fans just have to watch that on TV. We made the decision to set 600 seats aside for the people who have made this run so special, because people have been waiting, and we have been so close so many times before, and the tears of joy you've seen across the city — we want that to also be a part of the ceremony.

q.t: So, what's your advice for people that are heading to the parade?

a.t: Well, at this point, I would say, if you're not in a viewing pen, those are full. We've seen Knicks fans who showed up as early as yesterday evening who were waiting for this moment. And we know the parade begins at 10. But if you're heading into the city, you should still keep coming because this is gonna be a moment to remember. We have a big city. There's a lot of bars and restaurants you can be at, and this is going to be a moment that you're gonna feel across the five boroughs.

q.t: Just incredible. The parade is already at capacity. Subways have stopped going downtown. You've got 10,000 police on the parade route, so everybody is in a good mood. But are you confident everybody’s gonna be safe?

a.t: Absolutely. And I'm confident because we've seen the men and women of the NYPD perform this duty over the course of this final run and before that. And as you said, this is a parade of immense excitement across our city, and frankly, even across the region. It could very well end up being the largest parade in New York City history.

q.t: Our play of the day and more on the Knicks parade today here in New York. Joining us to talk about it is the mayor of the city, Zohran Mamdani. Mr. Mayor, thank you for joining us this morning. And you're not just wearing the jersey because they won, but you're a big Knicks fan. So, what does it feel like to be mayor during this historic moment in time?

a.t: It's hard to even put it into words. I mean, 53 years this city has waited for this moment — [27] years since we were last in the finals. And we know that Rick Brunson was on that ‘99 team. We know that they lost to the Spurs 4-1. And for his son to lead this team and this city, to beat that same team 4-1 in 2026 — it's a beautiful moment.

q.t: I don't blame you. Thank you so much.

a.t: Thank you.

q.t: Do they ever make you those green smoothies?

a.t: I have not asked.

q.t: What's your go-to breakfast?

a.t: Go-to breakfast? It's gotta be scrambled eggs. Some kind of avocados, tomatoes, a little bit of labneh.

q.t: Last question for you: You said at the beginning of the year that you're going to be getting a chef for Gracie Mansion that had a no-pork menu. Did you find a chef? What is that like? What's your relationship like with a chef? What do they make you for breakfast? I know Mayor Eric Adams likes his green smoothies. What does the chef make for you?

a.t: So, it is the same chef who's been at Gracie Mansion for many years. We don't have pork in our kitchen for what we eat. She's incredible. The team is incredible. And I think one of the beautiful things is having so many people around you who are making it easier for you to succeed in your work. It's what makes so much of this possible and I just appreciate what they do every single day.

q.t: She did make these comments. She did apologize yesterday on the debate stage. She made these comments when she was an adult — it was just about three or four years ago that she made these comments. I guess, where is the line? She made these comments last year. Was that too soon to run for Congress? Where is that line?

a.t: You know, I think the line for me is an acknowledgement and an affirmation of what you believe in in this moment and what you're fighting for. And too often in our politics, there isn't even a willingness to acknowledge that or even, you know, what we saw in her case, apologize for it. And I think that that reckons with how people feel and the willingness to be a leader that's also receptive to that.

q.t: Now, next Tuesday is also the primary, and you can endorse three congressional candidates — Brad Lander, Claire Valdez, and Darializa Avila Chevalier. But Chevalier has come under fire for past comments that she's made, calling to the abolish the police, criticizing the military, calling President Obama “evil,” calling President Biden a “rapist,” and a “war criminal.” She used profane language when describing other top democrats. She criticized interracial relationships, and she even took aim at Senator Bernie Sanders for quote, “liberal Zionism.” Sanders is throwing a rally for Chevalier tomorrow that you'll be attending. How do you reconcile the criticism and also helping campaign for her?

a.t: Well, I think first and foremost, I'm incredibly excited about her campaign as well as Claire's campaign and Brad's campaigns as campaigns that showcase the fact that the affordability agenda, the work of transforming the most expensive city in America into one that's affordable, can't be done alone. So many of the people who not just voted for me but canvassed for me did so with the hope of fulfilling this agenda and the knowledge that it would require partners at every level of government. These are the partners that would help to do that work. And when it comes to Darializa, you know, she recently was asked this question herself and she apologized for some of the remarks. She spoke about regret [for] the language that she used. I think she also showed the fact that her campaign is being run on what she is fighting for today and that is a message I think is resonating with many across her district.

q.t: Now, next week, the Rent Guidelines Board will be deciding whether or not to implement a rent freeze, but according to the Board's own numbers, the 2026 Rent Guidelines Board Price Index, the total cost of maintaining a building has gone up by 5.3 percent. Do you think it's fair to landlords right now to freeze the rent? And if they do freeze the rent, would it be helping or finding ways to help landlords who maybe can't afford repairs?

a.t: Well, I think first, the Rent Guidelines Board is an independent board, and they'll make their independent decision. I’ve been clear that I do believe that tenants deserve relief, and also my belief in tackling the cost-of-living crisis is true for everyone. So, when I've spoken to landlords, especially for affordable housing, they've told me that one of the costs has skyrocketed in recent years, and that is their insurance. And one of the decisions we made in our executive budget was to invest more than $100 million in the next few years on creating a city-backed insurance fund that can decrease those costs for these kinds of landlords so that we can actually do the work of maintaining ownership of these buildings and the quality of habitation for those who are [their] tenants. And when it comes to the Board, they've found that, as you said on the cost, they've also found that revenues have increased for landlords, and I think they're balancing all of this as well as the testimonies.

q.t: Now, there's one item in the budget that's gotten some attention, the Office of Mass Engagement — which takes your campaign strategy of meeting people where they're at, at their homes, knocking on doors, canvassing — to get the message of the priorities of your administration out to regular people. But it has drawn some ethical concerns, and this office was supposed to have a budget of about $5 million and now that's grown to about more than $50 million. Why did that budget grow and why this year having such a budget with such a massive amount, more than $50 million, during a time when there is a budget crisis?

a.t: I would just correct the record, in the vast majority of that $50 million [are] pre-existing responsibilities prior to our administration. So that Office of Mass Engagement is also an umbrella office that brings in existing initiatives and work, like the Community Affairs Unit or Public Service Unit, and that work has to carry on because many New Yorkers have looked to those agencies as ways that they can interact with the city. In terms of what's new; we're talking about a much smaller percentage of that amount of money. And to your point, it's not just about sharing what the administration is doing. We want New Yorkers to be a part of that. So, we recently had a final hearing of the Rent Guidelines Board. As you know, the Rent Guidelines Board determines the rent increase or lack thereof for more than 2 million New Yorkers. Yet, last year, [fewer] than 1,000 New Yorkers — I think it was 4 or 500 — testified. The percentage of those who were impacted versus those who were involved is minuscule. And so, we wanted to knock on doors to let people know not how they should testify, but that they should. And that's one of the key jobs that they've been doing.

q.t: Now, you have two weeks before the city's budget is finalized, sort of. The state gave the city nearly $8 billion in assistance over the next few years. But Governor Hochul says this is it, and she's not going to be giving the city extra assistance next year. Would you take that to mean that she's going to not be doing the increased taxes on millionaires, for example? Is that something you're still going to be looking for?

a.t: I will always believe in the importance of having the wealthiest pay a little bit more in taxes so that everyone can afford a life in the city. And I'll tell you that my focus right now is on these next few weeks, as you said. It's not just finalizing the city budget. It's not just the parade tomorrow. It’s the World Cup. It's July 4. It's America 250. So, for me, that's the focus right now, but I look forward to starting the budget process for next year as we continue to advocate for our city.

q.t: Do you think you'll have the police commissioner stay on for the full four years of your term?

a.t: I think that we're working very well together right now and I'm excited to keep that going.

q.t: How is your relationship like with the police commissioner? Do you see it as a lasting partnership?

a.t: I see it as something that is fulfilling our mutual desire to deliver a safe city to New Yorkers. And I'm so proud of the results we've seen over these last six months, as we've seen crime drop to historic lows, and as we’ve seen this partnership be one that can deliver on that wish to ensure that the greatest city in the world is also going to be the safest city in the world.

q.t: Now, you recently approved to increase the NYPD's headcount. The headcount is 35,000 uniformed officers and it went over that cap by about 370 officers. We've seen some criticism from it — from the Democratic Socialists [of America] — but why is it so important to have these additional officers, especially as we're looking at this summer with the World Cup, the Knicks — which is sort of wrapping up now — but the possibility of a Taylor Swift wedding here in New York City. Tell us more about why this was needed.

a.t: You know, these are officers that are going to be added because of two specific reasons that were presented to me. And the first was the fact that within our NYPD, there isn't sustained training after an officer gets through the Academy. And this is a desire to ensure that training is a regular part of serving in this Department. And that's the bulk of these additional officers. The other is that when we looked at the Bronx, we found that the Bronx was being treated differently than Brooklyn, than Manhattan, than Queens. It had one Borough Command, whereas these other boroughs, with comparative levels of demand had two. And so, we made the decision to split that command into two, which increases response times and also puts it on parity with these other boroughs. And these are critical reasons of why we made this decision. And I also appreciate that the criticism that we receive, is criticism still coming from a place of wanting this to be the best possible city. And we appreciate that criticism. And this is why we make those decisions.

q.t: Is there anything else though that this committee is requiring you to do as a part of this agreement?

a.t: That about covers it, and I would also just say that when it comes to this tournament, it's less of something that I view as a responsibility or a burden. It's more of an opportunity. This is the opportunity of a lifetime, and it's not just for those visiting our city for the first time. Also, for New Yorkers, you know, many of us who grow up and we have a very specific understanding of our city. Then a moment like this comes, and we get to view the beauty and the breadth of our city in its totality. So, we have a program where we're offering a $26 meal deal for more than 900 restaurants across the five boroughs. If anyone is interested, they can go to NYC Tourism's website and they can find that list and that's a way for New Yorkers to also explore their own city.

q.t: You said earlier this week that you're going to attend three World Cup matches as part of an agreement with the New York and New Jersey Host Committee. What else is in that agreement, because I can't get my hands on it to save my life, but what else are you required to do as part of this agreement?

a.t: It is about facilitating this as an experience, not just for New Yorkers, but also for those who are visiting the city. So you can see a lot of the work that we're doing through our World Cup Czar as well as through additional agencies, whether it's ensuring that match-day travel is smooth, whether it is ensuring that the city is working together with each of the fan fests across the five boroughs, or it's ensuring that we are making clear to each and every person visiting the city the many things that they can do in the city. And so, we take those responsibilities very seriously because this is a once-in-a-generation opportunity and we're so excited to have people come to the city.

q.t: The students across the five boroughs are pleading with you this week.

a.t: The youth vote — I'm not doing great with the youth vote right now.

q.t: You’re not going to cancel school?

a.t: No.

q.t: Now, as you know, Madison Square Garden owner James Dolan canceled the Knicks Game Four watch party outside MSG last week. Were you surprised that he did this, and have you had a conversation with him since?

a.t: Yeah, I've been in touch with Jim, and I would say that I'm less interested in relitigating the past and more about the fact of how we can work together to celebrate the moment of the city. And that is something that's bringing not just he and I together, but the entire five boroughs.

q.t: Now, there will be heightened security at the parade, and I think most people celebrating the Knicks on Saturday celebrated in a respectful, joyous manner. But there were people who didn't, and there was some violence on Saturday night; more than 60 arrests just from the Knicks celebration. And I think that kind of gets lost a little bit in the conversation, because it's not just all the arrests on Saturday night across the five boroughs — it's just to do with the Knicks celebration. And there were also school busses lit on fire, a teenager being shot. Are you worried that things are going to get out of hand at the parade and what sort of security measures are you looking for?

a.t: I think it's — as you said — that while we saw the last majority of New Yorkers celebrate in a way that was both respectful, responsible and appropriate, frankly, we did see a select number who behaved in a way that was unacceptable. And I'm really appreciative for the men and women of the NYPD who kept our city safe over the course of this finals run, and they do so every day. And I've made clear over the course of this run and every day that I've had the opportunity to, that there is no room for this kind of violence, whether towards someone who's next to you or towards a police officer. And what we're looking forward to when it comes to the parade tomorrow is a parade of celebration, of joy and responsibility. And I am confident that will be the case. The parade will begin at 10 a.m. However, when I've told anyone that it will be until 10 a.m., they tell me they're going to be there at 5 a.m. And I understand that because everyone's been waiting a long time. The viewing pens will open at 6 a.m. And we're reminding every New Yorker that there's going to be screening. There's gonna be safety and security procedures. So, we advise everyone to not bring a bag, make sure you are coming and you are ready to go through that process and to be there to celebrate.

q.t: So, as we can see, the stage is getting set up for the historic ticker-tape parade celebration for the Knicks. I hear that you are going to be having specially designed keys that you're going to give to the players tomorrow. Tell me more about it.

a.t: It's incredibly exciting. Those will be the first keys to the city that I've presented under our administration. And they are keys that have been designed for this moment. They carry the typography of the greatest living typologist in New York City, who helped to design not only what's being used at the 9-11 memorial, but also what is being used as the NYPD font, NYCFC — so much of what we know of as a city is going to be carried through in that and we're really excited to present it to the players.

q.t: Well, Mr. Mayor. Thank you very much for being here.

a.t: You’re very welcome.

q.t: Well, ladies and gentlemen, the mayor of New York City, Mamdani, right here inside the Radio Big Mack show. Appreciate you, man.

a.t: Always, my man, talk soon.

q.t: Wait, last thing, real quick before you go. How's the cats going?

a.t: I got like three shots left. They hurt now, too.

q.t: Mayor Mamdani, I appreciate you as always for taking your time. I know you're one of the busiest people in the world. You and Jalen Brunson right now. So, I appreciate you even giving me these five minutes.

a.t: Well, come on now. He's the king. I'm just the mayor. Thank you, my man.

q.t: Wow, so you got till June 26 to apply for that right now.

a.t: Yep, June 26th, go to myschools.nyc.

q.t: And now mayor, before you go too, tell me about the 2K program. How's that going on right now?

a.t: You know, this is something we're so excited about. We're right now in the middle of the application period. We're delivering our first 2,000 free childcare seats for two-year-olds and we're doing it across our city. So, whether you're Uptown — Inwood, Washington Heights; or you're in Fordham; or you're out in Queens, Ozone Park; or the Rockaways; or in Brooklyn and Canarsie and Brownsville; [or] parts of East New York, these are seats that are available for you. Instead of having to pay $20,000 a year for childcare for your two-year-old, you can apply at myschools.nyc before June 26. You can save that money, and you can actually build a family here in New York City.

q.t: That's dope. So, make sure you guys do that right now because you got an hour, but don't be on no CP time and wait [and] be like, “oh, let me just run to the store and then I'll do it.” Do it now so you guys can be out there, you know, [and] possibly get one of those 600 tickets.

a.t: Absolutely.

q.t: Nah, it's amazing. And I will be out there.
